En el PSOE, la consigna es no soltar la idea de la remontada. Después de una primera fase volcada en el votante situado a su izquierda, el partido abrió luego el foco hacia los socialistas desencantados o, en palabras de un dirigente, «alejados de la política por la crispación».
El cara a cara del jueves sembró el desconcierto en las propias filas. La Moncloa sostiene que la actuación de Sánchez respondió a una estrategia premeditada y, en todo caso, nadie en el partido cree que vaya a ser determinante en el resultado. Incluso los sectores críticos con el planteamiento del debate sostienen que la organización está 'enchufada'. «El estado de ánimo está infinitamente mejor que el candidato en el debate», resumió uno de esos dirigentes.
Sánchez ha imprimido a la campaña una intensidad que recuerda a la de 2023. Ha contado con la visita de Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, ha dado protagonismo a su mujer, Begoña Gómez, y ha vuelto a recurrir a formatos poco convencionales. Con ellos ha buscado desmontar la imagen de hombre frío y ambicioso que le penaliza y le impide crear un vínculo de empatía con el votante: el pódcast 'Keep it Cutre', 'Fuera de control' con Alba Carrillo, el programa de David Broncano e incluso la revista 'Lecturas'.
En ese recorrido ha incluido también 'Salvados'. Jordi Évole ya lo entrevistó en 2016, tras perder la secretaría general, en una conversación en la que muchos sitúan el origen de su victoria frente a Susana Díaz. Fue la primera vez que desplegó un discurso mucho más escorado a la izquierda, con el que conectó con la militancia de base. A la lista se suma una charla también con Plex, pareja de la cantante Aitana.
Nada de eso garantiza que el ánimo se traduzca en votos. El escenario es bastante más adverso que hace tres años, pero mantener viva la épica de la remontada es la única manera de evitar un resultado catastrófico. La batalla se libra sobre todo en 18 provincias en las que el PSOE se juega crecer o consolidar lo que logró entonces, de A Coruña a Zaragoza, con Madrid, Sevilla o Valencia entre ellas. En el partido creen que, si llegan a 135 escaños, todo es posible. En 2023 obtuvieron 121.

noticias.titulo: «No hay clientes gilipollas, hay personas más difíciles»
noticias.resumen: Marcos Granda no es chef pero luce con orgullo seis estrellas Michelin. «El éxito de un restaurante pasa por muchas personas», afirma el camarero más laureado de España
noticias.texto:
Marcos Granda | Camarero
«No hay clientes gilipollas, hay personas más difíciles»
Marcos Granda no es chef pero luce con orgullo seis estrellas Michelin. «El éxito de un restaurante pasa por muchas personas», afirma el camarero más laureado de España
Marcos Granda es el tercer español con más estrellas Michelin, pero su nombre apenas se conoce fuera del mundillo. Quizá porque no viste chaquetilla blanca ... ni enseña recetas en la tele. Él se reivindica orgullosamente como camarero. Nacido en Sotrondio (Asturias), se crio entre las mesas y la barra de una sidrería familiar. En 2004 abrió Skina, el primero de una colección de restaurantes en Marbella, Madrid y Gijón. Esta semana ha participado, junto a otros grandes de la sala como José Polo, Luis Baselga, Toni Gerez o Marian Martínez, en la tercera edición de Suite, uno de los pocos congresos gastronómicos donde los protagonistas no son los chefs.
-¿Por qué los niños sueñan con ser cocineros pero no con ser camareros?
-La televisión y los medios han convertido al chef en una figura reconocible, mientras que la sala sigue estando bastante olvidada. Antes ibas a un restaurante y querías conocer al maître, que te recomendara el pescado del día. Había grandes referentes en la sala, mientras que el cocinero estaba escondido y apenas se le conocía. Ahora es al revés. Necesitamos recuperar referentes para que los jóvenes vean en esta profesión una oportunidad de ser feliz. Y ¿por qué no? incluso un programa de televisión dedicado a la hospitalidad.
-Cuando un restaurante recibe una estrella, siempre la recoge el chef, ¿es justo?
-Michelin es una fiesta para los cocineros. Todo gira alrededor de ellos porque es una guía que premia fundamentalmente la cocina. Pero cuando consigues una estrella o cualquier otro reconocimiento, no me parece justo que todo repercuta en una única persona. Me gusta decir que yo solo no puedo. El éxito de un restaurante pasa por un montón de personas.
«En mi restaurante hago de aparcacoches para ser el primero en verte la cara»
-¿Camarero por vocación o por circunstancias?
-Por vocación. Me enamoré de esta profesión por la pasión y por el contacto con la gente. Es un oficio que te permite conocer a muchísimas personas y, sobre todo, hacerlas felices. Durante las dos o tres horas que están en un restaurante puedes influir, aunque sea mínimamente, en que tengan un momento entrañable. Eres un hilo conductor de esa felicidad. Para mí es una profesión increíble.
-¿Se puede aprender a ser hospitalario? ¿O hay que nacer con ello?
-Se puede aprender a ser sociable y hospitalario, pero tiene que partir de una vocación real y ciertas dotes personales. Tienes que ser alguien que quiere agradar y que le gusta servir. Hay que demostrar felicidad en todo lo que haces. Y eso va más allá del oficio, tiene que ver con tu manera de comportarte en todos los aspectos de la vida.
«No soporto el cortoplacismo ni a los camareros que hablan mucho de sí mismos»
-A la hora de contratar un camarero ¿qué valora más, la actitud o el currículum?
-Me fijo mucho en que no hable demasiado de sí mismo. También en el currículum, porque a veces parecen una novela de ciencia ficción y no se corresponden con la realidad. En España no tenemos costumbre de pedir referencias ni de contrastar demasiado las trayectorias. Me tira para atrás el cortoplacismo: gente que está seis meses en un sitio, nueve en otro, un año en otro. Me interesa el sentido de pertenencia. Cada casa tiene sus valores y lo que es bueno para un restaurante puede no serlo para otro.
-¿Cómo se reconoce a un buen camarero en los cinco primeros minutos?
-Es muy importante el lenguaje corporal. Cómo se acercan a una mesa, cómo se dirigen al cliente, cómo transmiten agradecimiento con cada gesto de su cuerpo. No es solo lo que dices. Hay que saber transmitirlo con tu manera de estar y de relacionarte con la gente.
-¿Qué es lo que menos soporta de un cliente?
-La altanería. Ese «¿tú no sabes quién soy yo?». Pero hay que saber llevarlos. Hay muchos tipos de clientes y a todos tenemos que estarles agradecidos por que hayan elegido venir. No hay un cliente gilipollas, hay personas más difíciles, pero en un restaurante, en un supermercado o en cualquier otro ámbito. Nuestra obligación es que se vaya contento, aunque tenga una actitud de mierda.
-¿Está matando la IA la conversación con el camarero?
-Hoy la gente tiene mucha más información, pero a veces no siempre sabe canalizarla. Soy anti IA, anti QR, no me gusta esa frialdad que transmiten. Me gustan los restaurantes con mantel y con cartas de vino que puedas tocar. La tecnología facilita la gestión, las reservas y permite conocer mejor los gustos del cliente cuando vuelve, pero yo sigo creyendo en el calor humano, en la conversación y en el vínculo emocional. Esa parte no la quiero perder.
-Viene de una familia hostelera, pero no soportaba trabajar con sus padres. ¿Tendemos a romantizar los negocios familiares?
-En casa las cosas tenían que hacerse como ellos decían y yo era una persona inquieta, con ganas de hacer las cosas de otra manera. Fue una relación complicada y salir a trabajar fuera fue también una forma de sobrevivir. Me habría gustado mejorar aquella sidrería del pueblo, llevarla hacia la excelencia, pero mis padres no supieron delegar. Los tiempos cambian y quizá tampoco tenían la formación que yo he podido adquirir después.
-¿Qué hay de aquella sidrería en sus restaurantes de hoy?
-La hospitalidad, el cariño y el agradecimiento. En el pueblo la gente venía a la barra a vernos, a compartir un rato. Eso he intentado trasladarlo a mis restaurantes. Me gusta recibir al cliente, últimamente estoy haciendo de aparcacoches: así soy la primera cara que ve cuando llega y es muy gratificante darle las gracias por haber elegido tu casa cuando se va. Con todos los restaurantes que hay en este país, somos afortunados de que hayan escogido el nuestro.

noticias.titulo: El caso cloacas se convierte en una gran hidra de consecuencias imprevisibles para el PSOE
noticias.resumen: Pedraz decidirá tras el 29-N si imputa al partido, pero mientras se ve forzado a investigar otra decena de ramificaciones
noticias.texto:
El caso cloacas se convierte en una gran hidra de consecuencias imprevisibles para el PSOE
Pedraz decidirá tras el 29-N si imputa al partido, pero mientras se ve forzado a investigar otra decena de ramificaciones
Y ahora también la trama de las eólicas de Forestalia amenaza con desembarcar en la macrocausa de las cloacas de Ferraz. Santiago Pedraz no da abasto ... . El titular de la plaza 5 de Instrucción de la Audiencia Nacional afronta un sumario cuyo perímetro nadie parece capaz de definir y que suma nuevos frentes.
La causa nació en mayo de 2025 en un juzgado de Madrid para investigar las maniobras de un personaje excéntrico, la fontanera Leire Díez, contra investigaciones que salpican a Pedro Sánchez, su familia y el PSOE. Hoy amenaza con superar en ramificaciones al mismísimo caso koldo, origen de todo.
Y con una decisión pendiente: si imputa al partido por financiar la cloaca.
El último capítulo de este crecimiento desmedido es la petición de un juzgado de Teruel para que Pedraz sume al puzle los supuestos tejemanejes de Leire Díez y Santos Cerdán con Transición Ecológica por los permisos de parques renovables.
Si Pedraz recoge el guante aragonés, la hidra sumará otra cabeza.
Ya investiga las cuentas de Ferraz; abogados que supuestamente financiaron la trama; presuntos rescates fraudulentos de la SEPI; el grupo Hirurok; tentáculos en empresas públicas; posibles fondos europeos desviados a los cloaqueros; intentos de colonizar las cúpulas de la Guardia Civil y la Fiscalía.
También un presunto plan para matar a la jueza del caso del hermano de Sánchez; intentos de soborno y hasta la utilización del mismísimo Registro Civil para fines espurios.
- Ferraz
El 9 de octubre Pedraz rechazó investigar al PSOE como persona jurídica «en este momento». Faltaban indicios, según el juez, que ordenó aclarar pagos, servicios y controles.
Ferraz entregó el 17 de noviembre tres cajas y un pendrive sobre abogados contratados entre 2021 y 2025 para una pieza reservada. Las fuentes consultadas afirman que después de las elecciones decidirá si imputa al partido por malversación al financiar la cloaca, no solo a Santos Cerdán, que como secretario de Organización personificaba el aparato.
- Leire y el hombre de arriba
La UCO atribuye a Leire dos funciones: facilitar negocios públicos y buscar munición contra investigaciones. Por encima sitúa a Santos Cerdán, incluso «en un plano superior» al grupo Hirurok, la red financiera para los chanchullos propios de los imputados.
Anticorrupción atribuye al entonces mano derecha de Sánchez haber pactado 4.000 euros mensuales para Leire con fondos socialistas. Cerdán aparece además vinculado en esta red a Antxon Alonso, socio de Servinabar, la sociedad en la que los agentes le atribuyen un 45% oculto.
- Los abogados y el dinero
El rastro llega a los despachos de Ismael Oliver y Jacobo Teijelo, dos históricos letrados del PSOE. Los investigadores sospechan que sus honorarios encubrieron pagos a Leire u otros trabajos. Teijelo acabaría defendiendo al propio Cerdán.
La gerente del PSOE, Ana María Fuentes Pacheco, atribuyó determinados encargos a la Secretaría de Organización.
- Puente con Koldo
Carmen Pano, que dijo haber llevado bolsas de dinero a Ferraz, declaró que el despacho de Leticia de la Hoz, antigua abogada de Koldo García, le ofreció contraprestaciones para cambiar su versión.
- La trama verde contra la UCO
«Necesito a Balas», reclamó Leire al empresario Alejandro Hamlyn, investigado por fraude de hidrocarburos. Antonio Balas dirigía entonces y dirige ahora las investigaciones económicas de la UCO que cercan al PSOE.
La Guardia Civil investiga la obtención de información contra agentes y las presiones e informaciones reservadas: la trama verde.
Leire se reunió tres veces con Mercedes González, entonces directora general del cuerpo. El exdirector general Leonardo Marcos negó haber presionado a los investigadores. Ambos están imputados por participar en las supuestas maniobras para frenar a la UCO. El DAO del cuerpo, también.
- Los despachos de la Fiscalía
Leire y Teijelo visitaron dos veces a Diego Villafañe, entonces teniente fiscal de la Secretaría Técnica de la Fiscalía General. Después, Villafañe elaboró un documento que calificaba de «delirante narración» las acusaciones contra la fontanera.
Las órdenes del número dos de Álvaro García Ortiz para torpedear cualquier investigación de la cloaca en Extremadura están documentadas. El exfiscal general no ha sido citado a declarar. Todavía.
- Biedma, la jueza en la diana
Beatriz Biedma, instructora del caso contra David Sánchez, ejerce ya la acusación particular. La UCO sostiene que la cloaca llegó incluso a urdir un plan para «eliminarla» a través de sicarios de un clan.
La jueza denuncia maniobras para apartarla mediante denuncias y recusaciones del exjuez Luis José Sáenz de Tejada, investigado por organización criminal, calumnias, coacciones y delito contra la integridad moral.
- La publicidad y Europa
La campaña europea de 2024 ha abierto otra derivada. La UCO examina los pagos publicitarios del PSOE a Crónica Libre, relacionados con personas del entorno de Leire. Testigos cuestionaron su utilidad y precio: podría encubrir financiación de las cloacas.
De probarse, podría haber malversación de subvenciones electorales y financiación ilegal. Anticorrupción pide determinar primero de qué partida salió el dinero. La Fiscalía Europea ha solicitado información sobre una posible afectación de fondos comunitarios.
- Hasta el Registro Civil
La cloaca habría llegado al exviceministro venezolano Nervis Villalobos, relacionado con pesquisas contra el fiscal anticorrupción José Grinda. La investigación apunta a la concesión irregular de su nacionalidad española gracias a las gestiones de Díez y de Cerdán.
- Hirurok, SEPI y más empresas
Hirurok reunió a Leire, al expresidente de la SEPI Vicente Fernández y a Antxon Alonso. Según la UCO, esa presunta banda criminal intervino en el rescate de Tubos Reunidos, de 112,8 millones, y habría cobrado 114.950 euros a través de Mediaciones Martínez. Cerdán y Leire recibieron luego a directivos de Tubos en Ferraz.
Las pesquisas alcanzan Mercasa, Enusa, la mina de Cala y el Parque Empresarial Principado de Asturias. Aldesa contrató a Mediaciones Martínez y a Análisis Relevante, la empresa del testaferro de Zapatero.
- Forestalia, la última cabeza
El juez de Teruel Juan José Cortes ha acordado inhibirse en favor de Pedraz por posibles delitos de cohecho y prevaricación ambiental vinculados a Forestalia. El grupo ya figuraba entre los negocios de Hirurok: una inversión de 17,32 millones de Sepides en su filial Arapellet y 200.000 euros pactados para los intermediarios.
La investigación turolense examina autorizaciones del Ministerio para la Transición Ecológica, dirigido durante los hechos por Teresa Ribera, y del Gobierno autonómico del socialista Javier Lambán.
Forestalia amenaza con convertirse en otra patata caliente para Pedraz. Otra investigación compleja que se sumaría a un sumario ya ingobernable y de consecuencias imprevisibles para el PSOE.

noticias.titulo: La vida domótica
noticias.resumen: Media España presume y la otra media abre la boca atónita y orgullosa ante tanto pariente automático
noticias.texto:
A la última
La vida domótica
Media España presume y la otra media abre la boca atónita y orgullosa ante tanto pariente automático
Mis sobrinos presumen de sus casas domóticas. «Es estupendo, ya no tienes que estar en casa cuando llega el repartidor de paquetes, le abres desde ... el trabajo», presumen encantados y los tíos y las abuelas ponemos cara de asombro. Es verdad, cuánta utilidad. La otra tarde llamé a casa de mi hermano y me abrió desde el tren en que viajaba. ¿Y mis hermanas? Cuánta modernidad cada vez que encienden el robot de cocina desde el gimnasio y así, al llegar a casa, tienen el zumo vitaminado de frutas exprimido, las lentejas recién hechas y las albóndigas en su punto.
Media España presume de vida domótica y la otra media abre la boca atónita y orgullosa ante tanto pariente automático. Cuando, tomando café, alguien del grupo saca el móvil, teclea y anuncia que va a encender la calefacción, la Thermomix y la lavadora para que todo esté en su punto al llegar a casa, me acuerdo de mi madre, que llamaba a mi padre a la oficina a las tres. «José Ramón, ¿vas a tardar mucho?», preguntaba. «Diez minutos», respondía él. «Pues voy echando el arroz», anunciaba ella con precisión más maternal que domótica.
El otro día, recordé en una tertulia esa precisión arrocera y me compararon con Cebolleta, aquel abuelo pesado que dibujaba Vázquez en el DDT. Yo callé, avergonzado y antiguo, pero sonreí mientras imaginaba a dos hackers iraníes divirtiéndose: abrasaban domóticamente las albóndigas de mis sobrinas, encendían en julio las calefacciones de mis colegas modernos, abrían la casa de mi hermano innovador a las tres de la mañana… Y me acordé de mi padre, tan analógico el hombre que protegía la puerta de casa con dos trancas cruzadas que no abrías ni desde el tren ni desde Teherán.

noticias.titulo: Saber reír
noticias.resumen: Pero es que la de Sánchez suena rara. Y lleva varias de esas en pocos días, en pocas entrevistas
noticias.texto:
En diagonal
Saber reír
Pero es que la de Sánchez suena rara. Y lleva varias de esas en pocos días, en pocas entrevistas
Rosa Belmonte
Julia Otero preguntó a Pedro Sánchez sobre lo que Puigdemont había dicho de él (cínico, amoral...). Se fue por los cerros de siempre. Insistió Otero. ... Y Sánchez: «Discrepo. Jo, jo, jo». Sé que la forma correcta de escribir la risa en español según la Real Academia es ja, ja, ja. Pero es que la de Sánchez suena rara. Y lleva varias de esas en pocos días, en pocas entrevistas. Con Franganillo, con Griso, con Otero. Saber reír no es una condición imprescindible para gobernar, pero igual que a uno le puede disgustar el color de un traje, también le puede disgustar una risa. Y adorar otra. La de Christine Baranski, claro, como Diane Lockhart. Pero vamos a lo importante. Este año se han aprobado 41 decretos-leyes. Más que durante la pandemia. Entre ellos, «el decreto-ley de Maricarmen». El que pidió a Feijóo que no derogue. A la vez, dice que no ha visto una movilización como la que hay. Lo mismo acabamos riendo como Diane cuando gana Trump.

noticias.titulo: ¿España se ha vuelto sanchista?
noticias.resumen: Las urnas nos dirán si la sociedad empieza a aceptar lo que antes consideraba políticamente inaceptable
noticias.texto:
¿España se ha vuelto sanchista?
Las urnas nos dirán si la sociedad empieza a aceptar lo que antes consideraba políticamente inaceptable
Juan Carlos Viloria
Las elecciones generales del 29-N van a mostrar si en España se está abriendo o cerrando la llamada ventana de Overton, un famoso concepto ... de comunicación política que explica el rango de ideas u opiniones que una sociedad considera aceptables en un momento dado. La idea clave es que esa ventana puede desplazarse con el tiempo, haciendo que lo antes impensable, llegue a verse como aceptable. Núñez Feijóo hace campaña advirtiendo al electorado de que estas elecciones generales son las más importantes y trascendentales de los últimos cincuenta años. Independientemente de sus intereses, específicamente partidistas, hay una verdad de fondo en el argumento porque se trata de confirmar o desmentir que la sociedad española empiece a normalizar determinados comportamientos del poder político que hasta la llegada de la coalición progresista, y el llamado sanchismo, se consideraban mayoritariamente inaceptables cuando no tabú. El PP, pues, ha planteado la consulta en las urnas como una especie de Rubicón social mientras Pedro Sánchez, por el contrario, esta dando un marco festivo cuando no frívolo, pero sobre todo, continuista, con la idea de seguir cruzando líneas rojas en beneficio del «progresismo».
El cuerpo electoral tiene que decidir si la sociedad española normaliza, no tanto incorpora, legislaciones muy permisivas sobre eutanasia, aborto de menores sin supervisión, o matrimonio, adopción, vientres de alquiler igualitarios, que también. Pero, sobre todo, lo que se planea, después de la última etapa del sanchismo, es la preponderancia del poder Ejecutivo, del Gobierno, sobre los otros dos poderes, el Legislativo y el Judicial. Esa preponderancia hegemónica que se materializa en la colonización partidista de las instituciones que en los usos democráticos tradicionales siempre se debería respetar su independencia. Se trataría de comprobar si la sociedad española está dispuesta a aceptar el estrechamiento de la clase media en favor de una sociedad fiscalmente socializante y estatalizante. Se pondrá a prueba de las urnas si se ha aceptado el tabú de cambiar poder por amnistía a sediciosos o el desequilibrio presupuestario en favor de una parte.
Frente al modus operando sanchista de romper moldes, homologar y normalizar los «cambios de opinión» (Bildu, Amnistía, Sahara) y la incoherencia (pisos en Vallecas por chalets con piscina, demonizar fondos buitre y tener que dimitir por acumulación de propiedades), estaría la propuesta de cerrar la ventana de Overton que proponen desde el bloque de la derecha. Y que va desde métodos moralmente discutibles para frenar la inmigración ilegal, hasta adelgazar el estado en beneficio de la iniciativa privada y frenar la preponderancia de lo público en sanidad, educación e infraestructuras. Las urnas nos dirán si la sociedad empieza a aceptar lo que antes consideraba políticamente inaceptable.

noticias.titulo: Sánchez confirma que Zapatero le «aconseja» en la campaña electoral, pero sin participar en los mítines por «razones personales»
noticias.resumen: El actual líder socialista defiende al expresidente y asegura que sigue siendo «un activo del partido» durante una entrevista en 'Salvados'
noticias.texto:
Sánchez confirma que Zapatero le «aconseja» en la campaña electoral, pero sin participar en los mítines por «razones personales»
El actual líder socialista defiende al expresidente y asegura que sigue siendo «un activo del partido» durante una entrevista en 'Salvados'
Pedro Sánchez ha confirmado que José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero está colaborando con él durante la campaña electoral del 29-N, aunque no aparecerá en ninguno ... de los mítines ni actos públicos del PSOE. El actual líder socialista ha explicado que el expresidente le está ayudando y aconsejando de manera personal, pero que ha sido el propio Zapatero quien ha decidido mantenerse al margen de la actividad pública por «razones personales».
«Tiene mucha experiencia en campaña», señaló Sánchez durante la entrevista con Gonzo en 'Salvados'. El jefe del Ejecutivo ha defendido además la continuidad del expresidente dentro del partido, pese a la investigación judicial que le afecta por el caso Plus Ultra. «Para mí, José Luis es un activo del partido», afirmó, antes de insistir en que cree en su inocencia. El líder del PSOE ha recordado que debe prevalecer la presunción de inocencia y ha asegurado estar «convencido» de que Zapatero no ha cometido ninguna irregularidad.
Queda una semana de campaña. Y ya sabemos quién no aparecerá en la del PSOE.Esta noche (21.30h): #SalvadosPedroSánchez https://t.co/2c3xtefW9F
— Salvados (@salvadostv) November 22, 2026
Uno de los asuntos más delicados de la conversación ha sido el hallazgo de unas joyas en una caja fuerte de la oficina del expresidente, que han sido valoradas en más de un millón de euros. Sánchez ha considerado que «muy probablemente» Zapatero esté arrepentido de haberlas guardado. Asimismo, ha evitado pronunciarse sobre las posibles responsabilidades fiscales derivadas de este asunto y ha dejado en manos de la justicia la decisión sobre si existe algún delito. «Él defiende su inocencia al respecto y yo le creo», añadió.
El asunto de Zapatero ha sido, precisamente, uno de los momentos más incómodos de la entrevista. El propio Gonzo había adelantado que las preguntas sobre el expresidente habían generado más incomodidad en Sánchez que las relacionadas con Begoña Gómez o su hermano David. El periodista explicó que el presidente llegó a alargar algunas respuestas al percatarse de que el siguiente bloque de preguntas abordaría la situación del exdirigente socialista.
Más allá de la situación de Zapatero, Sánchez también ha abordado las consecuencias políticas de los casos de corrupción que afectan a su entorno. El presidente ha reconocido que el caso de José Luis Ábalos fue «muy duro» y que le hizo llegar a plantearse la posibilidad de dimitir y poner fin a la legislatura. A pesar de ello, ha defendido la gestión de su ejecutivo y ha asegurado que su Gobierno es «de los más limpios de la historia de la democracia». También, ha reivindicado la presunción de inocencia de Santos Cerdán.
Además, durante la conversación, el líder socialista se ha referido a la situación judicial de su mujer, Begoña Gómez, y de su hermano, David Sánchez. Sobre la primera, ha afirmado que «ha sufrido las consecuencias de la crueldad de la política», aunque ha reconocido que no le queda otra opción que confiar en la justicia.
Relación distante con Feijóo
Por otro lado, Sánchez ha asegurado que no se arrepiente de haber concedido la amnistía a los líderes independentistas y ha defendido que fue una medida necesaria para avanzar en la «normalización de la convivencia en Cataluña». Sin embargo, ha descartado convocar un referéndum de autodeterminación.
También, ha aprovechado la entrevista para volver sobre su reciente cara a cara con Alberto Núñez Feijóo. Sánchez ha insistido en que ganó el debate «de largo» y ha acusado al líder del PP de recurrir a los bulos y a la «mala educación». Además, ha reconocido que ambos mantienen una relación distante y que no conectan en lo personal.
Por último, ha explicado que la decisión de adelantar las elecciones generales llegó después de una comida con sus padres, cuyo criterio considera importante a la hora de tomar decisiones políticas.

noticias.titulo: Israeli attacks have turned Gaza into 'toxic wasteland', Oxfam says
noticias.resumen: The report says there are signs of possible contamination across almost all of Gaza as a result of Israel's actions.
noticias.texto:
Israeli attacks have turned Gaza into 'toxic wasteland', Oxfam says
- Published
Gaza has been turned into "a toxic wasteland", with more than 99% of the Palestinian territory showing indicators of environmental contamination from Israeli military attacks, a new report from the non-profit organisation Oxfam says, external.
Heavy metals, explosive residues, and asbestos from destroyed buildings, dioxins and biological contaminants in the air, soil and water supply are threats to Palestinians now and potentially for decades to come, it says.
Oxfam International's executive director, Amitabh Behar, accuses Israel of "environmental war crimes" as part of an "ongoing genocide in Gaza."
"The destruction and contamination of Gaza will have fundamentally degraded the environmental conditions necessary for human safety and survival," he says.
Israel's government has been asked for its response to the report.
It has rejected genocide accusations in an ongoing case at the International Court of Justice as baseless and distorted. Israel maintains that its military campaign in Gaza is an act of self-defence against Hamas in response to the group's deadly attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, and that it takes steps to mitigate civilian harm.
Oxfam and the UK-based Conflict and Environment Observatory (CEOBS) used satellite imagery, remote sensing, spatial analysis and other open-source data to draw their conclusions in the most comprehensive report to date on the severe environmental impacts caused by three years of intense war in Gaza.
The report details how munitions used in Israel's intense bombardment, as well as the debris from destroyed buildings and infrastructure, all have an impact on the environment. In February, a UN special rapporteur stated that more than 200,000 tonnes of explosives were dropped on Gaza in almost two years - "the equivalent of the total energy of approximately 13 Hiroshima-type nuclear bombs".
Last year, the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) estimated that Israel's military operations destroying homes and infrastructure had generated more than 61 million tonnes of debris across the territory, with about 15% potentially carrying a high risk of contamination from hazardous materials.
"There are going to be chronic health impacts that are long term because a lot of these contaminants are persistent in the environment," Oxfam report author Lama Abdul Samad told the BBC.
She says that now and in future Gazans are likely to suffer from increased respiratory diseases, cancers, organ damage and a rise in birth defects and stillbirths.
With all six wastewater treatment plants out of operation in Gaza, untreated sewage currently makes its way into groundwater and the Mediterranean Sea. The health impact has recently been exacerbated by heavy winter storms causing rainwater to mix with wastewater and flow through streets and tent sites housing displaced people.
Testing types and levels of contamination is often not possible because Gazan laboratories have been destroyed and there are Israeli restrictions on the entry of specialist testing equipment and scientists. The BBC has approached the Israeli military for comment.
UNEP said security concerns also prevented its expert staff from previously travelling to Gaza.
The Oxfam report calls for a full, independent environmental assessment to be carried out in Gaza to identify contamination risks ahead of a clean-up. It says special attention must be given to the protection of workers involved.
Already, Gazan doctors have been reporting increased acute respiratory infections caused by dust and pollution from destroyed buildings and displaced people burning plastic, rags and cardboard to keep warm and cook food. Gastrointestinal diseases are linked to unsafe water and poor sanitation.
A Palestinian dermatologist, Dr Alaa Abu Hajar, told the BBC he had seen a five-fold increase in chronic skin diseases since the start of the war, putting this down to environmental pollution and overcrowded, unhygienic living conditions in tents and displacement camps.
"There are rodents, rubbish and sewage that's spread through the streets," he says. "Unfortunately, the age group most affected is children."
Farmers and those working in fishing say that pollution of the soil and sea mean they are unable to produce food that is safe.
"Sewage and wastewater are discharged into the sea without treatment and this is a great disaster," complains fisherman Abu al-Abed Sultan. "There is also rubble from destroyed houses that's dumped into the sea. When we lower our nets, we catch rubble and garbage. This harms the marine environment; the fish are affected and so are the fishermen."
At least 74,746 Palestinians have been killed since the start of the war in Gaza, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. The UN says that humanitarian conditions remain dire.
Israel has conditioned large-scale Gaza reconstruction on the full disarmament of Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups. In July, Hamas accepted a plan put forward by the US-led Board of Peace to give up its weapons in exchange for an Israeli troop withdrawal. However, the Israeli government said the proposal was insufficient.

noticias.titulo: Flights and train services cancelled in Belgium due to strike
noticias.resumen: A series of strikes have hit Belgium in recent months as the prime minister struggles to agree a budget to cut costs.
noticias.texto:
Flights and train services cancelled in Belgium due to strike
- Published
Hundreds of flights have been cancelled and public transport severely disrupted across Belgium as a result of a strike against planned austerity measures.
All air traffic has been halted at Brussels Airport in Zaventem as well as at Charleroi, home to low-cost airlines such as Ryanair.
Underground services have also been halted in capital Brussels, where large numbers of people joined a protest march.
The protest comes as Prime Minister Bart De Wever continues talks with his coalition allies over a budget to cut borrowing costs. King Philippe declined his resignation earlier this month, giving De Wever more time to negotiate.
No flights are taking off or landing at Brussels Airport between 07:00 and 21:00 local time (06:00-20:00 GMT) as a result of the strike by air traffic controllers.
"In total, 404 flights today cannot be operated, which has an impact on more than 50,000 passengers," Brussels Airport spokesperson Jeffrey Franssens said.
Reuters news agency spoke to Florence Faure, a French passenger who had arrived in Brussels from China's capital, Beijing, only to find that her flight to Paris Charles de Gaulle airport had been cancelled.
"Since our luggage was supposed to go on to Paris Charles de Gaulle, we didn't even collect it," she said.
A similar situation has affected Charleroi, where all flights were shown as "scheduled", regardless of the time of departure or arrival.
One passenger told Belgian broadcaster RTBF that she had received no warning and only discovered there were no flights when she arrived at the airport.
Philippe Naime, a teacher, was one of the tens of thousands taking part in the protest march in Brussels.
"Quite simply, no more money is being invested in education, and people are left to fend for themselves. But people do not have the means to do that," he told Reuters.
Public transport, schools and other public services are also facing disruptions.
The Belgian prime minister leads a five-party coalition.
One of its members, the socialist Vooruit, has been refusing to endorse plans agreed by the other four. It wants to raise taxes on the rich and for there to be fewer cuts to pensions and the health sector.
De Wever met King Philippe on Monday for the third update since the impasse.
"While expressing regret over the lack of significant progress, the king encouraged the prime minister to persevere in order to reach an agreement as soon as possible," the royal palace said in a statement.
The leader of one of the country's main unions, FGTB, said the government had alternatives to "dismantling the social protection system".
Bert Engelaar, head of the union, called for "a genuine wealth tax, fair taxation, and the elimination of tax loopholes".
"Political responsibility is not about keeping a government afloat at all costs. It's about knowing when to stop," he added, praising the Vooruit party.
Another union leader, Ann Vermorgen of the CSC, criticised government plans to cut bank holidays when they fall on weekends.

noticias.titulo: Mexican soldiers attacked in wake of drug lord's arrest
noticias.resumen: Eight suspects are arrested after firing on soldiers trying to re-establish order following the arrest of 'El Chapo Isidro'.
noticias.texto:
Mexican soldiers attacked in wake of drug lord's arrest
- Published
Mexican soldiers have detained eight alleged members of a drug cartel whose leader was arrested on Friday, sparking a wave of violence in northern Sinaloa state.
The Mexican defence ministry said the soldiers were shot by the suspects on Sunday while on patrol in the town of Sinaloa de Leyva, trying to re-establish order in the wake of the arrest of Fausto Isidro Meza Flores.
Meza Flores, also known as "Chapo Isidro", was on the FBI's 10 most wanted list and had managed to evade capture for years.
The ministry said the eight had also been involved in the retaliatory violence unleashed by Meza Flores's cartel in the hours after his arrest on Friday.
In a statement published on social media, external, the ministry of defence said that one of the detainees was under age.
It added that its special forces had seized six vehicles as part of their operation, two of which had been fitted with bullet-proof armour and gun turrets.
The US Department of Justice described Friday's arrest of Meza Flores as "a spectacular military operation" and congratulated Mexico's military and special forces on his capture.
It said that the US Homeland Security Task Force had supported the Mexican military and praised the "bilateral effort".
Mexico's defence ministry said its special forces had used stealth and surprise to reach the home of the wanted man.
They also established a security perimeter to prevent Meza Flores from escaping and cartel reinforcements from arriving.
Nevertheless, a bloody firefight ensued.
Along with Meza Flores, his second-in-command, known as "SerafÃn", and his financial operator, were also arrested and quickly transferred by air to Mexico City.
As news of their arrest spread, members of their cartel erected barricades on major roads and set cars and some shops alight.
There were also reports of shoot-outs between the security forces and cartel members.
The prosecutor's office in Sinaloa says 17 people, four of them members of the Mexican security forces, were killed as a result of the violence on Friday and early Saturday.
Who is 'Chapo Isidro'?
US Assistant Attorney General A Tysen Duva has described Meza Flores as "the most dangerous man in Mexico".
"For decades Meza Flores has promoted the terrorist objectives of the Sinaloa cartel," Duva said, accusing him of "flooding the United States with deadly substances".
The 44-year-old is believed to have started his criminal career with the JuÃ¡rez cartel decades ago.
He later moved on to become the right-hand man of the leader of the BeltrÃ¡n Leyva Organisation, a drug gang once allied to the Sinaloa cartel before the two groups split and became bitter enemies.
As early as 2013, the US Treasury identified Meza Flores as the leader of his own drug-trafficking organisation, named after him.
The US Treasury said at the time, that the Meza Flores drug trafficking organisation was responsible for "the distribution of large quantities of methamphetamine, heroin, marijuana, and cocaine to the United States".
It added that the turf war between the Meza Flores cartel and the Sinaloa cartel had "resulted in the quadrupling of drug-war killings" in between 2009 and 2013.
According to think tank Insight Crime, external, Meza Flores himself kept a low profile over the last decade while continuing to run his cartel out of Guasave, in Sinaloa state.
The head of the US Drug Enforcement Administration said that his capture was a "significant blow to a ruthless criminal organisation that has used extreme violence to traffic deadly drugs, including fentanyl, a designated weapon of mass destruction, into American communities".
His arrest, and the co-operation between US and Mexican officials which led to it, will be seen as a win for the government of Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum.
Sheinbaum has stressed that she is keen to work with the US authorities to capture high-profile target as long as Mexican's sovereignty is respected.

noticias.titulo: Kenya and DR Congo agree to restore ties after tensions over conflict
noticias.resumen: The two leaders committed to upholding sovereignty and "non-interference in the internal affairs of states".
noticias.texto:
Kenya and DR Congo agree to restore ties after tensions over conflict
- Published
Kenya's President William Ruto and his Congolese counterpart Felix Tshisekedi have agreed to restore full diplomatic ties between the two countries following tensions over the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.
Relations between the two countries have soured since 2023 when DR Congo accused Kenya of hosting leaders launching a rebel alliance, including the M23.
This led DR Congo to recall its envoy to Nairobi. Relations deteriorated further when Kinshasa refusing to accredit Kenya's nominated ambassador.
On Sunday, the two leaders affirmed their commitment to "sovereignty, territorial integrity, non-interference in the internal affairs of states".
The agreement was announced in a joint statement issued after the summit held in the town of Oyo in Congo-Brazzaville, facilitated by the nation's President Denis Sassou Nguesso, with Togolese leader Faure Essozimna GnassingbÃ© as mediator.
Tshisekedi and Ruto also agreed to "good neighbourliness and peaceful settlement of disputes" as well as "strengthen cooperation within regional mechanisms".
DR Congo and Kenya are both members of the East African Community (EAC).
DR Congo, which joined in 2022, is the latest entrant to the bloc, but its membership has been complicated by its accusation that Rwanda, a fellow member, backs the M23 rebels. Rwanda denies the claims despite overwhelming evidence.
DR Congo has also accused Kenya of hosting Congolese political and rebel leaders whom it says are working to destabilise the country.
When the Congo River Alliance (AFC), a political-military alliance including the M23, was launched in Nairobi in 2023, DR Congo responded by recalling its ambassador to Kenya.
The tensions were stoked further in March last year after Kenya named a consul-general to Goma, the capital of DR Congo's North Kivu region, after it fell to M23 forces, who control many eastern parts of the country.
DR Congo said naming the envoy amounted to disrespect for the country's territorial integrity and seemed to legitimise the group's occupation.
- Suited and booted: How Joseph Kabila went from president to rebel leader 
  - Published31 October
Relations deteriorated further after Kenya hosted a meeting of Congolese opposition figures, including former President Joseph Kabila, in October 2025.
Kabila was in 2025 sentenced to death in absentia on charges including war crimes and treason. He denied the accusations, but did not appear in court to defend himself.
He has since been named the leader of the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN), the new rebel coalition that took over from the AFC.
Sunday's meeting between Ruto and Tshisekedi also included other issues including deepening trade cooperation, economic development, and regional integration.
The two also sought to collaborate to control the spread of the Ebola virus.
On Sunday, the head of the World Health Organization (WHO), Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, said the frequency of attacks across the country's east had increased since the end of October, seriously affecting the Ebola response.
Tedros said heavy fighting in an area close to where the Ebola outbreak first emerged had disrupted work and the wider Ebola response.
More than 5,700 people have died and 11,000 infected with Ebola in DR Congo since the outbreak was declared in May.
The latest outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo species of the virus, has spread beyond DR Congo borders, with cases reported in Kenya, Uganda and Nigeria.

noticias.titulo: Presidential villa suffers water and power cuts, Nigerian leader says
noticias.resumen: Bola Tinubu says he was shaving last week when the water cut out - an experience familiar to many Nigerians.
noticias.texto:
Presidential villa suffers water and power cuts, Nigerian leader says
- Published
Nigeria's President Bola Tinubu says the presidential villa suffers from cuts in electricity and water - issues that are all too common for the country's ordinary citizens.
He said he was shaving last week when the water supply cut at the villa, known as Aso Rock, in Abuja.
He is seeking re-election next January and vowed to address these issues.
Tinubu made the disclosure on Sunday at a special prayer session organised in his honour by members of his family in Lagos.
He explained: "On the Wednesday of last week, I was shaving, and the water went off. In the villa, you won't know punishment dey dia too [thereâs punishment there too in Nigerian pidgin].
"The water went off. So we will correct all this. No light, no water, no electricity, no development. We have just started. We can do it, and we will do it for Nigeria,â he said.
Aso Villa serves as both the office and official residence of the Nigerian president. It is situated at the base of Aso Rock in Abuja.
Last year, 10bn naira (Â£5.5m; $7.2m), was allocated in the budget for the installation of a solar mini-grid in the Aso Villa as part of efforts to address rising electricity bills and unstable power supply.
Some reports say it has been completed and is in the testing phase, with plans to fully disconnect the facility from the national grid soon.
- Can Nigeria's president regain voters' trust after painful first term? 
  - Published12 November
- Search and rescue teams race against time after Nigeria boat tragedy 
  - Published1 hour ago
Nigeria has long endured electricity shortages, but recent severe disruptions have been caused primarily by insufficient gas supplies and declining hydropower output, rather than the usual nationwide grid collapse.
Persistent blackouts in Lagos, Abuja and elsewhere have forced distribution companies to implement rotating power cuts, severely impacting households and businesses.
The country also suffers from chronic water shortages, the result of a structural crisis rooted in the gap between rapid urban population growth and decaying, inadequate public water infrastructure, leaving millions without reliable supplies, especially in Lagos.
Tinubu made a high-profile electricity promise during the 2023 election campaign, but the exact wording and how binding it is has become a major point of contention ahead of the election on 16 January 2027.
In 2022, months before the last presidential election, Tinubu said: "Whichever way, by all means necessary, you will have electricity, and you will not pay for estimated bills any more. A promise made will be a promise kept.
"If I don't keep the promise and I come for a second term, don't vote for me, unless I give you adequate reasons why I couldn't deliver,â he said.
Despite the continuing power cuts, some of his supporters point to improved electricity supplies in rural areas as well as a recently approved $2bn (Â£1.5bn) investment in a new EastâWest Super Grid, designed to expand electricity transmission capacity and strengthen the national grid, as evidence that he is doing his best to keep to his promise.
Tinubu defeated the countryâs former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar as well as former Anambra state governor Peter Obi in 2023 and the three are seen as the strongest contenders once again.

Ukraine shares video of strikes on Russian ships off Libya
Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky has shared footage on social media which he says shows strikes on Russian vessels off the coast of Libya on Sunday.
A Russian warship was sunk by Ukrainian drones and the attack also targeted a second vessel, a cargo ship which was being used to transport weapons, Zelensky said.
Footage verified by the BBC shows a ship ablaze at Benghazi's port.
The local health ministry said it had received injured people from a commercial ship that was targeted off the coast. It is not clear whether this is the same vessel as the one Ukraine has claimed responsibility for.
Following the strikes, the Kremlin warned of an "escalation of tensions in the region", but declined to comment directly on the attacks in Libya.

noticias.titulo: Five takeaways from the failed climate talks COP31
noticias.resumen: The COP31 summit in Antalya was the longest-running climate talks in UN history.
noticias.texto:
Five takeaways from the failed climate talks COP31
- Published
The COP31 summit in Turkey came as evidence of climate change could not have been clearer - 2026 brought glacier collapses, record European heat, and wildfires across Asia - but also when geopolitical divisions could not have been deeper.
The result was the longest-running climate talks in UN history failed to deliver on its central political agreement â the Antalya Pacts - to further climate action.
Despite two countries, Australia and Turkey, leading the charge in their joint hosting of the negotiations, they could not bring the nations together.
After a dramatic and fractious final day where countries walked out over the absence of mention of fossil fuels in the text and money issues, questions are being asked more loudly than ever before about whether the COP process can still deliver.
Here are five, key takeaways from the talks which the hosts hoped would become known as the "implementation COP".
The world is preparing for life beyond 1.5C
This was the first COP since the UN warned that global temperatures are expected to exceed 1.5C degrees above pre-industrial levels. That is the threshold which countries agreed not to breach as part of the Paris Climate Agreement signed in 2015.
The draft agreement had acknowledged the uncomfortable reality that climate action to date has failed on its most crucial of targets.
Without agreement, that recognition has been lost.
Almost exactly a decade ago a group of the world's climate scientists - the official UN body the IPCC - warned what would happen if temperatures rose 1.5C vs 2C:
- Sea level rise would be 10cm higher - that would expose 10 million more people to flooding, external
- The ocean would become more acidic risking irreversible damage to some marine life
- Extreme heat - that's hot days and nights - in every inhabited part of the world
Throughout the talks and during the final day, many countries still acknowledged that the target remained their north star of climate action.
"This COP sought to confront hard truths â that global warming is set to overshoot 1.5C and that we must act with even more urgency to reduce emissions," said UK Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh at the close of the talks.
The draft had called for that overshoot to be kept as small and short-lived as possible â it also suggested something called carbon dioxide removal (CDR).
This is a process which takes greenhouse gases out of the atmosphere and has not been explicitly mentioned in a COP final agreement before.
Carbon dioxide can be removed naturally by planting trees - although there are limits to the scale and permanence of that.
There are other technological solutions, but these are controversial, external and are not well advanced.
Countries divided over approach on fossil fuels
This year's negotiations have exposed a troubling problem - consensus does not last forever.
On the central political agreement â the Antalya Pacts â countries could not bridge the divide on including language on fossil fuels.
And yet the very same pledge had been made just three years ago at COP28 in Dubai.
Rich nations also failed to put a figure to how much more money could be given to developing countries to adapt to climate change.
This is despite there already being a commitment from last year to triple the figure by 2035 from $40bn (Â£30bn) - but the interpretation of that pledge remains contested.
If governments cannot even agree to reaffirm commitments they've already made, it raises troubling questions about their ability to work together as the climate crisis intensifies.
- Longest-ever UN climate talks end with no deal as deep divisions exposed 
  - Published9 hours ago
Minister Chris Bowen from Australia, who was co-leading the negotiations, pointed out at the end of the talks that the world is a very different place from when these commitments were struck just a few years ago.
"The situation coming into this COP was the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory".
That was made apparent during the final meeting when pointed remarks were delivered. EU representative Darragh O'Brien said the talks had been "hijacked by some oil states".
Russian delegate Sergei Kononuchenko switched from Russian to English to directly address the EU delegation. He accused them of providing climate finance only in the form of loans to developing nations: "This is an old colonial distribution of labour under a new banner".
It is a serious blow not just to climate action, but to multilateralism itself - the idea that countries can put aside their differences on other issues to tackle problems they can't solve alone.
COP31 had some good news
Much of the coverage of COP31 has focused on the failure to get the central political agreement passed.
But much of the work at these summits is putting into action agreements made at previous meetings.
On money that is going towards adaptation for example, countries need to agree how is it being distributed, is it making an impact and how can this be tracked, and which areas are particularly vulnerable.
In fact, there were 164 other items on this year's agenda that were being thrashed out in the negotiating rooms.
And some of those were agreed at the talks.
The funds raised from a global system of carbon credits â money given in exchange for releasing greenhouse gases â will go towards helping developing countries adapt to the impacts of climate change.
They agreed to advance a just transition framework designed to protect workers and communities as global economies shift toward clean energy.
But there were many more that could not be agreed and some will now be picked up at COP32, including crucially the work programme responsible for driving forward action on cutting emissions.
Renewable energy growth remains unstoppable
What governments agree in the COP negotiating rooms is only part of what determines the speed of the energy transition.
The International Energy Agency's latest World Energy Outlook, external points to another powerful force: energy security.
It says the disruption to oil and gas supplies through the Strait of Hormuz has been the biggest energy supply shock in history. The longer the uncertainty continues, the stronger the incentive for countries to switch from imported fossil fuels to electricity generated at home.
The economics have been changing too.
Solar panels, batteries and electric vehicles have become increasingly competitive.
As clean energy develops its own commercial momentum, formal negotiations may become less important in determining its direction and pace.
Against the headwinds of inflation new investment announcements emerged at COP as part of the "Action Agenda".
This is the part of the COP process that tries to mobilise action outside of formal talks from businesses, investors and cities â this year the focus was on electrification. Turning more of our energy from fossil fuels to electricity.
"We are not entering the age of electricity, we have arrived at the age of electricity," Fatih Birol, head of the IEA, told the BBC. He says energy security and climate policies are now "closely aligned".
That doesn't make COP irrelevant.
Governments still have a crucial role in facilitating the transition, according to Dr Jennie Dodson, a senior director at the World Business Council for Sustainable Development which includes among its members the likes of Amazon and Apple.
"A key message from business is we can go so far, a lot of it is cost competitive, but there are policy barriers both around infrastructure and permitting".
The COP process needs to change
COP31 has shown how the role of these annual UN climate conferences is changing.
For the first 30 COPs, the emphasis was on building the international framework for tackling global warming.
The great diplomatic breakthrough came in Paris in 2015, when almost every country agreed to keep global warming well below 2Â°C and to pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5Â°C.
Paris also established machinery designed to turn promises into progress. Every five years, governments assess collective progress in a global stocktake and submit new national climate plans, known as NDCs.
Then came further agreements: a fund for climate damage at COP27, a commitment to transition away from fossil fuels and triple renewable energy capacity at COP28, a new climate finance target at COP29 and increased support for adaptation at COP30.
The international architecture for tackling climate change has, in other words, largely been built.
Now comes the harder business of making it work. That's why this year's conference in Antalya, Turkey, had been billed as an "implementation COP".
COP collapses: What's the future for climate action?
The COP summit in Turkey has failed because of a row about even mentioning the cause of climate change. Is there a way the world can move forward with coordinated climate action?
The emphasis now is shifting towards delivering commitments already made. Camilla Born, who helped develop the UK's strategy for COP26 and now heads the campaign group Electrify Britain, told the BBC this is making COP more procedural - less about fundamental negotiations than ensuring the machinery actually works.
This could mean doing away with a cover text â the central political agreement that countries sign up to with new pledges.
It is not a requirement to have one, and for many years countries managed without. Australia chose to push one for this COP, and it is where they fell down.
On many of the procedural issues Camilla Born spoke of, they did agree things. That may be important. It isn't necessarily exciting.
And there is a fundamental limit to what this machinery can achieve. Under the Paris Agreement countries have no mechanism to force them to meet their emissions targets.
So, when critics berate the COP process for failing to tackle the problem fast enough, it isn't really the system that is at fault, says Alden Meyer, a veteran climate negotiator now at the climate think tank E3G.
The COP process, he suggests, is "like a mirror that we hold up to ourselves every year". If the reflection is disappointing, the problem is the governments, not the mirror.
Sign up for our Future Earth newsletter to keep up with the latest climate and environment stories with the BBC's Justin Rowlatt. Outside the UK? Sign up to our international newsletter here.

noticias.titulo: Anti-austerity strike spurs transport chaos across Belgium
noticias.resumen: National strike against planned austerity causes widespread disruption, with government's fate hanging in the balance.
noticias.texto:
Anti-austerity strike spurs transport chaos across Belgium
National action against planned austerity measures causes widespread disruption, with government’s fate hanging in the balance.
Transport services across Belgium have been disrupted, with hundreds of flights and trains cancelled, as trade unions called a national strike to protest against the federal government’s austerity measures.
Monday’s walkout grounded planes across the country after air traffic controller Skeyes said it was unable to provide regular services at Belgian airports.
In a statement on its website, Brussels airport said that “unfortunately, all departing and arriving flights from 7am to 9pm local time (06:00-20:00 GMT) will have to be cancelled”.
Air traffic was also halted on Monday at Brussels’ Charleroi airport, which is used by low-cost airlines such as Ryanair.
The Board of Airline Representatives in Belgium, which represents about 25 carriers, said the strike would be the 11th affecting Belgian airspace in as many months.
The national strike has also caused disruption to buses, trains, schools, and other public services. Belgium has faced repeated cost-of-living protests and strikes in recent months, with much of the anger directed towards Prime Minister Bart De Wever and his attempts at cost-cutting.
The Belgian government is trying to save 10 billion euros ($10.9bn) in the coming years to reduce the country’s high deficit, but the issue is dividing the ruling coalition and threatens to collapse the government.
De Wever has already offered King Philippe his resignation, but the monarch refused to accept it, giving him more time to find a solution to the budget impasse. The prime minister has now set a new December 31   deadline for his government to reach an agreement on next year’s budget, after another week of talks ended without a result.
“Should we not have a budget agreement [before the end of the year], the government will effectively be unable to govern, thereby bringing its existence to an end”, De Wever’s office said in a statement.
The government is looking at spending cuts, notably in healthcare, and a VAT increase to bring down the deficit, but unions have been pushing for taxes on high earners to offset some of the cuts, as protests against rising living costs continue, not only in Belgium but across Europe.

noticias.titulo: COP31 has failed. The climate system is working as designed
noticias.resumen: The failure exposes a diplomacy that protects fossil-fuel power while leaving vulnerable countries to pay the price.
noticias.texto:
COP31 has failed. The climate system is working as designed
The collapse in Turkiye exposes a diplomacy that protects fossil-fuel power while leaving vulnerable countries to pay the price.
COP31 ended without an overarching agreement on Sunday in Antalya, Turkiye, after nearly 200 countries failed to agree on a final climate pact. The proposed text could not even name the principal cause of global warming: fossil fuels. The European Union, several Pacific island states and other governments rejected it, while oil-producing countries resisted stronger language. After three decades of annual summits, this was the first such breakdown since 2009.
It is tempting to call this an extraordinary diplomatic failure. But the collapse reveals something more enduring. Climate negotiations have become remarkably effective at keeping governments at the table while avoiding the economic changes that meaningful climate action requires. The system is not designed literally to produce no agreements; it is designed to accommodate interests powerful enough to prevent decisive ones.
Consider what happened in Antalya. The EU objected that the final draft did not even mention fossil fuels. Yet the omission was not a clerical oversight. Earlier language on moving away from oil, gas and coal had been weakened as negotiations proceeded. The summit could not agree on how to implement the agreement reached at COP28 in Dubai in 2023 to transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems. What should have been the starting point for action became the point at which diplomacy broke down.
The contradiction is built into the negotiating process. Under the Paris Agreement, governments determine their own emissions commitments, with no enforcement mechanism to compel a country to stop expanding fossil-fuel production. COP decisions also depend on consensus, giving determined holdouts considerable leverage. The result is an international forum in which the most reluctant participants can limit what everyone else is allowed to say, let alone do.
That does not mean all countries are equally responsible. Nor does it mean that every COP has achieved nothing. The Paris framework helped establish common goals, and climate summits have encouraged investment and cooperation. Antalya itself adopted limited decisions on other matters, including one on a just transition. But these gains cannot substitute for a credible timetable to wind down fossil-fuel extraction. The distinction matters: diplomatic activity is not the same as structural change.
Indeed, fossil-fuel power operates well beyond the conference hall. Producing states defend revenues and geopolitical influence, while consuming states continue to rely on cheap energy and established infrastructure. Even governments that speak forcefully about climate ambition face incentives to protect their own industries and voters from immediate costs. The global energy transition is therefore not simply a technological problem. It is a struggle over who must relinquish assets, profits and power.
This helps explain the appeal of technological promises. The failed Antalya draft promoted carbon-removal technologies to deal with warming beyond 1.5C, while disagreements also centred on carbon capture and storage. Such approaches may have limited roles in reducing or counterbalancing emissions from difficult-to-abate sectors. But when presented as substitutes for reducing extraction, they allow governments and corporations to promise that future machines will repair the damage of continued emissions. The political benefit is immediate; the promised atmospheric benefit remains uncertain.
The same structural inequality shapes climate finance. Countries that contributed least to historical warming face mounting costs from droughts, floods, displacement and adaptation. Yet the proposed $120bn adaptation target disappeared from the revised text and disputes over financial commitments helped sink the talks. Wealthy governments can celebrate climate ambition while leaving poorer countries to borrow, divert public spending or simply absorb losses.
This is precisely why climate finance cannot be treated as discretionary charity. It concerns responsibility for harms produced through an unequal world economy. Grants, predictable funding and meaningful decision-making power for affected countries are not extras to be negotiated after emissions targets. They are conditions of a transition that poorer countries can undertake without sacrificing education, healthcare and basic development.
There is also a danger in allowing the EU to emerge from Antalya as the uncomplicated defender of climate justice. Its refusal to accept a pact silent on fossil fuels was justified. But wealthy countries cannot demand ambitious language abroad while resisting the financial obligations and domestic changes that would give it substance. Conversely, some developing countries depend on fossil-fuel income or need affordable energy. A just phaseout must distinguish their circumstances from those of rich, historically high-emitting economies.
What would a different climate politics look like? It would begin with enforceable plans for ending new fossil-fuel expansion and phasing down production, with richer countries moving first and fastest. It would fund adaptation and loss and damage through reliable, primarily grant-based transfers rather than debt-creating loans. And it would give countries most vulnerable to climate change greater influence over the decisions that determine their futures.
None of this requires abandoning multilateralism. It requires refusing to confuse its survival with success. When consensus rules repeatedly protect the interests most responsible for the crisis, governments must also pursue complementary agreements, domestic regulation and coalitions willing to move faster. Otherwise, the promise of universal participation becomes a mechanism for universal delay.
The collapse of COP31 is a warning, not because climate diplomacy has suddenly stopped working, but because its limits have become impossible to disguise. The world does not lack knowledge of what causes warming. It lacks a political system willing to confront those who benefit from causing it. Until that changes, each summit will be judged by the agreements it produces, while the atmosphere registers the emissions it fails to prevent.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

noticias.titulo: Iran says it will use ‘all available means’ to counter US blockade
noticias.resumen: Ministry of Foreign Affairs says Iran will use all tools to confront the naval siege and defend itself.
noticias.texto:
Iran says it will use ‘all available means’ to counter US blockade
Ministry of Foreign Affairs says Iran will use all tools to confront the naval siege and defend itself.
Iran says it will use all means at its disposal to counter a United States naval blockade imposed during the nine-month US-Israel war on Iran.
The US blockade was imposed on April 13, lifted in June after Washington reached a draft understanding with Tehran, then restored on July 14 after the agreement collapsed.
“We will certainly not tolerate these actions and will use all available means to counter US aggression,” Iranian Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said at a news briefing on Monday.
“You should bear in mind that what the Americans have described as economic sanctions, an economic blockade and a naval blockade undoubtedly constitute an act of military aggression against Iran,” Baghaei said.
“Under these circumstances, Iran is entitled, pursuant to Article 51 of the UN Charter, to use any means at its disposal to defend itself.”
The war broke out on February 28 when the US and Israel carried out air strikes that killed Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and other senior officials.
The conflict has since expanded after Iran launched missile and drone attacks across the region and with armed groups it backs in Lebanon, Yemen and Iraq also entering the fray.
The Strait of Hormuz has become the focus of the conflict with Iran continuing in its efforts to block the waterway, which is vital for oil and natural gas shipments.
In an attempt to force Iran to halt efforts to block the strait, the US imposed a blockade on Iranian ports and later announced a series of economic sanctions and launched a task force to disrupt land routes into Iran.
Iranian forces have made multiple announcements in recent weeks that ships have caught fire while trying to use routes that Tehran considers off-limits.
TankerTrackers.com said last week that a tanker was loading Iranian crude oil in the Gulf via ship-to-ship transfer and could become the first vessel to successfully export the country’s crude since the US reimposed the blockade in July.
Baghaei said on Monday that reports about Iranian ships loading oil are “speculation”.
Visible Iranian crude exports decreased to near zero in recent months due to the blockade.
Al Jazeera’s Resul Serdar Atas, reporting from Tehran, said the US blockade is hurting Iran economically.
“Iranians are aware of that and they are publicly admitting it because more than 80 percent of the country’s imports and exports happen through the Strait of Hormuz or southern ports of the country,” he said.
“Iranians are now looking increasingly for options to put an end to the US naval blockade,” our correspondent said, adding that military action against US military assets around Iran is being discussed.
“Escalation is now the main option on the table,” he said.
Diplomatic efforts to resolve the war remain stalled, especially since the collapse of a June agreement that laid out a path to a permanent settlement.
Iran has said Hormuz could be open within two days if Washington meets its conditions, including halting hostilities, lifting the blockade and waiving sanctions.
“If the American side fulfils its commitments, security can be restored to the Strait of Hormuz and the region in the shortest possible time,” Baghaei said.

noticias.titulo: How the US, China and Russia are competing for Africa’s mineral wealth
noticias.resumen: The US, China and Russia are vying for Africa’s mineral wealth, raising questions about who stands to benefit.
noticias.texto:
How the US, China and Russia are competing for Africa’s mineral wealth
The US, China and Russia are vying for Africa’s mineral wealth, raising questions about who stands to benefit
From cobalt mines in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) to lithium deposits in Mali and uranium reserves in Niger, Africa’s mineral wealth is becoming an increasingly important arena of competition between the United States, China and Russia.
China dominates several critical mineral supply chains, while Russia has expanded its influence through security partnerships, particularly in the Sahel. The US, meanwhile, is seeking to secure access to strategic resources through diplomacy, investment and infrastructure projects.
The rivalry extends beyond mining to ports, railways and trade routes connecting Africa’s resources to global markets.
But as foreign powers compete for access, what do African countries stand to gain?
Why are global powers interested in Africa’s minerals?
Africa holds substantial deposits of cobalt, lithium, copper and uranium, resources vital to industries ranging from electric vehicles and renewable energy to advanced technology and defence.
For Washington, securing critical minerals has become a strategic priority amid concerns about dependence on China.
In February, President Donald Trump announced Project Vault, a $12bn initiative to establish a strategic mineral stockpile for US industries.
China has spent years investing in African mining, processing and infrastructure.
Trade between China and Africa reached a record $348bn last year, according to Chinese customs statistics, cementing Beijing’s position as the continent’s largest trading partner.
Russia’s economic footprint is considerably smaller. Moscow has instead relied heavily on military cooperation and security partnerships to expand its influence, particularly in countries that have distanced themselves from Western governments.
Its Africa Corps, established in 2023 under the Russian Ministry of Defence, has taken over much of the Wagner Group’s former operations on the continent.
Gold has also become strategically important to Moscow. A 2024 RAND Europe study commissioned by the United Kingdom’s Foreign Office identified the precious metal as a major feature of Russia’s engagement in Africa.
Why is the DRC central to the competition?
The DRC is the world’s largest producer of mined cobalt, accounting for an estimated 73 percent of global production in 2025, according to the US Geological Survey.
China has established a powerful position in the country’s mining industry, with Chinese companies owning or holding stakes in several major copper and cobalt operations.
Beijing also dominates global cobalt refining, giving it considerable influence over supply chains even when minerals are extracted elsewhere.
Washington is seeking to challenge that position.
Last December, the US and DRC signed a strategic partnership agreement aimed at expanding US access to critical minerals and supporting investment in infrastructure and processing.
Under the agreement, Kinshasa is to identify strategic mining assets and exploration areas, giving American and eligible partner investors rights of first offer on designated projects.
But securing agreements is different from developing mines and processing facilities.
This month, DRC Economy Minister Daniel Mukoko Samba urged Washington to translate the partnership into tangible investments, saying its success should be measured by completed projects rather than signed agreements.
Kinshasa wants investment to support domestic mineral processing, electricity access and economic development, rather than simply increasing raw material exports.
Why are transport corridors part of the rivalry?
Control over mineral supply chains depends not only on mines but also on the infrastructure needed to move resources to international markets.
China has made infrastructure investment central to its engagement with Africa through the Belt and Road Initiative, under which dozens of African countries have signed cooperation agreements.
The US, alongside European and African partners, is backing the Lobito Corridor, a transport network linking Angola’s Atlantic coast to the copper and cobalt-producing regions of the DRC, with a planned railway extension into Zambia.
The corridor is intended to provide a more efficient route for mineral exports while strengthening regional trade.
For Washington, it also offers an opportunity to diversify supply chains and reduce dependence on Chinese-dominated networks.
For African countries, the project could lower transport costs and attract investment. But its wider benefits will depend on whether it also supports local industries and communities.
Why is the Sahel another focus?
Mali and Niger possess significant deposits of lithium, gold and uranium, but political upheaval and armed group activity have complicated foreign investment.
Following military coups and deteriorating relations with Western governments, both countries strengthened security ties with Moscow, as did neighbouring Burkina Faso.
Russia deployed Africa Corps personnel across the region, consolidating its position as a security partner to military-led governments.
Washington is now seeking to rebuild relations.
In February, senior US State Department official Nick Checker visited Mali, signalling a desire to reset ties and reaffirming Washington’s respect for the country’s sovereignty.
The diplomatic outreach comes as foreign companies pursue opportunities in the region’s mining sector.
Mali produced an estimated 9,400 tonnes of lithium last year, according to the US Geological Survey, making it one of Africa’s leading producers.
Chinese interests are involved in the Goulamina lithium mine, while a subsidiary of Russia’s state nuclear corporation Rosatom secured an exploration licence for the Bougoula lithium project two years ago.
US commercial interests have also pursued opportunities in Mali’s gold sector.
In neighbouring Niger, uranium has become a focus of renewed US economic engagement following the withdrawal of US troops in 2024.
In September this year, the US International Development Finance Corporation approved financing of up to $414m for the Dasa uranium project, developed by Canadian mining company Global Atomic.
The financing remains subject to conditions, including securing a viable route to transport uranium from the landlocked country.
The project illustrates Washington’s efforts to rebuild economic ties even as Russia maintains a security presence in Niger.
What does Africa stand to gain?
For African governments, growing competition among foreign powers presents opportunities to attract investment, diversify partnerships and negotiate better terms for their mineral resources.
But it also carries risks.
Foreign ownership of mines and processing facilities can leave producing countries dependent on raw material exports, while insecurity, corruption and weak infrastructure can limit the benefits reaching local communities.
The challenge for African governments is to turn international interest into investment that creates jobs, expands domestic processing and strengthens local economies.
As Washington, Beijing and Moscow compete for Africa’s mineral wealth, the real test for African countries may be not which global power wins the race, but how much of the wealth they can retain.
