noticias.titulo: Inside the talks between student protest leaders and Macron’s government
noticias.resumen: Al Jazeera interviews two French student leaders who have met with top government officials as protests continue.
noticias.texto:
Inside the talks between student protest leaders and Macron’s government
Al Jazeera interviews two French student leaders who have met with top government officials as protests continue.
Paris, France – High school student Marius Mensil has participated in several meetings with top officials, including President Emmanuel Macron, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, and Education Minister Edouard Geffray, aimed at addressing the concerns of thousands of protesting students.
“They’re very good at listening to us. They welcome us, smile at us, tell us, ‘Yes, you’re right, your demands are legitimate’, and in the end, they do nothing,” the 17-year-old told co-leader of the French high-school students’ union, Union Syndicale Lyceenne (USL), told Al Jazeera.
Held in government offices in Paris, the meetings have, on occasion, lasted as long as two hours, he said.
“With Geffray, it was mainly an exchange of arguments. We’d present our demands to him, and then he’d try to explain why they weren’t feasible,” said Mensil. “He used very technical language to try to confuse us. Macron and Lecornu were much more attentive. They took notes, smiled and gave us winks – in short, they did everything they could to show us that our demands were being heard. All of this, of course, was just a way to avoid making any concrete commitments.”
The student movement first began at high schools in the overseas territory of Mayotte. Then it moved to mainland France, with a high school in Creteil, a suburb southeast of Paris in the Val-de-Marne region, on September 17. Protests quickly spread to neighbouring Saint-Denis and the rest of France, and were joined by groups with other grievances.
For two months, students have blocked their schools’ entrances and taken to the streets, demanding an overhaul of the education system.
“It’s been clear ever since Macron took office – and even before – that conditions have deteriorated year after year. With every budget, there are fewer teachers. There are cuts to local governments, who manage school facilities,” Mesnil told Al Jazeera. “We’re not asking for five-star restaurants, MacBooks, or castles… We’re asking for enough teachers, buildings where the ceilings aren’t falling on our heads and class schedules adapted to our biological rhythms.
“We’re asking that, once we’ve earned our high school diploma, we can study at university.”
In response to the protests, officials invited high school students to voice their concerns. Since late October, representatives have attended several meetings, but despite some concessions, students say their demands remain unmet.
A key demand is to entirely reconstruct Parcoursup, the university admissions programme. Students claim the system is discriminatory and lacks transparency, with rejected students saying they are unable to find out why they were not accepted. The system and some degree programmes also value the academic standing of an applicant’s high school, meaning top students in disadvantaged areas may be overlooked.
They are also calling for an emergency plan to renovate failing school infrastructure. Some student groups and unions also want more teachers on permanent contracts and an additional 10 billion euros ($11bn) devoted to education.
In response to the protests, the government recruited 920 substitute teachers in early October and plans to hire 3,000 more. Next year’s budget includes an increase to cover more substitute hours for each high school.
The government also agreed to commit 1 billion euros ($1.1bn) per year through 2030 to building renovations, and to offer more opportunities for high school representatives to participate in national education discussions.
When contacted by Al Jazeera, the Ministry of Education responded with a statement that Geffray and the minister of higher education, research and space, Philippe Baptiste, sent to students on October 26.
In that statement, the education minister promised to cap class sizes at 28 students at the start of the next academic year in 2027 at “the most disadvantaged schools”, and reduce specialised course sizes. Although some high school students are still calling for Parcoursup to be abolished, the government has agreed to update the controversial platform “to help you plan your academic path with greater peace of mind”.
“Some measures will be implemented very quickly, while others will be included in the 2027 budget bill, which will be introduced in the coming weeks,” Geffray said.
Mesnil called the measures “a few crumbs”, but believes the concessions show that the student movement is making waves.
“The government is starting to give in,” he said. “Gen Z, together with the workers, have forced Macron to back down on some initial points, and we’re very happy about that.”
Beyond meetings, the government opened “High school students, the floor is yours”, a consultation platform for students to submit their opinions and complaints. More than 100,000 submissions were sent in during the 18 days it was open, starting on October 6. About 70 percent said the current school system is “ill-suited to their needs”, citing days that are too long and intense, with poorly structured schedules.
Many French high school students are in class from 8am to 6pm, with few breaks and heavy homework on top of the course load.
More than half of respondents, 56.3 percent, said buildings were dilapidated, improperly insulated and poorly equipped. Participating students also cited absent teachers, class sizes, the Parscoursup platform and negative mental health effects.
Students in disadvantaged areas say conditions are even worse in their suburbs.
Bilal Narjissi, 17, from the Paul-Eluard school in Saint-Denis and a member of the Renouveau Lyceen student union, took part in recent meetings with government officials and said they do not include many students from less advantaged schools.
“In schools in the suburbs and in rural areas, roofs have collapsed, there are water leaks, rats, and classes with 30 students,” he said. “Young people today are pushed to pursue higher education, but they aren’t given the means to succeed.”
Narjissi has invited a special adviser to the prime minister to visit Paul Eluard.
“It would be truly symbolic if he were to come by and we could take him on a tour of the high school, show him the conditions there, and talk to him,” Narjissi said.
Narjissi described the first meeting with officials he attended as “very relaxed”, saying they seemed “very open to dialogue”.
But he added that the economy, education and labour ministries “were quite firm in their positions – for example, on reforming the baccalaureate,” Narjissi said, referring to the final high school exam.
The 2018 high school reforms by former Education Minister Jean-Michel Blanquer introduced “more subject concentrations, shortened the final exam, and placed greater emphasis on grades”, according to Rafaela Uzan, research associate for Europe studies at the Council on Foreign Relations. “But critics argue the abundance of concentration options exacerbated social stratification and made school days longer,” she wrote in a recent paper.
Narjissi said the exchange with officials “was still fairly constructive”, but he is unsure if the students are really being heard “because, so far, there still aren’t any real, concrete responses to our expectations”.
Until they receive those, students say they will continue to protest.
“We’ve managed to establish a balance of power through our mobilisation,” he said.
Student representatives were scheduled to meet with the prime minister again on Monday.
“We hope there will be announcements that live up to our expectations. We’re happy to attend these meetings, but if it’s just to talk and, ultimately, there are no concrete political results, then there’s no point,” Mesnil said.

noticias.resumen: Iceland’s former PM warns climate change remains an existential threat as global power politics sidelines action.

Talk to Al Jazeera
Former Icelandic PM says world’s great powers are flexing their muscles
Iceland’s former prime minister warns climate change remains an existential threat as global power politics sidelines action.
Iceland’s former prime minister says that although climate change has fallen lower down on the international political agenda, it remains an existential crisis.
Katrin Jakobsdottir says our warming world is not just a catastrophe for nature, but a health and security emergency that cannot be ignored.
Her country is on the front lines of that emergency, with the Arctic warming at four times the rate of the rest of the world.
Almost all of Iceland’s glaciers are rapidly retreating – one was declared “dead” in 2019.
Jakobsdottir says it all comes at a time when the world’s biggest powers are flexing their muscles – and the politics of compromise are being squeezed out.

noticias.titulo: COP31: What next after UN climate talks collapse
noticias.resumen: UN member states fail to agree on how to fast-track action to reverse global warming in a blow to climate agenda.
noticias.texto:
COP31: What next after UN climate talks collapse
UN member states fail to agree on how to fast-track action to reverse global warming in blow to climate agenda.
United Nations climate talks have ended in collapse after countries deadlocked over the phasing out of planet-warming fossil fuels, aiding energy transition for developing countries and the response to natural disasters.
Known as COP31, the conference in Antalya, Turkiye, ended on Sunday as the European Union and others rejected a final deal they said was too weak to advance the fight against global warming.
The longest UN climate summit on record brought to the fore the divide between major polluters driving climate change and smaller nations bearing the brunt of its impact, after a year of climate-linked disasters from Europe to Asia.
It also laid bare the world’s inability to keep the Paris Agreement pledge to limit global warming to the 1.5C (2.7F) mark, which scientists expect to overshoot in a few years.
So what’s next for the fraught UN process and what else can nations do to deliver promises that have too often missed their target?
Why did COP31 collapse?
The 11-day-long negotiations that began on November 9 were stalled after oil-producing states blocked any mention of phasing out fossil fuels in the final deal put forward by the president of COP31, Turkiye, and main negotiator Australia.
Saudi Arabia and fellow members of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) opposed any mention of a fossil fuel phase-out, while insisting instead on carbon capture, the technology criticised as costly and ineffective.
Cosima Cassel, programme lead in Climate Diplomacy and Geopolitics at environmental think tank E3G, said petrostates attempted to slow momentum on the energy transition “following the disruption of the Strait of Hormuz and the projected decline in their incomes as global demand for fossil fuels falls”.
The European Union and several nations particularly vulnerable to climate change said they could not accept a text that failed to mention the main driver of global warming.
The revised text of a deal that emerged early on Sunday was angrily rejected after some 130 nations sent a letter to the presidency stating that a deal would have to mention a path for transitioning away from fossil fuels.
On the contrary, the text made no mention of fossil fuels while promoting carbon capture.
“A small group of blockers set the outcome against the clear position of a large majority,” Cassel told Al Jazeera. “These dynamics raise questions about the role of oil and gas exporters in undermining the only forum where vulnerable countries get to advance their concerns.”
Crucially for developing countries, there was also no progress on the funds needed to help them transition their energy systems and respond to natural disasters.
Under the 2015 Paris Agreement, developed countries are required to provide financial support to developing nations. However, the US-Israeli war on Iran and Russia’s war on Ukraine strained national budgets, leaving wealthy nations unwilling to commit trillions of dollars in climate finance.
Sebastien Duyck, senior attorney at the Center for International Environmental Law (CIEL), said wealthy developed countries, which denounced the obstruction by fossil fuel-producing nations, showed “considerable hypocrisy”.
“You cannot demand a just transition from others while failing to pay your fair share of its costs,” Duyck told Al Jazeera. “We need less finger-pointing and political theatre and more accountability. All major economies, particularly the wealthiest, must deliver on their existing legal obligations and climate finance commitments ahead of COP32.”
What’s next for the UN process – and for the planet?
The collapse of the climate talks in Turkiye has renewed questions about reform of its consensus-based process, centred around the principle that all countries must agree to the reforms.
The commitment to moving away from fossil fuels – including natural gas, coal and crude oil – was considered a landmark achievement of COP28 in Dubai, United Arab Emirates. But even then, the deal stopped short of calling for a “phase-out”, amid fierce lobbying from oil-producing countries.
Amid concern that fossil fuel producers wield more power than those who want to accelerate the transition to a low-carbon world, many believe the COP process remains important as a platform that brings together virtually every country in the world.
“The UN process remains the only forum where every country has a voice and a chance to shape outcomes and it is worth protecting and fighting for,” said E3G’s Cassel.
However, calls for reform are multiplying and a second tier of COPs – the Global Climate Action Agenda – is rising in prominence. Often called just the Action Agenda, the voluntary implementation pillar of the UN Climate Change process is bringing in real-world actors such as financial institutions, cities, regions, businesses and civil society on a voluntary basis.
“That spirit of collaboration stands in stark contrast to the adversarial dynamics that too often dominate the formal negotiations,” Cassel said.
Other routes are also being pursued. An International Court of Justice advisory opinion last year confirmed that states have a binding legal obligation to combat climate change. In April, the Santa Marta initiative convened 57 countries to promote non-binding cooperation around fossil fuel phase-out.
Duyck, at CIEL, said “the failure of governments to agree at this conference does not make the science any less clear or their legal obligations any less binding.” “A fair and orderly transition away from fossil fuels remains both an imperative and a collective responsibility,” he added.
The UN Environment Programme last year said the world would exceed the 1.5C (2.7F) mark – the internationally agreed-upon target set under the Paris Agreement – “very likely” within the next decade.
Without any meaningful action, the planet will warm 2.3 to 2.5C (4.1 to 4.5F) by 2100, the report said.
Joeri Rogelj, professor of climate science and Policy at Imperial College London, said a starting point would have been to renew commitments made at COP28 in Dubai, where nations had agreed to transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems, triple renewable energy capacity globally and double the global average annual rate of energy efficiency improvements by 2030.
Instead, “even simply echoing these agreed outcomes was politically too challenging for some countries with strong vested interests in fossil fuels,” he told Al Jazeera.
“The commitments needed are clear: global greenhouse gas emissions must decline to slow the rate of global warming,” Rogelj told Al Jazeera.
“This failure risks further delaying meaningful global emissions reductions, with the poorest and most vulnerable countries and communities bearing the greatest consequences.”

noticias.titulo: Ukraine claims drone strikes on Russian ships off Libya: What do we know?
noticias.resumen: Drone strikes on two Russian vessels near Libyan coast fuels fears of Ukraine war's spread.
noticias.texto:
Ukraine claims drone strikes on Russian ships off Libya: What do we know?
Drone strikes on two Russian vessels near Libyan coast fuels fears of Ukraine war’s spread.
Ukraine has claimed responsibility for sinking a Russian warship and striking a cargo vessel off Libya’s coast, raising concerns about the Russia-Ukraine war widening geographically.
“It all took place off the coast of Libya. Our warriors deployed seven Ukrainian-made naval drones,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a post on X on Monday.
The attack targeted the Russian corvette Merkury and the cargo vessel MV Angara, which Zelenskyy said was used to transport weapons.
The attacks come amid an intensifying Ukrainian campaign targeting Russian naval assets, energy infrastructure and vessels linked to Moscow’s so-called shadow fleet, which helps Russia circumvent Western sanctions.
The developments have also raised questions about the involvement of foreign powers in a divided Libya, and the risk of drawing other nations into the conflict, nearly five years after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Here is what we know about the attacks, who may be behind them and what they mean for the expanding reach of the war.
What do we know about the attacks?
The Russian Navy’s Merkury was struck at the Benghazi naval base in eastern Libya on Sunday, triggering an explosion and fire.
Satellite imagery showed most of the corvette had capsized and sunk, with only its bow visible above water.
Zelenskyy confirmed the sinking on Monday, saying a Russian Kamov Ka-27 military helicopter was also destroyed.
“Our second target was the Russian dry cargo vessel MV ANGARA, which the enemy used to transport weapons. Result: target hit,” he added.
A day earlier, the Russian cargo ship Sparta II was struck by drones in the Gulf of Finland. The vessel caught fire and drifted into Finnish waters. All 16 crew members were evacuated, with one slightly injured.
In Finland, the military assessed the vessel was likely struck by Ukraine. Russian authorities said two drones hit the Sparta II in international waters. Kyiv has not publicly claimed responsibility for Sunday’s attack.
Zelenskyy said his country would continue to launch operations in designated maritime areas in response to Russia’s aggression.
Kyiv’s attacks come as Russia has intensified its air attacks across Ukraine, using ballistic missiles, drones and guided bombs. Energy facilities, bridges, Black Sea ports and other civilian infrastructure have been targeted in Ukraine, which has countered with attacks on Russian energy sites and other targets.
What have Libya and Russia said?
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov described Ukraine’s attacks off the coast of Libya, as well as the targeting of Russian cargo vessels in the Baltic Sea, as a “very dangerous trend”.
Peskov warned Ukraine of “painful” consequences. “The Defence Ministry is dealing with this matter, and information will also be provided through the Defence Ministry if deemed appropriate,” he said.
Libya’s eastern administration condemned the attack as a violation of its sovereignty and said it had requested an international investigation through the United Nations.
“The Libyan government will not allow Libyan ports, territory or territorial waters to be turned into an arena for settling scores or exporting international conflicts,” it said.
Saddam Haftar, son of renegade military commander Khalifa Haftar, said Libya’s security and sovereignty are a “national responsibility that cannot tolerate political posturing or the exploitation of incidents to promote accusations and stir up fears”.
“Rather, it requires prioritising the national interest and dealing responsibly with everything that affects our country’s security and stability,” he said in a statement on Facebook.
The rival UN-recognised government in Tripoli also commented on the incident, saying it was concerned by “risks posed by involving civilian ports and facilities in activities linked to external conflicts”.
Meanwhile, the UN has called for an independent investigation into Sunday’s drone attacks.
On Monday, the UN Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL) expressed “serious concern” over the attacks, calling for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation”.
“Libya cannot afford and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts,” UNSMIL wrote in a post on X.
The oil-rich nation has been divided between the government in Tripoli and a rival administration in the east since the overthrow of longtime ruler Muammar Gaddafi in 2011.
In September, Libya denied reports by CNN that it allowed Ukraine to use a military base in the northwest of the country to launch drones against vessels from Russia’s “shadow fleet” in the Mediterranean.
The origin of Sunday’s attack is still not confirmed.
How many Russian vessels have been attacked in recent weeks?
At least four Russian vessels have reportedly been targeted in November, including the Merkury, MV Angara and Sparta II.
The Finnish military also reported detecting a strike on a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland in the Baltic Sea during Ukrainian drone attacks the previous week.
In March, a Russian LNG tanker sank off Libya’s coast following an attack Moscow blamed on Ukraine.
In December 2025, Ukraine claimed responsibility for striking a Russian-linked oil tanker in the Mediterranean.
Is the Ukraine-Russia war expanding geographically?
Academic Alexey D Muraviev says the conflict has already expanded beyond Ukraine.
“The Mediterranean has firmly become an external theatre of operations, particularly maritime operations,” Muraviev, senior research fellow in defence and strategic studies at Edith Cowan University, told Al Jazeera.
He said the vessels targeted in Libyan and Finnish territories were likely involved in transporting military equipment or other supplies to Africa, potentially supporting Russia’s Africa Corps, which operates alongside Moscow-aligned governments.
Muraviev said Ukrainian forces had previously confronted Russian security personnel in Africa, demonstrating that the conflict had already extended beyond its original battlefield.
“Even in this sense, there have been cases when the war in Ukraine effectively extended onto the African continent,” he said.
The sinking of the Merkury, commissioned in 2023, would also weaken Russia’s naval capabilities, Muraviev said.
However, the academic warned that the Gulf of Finland was particularly sensitive because of its geography and the proximity of Russian and NATO forces.
“In my personal view, it is an area where a possible clash between Russia and NATO is quite possible,” he said.
Muraviev added that the attacks could have wider implications for global shipping, which is already facing heightened security threats around the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb.
“[The attacks] just add additional risks to marine operators from across the world,” he said.

noticias.titulo: CAS decision on Senegal’s AFCON 2025 title appeal on Tuesday
noticias.resumen: Senegal are contesting CAF's decision to declare Morocco champions, despite Senegal winning the final 1-0 in January.
noticias.texto:
CAS decision on Senegal’s AFCON 2025 title appeal on Tuesday
Senegal are contesting CAF’s decision to declare Morocco champions, despite Senegal winning the final 1-0 in January.
The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) will release its decision on Senegal’s appeal against being stripped of this year’s Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) title on Tuesday.
Senegal are contesting the decision of the Confederation of African Football (CAF) to declare Morocco champions, despite Senegal beating the hosts 1-0 in extra time in January’s final in Rabat, and the outcome will be announced on Tuesday, the court confirmed on Monday.
It did not give a time for the announcement.
CAS heard the arguments of Senegal, Morocco and CAF in Lausanne in early October.
It had initially promised a decision within days of the hearing on October 8 but then decided to issue a complete ruling, including legal grounds, known as a CAS Award. That process requires several weeks.
CAS Awards hold the same value as a national court judgement, enforceable in accordance with the New York Convention on the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral Awards. Awards may be enforced by sports federations or state courts, depending on the circumstances.
In the final, Senegal walked off the pitch for 14 minutes after a penalty was awarded against them late in regulation time, with several players returning to the dressing room in protest before they resumed play.
Morocco missed the spot kick, sending the match into extra time, where Senegal scored the winner to secure victory.
However, they were stripped of the title two months later after CAF’s Appeal Board ruled that Senegal had forfeited the match by walking off the pitch, overturning the result and awarding a 3-0 victory to Morocco.
Senegal appealed the CAF ruling to sport’s highest court, CAS, on March 25, but it was heard some six months later. The basis of its arguments is that the referee’s decision is final and he allowed the match to be completed.
The CAS panel is presided over by French sports law expert Gerald Simon, with assistance from Italian international law professor Luigi Fumagalli and Hamburg-based lawyer and professor of law at the University of Zurich, Ulrich Haas.

noticias.titulo: Why is Bangladesh’s Grameen Bank under attack?
noticias.resumen: Leading financial institution has found itself at centre of tensions amid violence by Sheikh Hasina supporters.
noticias.texto:
Why is Bangladesh’s Grameen Bank under attack?
One of Bangladesh’s best-known financial institutions has found itself at centre of political tensions amid protests and violence by supporters of ousted PM Sheikh Hasina.
Dhaka, Bangladesh – When attackers stormed a Grameen Bank branch in Kashiani last week, they did not just damage furniture and equipment. They also destroyed records accumulated over nearly three decades.
Solaiman Morol, the branch manager in Bangladesh’s Gopalganj district, said about a dozen men arrived on the afternoon of November 18 carrying machetes, petrol and tools to break the locks. Staff members were away on field visits.
The attackers looted the branch and tried to cut open its vault with a grinder. They took out about 40 sacks of vouchers and other documents and set them on fire. They also looted steel cupboards, filing cabinets, chairs, tables and other equipment. A staff member’s rice cooker was among the items taken away. “They said that after burning the records, nobody would have to repay their loans,” Morol said.
Videos of the attack later appeared online. Morol said he heard slogans including “Joy Bangla” and “Joy Bangabandhu”, associated with ousted former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina’s Awami League, as well as calls to burn what the attackers described as “Yunus’s den”.
The branch has not been able to resume normal operations. Staff members have received threats and customers are worried about the safety of their deposits and loan records.
“A bank depends on trust. This is impacting our customers’ confidence. People who have deposits with us are becoming frightened,” Morol said.
It wasn’t a one-off incident.
Grameen Bank under attack
The attack was part of a wider wave of violence against Grameen Bank. Its latest internal memorandum, dated November 23, records 97 attacks on branches and offices between November 10 and 23.
The attacks have put the Nobel Prize-winning institution founded by Muhammad Yunus at the centre of Bangladesh’s political tensions, months after he stepped down as chief adviser following Hasina’s removal from power in August 2024. Hasina supporters set fire to police stations and the homes of local MPs, and allegedly killed three BNP members in Faridpur and Narail.
In a statement on Monday, Yunus called “the systematic assault” on Grameen Bank “unbelievably shocking”, noting that bank officials and borrower-members “narrowly escaped fatal injury” in several incidents.
Grameen Bank is one of Bangladesh’s best-known financial institutions. It pioneered a model of microcredit that provides small loans to people who often cannot access conventional banking services.
About 90 percent of its ownership belongs to its borrower-members, while the government holds the remaining 10 percent. It has around 10.6 million members, most of them rural women, according to its managing director, Sarder Akhter Hamed. Around 5.5 million borrowers have outstanding loans worth more than Tk19,000 crore ($1.53bn). Members also hold deposits of around Tk25,000 crore ($2bn) with the bank.
“There are many people in the communities we serve whom other banks and financial institutions are unwilling to lend to. We stand beside them and provide access to credit,” Hamed said.
The attacks have disrupted the bank’s work and left staff members worried about their safety. Hamed said the institution has around 21,000 employees and that the violence had affected them psychologically. “There is a sense of insecurity,” he said.
Is the Awami League targeting Grameen Bank – and why?
The government has blamed the Awami League, the party of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, for the attacks.
“The government is making every effort to maintain law and order,” Ziauddin Ahmed, additional secretary in charge of the political wing at the Ministry of Home Affairs, told Al Jazeera.
The attacks come amid renewed political activity by Hasina’s supporters, which has led to serious unrest in parts of the country, for example Gopalganj, her ancestral district. Hasina supporters have set fire to police stations and the homes of local MPs, and allegedly killed three BNP members.
Political analysts say Grameen Bank has become a symbol through which some Awami League supporters can direct their anger at Yunus, under whose interim rule Hasina’s party was banned from electoral politics. During Yunus’s stint as Bangladesh’s leader, Hasina was also convicted by a tribunal for massacres carried out against protesters who challenged her rule in 2024. Hasina faces a death sentence, but has recently asserted that she intends to return to Bangladesh from India, where she has lived in exile since she was ousted.
Mubashar Hasan, a researcher at the humanitarian and development research initiative at Western Sydney University, said the timing was significant.
“Her party has spent the week pushing for her return. Grameen Bank is the easiest symbol of Dr Yunus they can reach,” he said. “For the Awami League’s hardliners, Yunus is the face of their fall, so burning his bank is a way of hitting back at him.”
The attacks, Hasan argued, may also be intended to demonstrate that the party still has a presence on the streets, despite the ban. “Some of these attacks look like a performance of strength, especially in Gopalganj, to tell supporters ‘we are still here’,” he said.
Asif Mohammad Shahan, a professor in the department of development studies at the University of Dhaka, sees the violence as part of a broader political strategy.
He said the Awami League had two possible routes after the August 2024 uprising: acknowledge its mistakes and seek political rehabilitation, or try to force its way back into politics. In his assessment, the party has chosen the latter.
“The attack on Grameen Bank is actually an effort of sending a message of ‘politics of revenge’,” Shahan said.
He said the attacks could also be intended to provoke the government into a heavy-handed response, allowing the party to portray itself as a victim and challenge the government’s legitimacy.
Why is Grameen Bank particularly vulnerable, and who is paying the price?
The bank’s ownership structure makes the attacks especially consequential. Most of its shares belong to the poor women who depend on it for loans, savings and other financial services.
“When a branch burns, it’s their loan files, savings records and repayment schedules going up in smoke,” Hasan of Western Sydney University said.
He warned that disruption could push borrowers towards informal lenders and make it harder for them to continue their repayment cycles.
The damage is already affecting the bank’s operations. Hamed, the Grameen Bank managing director, said the institution had suspended the accrual of interest on outstanding loans at branches unable to operate because of the attacks.
The bank is also trying to protect its staff and property. Some branches have increased security and moved staff from locations considered particularly risky.
But the consequences extend beyond damaged buildings and lost records: At stake is also the confidence of customers in the bank.
Why is the BNP government struggling to stop the attacks?
The attacks have also raised questions about the ability of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s government to maintain law and order.
Ahmed, the Home Ministry official, said “it would be wrong to say that the government is struggling to contain the situation”. Police headquarters told Al Jazeera that eight cases had been filed and eight people arrested in connection with the attacks. “The problem is that our police force is somewhat short of manpower,” Ahmed said.
Shahan said the government’s response was being constrained by the knowledge that a tough crackdown could give the Awami League the chance to play victim. “The Awami League is baiting the government into attacking it so that it can quickly switch to playing the victim and try to delegitimise the government,” he said.
Hamed said police had responded whenever the bank sought help and in some cases had provided advance warnings about possible attacks. “For the most part, however, we have had to remain alert and protect ourselves,” he said.
“If the law-and-order situation in the country improves, confidence and trust [in the bank, too] will automatically return,” he said.

noticias.titulo: Occupied West Bank ‘military zones’ become de facto Israeli settler land
noticias.resumen: Closed military zones in the occupied West Bank are being seized by settlers as staging posts for pogroms.
noticias.texto:
Occupied West Bank ‘military zones’ become de facto Israeli settler land
Closed military zones in the occupied West Bank are being seized by settlers and made into staging posts for pogroms against Palestinians.
Ramallah, Occupied West Bank – Saleh Zahran had a room on his family’s land with a television, a fireplace, a fridge and solar panels. The kids would play in the groves, and the men stayed up late at night watching the stars.
“We’d cook, eat, drink, spend a whole day from morning to sunset,” he says.
Zahran, 39, inherited the farmland, with 120 olive trees, in Deir Abu Mishal, a village west of Ramallah, from his grandfather and father, splitting it among his brothers.
Between 70 and 80 percent of people in the village, which falls in Area B, under joint Israeli-Palestinian control, live off the land, and just a few years ago, there were no settlers nearby.
“We’d come and go whenever we wanted, pick our fruit at our own pace, sell, build, and marry off sons from the olives. Now, it’s all gone,” he told Al Jazeera.
Since settlers set up an outpost in Area B about 1km from his land in June, nobody in his family had been able to reach it. Settlers attacked their cars, and his elderly father was pepper-sprayed while trying to reach the farmland, he says.
On November 10, an Israeli High Court decision granted the village two days of army “coordinated” harvesting, something once unthinkable in Area B.
Zahran set out with his brothers to reach their lands for the first time in five months, but about 20 settlers came at them. They threw stones, smashed the family’s truck and his brother’s four-wheeler and slashed the tyres. He saw no soldiers, and police never arrived despite their calls.
The next day, the army and its liaison office were present. But farmers were held up until about 9am, shown a map of permitted areas, and told to leave by 2:30pm. Ghiyath Nasser, their lawyer, says villagers could reach less than a third of the area in question, so Zahran could harvest only about 20 of his 120 trees.
After five months, Zahran finally reached the farm room that day only to find settlers had stolen or smashed his belongings and were drawing water for their sheep from the two wells he had restored. The saplings he had planted last year had died of thirst.
On paper, it is the settlers who are barred from the Zahran family’s property and the land around Deir Abu Mishal. But in practice, it is Palestinian owners like Zahran who are kept out.
Nasser says that after his first legal petition, the army twice demolished the outpost – which was immediately rebuilt both times – then declared the site a closed military zone for Israelis only. That, Nasser argues, means soldiers cannot demand permits or “coordination” from Palestinian owners – their job is to keep settlers out.
“Sometimes they declare an area closed to settlers, but in the application they close it to Palestinians,” said Wail Qut, a lawyer with the Jerusalem Legal Aid and Human Rights Center (JLAC), who is from Madama, south of Nablus.
Kerem Navot and Peace Now’s July report found that, at the end of 2025, farm outposts effectively controlled more than 1 million dunams (247,105.4 acres), about 18 percent of the West Bank — roughly 750,000 dunams (185,329 acres) taken since late 2022.
‘A de facto closure’
In Madama, closures came first, and the outposts followed. Qut says its northern land was never declared a closed military zone, but the effect was the same.
About five years ago, the army gated the road from the village to Nablus, citing security concerns, he says. It was the only access to as much as a third of Madama’s land. The Israeli High Court dismissed the villagers’ petition after the army said farmers could reach the land on foot or by animal and apply for permits.
“It’s a de facto closure, though,” said Qut, with farmers still barred from entering.
Then, last April, an outpost of what Qut estimates are now 10 caravans appeared inside the closed area. He said the army suddenly reopened the gate for the settlers to use. Qut and his brother were stopped by a settler in the same area when they tried to pick olives there this year, forcing them to leave under armed threat.
Dror Etkes, founder of Kerem Navot, which tracks settler land takeovers, says such closures without orders are common across the occupied West Bank. “There is no vacuum in the West Bank,” he said. “Once an area is closed to Palestinian access, settlers sooner or later will come and take it over, and this is exactly what happened in Madama.”
But Qut finds the courts complicit too. When JLAC petitioned over the outpost north of Madama in September, the court gave the state until May 2027 to respond, rather than a few days, as Qut expected.
‘On the pretext of I don’t know what’
On November 13, a wedding was due to take place in al-Mughayyir, located at the northeastern edge of the Ramallah governorate. “Despite the pain and the suffering, people rejoice,” said Samir Abu Alia, 60, a village council member whose cousin’s son, Hassan Abu Alia, 30, was the groom. But soldiers violently cut the festivities short.
“The moment the patrols came down, they surrounded the hall, 20 army jeeps, and started throwing stun grenades between the men and the women,” recalled Abu Alia. Soldiers took the groom and relatives away from his bride for two hours. Abu Alia and others say the groom was beaten.
It began earlier that day on the eastern plain, when a settler grazing his flock inside a closed military zone claimed someone from al-Mughayyir had thrown firecrackers or shot at him, although he was unhurt. Soldiers accepted the settler’s claim at face value and then sealed and raided the village. The army quickly targeted the wedding, claiming there were gunshots and firecrackers, which attendees deny.
About 80 percent of al-Mughayyir’s 43,000 dunams (10,625.5 acres) lies beyond its eastern entrance, closed for years. Abu Alia says villagers can now move freely in only about 900 dunams (222.4 acres). “The rest of the land they’ve taken over, they stop people from reaching it, on the pretext of a military zone, on the pretext of security, on the pretext of I don’t know what.”
Here, the outpost came first. Village council member Marzouq Abu Naim says the first outpost on the eastern plain appeared in 2018 and has grown from 200 dunams to 5,000 dunams. He counts a dozen around the village. “One of the settlers comes, brings a tent, pitches it on a hilltop … the second day, the third day, you find there’s facilitation, something not normal: [authorities] run him water, they run him electricity, they lay a road to this tent,” he said.
According to Abu Naim, when villagers tried to use the eastern entrance about two months ago, settlers attacked and tried to burn cars and tractors, and the army did nothing to intervene.
Abu Naim, whose son, Jihad, 32, was shot dead by a settler during an invasion of the village school in April, also lost a 10-dunam grove of about 250 olive trees. “It wasn’t me who planted them, or my father — our grandfathers planted them.”
In August 2025, after a shooting wounded an Israeli teenager, the army ordered olive trees beside a settler road through the plain cleared as a “security threat”, and settlers joined in. Locals say more than 10,000 trees were eventually uprooted, including 230 belonging to Abu Alia.
Documents from the Israeli NGO Yesh Din show the area was closed for 30 days to “preserve the aims of the clearing”. Renewed in October 2025, the order extended to July 2026 with redrawn boundaries, and again through December.
The order bars everyone without a permit, settlers included. But Yesh Din’s legal objection says it is enforced only against the owners, while settlers graze, plough and build on their plots. When the army’s legal adviser declined to enforce the closure against settlers, he referred Yesh Din to the Israeli Defence Ministry’s legal adviser instead, which the NGO says was an effort to absolve the army of responsibility.
Lior Zur, a Yesh Din lawyer representing the petitioners, told Al Jazeera, “Through this policy of selective enforcement, the military turns closure orders into a mechanism for transferring possession of land from its lawful Palestinian owners to settler trespassers.”
The ‘height of injustice’
The pattern runs across the West Bank. In March, a closed zone around Duma was enforced against Israeli solidarity activists protecting Bedouin families, rather than settlers; after soldiers removed the activists, settlers invaded the encampment, forcibly displacing the community the next day.
In Burin, farmland sits in closed zones renewed every month or two; settlers have gutted five greenhouses in these closed zones already. In Taybeh, an August order barred Israelis and foreigners, but settlers and outposts remained, including one near the edge of Area B that led to another unevenly enforced closed zone.
Similar cases have occurred in Ein al-Duyuk, Qusra, Umm al-Khair and elsewhere. In closed and firing zones the Israeli army has not used for decades, Etkes said, settlers are “filling in”, even though the orders formally apply to settlers, too.
The result, this olive harvest season, has been unprecedented levels of violence and access restrictions. The United Nations Humanitarian Country Team for the occupied Palestinian territory said on November 20 that more than 400 settler attacks that caused casualties or damage had been recorded since September, more than in any previous season. The infrequent “coordination” access windows, it said, are often followed by “cancellations, denial of entry, expulsion or attacks”.
“What started as local initiative has been adopted by the military and is today, maybe not a declared policy, but an implemented policy,” said Etkes. The outposts are “not legal, but they are completely supported by the military, by the government, without officialising it”. The Israeli Civil Administration has leased large areas of the West Bank to settlers for grazing, which they never do for Palestinians, Qut said.
“Military closed-zone orders and settler takeovers of Palestinian land are two complementary practices,” said Yair Dvir, spokesperson for Israeli NGO B’Tselem. “The military uses these orders to drive Palestinians off their land, while settlers are frequently allowed to remain or establish outposts.”
Back in Deir Abu Mishal, olives are rotting on trees as the season ends. Zahran’s three young children ask why they cannot return to the farm room for barbecues and the olive harvest. He tells them it is too dangerous. “Four or five settlers stop a whole village, 5,000-6,000 people, from going to the land,” Zahran said. “We are living the height of injustice.”

noticias.titulo: At least 15 killed in Ukraine’s Kyiv region as Russia intensifies attacks
noticias.resumen: Mulitple strikes unleashed days after Putin promises a ‘painful’ response to Ukrainian attacks.
noticias.texto:
At least 15 killed in Ukraine’s Kyiv region as Russia intensifies attacks
At least 15 people are killed in multiple attacks, days after Russian President Putin promises a ‘painful’ response to Ukrainian attacks.
Rescuers in Ukraine have raced to find residents trapped under the rubble of a block of flats that partially collapsed in a Russian strike after attacks on the Kyiv region killed at least 15 people.
Moscow has been pummelling Ukraine with nightly drone and missile barrages as the war-torn country braces for another winter while the full-scale invasion grinds through its fifth year.
An overnight strike on Dymer, about 45km (30 miles) north of the Ukrainian capital, hit a five-storey building, killing at least 11 people, Kyiv regional official Tymur Tkachenko said on Monday.
“Rescuers recovered the body of another person from beneath the rubble,” Tkachenko wrote on Telegram, confirming the death toll had risen to 11.
Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said earlier on Telegram that the dead included a teenager.
It said rescuers were searching for 11 people, including two children, who were “not responding or cannot be reached”.
Rescuers had managed to pull out survivors from the rubble, including a 79-year-old woman and a child, Tkachenko said.
Al Jazeera’s Audrey MacAlpine, reporting from Kyiv, said people were believed to still be under the rubble.
“Rescuers are still at the site, working to try to pull people out from under the rubble dead or alive,” she said.
A Russian strike on a supermarket killed three other people and wounded 15, including three children, in Vyshneve, a city just south of Kyiv, Mayor Illya Dikov wrote on Facebook.
“People had simply gone to the store to buy groceries. An ordinary shopping trip turned into a tragedy due to a Russian attack,” Tkachenko said.
A strike on a private home in nearby Bila Tserkva killed one more person and set the building ablaze, he added.
Russia also struck a power substation in the Dnipropetrovsk region, Prime Minister Sergiy Koretsky said on social media.
Moscow has ramped up attacks on Ukraine and its energy network in particular as temperatures drop to around freezing.
Putin promised on Thursday that Russia would respond to Ukrainian attacks on the Kerch Bridge, a symbol of Putin’s rule over Ukraine’s Russian-annexed Crimean Peninsula, with “much more painful” attacks.
Ukraine hit the bridge three times in a week, severing the part of it used by vehicles and halting train services.
Ukrainian attacks hit Russia and beyond
Meanwhile, drones attacked oil storage facilities in Russia’s Tatarstan region, damaging several, but there were no immediate reports of deaths or injuries, according to the Interfax news agency, which quoted local authorities.
“A fire broke out there,” Al Jazeera’s Yulia Shapovalova reported from Moscow, adding that the attack targeted the facility in Tatarstan’s Almetyevsk area.
Shapovalova said drone attacks were also reported in the Novoshakhtinsk area in Rostov, hitting a petroleum products plant and causing a fire in a storage tank.
She added that an attack was also reported in the city of Perm in the Volga region, where a large oil refinery is located.
Our correspondents said the attacks in Tatarstan, which is about 1,000km (620 miles) away from the Ukrainian border, demonstrate Kyiv’s ability to penetrate deep inside Russia.
Kyiv confirms Libya attack
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Monday that Ukraine’s forces sank the Russian corvette Merkury, one of Russia’s newest ships, commissioned in 2023, near the coast of Libya using seven Ukrainian-made naval drones.
Zelenskyy said they hit a second target, the Russian dry cargo ship MV Angara. The Ukrainian president said it was used by Russia to transport weapons.
“We continue operations in designated waters,” he said on Telegram.
Zelenskyy added that a Russian Ka-27 combat helicopter was destroyed along with the corvette.

noticias.titulo: ‘Environmental crimes’: Israel blamed for toxic pollution in 99% of Gaza
noticias.resumen: A new report by UK-based charity Oxfam shows how Israel’s destruction of Gaza has created a ‘toxic wasteland'.
noticias.texto:
‘Environmental crimes’: Israel blamed for toxic pollution in 99% of Gaza
A new report by UK-based charity Oxfam shows how Israel’s destruction of Gaza has created a ‘toxic wasteland’.
Gaza turned into ‘toxic wasteland’ by Israel’s war, says new report
More than three years of Israel’s genocidal war has turned Gaza into “a toxic wasteland”, with poisoned water and contaminated soil threatening the survival of Palestinians in the enclave of 2.3 million people.
Israel’s use of explosives and incendiary weapons has caused environmental contamination across more than 99 percent of Gaza, according to a new report by Oxfam and the Conflict and Environment Observatory (CEOBS).
“Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza includes military assaults on its environment, which are environmental war crimes threatening life now and for generations to come,” said Amitabh Behar, Oxfam’s international executive director.
“The destruction and contamination of Gaza will have fundamentally degraded the environmental conditions necessary for human safety and survival. This would breach Israel’s legal obligations under international humanitarian and human rights law,” he said in a statement.
“Palestinians living in Gaza are being exposed to toxins in multiple ways through air, food, water and via direct contact with contaminated soils and debris.”
The report shows how Israel’s destruction of buildings and the environment has contaminated the air, soil, food and water in the enclave.
It also emphasises the urgent need for a full independent investigation to identify and reduce the risks to Palestinian lives.
Pollutants from bombardment, fires, rubble and untreated sewage can reach Palestinians through the air they breathe, the water they drink and the food they eat.
Oxfam’s report, which uses satellite imagery, remote sensing, scientific analysis and other open-source data, gives a comprehensive picture to date of the impact of the Israeli assault on Gaza, which has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians. More than 1,500 Palestinians have been killed since the so-called “ceasefire” was signed in October 2025.
In September 2025, a UN international commission of inquiry said Israel had committed genocide in Gaza. And the International Court of Justice is hearing a case of genocide against Israel. In January, the ICJ said it was plausible that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza.
The report came a day after world leaders failed to reach a consensus on climate change at the 31st Climate Change Conference (COP31) of the United Nations.
Air pollution
Explosions, fires and the destruction of buildings and infrastructure release pollutants that settle on rubble and soil.
Wind, traffic and debris clearance send them back into the air. Oxfam’s analysis points to the highest concentrations in Gaza City, Jabalia and the North Gaza governorate.
Israel’s continuous bombardment has also generated substantial greenhouse gas emissions, with further emissions expected from clearing debris and rebuilding.
A study cited in the report estimated direct conflict emissions at more than 1.3 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO2e) by January 2025.
61 million tonnes of rubble across Gaza
By October 11, 2025, Israeli ground operations directly affected about 283sq km (109sq miles) of Gaza’s 365sq km (141sq miles), or 78 percent of the area, Oxfam estimates.
The UN Environment Programme estimates that the assault since October 7, 2023, generated 61 million tonnes of debris, which is about 29 tonnes of rubble per person living in Gaza now. More than 90 percent of Palestinians have been forcibly displaced, most of them multiple times.
Oxfam estimates that the mountains of rubble would require 2.1 million dump truckloads to clear them, equivalent to 736 trips around the circumference of the entire planet.
The amount of rubble that needs to be cleared is about eight times the 7.65 million tonnes estimated in Iraq’s Mosul during the 2017 conflict.
The report identifies at least one potential contamination source across more than 99 percent of Gaza. Gaza City, Khan Younis, Rafah, Jabalia and the Salah al-Din Street corridor showed the greatest overlap of potential hazards.
Unexploded munitions can leach contaminants into soil and groundwater as their casings corrode. Damaged vehicles, batteries and fuel stores add to the risks along military routes and former positions.
A study cited by Oxfam estimated emissions across the wider conflict cycle at 33.2 million tonnes of CO2e, including an estimate of 31.4 million tonnes of carbon emissions that will occur from reconstruction.
According to a report by Palestinian Water Authority cited by Oxfam, Gaza’s daily water supply fell from 334,107 cubic metres before October 2023 to 54,747 cubic metres in June 2024, a drop of about 84 percent. By April 2026, emergency repairs had brought it back to 130,315 cubic metres a day, still 61 percent below pre-assault levels.
Nine of 61 reservoirs were operational, with combined storage sufficient to provide 18 litres per person for one day.
Gaza’s Coastal Aquifer historically supplied 81 percent of the territory’s water. Oxfam says 97 percent of the aquifer was already chemically polluted before October 2023.
Decades of overpumping amid Israel’s air, land and sea blockade of Gaza allowed seawater to seep in. Untreated sewage, farm runoff and waste disposal added to the pollution.
In July 2026, Gaza’s Ministry of Health detected faecal coliforms in 15 of 79 groundwater wells (19 percent) tested. Oxfam identified North Gaza, Gaza City and Deir el-Balah as the areas most at risk from contaminated drinking water. An assessment in 2021 reported faecal coliforms in 2 percent of wells.
July tests found that 61 of 79 wells (77.2 percent) had total dissolved solids above 1,000 milligrams per litre, 400mg above the level at which the World Health Organization says water becomes increasingly unpleasant to drink.
By April 2024, Israel’s assault had destroyed all six of Gaza’s wastewater treatment plants. An estimated 40,000 cubic metres of raw sewage enter the Mediterranean daily, enough to fill 16 Olympic-size pools.
By April 2026, 19 percent of pumping stations and about 30 percent of the sewer network still functioned at least partly.
Gaza’s waste collection fleet fell from 261 vehicles to 48.
Both main landfills remained inaccessible. Of at least 56 temporary dumps, only 11 were accessible and operating.
These sites generally lack barriers to protect soil and groundwater. By April 2026, an estimated 1.45 million people lived in areas affected by rodents and other pests.
Soil and food security
Before October 2023, Gaza’s farms supplied about 95 percent of the fresh vegetables people ate. By late 2025, more than 87 percent of cropland was damaged.
Oxfam says only 3 percent was accessible and undamaged.
By October 2024, the UN had reported that more than one million olive trees had been uprooted.
Oxfam identified more than 7,200 damaged greenhouses and documented the destruction of facilities that preserved and distributed Palestinian seeds.
Before the assault, Gaza’s fisheries produced about 4,660 tonnes of fish a year, with fish farms adding 750 tonnes.
In July 2026, an estimated 1.2 million people (59 percent) faced crisis levels of acute food shortages or worse, according to the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, cited by the report.
The report also records the loss of roughly 95 percent of cattle and a collapse in fishing.
The average daily catch from October 2023 to April 2024 was 7.3 percent of its 2022 level. Oxfam warns that contaminants could enter crops and seafood as production resumes.
Livelihoods and economic systems
Gaza’s gross domestic product fell by 83 percent in 2024 to $362m, the report says.
Damage to farms, workshops and factories has stripped people of income and the means to resume work. Debris removal, repairs and farming could expose workers to asbestos, silica and other hazards for years.
Among the commerce and industry establishments assessed, 92 percent sustained damage, including 72 percent that were destroyed.
A joint World Bank, European Union and UN assessment, cited by Oxfam, put direct physical damage at $35.2bn and economic losses at $22.7bn by October 2025.
It estimated recovery and reconstruction needs at $71.4bn over a decade, including $26.3bn in the first 18 months.
Health risks and long-term impacts
Disease prevalence in Gaza recorded more than 1.9 million cases of acute respiratory infection and about 81,000 cases of acute watery diarrhoea in January and February 2026. More than 36,000 of the diarrhoea cases were among children aged below five years. Gaza recorded more than 496,000 cases of acute watery diarrhoea in 2025.
In 2024, vaccine-derived poliovirus type 2 was detected in Gaza’s wastewater. A child was later diagnosed with paralytic polio, Gaza’s first reported case in 25 years. The report also cites the detection of multidrug-resistant pseudomonas in water at primary healthcare centres.
Legal, political and financial risks
Oxfam says the destruction of Gaza’s water, food and sanitation systems may be relevant to alleged crimes under the Rome Statute and to assessing whether Israel violated the Genocide Convention.
A genocide finding requires proof of intent to destroy a protected group, in whole or in part. Oxfam calls for full reparations where violations are established.
Its five-stage plan calls for securing access and reducing exposure, testing for contamination, screening sites and making essential repairs, treating contaminated sites and managing hazardous waste, then rebuilding with safeguards and long-term monitoring.

noticias.titulo: Artificial superintelligence ‘arriving’, warns top Meta executive
noticias.resumen: Meta Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang says humankind's actions over next year will have 'great consequence' for the world.
noticias.texto:
Artificial superintelligence ‘arriving’, warns top Meta executive
Meta Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang says humankind’s actions over next year will have ‘great consequence’ for the world.
Meta’s top AI executive has sounded the alarm about the risk of humanity losing control of AI, warning that superintelligence that far exceeds the human intellect is imminent.
Meta Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang issued the warning on Sunday after an employee at AI giant Anthropic announced that he had used Claude to solve the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most difficult problems in mathematics.
Wang said the breakthrough dwarfed any human achievement for “sheer intellectual might”.
The 29-year-old executive said the milestone showed that emerging AI models will be “clearly superhuman” at improving themselves, as well as “massively accelerating” research in fields such as biology, armaments and economics.
“Superintelligence is arriving,” Wang said on X.
“How humanity acts over the next year will have great consequence on what future world we live in.”
Wang, who co-founded Scale AI before joining Meta as the tech giant’s first chief AI officer last year, said it is unlikely humankind will be able to control AI that achieves unconstrained recursive self-improvement or is “1000x smarter and more capable than humans in every field.”
“Now that we are at a point where the scientific and technical problems on capability progress are likely solved, we must not only make progress in the extremely urgent areas of safety, alignment and security, but we have to start thinking through how we progress thoughtfully,” Wang said.
AI safety advocates have identified recursive self-improvement – where AI models become capable of advancing without human input – as a critical tipping point after which humanity could lose the ability to control the technology.
While the risks of frontier AI have stoked intense debate in Silicon Valley, there is no consensus on how to maximise the benefits of the technology without exposing humanity to catastrophic risks.
Meta has largely positioned itself on the more optimistic side of the debate, with CEO and cofounder Mark Zuckerberg rejecting calls by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman for a coordinated slowdown in development to beef up guardrails.
In an essay published in August, Zuckerberg lamented that discussions about AI were “filled with doom” and said the technology should lead to “more people sharing greater prosperity, health and freedom.”
In his post on Sunday, Wang criticised “lazy thinking” within the AI industry that he said treated superintelligence as inevitable.
“We should not be okay with a ‘handover’ of society to AI. We should endeavour ourselves to build a technology which delivers a positive future for humanity, where all humans have greater agency and empowerment,” Wang said.
“I strongly believe this is possible, but likely involves the whole industry taking meaningfully different actions from the “default path” in front of us.”

noticias.titulo: Widowed amid war and displacement: Sudanese mothers struggle to survive
noticias.resumen: War widows in Sudan face growing challenges supporting their children as the cost of living increases.
noticias.texto:
Widowed amid war and displacement: Sudanese mothers struggle to survive
Widowed by war and displacement, women in Sudan face growing challenges supporting their children amid rising living costs and shrinking humanitarian assistance.
Warning: This story contains descriptions of sexual assault that some readers may find disturbing.
Port Sudan, Sudan – In Sudan’s displacement camps, the stories of residents often follow similar paths, but each loss and hardship is a deeply personal experience.
Arafa Abdelaziz endured a dangerous 15-day journey from Omdurman to a displacement camp in Port Sudan in late 2023, after losing her husband and one of her two sons, who died early in the war.
Her husband died just days after fighting broke out between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in April 2023, leaving her to care for her remaining two children as their home city of Omdurman in Khartoum State came under bombardment.
Five months later, her eight-year-old son was killed by a stray bullet during clashes near Omdurman’s market.
“My son was playing outside the house with his friends when I suddenly heard a loud noise. When I went outside, I found that his head had been shattered by gunfire,” said the 33-year-old.
With the fighting between the SAF and RSF continuing in Omdurman, one of the centres of the power struggle between the two former allies at the start of the war, Arafa eventually decided to flee the city with her six-year-old son, who has a brain condition affecting his development.
She describes the journey to Port Sudan as a prolonged and horrifying ordeal. Near Jebel Aulia, south of Khartoum, RSF fighters intercepted the vehicle they were in and the passengers were robbed and assaulted.
“They asked every woman carrying a child how she wanted her son to be killed. I told them to kill me before they touched my son,” Arafa recalled.
When she confronted the fighters as they attempted to assault her child, one of them hit her with the butt of his rifle, leaving her unconscious for more than an hour.
“When I regained consciousness, I saw RSF fighters raping the young women who were travelling with us on the bus. Some were raped in front of their fathers. I felt it was the end,” she said.
In October 2026, UN Women reported that 12.7 million people, mostly women and girls, needed support for gender-based violence in Sudan – four times the pre-war figure.
The agency warned that sexual violence is being used as a weapon of war, with women and girls at risk while fleeing areas of fighting, in displacement camps and while searching for food, water and shelter.
Arafa said her greatest fear throughout the ordeal was for her younger son’s safety. When the fighters asked what valuables she had, she told them she owned nothing. They took two gold rings from her fingers and after severely beating her, let her continue her journey.
“I arrived in Port Sudan with nothing, having lost my husband. My son’s condition had worsened because of what we went through on the journey and because he could not receive his medication regularly,” she said.
It was Arafa’s first time in Port Sudan, so, having no family or friends there to support her, she headed to a school sheltering displaced families. She was later transferred to another displacement camp, where she now lives with her son. But reaching relative safety was not the end of her struggles. Her son’s condition fluctuates, and she remains worried about his health and future.
“Sometimes he imagines strange things because of his illness,” she said. “Yesterday, he told me he could see a lot of blood on the ground. It makes me think every day about his future with this condition.”
Arafa cannot afford his medication, so she has resorted to giving him medicine only when his condition deteriorates. She depends largely on aid distributed in the camp, as her needs and those of her son continue to grow.
“I’m afraid to leave him alone at home, out of my sight, in case he has a seizure or hurts himself,” she said.
The war in Sudan has killed as many as 150,000 people and forced millions from their homes, often to camps in impoverished neighbouring countries.
Income levels have dropped to 1992 levels and extreme poverty rates are worse than in the 1980s, according to the United Nations. Due to conscription, fatalities and emigration to other regions and countries for work, women have become the sole guardians in many displaced Sudanese households.
The UN’s 2025 Gender Snapshot found that 75 percent of female-headed households in Sudan were food insecure – three times the rate among male-headed households.
The Mashad Observatory has documented 72,202 cases of widowhood since the outbreak of war in Sudan in April 2023. That constitutes a complex humanitarian crisis which can lead to the collapse of household incomes, stability and protection systems. In the long term, it means transmitting deprivation, economic vulnerability and psychological trauma from one generation to the next.
These cumulative impacts can weaken social cohesion, exacerbate inequalities and undermine the capacity of local communities to recover from the consequences of war. This growing burden means fewer opportunities for women to work and increased dependence on humanitarian assistance, with long-term economic implications for Sudan, the group said.
“Their suffering is further compounded when women lose the primary source of household income or are forced to abandon their homes and communities without adequate financial resources or social support networks. Such circumstances may expose them to heightened risks of economic exploitation, gender-based violence, forced or early marriage involving their daughters and the interruption of their children’s education,” a spokesperson for the organisation told Al Jazeera.
“These pressures may also contribute to deteriorating mental health as a result of cumulative trauma, overwhelming responsibilities and the absence of appropriate psychosocial support services.”
With humanitarian agencies saying that Sudan’s 2026 response plan, which aims to reach 20.4 million people and requires $2.9bn, has received only 47% of the funding needed, there will be challenges in providing these families with the necessary support.
“Addressing this challenge therefore requires a transition from temporary emergency relief towards a comprehensive national strategy that places widows and female-headed households at the centre of Sudan’s recovery and reconstruction plans,” said the organisation.
“Such a strategy should include sustainable cash assistance, economic empowerment programmes, vocational training, access to decent employment, improved access to finance and productive enterprises, as well as guaranteed access to education, healthcare, legal protection and psychosocial support.”
Zahra Idris, 39, fled Khartoum with her husband and two children as shelling intensified, arriving in Port Sudan three years ago.
Her husband initially rented a house in the working-class neighbourhood of Al-Kasara. But when they could no longer afford the rent, the landlord evicted them. The family moved to a school shelter before being relocated to a displacement camp at the start of the school year.
Two months ago, Zahra’s husband died of heart disease, leaving her to care for their two children with little support beyond humanitarian assistance, which has become increasingly limited.
“Since my husband died, my fears have grown. I cannot go out to look for work until I complete the mourning period prescribed in Islam, which lasts four months and ten days,” she said.
Her 12-year-old son has an intellectual disability and requires regular medical care, something the family cannot afford given the rising cost of living.
“There is no one to help me. I just want my son’s condition to improve enough for him to attend a school for children with disabilities,” she said.
“Going from one organisation to another, looking for someone to cover my son’s medical treatment and education, cost me around 100,000 Sudanese pounds. That money could have covered our household needs for several days.”

noticias.titulo: Europe’s hot autumn of protests is a symptom of economic breakdown
noticias.resumen: European governments beholden to corporate interests no longer have the wellbeing of their nations as a top priority.
noticias.texto:
Europe’s hot autumn of protests is a symptom of economic breakdown
European governments beholden to corporate interests no longer have the wellbeing of their nations as a top priority.
Europe is in the grips of a “hot autumn”. For several weeks now, French students have led mass protests against underinvestment in education, teacher shortages and dilapidated classrooms.
In Spain, mass protests broke out after the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home of 70 years, after her rent was hiked by 230 percent by an investment fund that bought the property. She died a fortnight later after being admitted to hospital.
Now the protests are spreading: to Italy, where upwards of one million people took to the streets of 50 cities last week; to Portugal, where tent encampments have sprung up to oppose rapid hikes in housing costs; to Germany, where riot police with water cannon confronted protesters opposing the creeping extension of conscription; and most recently, to the United Kingdom, where thousands of students joined a day of action on November 20 under the slogan “Fight for our future, not their wars!”
The common thread which has sparked these Gen Z protests is the rapidly rising cost of living. In the wake of the global pandemic, the war in Ukraine, US tariffs, and now the US-Israel war on Iran, global supply chains are breaking down, sending costs spiralling.
But this is only a symptom of a wider problem. Deregulation and neoliberal policies have allowed corporations to take over not only the economy but also politics. This has led to massive wealth concentration at the top and increasing precarity for the vast majority of the European population. The impact of climate change and the rollout of artificial intelligence (AI), threatening mass unemployment, are making the situation a lot worse.
If we want to change course, we need to fundamentally rethink how our economy works. And yet we are ruled by a political class which has lost its will to govern.
Of course, our rulers still clamour for the perks of office. But they are operating within a logic which prevents them from taking the action necessary to deal with the challenges humanity faces. In this crisis, the centre cannot hold, and support for both radical right and left-wing parties is growing rapidly.
The problem is this: 40 years ago, politicians came to accept that the free market held the answer to all our problems. Governments gave up trying to manage the economy. By handing the levers of control to the private sector, they were told they would unleash the forces of competition and economic growth, free from the sclerotic hand of the state.
As the decades wore on, it became increasingly clear that the market looked less like multiple small businesses competing for customers and more like gigantic corporations forcing citizens, governments and the planet itself to bend to their will.
Power has been handed to monopolies, which have stretched supply chains to a breaking point, privatised profits while socialising costs, fuelled inequality and trashed the environment.
Key economic decisions once made by elected governments with at least a pretence of public interest in mind are today made in corporate boardrooms, with only the self-interest of their rich investors to trouble them.
When economic decisions are designed primarily to enrich the few, is it any wonder our public infrastructure is crumbling? The things we need to make life acceptable – housing, education, healthcare – have become no more than commodities from which the monopolists can profit.
Politicians are dismantling our welfare state, claiming that today we can no longer afford to care for the poorest. They have it the wrong way around. Rather, we cannot afford the rich.
In today’s crisis, some in Europe have come to accept the need for industrial strategy, for economic planning and government intervention; all tools which were abandoned at the onset of the “free market” era.
But these tools cannot be used properly without taking power back from the monopolies – fundamentally shifting the relationship between those who now own society and those of us who live in it. It requires a New Deal at least on the scale of President Franklin D Roosevelt’s policies in the 1930s in the United States.
And in some ways, our task is even bigger today. After World War II, European politicians built a new social contract: we would all share in the massive economic growth which would be unlocked as countries recovered from war and exploited the Earth as never before. With high growth, the poor could get richer even while the rich themselves did well.
In a world facing massive resource constraints, we can no longer operate in this way. Indeed, the richest countries have already used up their fair share of global resources.
One way out is to reassert Western dominance. The one economic area in which European governments will invest is the war machine. Even Germany’s steadfast commitment to balanced budgets – a commitment which it has disastrously imposed on the European Union with almost religious zeal – can seemingly be broken when the military demands it.
But military spending will not resuscitate European industry. Nor will it keep us safe. It will further empower the monopolies who soak up ever more of our taxes while bringing catastrophic conflict ever closer. This is not protecting us from invasion but protecting Europe’s ability to do what it wants, when it wants, where it wants. We cannot, any longer, build prosperity and security on injustice. The youth protests get that; just look at the explicitly antimilitary slogans on the streets of German cities.
A real solution requires a much bigger shift in thinking. We need to accept that Europe is entering a post-growth world, where society’s resources need to be fundamentally reallocated.
This change will not be easy. It needs politicians with the will and the ability to remove power from the corporations, to break up monopoly capitalism. And that will not come from above because, as American statesman Frederick Douglass said: “power concedes nothing without a demand”.
Europe’s youth demand radical change. Hope lies with them.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.
