noticias.titulo: Ukraine confirms it used naval drones to strike two Russian ships off Libya
noticias.resumen: Ukraine’s security service says seven drones were launched from mothership in operation that sank Merkury warship Europe live – latest updates Ukraine has confirmed it deployed naval drones in strikes on two Russian vessels off Libya on Sunday, including one that sank the corvette Merkury, one of Russia’s newest vessels. Ukraine’s security service, the SBU, said seven domestically made naval drones were launched from a mothership in the operation, which Volodymyr Zelenskyy described as “exemplary”. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Ukraine has confirmed it deployed naval drones in strikes on two Russian vessels off Libya on Sunday, including one that sank the corvette Merkury, one of Russia’s newest vessels.
Ukraine’s security service, the SBU, said seven domestically made naval drones were launched from a mothership in the operation, which Volodymyr Zelenskyy described as “exemplary”.
“We continue our operations in designated waters. We are responding to Russia’s aggression. We are developing Ukrainian weapons,” the Ukrainian president added.
Zelenskyy released video footage, filmed by an approaching drone, showing the drones as they smashed into the side of the warship at its berth in the Benghazi naval base, triggering huge explosions that lit up the night sky.
In its own statement, the SBU said: “The defence forces of Ukraine have once again demonstrated that the Russian military fleet and its logistics networks have no safe routes, even far beyond the Black Sea.”
Zelenskyy said the other vessel hit on Sunday, the dry cargo ship MV Angara, was being used by Russia to transport weapons.
The operation, conducted 1,500 miles (2,400km) from the frontline in Ukraine, was the latest daring long-range assault by Kyiv’s forces. Last week Ukraine hit the Kerch bridge – a key supply line to Russian-occupied Crimea – and the Russian Baltic seaport of Kaliningrad.
Residents in Benghazi heard loud explosions and saw flames at the naval base early on Sunday. Civil defence units rushed to the site and extinguished the fire, authorities in eastern Libya said.
The Merkury had docked to refuel and take on supplies as part of a cooperation agreement between Russia and the eastern-based government in Libya, the statement said without providing details about the vessel or its cargo.
Vladimir Putin had taken a personal interest in the ship. In 2019 he toured the St Petersburg yard where it was being built and backed naming it after a tsarist-era brig celebrated for fighting off two Turkish warships in the Black Sea in 1829.
At the 2023 Navy Day parade, the Russian president singled it out among 30 new vessels as evidence that Russia was “consistently building up the power of its fleet”. He hailed its St George flag as “a sign of the inviolability of our naval traditions” and said it was “gratifying” that the brig’s name had been revived.
Russian state media also talked up the ship. The news agency Tass called it the “newest missile corvette”, while the channel TV Tsentr claimed its stealth technology made it “invisible to radar”.
Divided Libya has emerged in recent years as a proxy battlefield. Moscow has long supported the breakaway government in Benghazi of Khalifa Haftar in its efforts use eastern Libya as a staging post for its military presence in north Africa and the Sahel.
More recently there have been reports of increasing Ukrainian operations. In April, the Associated Press reported that Ukrainian drone specialists had been operating at military sites in Misrata, Tripoli and Zawiya in Libya’s west. In September Libyan authorities denied reports by CNN that it allowed Ukraine to use a military base in the to launch drones against vessels from Russia’s “shadow fleet” in the Mediterranean.
The rival UN-recognised government in Tripoli said in a statement it was alarmed by “risks posed by involving civilian ports and facilities in activities linked to external conflicts”.
There was no immediate comment from Russia about the strikes. The UN mission in Libya (UNSMIL), however, expressed “serious concern” over the attacks, calling for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation”. It said on X: “Libya cannot afford, and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts.”
Ukraine prides itself on its military industry, particularly its progress in drone technology, which it has extensively developed since Russia invaded more than four and a half years ago. It has repeatedly touted the effectiveness of its domestically produced drones, including naval drones deployed throughout the war to hit Russian ships and infrastructure in the Black Sea.
In 2024, the Ukrainian general staff announced it had destroyed the Russian landing ship Cesar Kunikov with naval drones off the coast of Ukraine’s peninsula of Crimea, which was annexed by Russia in 2014.
Ukraine has also claimed to have attacked Moscow’s so-called shadow fleet – believed to carry Russian oil to circumvent sanctions – including in the Mediterranean last December. In March, a Russian liquefied natural gas carrier sank off the Libyan coast following an attack that Putin blamed on Ukraine.
Additional reporting by Pjotr Sauer

noticias.titulo: Trump administration deported US citizen to Mexico, DoJ admits in court
noticias.resumen: Brian Morales García of Texas seeks damages after he was wrongly identified as undocumented in case White House wants dropped The Trump administration recently admitted in federal court that it deported a US citizen to Mexico after American authorities incorrectly concluded he was an undocumented immigrant. Attorneys for the US justice department made that admission on Friday while requesting the dismissal of a lawsuit for damages that the deported man – Brian José Morales García of Austin, Texas – has been pursuing against the federal government. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
The Trump administration recently admitted in federal court that it deported a US citizen to Mexico after American authorities incorrectly concluded he was an undocumented immigrant.
Attorneys for the US justice department made that admission on Friday while requesting the dismissal of a lawsuit for damages that the deported man – Brian José Morales García of Austin, Texas – has been pursuing against the federal government.
Morales García’s case took that turn as the White House has faced bipartisan criticism for the aggressive mass deportation campaign pursued by Donald Trump throughout his second presidency – widely seen as a factor in the electoral battering his Republican party suffered during the 3 November midterms, costing it control of Congress.
The Denver-born, Mexico-raised Morales García was riding with his boss to his job as an air-conditioning installation technician on 3 April when they were pulled over by state and local officers near Fredericksburg, Texas.
Morales García was his boss’s passenger and did not have his identification on him. The 25-year-old also told the officers that he had his birth certificate and social security card at home, but they didn’t believe him – so they called immigration agents, who detained Morales García.
Court filings recount how Robert Gil Jr, a US Customs and Border Protection agent, consulted records from Mexico that listed a Mexican birthplace for Morales García. Gil Jr also accused Morales García of saying he was born in Mexico and observed that he only spoke in Spanish, according to court records.
Morales García was deported on 7 April, with the Trump administration later accusing him in a media statement of being in the country illegally.
Morales García’s attorneys sued on 1 May, maintaining that he had falsely said he entered the US illegally and signed papers for a rapid deportation in response to threats of imprisonment by agents. His lawsuit, which seeks an unspecified amount of money, also contended that family and friends tried to deliver documents proving his US citizenship before this deportation.
But those efforts were unduly rebuffed, Morales García’s lawsuit said.
The Trump administration denied Morales García’s assertions, saying on Friday that he went to Mexico voluntarily and therefore lacked any basis to sue the federal government for damages. Nonetheless, in court filings on Friday, the administration conceded that Morales García “was permitted entry” back into the US on 30 August after it reviewed “information concerning plaintiff’s place of birth”.
“Plaintiff is a dual citizen of the United States and Mexico,” Justin Simmons, the US attorney for the western district of Texas, wrote in a court filing first reported by the Texas Tribune.
Americans are not required to carry proof of citizenship when going about their daily business. Lawyers across the US have seen cases such as Morales García’s, which begin after an encounter with local authorities demonstrate how those officials are generally not aware of the nuances of immigration policy.
Texas’s public safety department is among many US state and local agencies that collaborate with federal immigration authorities under their 287(g) program.
The judge presiding over Morales García’s lawsuit, Robert Lee Pitman, did not immediately rule on the Trump administration’s request on Friday to dismiss the case. The lawsuit also named unspecified local and state Texas law enforcement officers as defendants.
An October 2025 report by ProPublica found that immigration agents had detained more than 170 US citizens during the first nine months of Trump’s second presidency.
Meanwhile, the media statement incorrectly saying Morales García was in the US illegally is among several related to immigration enforcement under the Trump administration that has unraveled under scrutiny.
A Guardian analysis published in July reviewed Trump administration press releases on 26 cases of cars allegedly being used to assault immigration enforcement agents – and nearly all were either disproven or dropped.

noticias.titulo: Plant-based lunches could cut Australia’s emissions by 15m tonnes, new research shows
noticias.resumen: Nationwide change in lunch habits could cut more climate pollution than grounding every domestic flight Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Australians could collectively cut climate pollution by more than 15m tonnes – more than grounding every domestic flight – simply by changing what they eat for lunch. A nationwide shift to plant-based lunches could reduce food-related emissions by 29% – 15.4m tonnes per year – while saving the average household about $611 annually, according to a report by Bryant Research and not-for-profit ProVeg. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Australians could collectively cut climate pollution by more than 15m tonnes – more than grounding every domestic flight – simply by changing what they eat for lunch.
A nationwide shift to plant-based lunches could reduce food-related emissions by 29% – 15.4m tonnes per year – while saving the average household about $611 annually, according to a report by Bryant Research and not-for-profit ProVeg.
Nadia Schilling, the executive director of ProVeg Australia, said the findings highlighted the “huge difference” that relatively modest changes, like a meat-free Monday or a plant-based lunch, could make.
That might mean opting for a black bean burrito, a poke bowl with tofu, or a lunchbox with hummus and fresh vegetables – instead of a cheese and ham wrap – she said.
“We realise that Australians aren’t going to change their diets overnight,” Schilling said. “This is a really practical change where everyone wins. Lunch is a huge missed opportunity.”
Australia has the highest per capita food-related emissions in the world, the report found. It modelled the environmental, health and economic impacts for a range of Australia-wide dietary changes, finding the shift to 100% plant-based meals would cut dietary emissions by two-thirds, while just switching lunches would cut nearly one-third.
Emissions from domestic aviation are about 10m tonnes a year, according to government data.
The organisations behind the report, which promote moving from meat to plant-rich foods and alternative protein sources, called for a national campaign to increase vegetable consumption along with policy and funding support for plant proteins.
Almost one-third of global greenhouse gas emissions are connected to the global food system through land clearing, raising animals, growing crops, processing, packaging, transport and waste.
The National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) is reviewing the evidence about sustainability and diet as part of the first update of Australian dietary guidelines in more than 13 years. Draft guidelines are expected to be released for public consultation in December 2026.
An NHMRC spokesperson said the expert committee drafting the new guidelines had prioritised information on health impacts, but “information about the economic, social, and environmental sustainability of diets was then considered as one of the many factors that influence people’s ability to follow a healthy diet”.
Dr Diana Bogueva, who researches food sustainability at Curtin University, said relatively small changes in everyday eating habits – when adopted by a large number of people – could have a major impact on the environmental footprint of food production.
However, Bogueva, who was not involved with the report, said the environmental, health and affordability benefits of eating less meat depended on what foods replaced it.
Whole foods like legumes, grains, vegetables, nuts and seeds provided valuable fibre, vitamins, minerals and plant proteins, she said. “But not every plant-based product is automatically healthy,” Bogueva said. “Simply swapping meat for highly processed products does not necessarily improve the nutritional quality of the meal.”
Sustainable eating didn’t have to be expensive, she added, and some of the most nutritious sources of plant protein – such as beans, lentils and chickpeas – were also among the most affordable.
“We do know there are both health and environmental benefits if you reduce red and processed meat in your diet,” said Alexandra Jones, an associate professor at the George Institute for Global Health, who was not involved with the report.
But rather than focusing on swapping out one protein for another, the emphasis should be on “helping people eat more vegetables, legumes and minimally processed plant foods,” she said.
A good lunch could be as simple as an “old-school salad sandwich” on wholegrain bread, with lettuce, tomato, sprouts and beetroot.

noticias.titulo: Domestic violence perpetrators are misusing smart car features to abuse, researchers warn
noticias.resumen: Exclusive: Alarming report reveals how tracking and monitoring functions and digital key access have been used to facilitate abuse Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Earlier this year a man in Australia was found guilty of using a connected car app to harass his former partner, including restricting the speed at which she could drive, sometimes to 40km an hour . In 2022 in the US, a woman found her former husband had used a car app associated with her car to track her; the carmaker then allegedly refused to terminate the former partner’s digital access to the vehicle.
noticias.texto:
Earlier this year a man in Australia was found guilty of using a connected car app to harass his former partner, including restricting the speed at which she could drive, sometimes to 40km an hour.
In 2022 in the US, a woman found her former husband had used a car app associated with her car to track her; the carmaker then allegedly refused to terminate the former partner’s digital access to the vehicle.
In another case in the US in 2020, a woman found a baseball bat her former partner had used to threaten her in the back seat of her car.
These three cases form part of an alarming report by University of New South Wales researchers, released on Tuesday, which warned this was an emerging problem that could get worse. It found smart car functions that could be misused by perpetrators of domestic violence to facilitate abuse were prevalent across major car brands.
“There is an urgent need for carmakers to adopt safety by design principles from the early stages of designing both the apps and the cars,” said the report co-author Katharine Kemp, a data privacy and consumer protection expert at UNSW.
The researchers found that problems emerged as many of the cars’ functions – which include tracking and monitoring functions, remote control functions and digital key access – could be controlled remotely via an app.
The researchers said that there were three main scenarios that could open the functions to misuse: the abuser being the owner of the car and having created the account themselves; they were granted access as a secondary user of the car; or the victim survivor is impersonated and the perpetrator creates an account on their behalf.
The report said that the problematic functions are mainly marketed by the car manufacturers as being for the purpose of enabling the car owner to “keep an eye on” and protect their car.
It highlighted an advertisement on the carmaker Kia’s Australian website for “Kia Connect”. Kia was contacted for comment.
“Kia Connect is also bundled with geofence and time fencing alerts which let the owner know when another user strays outside preset limits of geographical areas or time limitations. It’s a perfect feature for anyone dealing with a family member who is borrowing the car,” the advertisement said.
The report mapped how prevalent potentially problematic functions were, and whether these functions were advertised by 15 of the top car brands.
One of the functions raised was geolocation, which allows the geographical location of the car in real-time or when it is parked, and was advertised by 100% of the 15 car brands, with some marketing it as “Vehicle Tracking”, “Vehicle Locator” or “Find My Car”. The researchers said this tool could be misused to track people.
The researchers found that 60% of the top 15 brands also advertised a “zone exit alert” which allows users to set an alarm if a car leaves a designated area. They warned this functions could be used to: “Set a zone of 3km from the family home to receive alert if the victim-survivor attempts to leave or fails to follow abuser’s rules limiting travel by the victim-survivor.”
Meanwhile, 20% advertise speed or acceleration restrictions. The explanation of this function by carmakers includes that it is to set speed limits for young drivers or valet parkers.
But the report warned this could be misused to set a speed limit of 40km/h so that a victim survivor cannot safely use highways or escape at speed.
The researchers also raised concerns about digital key access, which allows drivers to use their mobile phone to unlock the car or start the engine and was advertised by 67% of car brands in the Australian market. The report warns: “This function may also allow an abuser to remotely terminate or severely restrict the victim survivor’s ability to use the vehicle.
“An abuser can achieve this, for example, by remotely deactivating the victim-survivor’s digital key access or setting speed restrictions on the vehicle. This could effectively strand the victim-survivor in an unsafe location and/or limit the victim survivor’s ability to escape the abuser’s violence,” the report said.
‘Almost no accountability’ for manufacturers
Emma Buxton-Namisnyk, a co-author of the report, warned this was an emerging problem that could get worse.
“There’s really not a widespread understanding about how these technologies can be misused,” she said, adding that there was “almost no accountability” for car manufacturers to limit potential misuses.
The report recommended carmakers adopt principles which consider at the design phase how a function could be misused to facilitate abuse, and help determine if a function should not be offered because the risks outweigh the benefits.
Last year the eSafety commissioner, Julie Inman Grant, raised the alarm on the issue after receiving reports from frontline workers that cars were being used to monitor and track victim-survivors of domestic violence.
She called for improved industry safeguards, noting that it was estimated that more than 90% of new cars sold in Australia by 2031 would have embedded connectivity.
“We need urgent action to make them safer,” Inman Grant said.
The minister for social services, Tanya Plibersek, said in a statement to Guardian Australia that the government was considering what more it could do to crack down on the risk posed by smart devices, after developing a support service on technology-facilitated abuse that helps frontline workers navigate the issue.
“We’re seeing new frontiers of family and domestic violence emerge every day – we’ve seen smart fridges, cat feeders and electric vehicles all being weaponised to stalk, control and harm,” she said.
“We’ll consider what more we can do as we finalise our Second Action Plan to End Violence Against Women and Children.”

noticias.titulo: ‘Pervert glasses’ named word of the year by Macquarie dictionary, ahead of ‘nudify’ and ‘AI;DR’
noticias.resumen: Australian dictionary’s committee of word experts says winning term is ‘a succinct reflection of the state of the world in 2026’ Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast The backlash to “pervert glasses” has been swift and severe. Smartglasses such as Meta’s Ray-Bans, which have built-in cameras, microphones, and AI assistants have been banned at some Australian swimming pools and playgrounds, and condemned as a possible invasion of privacy. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
The backlash to “pervert glasses” has been swift and severe.
Smartglasses such as Meta’s Ray-Bans, which have built-in cameras, microphones, and AI assistants have been banned at some Australian swimming pools and playgrounds, and condemned as a possible invasion of privacy.
There are widespread fears about the glasses being used to film people, especially women, without their consent, and the resulting footage being posted on social media.
Now “pervert glasses” have gained a new layer of infamy: being crowned Macquarie dictionary’s word of the year.
The term “pervert glasses”, which also won the people’s choice word of the year for 2026, was described by the committee of word experts as a triumph of linguistics.
“The coinage pervert glasses is a succinct reflection of the state of the world in 2026 in so many ways,” they said.
“On the one hand, we’ve seen a massive acceleration in the capabilities of AI and products that integrate it. At the same time, the undeniably critical nickname mirrors the widespread calls to hit the brakes on this seemingly unchecked development.
“The name represents the year we’ve all endured, with AI, the manosphere, increasing surveillance in supermarkets, and more. Sure these new gadgets might be marketed as smart glasses or camera glasses, but it seems to us that pervert glasses paints a more apt reflection of the year.”
Honourable mentions from the committee went to “PMOS”, or polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, which has received greater recognition alongside spreading awareness of medical misogyny; “agentic”, which refers to the ability, especially of artificial intelligence, to make decisions independently; and “Marrickville pause”, a colloquial term referring to a temporary halt in conversation by people under Sydney’s flight path.
“Digital dementia”, which refers to short-term memory loss from a reliance on technology and artificial intelligence, received an honourable people’s choice mention.
The committee said digital dementia was “not a real medical diagnosis but that hasn’t stopped the fear of an increasing reliance on digital devices from resonating deeply”.
“People are finding that they’re struggling to navigate without Google Maps and to make and remember plans without iCal,” they said.
“It will be interesting to see if all of this outsourcing does in fact lead to impaired cognition in the long term.”
In a sign of the times, other words on the shortlist included “nudify”, referring to AI-generated pornography, and “AI;DR”, short for “AI; didn’t read”.
Last year, AI slop was dubbed the term that was the epitome of 2025 linguistics, with the committee saying it embodied the word of the year’s general theme of reflecting “a major aspect of society or societal change throughout the year”.
The committee’s choice and people’s choice winning words are chosen from the list of new entries included in the annual update of the Macquarie dictionary online. The people’s choice winner was selected from public votes cast on its website.

noticias.titulo: Up to 1.1m people eligible to join class action against Jetstar over alleged failure to refund Covid flights
noticias.resumen: Jetstar accused of issuing customers credits instead of cash refunds for flights cancelled between 2020 and late 2022 Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast More than 1 million Jetstar customers could be eligible to join a class action alleging the airline failed to refund them for flights it cancelled during the pandemic, the firm leading the lawsuit has said. The federal court on Monday confirmed it had ordered notices be sent to customers informing them of their eligibility to participate in, or opt out of, the lawsuit, with a potential trial set for March 2027. Contin
noticias.texto:
More than 1 million Jetstar customers could be eligible to join a class action alleging the airline failed to refund them for flights it cancelled during the pandemic, the firm leading the lawsuit has said.
The federal court on Monday confirmed it had ordered notices be sent to customers informing them of their eligibility to participate in, or opt out of, the lawsuit, with a potential trial set for March 2027.
Echo Law, the firm leading the class action, said it wanted to alert the public to the notices – which were due to be distributed to about 1.1 million people by 4 December – to ensure they understood it was not a scam.
The class action alleges Jetstar issued customers flight credits instead of the cash refunds they were entitled to for flights cancelled between 2020 and late 2022, after cancelling thousands of scheduled domestic and international flights.
Echo Law ran a separate class action against Qantas over its handling of Covid-19 travel credits, which the airline in March agreed to settle for $105m with no admission of liability.
In its case against Jetstar, the firm alleges the airline breached its legal obligations to customers by failing to provide refunds for cancelled flights, instead offering customers credit vouchers.
It alleges Jetstar misled customers and engaged in unconscionable conduct in breach of Australian consumer law.
It also alleges that, by holding customers’ funds that ought to have been refunded, Jetstar unlawfully benefited from this conduct.
Jetstar has denied the allegations and is defending the class action
“During the Covid-19 pandemic, Jetstar took a range of steps to respond to rapidly changing travel restrictions, while continuing to support customers affected by disruptions,” a spokesperson for the airline said.
“We provided customers with a range of options during this period depending on the circumstances, including travel credits, fee-free flight changes and refunds.”
They said the Jetstar Covid-19 vouchers remained valid as the airline had removed the expiry date in 2023.
However, Andrew Paull, a partner at Echo Law, alleged Jetstar’s policy of “pushing” customers to accept vouchers was designed to preserve the airline’s cash position.
“It held onto ordinary Australian’s [sic] money and expected customers to just be happy with credits, or in some cases nothing, when we allege they were entitled to cash refunds,” he alleged.
Paull alleged many customers had ended up paying Jetstar more than their original booking to use their credits on new fares, as they were led to believe they had little choice but to do so in order to avoid losing the value of their flights.
The firm’s lawsuit against Jetstar is scheduled for mediation in December and is expected to go to trial if the parties fail to reach an agreement.
Echo Law said the litigation funder Court House Capital was backing its class action against Jetstar.
Court House Capital’s chief investment officer, Heather Collins, accused Jetstar of seeking to “delay resolution while continuing to hold onto money that belongs to Australian families”.

noticias.titulo: Constitutional law expert brands defence bill allowing secret security rules ‘lazy and irresponsible’
noticias.resumen: Anne Twomey says lack of proper debate around bill is ‘flabbergasting’ amid concerns over extension of ministerial powers Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast Labor’s new defence bill is “lazy and irresponsible” lawmaking, one of Australia’s leading constitutional scholars has warned, claiming provisions for the government to secretly class any facility as a special security zone could raise serious legal issues. The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, claimed on Monday that critics of the “accelerating capability and protecting bases” bill were “jump[ing] at shadows”,
noticias.texto:
Labor’s new defence bill is “lazy and irresponsible” lawmaking, one of Australia’s leading constitutional scholars has warned, claiming provisions for the government to secretly class any facility as a special security zone could raise serious legal issues.
The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, claimed on Monday that critics of the “accelerating capability and protecting bases” bill were “jump[ing] at shadows”, accusing them of “absurd” claims. But parliamentary crossbenchers opposed to the bill, which was rushed through parliament with little public scrutiny, were joined on Monday by Prof Anne Twomey, who expressed alarm about what she called an increasing trend of ministers exercising discretionary powers without parliamentary oversight.
“Yes, it’s important we have defence legislation that’s flexible to deal with uncertain times, but let’s remember we’re trying to defend our democratic system of government, and we don’t want to throw it out at the same time,” Twomey told Guardian Australia.
In a video on her YouTube channel, Twomey – professor emerita at the University of Sydney – claimed it was “flabbergasting that it was not the subject of proper debate or scrutiny before this law was enacted”.
“This notion of permitting secret alterations to commonwealth, state and territory laws is a really serious development.”
The wide-ranging bill criminalises entering or photographing a defence security zone or a person or thing within, entering or leaving it, with a maximum penalty of up to seven years’ jail time, a $152,880 fine, or both. Security zones can include regular defence bases but can also extend to emergency, temporary or mobile sites as decided by a minister, with wide-ranging powers to “effectively do anything”.
Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here
The minister can make a “capability declaration”, which allows for certain activity to be carried out “without contravening certain other laws, or changes the way that other laws apply” – including state and territory laws. Such a declaration can also be held back from being declared as a legislative instrument.
After passing the Senate last week, the final bill passed the lower house on Monday evening. Labor and the Coalition supported the bill, with only a handful of crossbenchers – including Kate Chaney, Monique Ryan and Andrew Wilkie – resisting.
The Greens, David Pocock, Digital Rights Watch and other civil society groups also strongly opposed the bill. But Albanese, in his first public comments on the legislation, said “people shouldn’t jump at shadows”, claiming the powers were necessary and “just practical”.
“It will be accountable obviously for things that are designated, but we live in unsafe times,” he said on Monday.
“I find it remarkable in 2026, there’s a question over whether we need to designate areas as being protected. And we live in times where we know there are more conflicts in the world today than at any time since world war two.”
The Greens leader, David Shoebridge, called the changes “extreme wartime powers” and “an assault on civil liberties”, claiming people may be charged for breaking laws they were not even aware of.
Pocock said Albanese’s response was “disingenuous”.
“We need to protect sensitive defence facilities from threats posed by drones and other technologies. But that doesn’t mean handing the defence minister extraordinary powers without proper safeguards,” he told Guardian Australia.
“At a bare minimum, far stronger safeguards are needed around the use of ministerial powers, the need to protect civil liberties and greater transparency.”
Twomey, in her video, branded the legislation “quite disturbing”, noting declarations could be made secretly – which she said raised “serious rule of law issues” – and called out what she said was a concerning movement of giving ministers more discretionary power.
“Instead of working out what laws need to change to accommodate defence needs and then balancing them against the needs and rights of the community, the parliament has effectively just given up and instead given the power to the minister or indeed senior public servants or defence officers to make decisions that exclude the application of existing laws to defence activities.
“This is a lazy and irresponsible abandonment by parliament of both its scrutiny and its lawmaking roles, raising the risk that these powers will be misused in the future.”

noticias.texto:
Moscow accuses Estonia of acting 'on verge of unleashing open war with Russia'
Russia has accused Estonia of acting “on the verge of unleashing open war” claiming it was “tacitly providing its airspace for Ukrainian drones” to attack Russia and, erm, made “hasty accusations lacking any evidence” against Moscow.
Estonia, just like other Baltic countries, has repeatedly denied any suggestions they allowed for Ukrainian drones to operate from its territory.
“Tallinn apparently isn’t seriously considering the consequences of such a move. Closing the state border would primarily deal another blow to the Estonian economy and would boomerang on both Tallinn itself and its EU and Nato allies,” Russia said in a statement.
The statement blamed Estonia’s decision as “the latest anti-Russian stunt,” saying it “adds to the numerous hostile actions undertaken by this Baltic state in recent years.”
In a particularly worrying part of the statement, Russia also once again attacked Estonia for what it said were “repressive measures” against Russian-speaking residents – a point repeatedly denied by Estonian authorities.
“The head of the Estonian diplomatic mission was informed that such an unjustified policy of cultivating comprehensive hostility towards our country will continue to have a destabilising effect on the situation in the region and negatively impact both the well-being of Estonian residents and the already dire economic situation of this Baltic country,” it said.
The statement concluded with the Russian side “reserving the right to take comprehensive political and diplomatic measures aimed at protecting Russia’s national interests and the legitimate rights of its citizens.”
It needs to be said that there is no evidence, at least available to us, that would confirm Russia’s version of events on most points covered in their statement.
Estonia has repeatedly denied on the record pretty much everything that Russia is alleging in its statement.

The statement concluded with the Russian side “reserving the right to take comprehensive political and diplomatic measures aimed at protecting Russia’s national interests and the legitimate rights of its citizens.”
Ukrainian operation to sink Russian warship is the latest of Kyiv's daring long-range attacks
Peter Beaumont
The operation to hit the Russian warship in Libya, conducted 1,500 miles (2,400km) from the frontline in Ukraine, was the latest daring long-range assault by Kyiv’s forces.
Last week Ukraine hit the Kerch bridge – a key supply line to Russian-occupied Crimea – and the Russian Baltic seaport of Kaliningrad.
Residents in Benghazi heard loud explosions and saw flames at the naval base early on Sunday. Civil defence units rushed to the site and extinguished the fire, authorities in eastern Libya said.
The Merkury had docked to refuel and take on supplies as part of a cooperation agreement between Russia and the eastern-based government in Libya.
Vladimir Putin had taken a personal interest in the ship. In 2019 he toured the St Petersburg yard where it was being built and backed naming it after a tsarist-era brig celebrated for fighting off two Turkish warships in the Black Sea in 1829.
At the 2023 Navy Day parade, the Russian president singled it out among 30 new vessels as evidence that Russia was “consistently building up the power of its fleet”. He hailed its St George flag as “a sign of the inviolability of our naval traditions” and said it was “gratifying” that the brig’s name had been revived.
Russian state media also talked up the ship. The news agency Tass called it the “newest missile corvette”, while the channel TV Tsentr claimed its stealth technology made it “invisible to radar”.
Two survivors pulled out from rubble after Russian attack kills 11 near Kyiv
Rescuers pulled a seven-year-old boy and a 79-year-old woman alive from the rubble of a residential building in the town of Dymer in Ukraine’s Kyiv region as the death toll from Sunday’s Russian attack reached 11, officials said on Monday, as reported by Reuters.
The survivors, who were trapped for 22 hours, were identified only as Davyd and Valentyna, emergency service spokesperson Viktoriia Ruban said, without providing their full names.
Doctors were treating the boy, who was rescued from the wreckage on Sunday, and his parents were with him, Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Monday in a post on Telegram.
Rescuers were combing the rubble of a residential building, after retrieving several bodies overnight.
Zelenskyy said the fate of two people was still unknown. Search operations had to be halted several times because of the threat of further Russian attacks and the danger from Shahed drones, he said.
Russia summons Estonia's charge d’affaires in Moscow
Russia’s foreign ministry has summoned Estonia’s charge d’affaires in Moscow, Russian state news agency Tass reported,after a suspected sabotage attack on a drone maker in the Baltic state. It comes after Estonia, a Nato and EU member, announced it would close its road border crossings with Russia on security grounds for at least six months.
In a post on X on Friday, the Estonian foreign ministry wrote:
Today, the Estonian government decided to close road border crossings with Russia from 1 December in response to Russia’s continued hostile activities against Estonia and Europe.
The decision follows Russia’s ongoing sabotage and hybrid operations across Europe. Closing the crossings will reduce opportunities for Russian intelligence services to recruit people, organise sabotage and circumvent sanctions, helping to protect the security of Estonia, the EU and the Schengen area.
Estonia – which shares a border of about 220 miles (338 km) with Russia – currently has five crossing points where travellers can enter or leave Russia, according to the government.
In other news, the EU has expressed disappointment in the collapse of the Cop31 talks in Turkey where countries failed to reach a major new deal to tackle the escalating climate crisis.
Earlier today, the commission spokesperson Anna-Kaisa Itkonen said:
The European Union did not support the final draft because the interests of a few were allowed to obstruct the ambition needed by many.
The EU is responsible for 6% of global emissions and therefore for us, it was important to bring the countries that are responsible for the 94% of global emissions on board.
But the bloc faces accusations of hypocrisy for taking this posture at international climate summits while some of its member states have backed new fossil fuel infrastructure at home and give inadequate financial support for developing nations to adapt to the impacts of rising temperatures.
Amid this backdrop, the Cop31 summit became the longest-ever UN climate conference in history on Sunday, with talks stretching two days past their scheduled end time. Environment and climate correspondent Graham Readfearn joined Nour Haydar to unpick exactly what happened in our Full Story podcast:
Kremlin warns of Baltic escalation after Ukraine strike on cargo ship
Meanwhile, Moscow warned about worsening security in the Baltic Sea after a suspected Ukrainian drone strike on a separate Russian cargo ship at the weekend, AFP reported.
“It is indeed a very dangerous trend, the expansion of terrorist activity in the Baltic region... This is very dangerous. It is, of course, leading to an escalation of tensions in the region,” Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told reporters.
On Saturday, Finland said it had detected a drone attack in international waters on a Russian cargo vessel that later began drifting towards Finnish waters.
The ship, identified as the Sparta II, was anchored about 90 kilometres (nearly 50 nautical miles) east of Helsinki while efforts to put out a fire on board were under way, but was later towed towards Russian waters.
Peskov said Russia “would like to hope that the Baltic states will somehow use their influence” on Ukraine to “warn it against continuing such dangerous terrorist practices”.
Lying at the easternmost end of the Baltic along the coasts of Finland, Estonia and Russia, the Gulf of Finland is a key maritime passage for Russia, leading to the former capital, St Petersburg.
Russia's calls for return to pre-1997 European security order 'unacceptable,' Rutte says
Nato’s Rutte got a question on Russia’s demands to rewrite the European security order as part of the Ukraine peace settlement.
“We are all totally clear that the proposals Russia put forward in 2021, basically going back to … for Nato to basically move backwards from where we are now and to the 1997, borders are unacceptable. And there’s nobody in Nato who thinks this is a good idea.”
Rutte also gets pushed a bit on the Polish incident last week, as he says:
“It is clear that this is a dangerous incident. It comes from Russia. Whether it is intentional or not has to be decided, of course, by authorities. I will never speculate. I can only comment on that when we have the evidence coming out of, of the system, where Poland and other Nato allies work together to assess what exactly happened.”
Over in Berlin, Rutte is still diplomatically answering questions from national delegations and avoiding many any news.
So far his most entertaining line was about making sure he never forgets to mention Italy as a key Nato ally, because he doesn’t want to fight Italy’s defence minister, Guido Crosetto.
“If I would ever forget about Italy, then the defence minister, Guido Crossetto, whom you don’t want to get into a fight with given his build, will remind me quite forcefully, I can assure you.”
Meanwhile, Rutte is still answering questions at Nato’s parliamentary assembly – on the Arctic security and the expected review of US force posture in Europe, among others – but he’s bravely avoiding saying anything remotely new so far.
Albania denies Ukrainian drones that sank Russian warship were launched from its territory
Meanwhile, Albania has strongly denied suggestions that the naval drone attack against the Russian warship in Libya originated from its territory.
“The reports in question are inaccurate and do not reflect the facts. Albania was not involved in this incident, and its territory was neither used nor made available for the launch or facilitation of such an attack,” Albania’s ministry of foreign affairs said.
It added:
“We categorically reject these allegations, which have been presented without verifiable evidence. We call on those responsible for disseminating them to correct the record and to exercise accuracy, due diligence and responsibility when reporting on matters of such sensitivity.”

noticias.titulo: Twenty Gaza students due to leave for Ireland after winning visa battle
noticias.resumen: Group’s evacuation follows campaign to overturn decision to deny visas to more than 60 students from territory Twenty students from Gaza are to travel to Ireland to take up scholarships after winning a battle for visas that undercut the Irish government’s reputation as a champion of Palestinians . The group is due to leave the territory on Monday under strict Israeli controls and travel via Jordan to Dublin to take up places at Irish universities. Another group is expected to follow next month. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Twenty students from Gaza are to travel to Ireland to take up scholarships after winning a battle for visas that undercut the Irish government’s reputation as a champion of Palestinians.
The group is due to leave the territory on Monday under strict Israeli controls and travel via Jordan to Dublin to take up places at Irish universities. Another group is expected to follow next month.
The evacuation comes after a four-month campaign to overturn a decision by the Irish Department of Justice to deny visas to more than 60 students in Gaza who had been offered scholarships in Ireland.
The decision dismayed opposition politicians and other critics who accused the department of betraying Ireland’s record of solidarity with Palestinians.
The government backed down last week after a Dublin high court ordered the department to reconsider the decision. The minister for justice, Jim O’Callaghan, approved 48 visas. The first group is expected to arrive on Tuesday, with the remainder coming in late December.
“It’s a mix of feelings I still can’t fully describe,” Amir Alareer, 26, who is to study cybersecurity and artificial intelligence at University College Dublin, said via email on the eve of his departure from Gaza.
“There is hope and relief after months of waiting and fighting for this moment. But it is hard to feel complete joy when I am leaving my family behind in Gaza, and when 28 of my fellow students, who hold the same visas and share the same dreams, are still here waiting.”
The students originally expected to come in summer, and had supporting paperwork from Irish universities, but in July the Department of Justice rejected the visa applications. “The refusals hit us hard,” said Alareer.
The department demanded bank statements, proof of intention to return and other documents and said any appeal would have to be made by post, saying screening and verification were integral to the immigration system.
The students said such documents had not previously been requested and that Gaza’s banking and postal service had been destroyed. Ivana Bacik, a legislator and leader of the Labour party, accused the department of using “spurious reasons” amid a hardening of immigration policy.
Alareer helped to lead a campaign from Gaza that was backed in Ireland by demonstrators, a petition and an open letter signed by actors, writers and artists including Hozier, Nicola Coughlan and the rap group Kneecap. “Running a campaign from Gaza, through blackouts and displacement, was not easy, but I knew that if we stayed silent, our case would be forgotten,” said Alareer.
In October, the high court ruled that there were “significant and demonstrable errors” in the refusal of a visa to Shaymaa Abudalu, a 20-year-old who had been offered an engineering scholarship at University College Cork, and who was the lead case in a batch of similar lawsuits. A high court judge welcomed the decision last week to grant 48 visas and said “huge progress” had been made.
Among the students are five members of a dance troupe who have been offered places at the Irish World Academy of Music and Dance at the University of Limerick.
Alareer, who studied engineering at Al-Azhar University – Gaza, said Israel’s attacks on Gaza had destroyed his home and displaced the family several times. “The hardest experience of all was the famine, when we couldn’t find even a single kilo of flour.” Floods have impeded recent relief efforts.
His family was proud of his scholarship, he said, but saying goodbye would be hard. “They are happy that I finally have this opportunity, but leaving them behind after everything we have been through together is incredibly difficult.”
After studying software and innovation in Dublin, Alareer plans to return to Al-Azhar University and establish a cybersecurity department. “I want to build a generation of Palestinian engineers and researchers who can protect our digital future. Gaza will be rebuilt, and its systems must be rebuilt securely, by its own people.”

noticias.titulo: Arctic air brings colder temperatures to Europe this week
noticias.resumen: After a warmer-than-average November so far globally, a cold snap is on the horizon in parts of Europe While average global temperatures continue to set records through one of the strongest El Niños on record, temperatures across a large swathe of Europe could plunge this week, as Arctic air sweeps in. On Friday, the global average temperature was 2.12C higher than the preindustrial average, the biggest ever anomaly and equivalent to 1.22C above the 1991-2020 climate average. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
While average global temperatures continue to set records through one of the strongest El Niños on record, temperatures across a large swathe of Europe could plunge this week, as Arctic air sweeps in.
On Friday, the global average temperature was 2.12C higher than the preindustrial average, the biggest ever anomaly and equivalent to 1.22C above the 1991-2020 climate average.
But in parts of Europe, high pressure building over Scandinavia and low pressure shifting south-east into western Russia will open a corridor of cold air from the north. Temperatures in the Baltics and in countries such as Germany, Poland and Ukraine are likely to fall widely below zero from Monday, with ice days – in which temperatures stay below 0C all day – expected from midweek. By the weekend, temperatures could be 5-15C below average, reaching double-digit negatives on higher ground.
The low pressure over eastern Europe and western Russia will bring extensive snowfall. Southern Poland, Belarus, eastern Ukraine and south-eastern parts of the Baltics will be the first to see widespread snow, which could reach up to 10cm in southern Poland.
Later in the week, as a smaller area of low pressure pushes into western and central Europe, significant snow is expected to spread across southern Germany, Austria and Czechia, where depths of 10-20cm could build. The Alps could get a significant dumping of snow, a welcome boost for the region’s ski resorts which will open in the coming weeks.
Into the weekend and the start of December, high pressure is set to remain dominant across northern Europe, maintaining below-average temperatures in central and eastern Europe and possibly extending into the Balkans. There are also hints that the sudden stratospheric warming earlier this month could finally begin influencing the lower atmosphere, with high pressure extending farther west and perhaps bringing cold easterly winds into western Europe and the UK, although confidence on this is low.
The cold in Europe is in stark contrast to the global picture. This October was the warmest on record, with an average global temperature of 15.35C, 0.9C above the 1991-2020 average and 1.75C above the estimated preindustrial level. It was the third month in a row above 1.5C, following August and September, and while parts of Europe, including the UK, have seen below-average temperatures so far this November, global temperatures this month have continued to run above average.

noticias.titulo: Chamonix mayor plans tourist limits for Alpine beauty spot

noticias.texto:
In the Alpine town of Chamonix, most tourist paths lead to the national park with spectacular views across Mont Blanc and the shrinking blue glaciers. In the summer, up to 4,000 tourists a day hike or take the cable car to the lakes high in the Aiguilles Rouges nature reserve.
Many of them descend disappointed. Once a place of nature and tranquility, the beauty spot’s visitor numbers have more than doubled since 2020, spoiling the experience and leaving trails of litter, threatening the environment and wildlife.
Now Chamonix plans to become the first town in the Alps to introduce visitor quotas, to limit the number of hikers around Lac Blanc and the Lacs des Chéserys.
The town’s mayor, Francois-Xavier Laffin, announced last week that from next June tourists would be required to book in advance to visit the area. After booking, they will receive a QR code granting them access.
Laffin championed the quotas after visiting Marseille, where a similar scheme was introduced limiting access to the Calanques national park in 2022. He said the aim was “reserve to preserve”, adding that visiting the mountains would still be free but subject to conditions.
Laffin said mass tourism was having a major impact on the environment, wildlife and on visitors’ enjoyment of the reserve. “Lac Blanc is one place we cannot let continue to deteriorate” he said, adding that the council was looking at additional regulations in other areas.
The plan, which needs the final approval of the local prefect, would restrict the number of visitors to the Lac Blanc area to between 600 and 1,000 a day for four months from June to September.
Christian Schwoehrer, the director of the Haute-Savoie Nature Conservation Agency, which manages the reserve, said: “We will see how it works for the next three years and if it does then it will be extended and maybe applied to other areas. This is a nature reserve but when there are thousands of visitors a day there’s no peace for the protected species or local people and we need stronger measures to control this.
“At points of entry [to the reserve] there will be ‘eco guards’ to verify that people have reserved. If they haven’t, they could be fined, though our intention is to avoid fining people by making sure they know in advance and cannot say they weren’t warned.”
The quota plan has met some local opposition from the land’s legal owners. Lac Blanc sits in just under 3 sq miles of private estate held by 35 families under a historic entity that has existed for centuries and is now managed by the Montagne de Chéserys company.
One of the landowners, Guillaume Ravanel, a mountain guide, agreed tourist numbers need controlling but suggested visitors should be asked to pay a small entry fee to access the reserve.
Frédéric Charlet-Berguerand, a co-manager of Montagne de Chéserys, told Le Monde: “This quota system is innovative and virtuous.” Contacted by the Guardian, he added: “That said, there will be no quotas on our private property until they are approved by a meeting of the owners,” due to be held in December. “Let’s not put the cart before the horse.”
Laffin said the quota plan would cost about €590,000 for the three-year “experimental” period. Financing has yet to be arranged but he said part would be raised by Chamonix and other local authorities and the town would be applying for a grant from the government’s “green fund” to help protect the environment. Private sponsors are also being sought.
The mayor, elected in March, has made managing tourist numbers a priority. He is also looking at tighter controls on the three-week Ultra-Trail du Mont Blanc, an ultramarathon circling the Mont-Blanc massif through France, Italy and Switzerland that begins in Chamonix. The event, started in 2003, now attracts 10,000 runners and up to 50,000 visitors each August.
Schwoehrer said summer crowds meant local people were avoiding the reserve. A recent survey found that 55% of visitors who ascended to Lac Blanc said they were disappointed by the experience, he said.
“We don’t want to stop people going there, just have a few stronger rules. It’s a compromise to ensure that visitors have a good experience and at the same time the natural environment is protected.”

noticias.titulo: From mocked to mainstream: how Spain’s far-right Vox transformed its fortunes
noticias.resumen: Party that won just 0.2% of the vote in 2016 is on course for almost 20% this time and could be part of next government Almost exactly eight years ago, a video clip of a stocky, bearded man riding a horse through western Andalucía went viral in Spain . The rider was Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right Vox party, the soundtrack was a bombastic snatch of the Lord of the Rings score, and the caption was an equally unsubtle callback to the 700-year fight to wrest the Iberian peninsula from Islamic rule. “La Reconquista comenzará en tierras andaluzas,” it read – the reconquest will begin
noticias.texto:
Almost exactly eight years ago, a video clip of a stocky, bearded man riding a horse through western Andalucía went viral in Spain. The rider was Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right Vox party, the soundtrack was a bombastic snatch of the Lord of the Rings score, and the caption was an equally unsubtle callback to the 700-year fight to wrest the Iberian peninsula from Islamic rule. “La Reconquista comenzará en tierras andaluzas,” it read – the reconquest will begin on Andalucían soil.
Celebrated by some, jeered by others – and inventively lampooned by those with sufficient skill and time on their hands – the video didn’t seem quite as amusing three weeks later when Vox broke through into the political mainstream by winning 12 seats in Andalucía’s regional parliament.
Until that moment, the prevailing wisdom had been that Spain’s experiences of the Franco dictatorship had inoculated the country against the far right, and that Vox was a tiny, fringe outfit whose prospects were terminally limited after it had picked up just 0.2% of the vote in the 2016 general election.
Fast-forward to late 2026 and the horseman seems less comical still. Vox, now the third largest party in Spain, is poised to pick up almost 20% of the vote in the snap general election on 29 November and, very possibly, to form a coalition government with the conservative People’s party (PP).
Abascal is going all out as the campaign enters its final days, peppering his patriotic appeals with familiar, baseless conspiracy theories. Last week he suggested that the socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, was conspiring with dark forces to undermine democracy and change the country’s demographic makeup.
“The next elections may be the last that Spaniards get to decide,” he posted on X. “That’s what Sánchez and his accomplices at home and abroad are working toward … Vote so you don’t get replaced.”
Catalan catalyst
How did Vox’s fortunes transform so massively and so quickly? The party was founded in late 2013 by disenchanted PP members who felt the conservatives had grown too indulgent of the demands of Basque and Catalan nationalist parties, but it struggled to make its mark. The highlight of its early years, during which it relied on hefty sum donated by the Iranian exile group the National Council of Resistance of Iran, was unfurling a large Spanish flag on the Rock of Gibraltar.
All that changed in the autumn of 2017 when a Catalan push for independence pitched Spain into crisis and left the PP government looking soft and ill-prepared. The crisis proved a godsend for Vox, simultaneously vindicating its distrust of Catalan and Basque nationalist parties and allowing it to position itself as an uncompromising defender of Spanish unity.
“Vox’s initial growth was driven by a reaction to Catalan nationalism – specifically, the sense around 2017 that Spain might fall apart,” says Miguel González, an El País journalist who covers Vox and the author of a new book, The Extremist Galaxy: Funders, Allies and Strategies of the New Far Right.
It gave Vox the profile it needed to pursue what González considers its most significant move: dragging immigration into mainstream politics and forcing a rattled PP to lurch further to the right.
“It was only an issue in a few specific places with high levels of immigration – such as El Ejido in Almería, or certain areas in Murcia,” González says. “[But] Vox has managed to put this issue on the political agenda, and, what’s more, the PP has gradually come to adopt some of their positions.”
This summer’s mass influx into Spain’s north African territory of Ceuta, when more than 80,000 men, women and children crossed over from Morocco, is a case in point. Abascal called it “an invasion and an act of war promoted by Morocco”, while the PP’s leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo urged the expulsion of all who had entered, regardless of their age and individual circumstances.
The PP’s efforts to stop its voters slipping into the embrace of its far-right rival have led it into all sorts of contortions. Although Feijóo’s predecessor, Pablo Casado, famously rounded on Vox in 2020, accusing Abascal and co of peddling a politics based on “fear, anger, resentment and revenge”, the PP has repeatedly entered into regional coalition governments with Vox and now runs four of Spain’s autonomous regions with the party.
Vicente Valentim, a professor of political science at Spain’s IE University and the author of The Normalisation of the Radical Right, says that when centre-right parties adopt the language and postures of the far right, they end up legitimising it.
“After the initial normalisation moment when these parties first become successful – entering parliament etc – there’s a second step,” he says. “The centre right moves closer to them, starts speaking the same way that they do, starts going into coalitions.”
This can prove electorally expensive, he says. “The PP has moved closer to Vox, and when you have two parties that have such similar views on an issue as important as immigration, [some] voters simply prefer the original to the copy, and so they’re going to vote for Vox.”
Hate figures
Alongside a fixation on immigration, Vox has also brought its predilection for hate figures into the mainstream of Spanish politics – be they the secessionist former Catalan president Carles Puigdemont, the former leader of the leftwing Podemos Pablo Iglesias, or Sánchez.
“Vox talks about traitors and about criminals,” says González. “What Vox is doing isn’t offering political assessments, it’s making legal judgments.”
Abascal’s loathing of Sánchez is well documented – in 2023, the Vox leader said a day would come when the Spanish people would “want to see [Sánchez] strung up by his feet” – and his party’s manifesto vows to “undertake legal proceedings to have Sánchez and his government prosecuted for treason and crimes against the security of the state, based on their actions during the invasion of Ceuta”.
The party’s increasingly strident language has been matched by a more recent refusal to sever ties with some of the more extreme figures in its ranks and in its orbit.
In the run-up to the first of the two general elections in 2019, Vox was forced to drop the historian and commentator Fernando Paz from its list of candidates after Jewish groups complained about his “denialist and revisionist” approach to the Holocaust. Today he sits on the honorary board of the Foundation for the Defence of the Spanish Nation, a Vox-aligned platform of which Abascal is a co-founder and board member.
One pro-Israel lobbying group has expressed concerns in the past about Jordi de la Fuente, a Vox member and former neo-Nazi party leader who heads the Solidarity trade union, which was created by Vox. De la Fuente, who is awaiting trial for his alleged role in a violent attack on a centre housing unaccompanied migrant children in 2019, is standing as Vox’s candidate in Tarragona. Vox has insisted its candidate is innocent of a charge of “inciting hatred, hostility, violence or discrimination on the grounds of national origin”.
Alejandro Baer, a sociologist at the Spanish National Research Council who specialises in memory, genocide studies and contemporary Jewish studies, says: “A few years ago, the party was forced to distance itself from them, but now they don’t seem to represent a liability. Vox appears to be sufficiently consolidated and legitimate to openly incorporate people with backgrounds in these extremist spaces.”
Generation gap
Vox’s trajectory is plain to see in Rioja, a small town in the eastern Andalucían province of Almería. Long a socialist stronghold, Rioja was the only municipality where Vox finished first in May’s regional election – a poll that resulted in another PP-Vox coalition, after the conservatives lost their absolute majority. And yet the quiet town, whose palm trees and bougainvillaeas rustle in the warm November breeze, doesn’t exactly have the feel of a far-right frontier. Its divisions appear more generational than political.
Few of the younger people walking down the main road that bisects Rioja are surprised by Vox’s strong showing here. Fewer still appear bothered by Sánchez’s warning that a PP-Vox coalition will “roll back progress” and lead to the loss of hard-won social advances.
“My own ideology tends more to the right,” says Patricio López, 29, who works in an agricultural company. “I’ve noticed that people of my age tend to be more rightwing than leftwing, and I think that’s because they feel like they’ve been shortchanged. Housing, for example, is a much bigger issue for young people than it is for older people. And the left hasn’t looked after young people over the past eight years.”
One older resident, however, believes Vox’s surge in Rioja has more to do with protest votes from the young and the proximity of a large military camp than a rejection of its socialist past.
“I think it was just a gesture of distrust and revenge in the way Spanish politics is these days – it’s pure partisan theatre and it’s all very Game of Thrones,” says Rafael Ruiz Martínez, 63, who works for the local council. But he adds: “For those of us who lived through some of the Franco era, the Vox stuff doesn’t sound good.”
Another younger local man, who prefers not to give his name, agrees many people are sick of traditional politics and of a political class that has failed them.
“I reckon whoever gets in – whatever their political stripe – will do what others have done; they’ll dip into the till,” he says. “But politics is politics and people want a change.”

noticias.titulo: Israel’s destruction of Gaza has created a ‘toxic wasteland’, experts find
