noticias.texto:
Israel’s destruction of Gaza has left a devastating environmental legacy with poisoned water, contaminated soil and toxic air threatening the life-support systems that the population depends on for survival, according to a report.
Israel’s military assault has created widespread contamination across the entire strip, the report by Oxfam and the Conflict and Environment Observatory (Ceobs) finds, with heavy metals, explosive residues, asbestos from destroyed buildings, and sewage making the air, soil and water dangerous for Palestinians for decades to come.
Oxfam International’s executive director, Amitabh Behar, said: “Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza includes military assaults on its environment, which are environmental war crimes threatening life now and for generations to come.”
He said the “destruction and contamination of Gaza” have “fundamentally degraded the environmental conditions necessary for human safety and survival” and breach Israel’s legal obligations under international humanitarian and human rights law.
“Palestinians living in Gaza are being exposed to toxins … through air, food, water and via direct contact with contaminated soils and debris. These risks will persist for generations to come, unless clean-up, remediation and recovery actions are prioritised.”
In 2025 and earlier this year, the UN independent international commission of inquiry found that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza and that Israeli officials, including the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, incited these acts. The Israeli mission in Geneva said Israel rejected the commission’s “libellous sham”. Netanyahu is separately wanted by the international criminal court (ICC) for war crimes.
Oxfam’s report gives the most comprehensive picture to date of what it calls the “toxic wasteland” created by the Israeli assault which has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and wounded at least 175,000, while thousands still remain unaccounted for under the rubble.
Using satellite imagery, remote sensing, scientific analysis and other open-source data, it concludes contamination in Gaza is “widespread, severe and consequential, with serious implications for public health and civilian survival”.
Behar said: “It is horrifying to begin to understand the extent of toxic contamination being faced by the population, who can neither escape nor protect themselves properly from the dangers. In an area as small, oppressed and densely populated as Gaza, continuous exposure is inevitable, with people surrounded by waste and sewage, spreading pests and the risk of disease growing.
“Raw sewage is pouring into the sea and leaking into the ground, while the destruction of Gaza’s sanitation systems leaves people with little protection from the contamination around them.”
He added the “associated health consequences will be severe, with children and pregnant women among those facing the highest risks”.
The UN Environment Programme (UNEP) estimates that Israel’s military operations have generated more than 61m tonnes of debris across the territory, turning Gaza’s destroyed homes, neighbourhoods and infrastructure into a vast reservoir of potentially hazardous materials.
The report’s author, Lama Abdul Samad, a global water and sanitation specialist at Oxfam, said tackling the environmental damage in Gaza will be “highly challenging because contamination is dispersed across the urban rubble, farmland, water systems and soils, while unexploded ordnance continues to restrict safe access to most areas”.
“The analysis highlights the urgent need for Israel to grant access for a detailed environmental assessment on the ground to clarify the risks to public health and identify options for urgent harm-reduction measures. Restoration is likely to require extensive clearance, monitoring and specialised remediation of affected areas from contaminants such as explosive residues, organic pollutants and heavy metals.”
Behar said that as international attention increasingly turned to Gaza’s reconstruction, environmental recovery must not be treated as an afterthought, but as a vital undertaking in parallel.
“Rebuilding Gaza without simultaneously understanding and addressing the extent of environmental contamination risks creating long-term public health consequences for generations to come,” he said.
A spokesperson from the Israeli embassy in the UK questioned the methodology underpinning the report, saying its reliance on satellite imagery and what they described as unverified assumptions “falls short of professional standards”.
They added: “Hamas itself claimed to have excavated more than 500 km of tunnels beneath Gaza, exceeding the total route length of the London Underground. A report on Gaza’s soil and groundwater that fails to examine excavation on that scale is fundamentally incomplete. That omission undermines the credibility of its conclusions.”

noticias.titulo: Ian Huntley killed by inmate in ‘cold-blooded murder’ planned weeks in advance, court told
noticias.resumen: Jurors hear Anthony Russell killed Soham murderer by hitting him repeatedly over head with metal bar A prisoner killed the Soham murderer Ian Huntley with a heavy metal bar in a “cold-blooded” attack that had been planned weeks in advance, a court heard. Jurors were told that Anthony Russell, 44, repeatedly hit the 52-year-old over the head in the attack at the high-security HMP Frankland, near Durham. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
A prisoner killed the Soham murderer Ian Huntley with a heavy metal bar in a “cold-blooded” attack that had been planned weeks in advance, a court heard.
Jurors were told that Anthony Russell, 44, repeatedly hit the 52-year-old over the head in the attack at the high-security HMP Frankland, near Durham.
Matthew Bean KC, prosecuting, told jurors at Newcastle crown court that they may feel no sympathy for the Soham killer, who murdered Holly Wells and Jessica Chapman in 2002, but the case was not about his “appalling actions” but the manner in which he had died.
Russell denies a single count of murder.
Bean said: “At shortly after 9am on 26 February 2026, the prosecution say that the defendant in this trial, Anthony Russell, murdered Ian Huntley, by striking him repeatedly to the head with a heavy metal bar. The prosecution case is that this was a cold-blooded murder that had been planned weeks in advance of its execution.
“It happened in a prison, HMP Frankland, where both Anthony Russell and Ian Huntley were serving prisoners. At the time, both men were serving sentences of life imprisonment for offences of murder.
“The defendant, Anthony Russell, you will hear, had previously been convicted of the murder of three people, these offences having taken place in October 2020. The name of the man he killed, Ian Huntley, will be known to many, if not all of you.
“He had been convicted of the murder of two girls, Holly Wells and Jessica Chapman, that took place in the village of Soham in Cambridgeshire in August 2002. These were offences that, for entirely understandable reasons, aroused feelings of disgust and anger.
“Due to the nature of his offences, you may feel little or no sympathy for what happened to him. More than that, the prosecution do not ask for sympathy.
“Ultimately, this case is not about the appalling actions of Ian Huntley during his life, but the manner of his death. The prosecution well understands the emotions that may be stirred during this trial.
“It is essential, however, to be true to your oath or affirmation, to put emotion to one side, to try this case on the evidence and the evidence alone, and to come to verdicts based on that evidence.”
Bean told jurors the two murderers were held on A wing at the high-security prison and there had been “tension” between them in the months leading up to the killing.
About a year earlier, in March 2025, prison staff witnessed an argument between them in which they threatened one another and had to be separated.
They later agreed with staff that nothing further would happen, the court heard.
About 10 months later, Russell was seen with a black eye, and told staff he had fallen.
Bean said: “Some members of staff believed, however, that someone had assaulted him and you will hear some evidence during the trial that indicates that it may have been caused by Ian Huntley.”
Those incidents were the only two issues between the men in the prison records, the court heard.
The trial continues.

noticias.titulo: Former Tory PMs ‘can’t face up to their bad Brexit deal’, says Burnham – UK politics live
noticias.resumen: Rishi Sunak joins other former Tory PMs in urging Burnham not to reopen the debate on Brexit In her speech, Louise Haigh announced that Juergen Maier, chair of Great British Energy, has been appointed as the government’s northern economy and reindustrialisation commissioner. She said: Giving business the confidence to invest here, and create good jobs in our industrial heartlands. Creating good quality jobs in all parts of the country. The role of the private sector is essential to fulfilling that. That is why I am delighted to announce today a new northern economy and reindustrialisation comm
noticias.texto:
Burnham says Tory ex-PMs urging him not to review Brexit 'can't face up to the bad deal they did'
Speaking to reporters this morning, Andy Burnham also accused the four former Tory PMs who have urged him not to reopen the Brexit debate (see 11.48am) of refusing to accept how bad the settlement they achieved for Britain actually was.
Asked about their comments, he said:
I’m not sure they’re the people I’ll be listening to here because they left Britain with a bad Brexit deal.
They’re stuck in the past because they can’t face up to the bad deal that they did.
I’m not a prime minister that’s going to be stuck in the past. I want to lead Britain forward to a more hopeful future, get the economy growing again, get the cost of living down for people, lower energy bills.
All of these things can be achieved by a more positive, constructive relationship with the European Union.
I believe it will be better for Britain to take this path, and I won’t be listening to those voices who put us here in the first place.
Burnham's deal with EU will increase costs for food companies importing fresh produce from outside EU, trade body says
A food industry executive told the World at One that he did not accept Andy Burnham’s claim about the food standards deal agreed with the EU on Friday cutting prices for consumers. (See 1.30pm.)
Nigel Jenney, chief executive of the Fresh Produce Consortium, said that while Burnham was talking about advantages for food exporters, the situation was not the same for food imports.
He said around 65% of fresh produce consumed in the UK was imported, and that the deal would lead to more checks being imposed on imports coming from outside the EU.
Currently, checks on fresh produce being imported from outside the EU are minimal, he claimed.
He went on:
Many of those products that are subject to no checks will be subject to 100% checks. That is tens of thousands of consignments on a daily, weekly, annual basis. It is massive for our industry.
Sadly, all these costs and fees are officially controlled by our government and others. Therefore we cannot absorb these costs as an industry. We simply don’t enjoy those margins.
So these costs, which we estimate to be at least £300m a year, will be passed on to consumers in the months to come unless the government takes the opportunity to adjust the agreement to facilitate great value fresh produce from the rest of the world in UK stores.
Sam Lowe, a consultant and trade specialist, told the programme that he was surprised the government chose to promote the benefit of the Friday deal by focusing on lower costs for consumers because the main benefit was likely to be felt by companies exporting food, not importing it.
For food importers, he accepted that there would be more checks for items being imported from outside the EU, which would lead to “cost pressures”.
But people importing items from the EU might see some reduction in checks because, even though the UK largely chose not to impose fresh regulations after Brexit, some new requirements have been coming in, he said.
Burnham says Tory ex-PMs urging him not to review Brexit 'can't face up to the bad deal they did'
Speaking to reporters this morning, Andy Burnham also accused the four former Tory PMs who have urged him not to reopen the Brexit debate (see 11.48am) of refusing to accept how bad the settlement they achieved for Britain actually was.
Asked about their comments, he said:
I’m not sure they’re the people I’ll be listening to here because they left Britain with a bad Brexit deal.
They’re stuck in the past because they can’t face up to the bad deal that they did.
I’m not a prime minister that’s going to be stuck in the past. I want to lead Britain forward to a more hopeful future, get the economy growing again, get the cost of living down for people, lower energy bills.
All of these things can be achieved by a more positive, constructive relationship with the European Union.
I believe it will be better for Britain to take this path, and I won’t be listening to those voices who put us here in the first place.
Andy Burnham has revived claims that the food standards deal he agreed with the EU on Friday will cut prices for consumers.
Visiting a Morrisons’ regional distribution centre in Kent, Burnham said:
We’re here at Morrisons, and they have told me that the deal will lift the pressure off the weekly shop.
They’ve just shown me a stack of paperwork which they have to fill in when they export from here to their store in Gibraltar.
If you remove that paperwork, that red tape, you can lower the cost, and they say it will lower the pressure on the weekly shop.
This deal is not about re-joining. That’s not what’s on the table here.
It’s just a better, practical working relationship with the European Union.
In an interview with the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg yesterday, Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, conceded that the British Retail Consortium has said the deal is “unlikely to have any impact on prices in the near future”. But he said the BRC has also said the deal should “reduce pressure on trading costs”, which implies it should cut prices.
Badenoch claims Good Friday agreement won't stop Tories leaving ECHR, saying 'it's not issue unless people make it one'
A conference attendee from the Law Society of Northern Ireland asked what impact the Tory plan to leave the European convention on human right (ECHR) would have on Northern Ireland, where deals like the Good Friday agreement and the Windsor framework are based on the UK being party to the ECHR.
Badenoch said the Tories had already been looking at this. She said human rights laws did not start in 1998, and that “quite a lot of the human rights legislation which we have we can put back into common law and into statute”. She went on:
We’ve also looked at potential conflict with the Good Friday agreement, and we don’t see why that should be an issue. It’s not really an issue unless people choose to make it one.
We look at the wording of the text. There is no conflict.
She defended the proposal to leave the ECHR.
At the moment, we cannot remove people who don’t belong in this country. We are not able to stop the vexatious prosecution of our veterans. We’re not even allowed to decide who gets benefits and who doesn’t.
But she conceded that implementing this policy “is going to require cooperation from Stormont and even with the Republic of Ireland itself”. Those conversations had started, she said. She added:
I want people to be reassured that we understand the significant difficulties of this. We’re not pretending that this is an easy thing to do.
And what I have said is that we need to explain the plans we’re going to deliver.
Badenoch says when she was business secretary in the last government, she felt like she was “the customer complaints department of the government”. She said she was constantly dealing with businesses protesting about decisions taken by other departments, like the Treasury. Now she is in charge, she says.
Badenoch said the Tories have a five-point plan to boost growth. She proposed: 1) cutting the cost off energy; 2) making the labour market more flexible by repealing parts of the Employment Rights Act; 3) cuttting taxes; 4) getting rid of red tape; and 5) championing business.
Badenoch tells CBI that business should worry about state control under Labour
Badenoch told her CBI audience that they should ignore what Louise Haigh told them this morning. (See 10.58am.) She said:
[Haigh] told you that public control of business should not alarm anyone in this room. You should be alarmed because what they mean by public control is state control – controlled by Labour politicians.
And don’t forget, these are the same Labour politicians who didn’t know that putting up national insurance would make it more expensive to hire people. These are the same Labour politicians who didn’t understand that equalising the minimum wage would destroy jobs for young people.
So yes, I would be alarmed if politicians with that level of ignorance were coming for your business.
Badenoch complains about 'too many politicians', like Burnham, being obsessed with Brexit
Kemi Badenoch is now addressing the CBI conference. She starts by saying she was not an MP at the time of the Brexit referendum, and that she cannot believe that Andy Burnham has chosen to reopen the debate on this topic. She says:
I know I speak for the majority of people when I say reopening the Brexit debate is the last thing our country needs right now. There are many more urgent priorities.
I’m not saying that Britain’s relationship with the EU doesn’t matter. Of course it matters. But, for too many politicians, the EU question has become a totemic issue around which their entire existence revolves.
In 2016, some people thought that all our problems would be solved by leaving the EU. Now others, including the prime minister, seem to think that all our problems would be solved by rejoining. Both sides are wrong.
It is quite bold for Badenoch to complain about people like Andy Burnham being obsessed with Brexit because, for much of the past decade the Conservative party acted like a pro-Brexit cult; there were many MPs, like Badenoch herself, whose careers would never have flourished if they had not been hardline Brexiters.
But, as explained earlier (see 11.48am), the party now has a clear incentive to change the subject.
Farage claims British business has 'done well' since Brexit in areas where it has diverged from EU law
We have also had overnight quotes from Reform UK about what Nigel Farage will say when he speaks to the CBI conference later. He will argue that the UK has “done well” in areas where it has diverged from EU law, and he will pledge to repeal the deal if he wins the next election. He will say:
Where we have actually used our freedom and diverged, British business has done well. In precision breeding and agricultural technology we are moving faster than the EU’s cautious system and developing crops that need fewer chemicals and deliver higher yields. In the City we have begun to tailor the rules to our strengths instead of copying one-size-fits-all directives. In AI and novel foods our lighter-touch approach is attracting investment that the EU’s heavier regime is scaring off.
Divergence is our strength. Going backwards into the EU’s orbit would be a disaster for the very British businesses that are trying to compete and innovate. The future is an independent Britain that sets its own rules, trains its own people and lets competition flourish, not a country that hands the advantage back to Brussels and the biggest corporates. That’s why only Reform have committed to reversing the Brexit reset deal in full.
Farage is wrong on his final point; in his interview with the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg yesterday, Alex Burghart, the deputy Conservative leader, said the Tories would abandon the deal if they won the next election. Asked if they would do this even if it led to positive outcomes, he replied: “I don’t think that there will be good outcomes from it.”
Badenoch says Burnham's deal with EU 'terrible', and UK should be focusing more on trade where growth much higher
Kemi Badenoch is going to use her speech to the CBI to repeat Tory claims that Andy Burnham’s deal with the EU on Friday was flawed. According to extracts released in advance, she will say:
Of course [Burnham] got a terrible deal, because he made it clear he wouldn’t turn it down.
It is also thinking way too small.
To put 0.4% [the amount Burnham says the deal will increase GDP] into perspective, at the budget last month the OBR cut its forecast for economic growth next year from 1.6% to just 1%.
It’s not even going to get us back to where we were.
You have to weigh the benefits up against the cost.
Of course, Europe will always remain an important market. but it is not the market of the future.
France has been growing at 0.9% a year since Brexit, Germany at 0.1%.
Compare that with India which is growing at 7%, Indonesia at 5%. Even the US, at 3.5%.
Sunak joins list of former Tory PMs saying Burnham wrong to open debate on rejoining EU
Rishi Sunak has become the latest former prime minister to argue that Andy Burnham is wrong to open up a debate about the case for reversing Brexit.
In an interview with Sky News broadcast today, the former Tory leader said:
I think Andy Burnham himself has said he wouldn’t want to go back into Europe when it comes to areas like financial services or technology and that’s because they’re so critical to our future growth …
I certainly wouldn’t reopen up this whole debate about rejoining the EU. Obviously, it’s divisive. But we saw last time around, it was also all-consuming. So it ends up being a huge distraction for government.
Boris Johnson, David Cameron and Theresa May have also all argued that Burnham is making a mistake. Here is Peter Walker’s take on May’s intervention yesterday.
Many commentators have argued that the Tory criticisms of Burnham on this issue are self-interested, for two reasons. First, given that Conservative governments delivered Brexit and that it is now widely regarded by voters as a mistake, the party would rather avoid talking about it in the first place. Second, a debate on rejoining would split the Tories, because almost a third of their supporters would be in favour.
What Haigh told CBI about government plans to curb powers of quangos
And this is what Louise Haigh said in her speech this morning about curbing the power of quangos. (See 9.32am.)
The prime minister is clear eyed about the limitations of centralised government, and the failings of politics. That is why we are rewiring the state.
Over decades, politicians were content to duck accountability by giving responsibility away from ministers to a sprawling web of regulators and arm’s length bodies.
More than twenty statutory consultees, all with veto power …
Notionally bound by statutory deadlines, but obfuscation has become habitual …
As part of rewiring the state we will reform arm’s length bodies to increase public control
We will take a look at each of their functions and pose the challenge: what should be devolved, what can be dissolved and what could be delivered departments We’ve already begun that process with the Environment Agency, Natural England, Ofwat and the Drinking Water Inspectorate
Where decisions are intrinsic to the fabric of a place, those powers and responsibilities must be made in that place, not in Whitehall.

noticias.titulo: Environment Agency and Natural England face axe in Labour quango cull
noticias.resumen: Louise Haigh says the two environmental regulators are being reviewed as part of shake-up of arm’s length bodies Ministers are considering abolishing two of England’s biggest environmental regulators in an attempt to give politicians greater control over what gets built and where. Louise Haigh, the de facto deputy prime minister, said on Monday that the Environment Agency and Natural England were being reviewed as part of a wider shake-up of arm’s length bodies. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Ministers are considering abolishing two of England’s biggest environmental regulators in an attempt to give politicians greater control over what gets built and where.
Louise Haigh, the de facto deputy prime minister, said on Monday that the Environment Agency and Natural England were being reviewed as part of a wider shake-up of arm’s length bodies.
Successive governments have argued that reforming or scrapping large environmental watchdogs would help free companies to build more houses and infrastructure. Environmentalists, however, warn such a move would endanger wildlife and do little to boost growth.
Haigh told the CBI conference on Monday: “Over decades, politicians were content to duck accountability by giving responsibility away from ministers to a sprawling web of regulators and arm’s length bodies, more than 20 statutory consultees, all with veto power, notionally bound by statutory deadlines. But obfuscation has become normal.”
She added: “As part of rewiring the state, we will reform arm’s length bodies to increase public control. We will look at each of their functions and pose the challenge: what should be devolved, what can be dissolved and what can be delivered by departments?
“We’ve already begun that process with the Environment Agency, Natural England, Ofwat and the Drinking Water Inspectorate.”
The proposals have angered many in the environmental world. Tony Juniper, the chair of Natural England, said his organisation had helped speed up building by reviewing rules such as those that protect bats and newts.
Supporters say Natural England and the Environment Agency enforce legal duties that would still have to be enforced even if they did not exist. “A healthy natural environment is vital for economic development and at Natural England we are very proud of all the work we have done during recent years to unite our national ambitions for growth while achieving nature’s recovery,” Juniper said.
“It’s never been the case that healthy nature is in opposition to economic development, but actually enables it. It’s possible to do both.”
Craig Bennett, the chief executive of the Wildlife Trusts, said: “For over 16 years, politicians have been claiming that the regulations and regulators who protect English wildlife are some sort of obstacle on a path to prosperity. They are not. For over 16 years, protections have been chipped away and the woods, meadows, skylarks and hares they protect are suffering a death by a thousand cuts.”
Ministers in successive governments have taken aim at both the Environment Agency and Natural England for blocking housebuilding in particular. The former prime minister Rishi Sunak wrote this weekend in the Sunday Times: “Natural England was able, without explicit parliamentary consent, to issue planning advice which held back the construction of 100,000 homes.”
Many of those frustrations were shared by the former chancellor Rachel Reeves, who blamed environmental regulators for choking economic growth by demanding developers build expensive wildlife protections such as the £100m “bat tunnel” over the HS2 high-speed rail line.
She told Sky News on Monday morning: “We’ve had successive governments complain about this, but unfortunately, successive governments have created more of these and pushed more decision-making out of their own departments, so that then when they make decisions they don’t agree with, they turn around and look in horror.”
Many of the proposals are likely to follow the recommendations made in a report by Jon Cunliffe last year, who proposed replacing Ofwat with a new super-regulator that would take in powers from Natural England and the Environment Agency.
Last month, the Conservatives announced that if they won power they would abolish both agencies, saying this would help create more new homes.
She told her business-dominated audience it should not fear public control of companies currently in the private sector, saying it would help bring long-term certainty for investors. “We’ve built a hulking, complex behemoth of a regulatory state. It satisfies no one – not consumers, not investors. That is why public control should not alarm anyone in this room. It’s not ideological. It’s pragmatic, and it’s essential for people, for places, and for business.”

noticias.titulo: Flagship UK gigafactory plan in turmoil after it loses second builder in five months
noticias.resumen: Tata-owned Agratas plant to build EV batteries for sister company Jaguar Land Rover seen as crucial for long-term health of British car industry One of the UK’s flagship electric vehicle battery projects has been thrown into turmoil after its second building contractor in five months walked away, adding to questions over when Jaguar Land Rover cars will use British-made batteries. The £5.2bn gigafactory in Bridgwater, Somerset, is being built by Agratas, to provide batteries for Britain’s largest automotive employer, its sister company. Agratas and Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) are both part of Indi
noticias.texto:
One of the UK’s flagship electric vehicle battery projects has been thrown into turmoil after its second building contractor in five months walked away, adding to questions over when Jaguar Land Rover cars will use British-made batteries.
The £5.2bn gigafactory in Bridgwater, Somerset, is being built by Agratas, to provide batteries for Britain’s largest automotive employer, its sister company. Agratas and Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) are both part of Indian conglomerate Tata Group.
The UK government has pledged £380m in financial support for the factory because it is seen as crucial to the long-term survival of the British car industry, but the build has suffered several setbacks. The construction specialist contracted by Agratas, TSL, has decided to leave the project after failing to agree terms with the battery company, according to three sources.
Batteries are among the important parts of EVs, but global supply is dominated by China, South Korea and Japan. Successive Conservative and Labour governments have strongly supported efforts to build a British battery supply chain, and it also fits with Andy Burnham’s hopes to “reindustrialise” the UK. Not all of the subsidy has yet been paid out.
Tata announced the gigafactory in 2023, aiming for a 2026 start of production with as many as 4,200 employees, before pushing it back to 2027. Replacing the lead contractor for the second time in five months is likely to add to doubts over whether Agratas can hit its latest target of January 2028 – although the company has not yet pushed back its planned start date.
A spokesperson for Agratas said: “We are on track to meet our customer requirements.
“The Somerset site is a large and complex industrialisation project, and all of our supplier partners are supporting us well as we prepare for the facility’s launch phase.”
The inability to reach an agreement with TSL, formally known as Tonroe Group, stemmed from disagreements over the timeline and cost of the project, two sources said.
TSL is expected to leave the site within two or three months, leaving no other main build contractor lined up. However, it is thought that NG Bailey, the project’s mechanical, electrical and plumbing contractor, could be one option to take over the entire build.
The issues at the heart of the dispute are similar to those with TSL’s predecessor, Sir Robert McAlpine (SRM). Agratas fired SRM at short notice in June, and one source suggested discussions over the terms of its departure remain ongoing.
Morale within Agratas has also been hit by the company’s decision to relocate some workers from Coventry, in a building shared with other Tata Group companies, to Somerset.
Some of those workers are expected to take redundancy rather than uproot families and move 120 miles away. If they did so it would continue a stream of senior staff leaving the business in recent months, two sources said.
The UK’s only operating gigafactory, AESC’s plant in Sunderland, north-east England, has also faced problems as carmakers have scaled back plans for EVs, with governments delaying bans on petrol and diesel cars. The Guardian revealed in August that AESC had shelved expansion plans after it failed to agree a separate deal to supply JLR.
It is understood that JLR has secured batteries from other suppliers, so its plans to increase sales of new electric Land Rovers and Jaguars will not be affected. However, those initial cars will not have British-made batteries, although the manufacturer could also avoid EU tariffs under “rules of origin” if it uses batteries made in Europe.
Agratas has made some progress at the Somerset factory, as well as another site in Sanand, western India. Some Agratas managers have travelled to India this week to share experiences with their counterparts in India and discuss the UK situation.
The shell of the building site in south-west England is mostly complete, and National Grid has started work on the electricity substation that will provide the large amounts of power needed to make batteries.
People close to the project suggest Agratas could still succeed in producing batteries and avoid the fate of an earlier rival project, Britishvolt, which collapsed after failing to secure firm orders. The former Britishvolt site in north-east England is now being turned into a datacentre for artificial intelligence – a potentially attractive prospect for an empty building with a high-capacity connection to the electricity grid.
Agratas was approached for comment. TSL declined to comment. JLR declined to comment. NG Bailey was approached for comment.

noticias.titulo: Asylum seekers removed from UK subjected to ‘unnecessary and intimidating’ force
noticias.resumen: Incidents include suicidal man being carried on to plane in waist, leg and ankle restraints, official report says “Unnecessary and intimidating” behaviour was used against asylum seekers being deported under the UK’s controversial “one in, one out” scheme, including a vulnerable person being carried on to a flight in restraints, according to a report. Many of those deported to France under the scheme – which involved one asylum seeker who arrived in the UK in a small boat being forcibly returned to France in exchange for another in northern France brought legally to the UK to claim asylum – ha
noticias.texto:
“Unnecessary and intimidating” behaviour was used against asylum seekers being deported under the UK’s controversial “one in, one out” scheme, including a vulnerable person being carried on to a flight in restraints, according to a report.
Many of those deported to France under the scheme – which involved one asylum seeker who arrived in the UK in a small boat being forcibly returned to France in exchange for another in northern France brought legally to the UK to claim asylum – have fled conflict zones and are survivors of torture or trafficking.
According to freedom of information data shared with the Guardian about Home Office deportation charter flights between July and September 2026, 26 use-of-force incidents were recorded on 26 deportation charters – 21 to France and the others to Albania, Lithuania and Romania. Not every deportation flight involved a use-of-force incident.
After reviewing body-worn footage of four previous deportation flights to France the HM inspectorate of prisons team identified nine incidents of use of force, at least one that was not formally recorded by escorts. Monday’s HMIP report looked specifically at the deportation charter flight to France on 4 September.
In the case of the three documented use-of-force incidents on the flight, one man described by inspectors as “fragile”, who was not eating consistently, posed no threat and had no history of active resistance or violence, was taken from his cell by staff in full protective gear including helmets and riot shields and was placed in a waist restraint belt and leg restraints, even though he had not resisted. Techniques to carry him out were found to be “poorly applied” and “disproportionate”. During the flight he “remained slumped and non-communicative”.
In a second case a man who was on constant suicide watch was carried out to the plane in a waist restraint belt, along with leg and ankle restraints. In a third case a man was placed in a waist restraint belt because he said he was not going to comply with his removal.
The Guardian has previously highlighted concerns about the state in which one in, one out asylum seekers were being returned to France. A report from Samusocial de Paris, which was commissioned by one of France’s regional health agencies to provide healthcare to returned asylum seekers, found: “Consultations are revealing signs consistent with recent physical and psychological violence as well as the consequences of prolonged detention in conditions described as particularly degrading.”
It states that the physical and psychological conditions documented are “explicitly linked to the implementation of the France-British agreement”.
The HMIP report said inspectors “mostly observed caring and respectful interactions” but also found that leadership of collection teams was “not always active enough to address some unnecessary and intimidating behaviour”.
A bodyworn video camera that doubled as an interpreting tool was found not to work effectively and many asylum seekers were unable to access either adequate interpretation or lawyers to represent them.
Inspectors also found that the asylum seekers were referred to by numbers rather than by their names and that those taken to the plane by van were given bags to urinate into.
The Guardian reported in November that despite the scheme ending in October, there were still incidences of people being removed.
Emma Ginn, director of the charity Medical Justice, said: “This report’s findings come as no surprise. Medical Justice has long evidenced the severe and avoidable harm of the government’s dehumanising mistreatment of vulnerable people during immigration enforcement – it cannot be described it as accidental.
“Our independent clinicians assessed that most of our clients detained under the one in, one out scheme had clinical evidence of torture. It should be a source of shame that torture survivors have been mistreated and retraumatised in UK immigration removal centres and while being deported back to France having suffered additional severe harm here.”
The Home Office has been approached for comment.

noticias.titulo: Russia may be planning to launch nuclear weapons in to space, says German intelligence
noticias.resumen: German media has reported a rise in concern over Russia’s ambitions to use weapons to destroy enemy satellites The German government has said it is taking very seriously reports that Russia may be planning to launch a satellite armed with a ⁠nuclear weapon ⁠into ​space later this year. The move – if confirmed – would be a breach of 1967 Outer Space Treaty of which Moscow is a signatory as well the 1963 Partial Nuclear Test Ban Treaty – which prohibit the placing of nuclear weapons in Earth’s orbit and test detonations in space. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
The German government has said it is taking very seriously reports that Russia may be planning to launch a satellite armed with a nuclear weapon into space later this year.
The move – if confirmed – would be a breach of 1967 Outer Space treaty of which Moscow is a signatory as well the 1963 Partial Nuclear Test Ban treaty – which prohibit the placing of nuclear weapons in Earth’s orbit and test detonations in space.
The reports by a group of German media outlets reported, based on what they said were assessments by western intelligence agencies, come amid a recent rise in concern over the increasing militarisation of space which had the US Air Force secretary, Troy Meink, admit for the first time in September that Washington had deployed “on-orbit space control weapons”.
Germany’s Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND) intelligence service and armed forces have exchanged intelligence showing that a Russian satellite, named Sputnik-S, was assembled several years ago and is stationed in the Moscow region, a report by broadcasters NDR and WDR, and newspaper Sueddeutsche Zeitung said.
According to the reports, warnings in early November said the satellite could be launched within 60 days and would be operational shortly afterwards.
“No, we haven’t seen the report. But there are so many ‘alleged’ and ‘possible’ claims in it, attributed to who knows whom, that it’s certainly hardly worth taking them seriously,” Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told reporters.
The Russian embassy in Berlin said it was not aware of any such plans describing the reports as “unfounded allegations regarding the space activities of the Russian Federation” and calling them “part of a propaganda campaign”.
Moscow’s space measures, the embassy added, proceed “in accordance with international obligations” and serve “exclusively peaceful purposes”.
In 2024, Russia denied assertions by US officials that Moscow was developing a weapon that could destroy enemy satellites by setting off a nuclear explosion in space and triggering an electromagnetic pulse (EMP) to disable the electronic systems of nearby satellites.
US officials have alleged that Russia has for years been developing a nuclear weapon capable of destroying entire satellite networks, such as SpaceX’s vast Starlink internet system that Ukrainian troops have been using.
Concern has been mounting in recent years in Europe and the US that Russia has been seeking to develop an anti-satellite weapon system which experts believe would probably employ an EMP wave.
Two years ago, the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, denied the claim after then US president Joe Biden’s national security spokesperson John Kirby confirmed that the Russian Federation had been developing a “troubling” anti-satellite weapon.
“We’re not talking about a weapon that can be used to attack human beings or cause physical destruction here on Earth,” Kirby said.
Biden told reporters in 2024 that he believed Russia was developing the “capacity to launch a system into space that could theoretically do something that was damaging … my hope is it will not”.
While EMPs can occur naturally, it has long been understood that nuclear detonation has the ability to harm electronic systems, including energy networks, with both the US and Russia conducting high altitude tests in the early 1960s.
There has been increasing discussion over fears that Russia may be planning to place a nuclear weapon in space. Germany’s top military space commander earlier this year said he could not rule out that Russia was working on technology to place a nuclear warhead in space, warning that such a move could cripple satellite services and make parts of the orbit unusable for decades.
“At the very top end of escalation, there is the suspicion that Russia may be working on technology to place a nuclear explosive device in orbit,” Maj Gen Michael Traut, commander of the German Space Command, said in an interview with Politico.
Asked whether he considered that realistic, Traut said: “I cannot rule it out.” He added that a nuclear detonation in space could impact up to a third of satellites in low Earth orbit with massive global consequences.
Suspicions over Russia’s ambitions to place weapons in space were given fresh scrutiny in 2022 with the launch of the Kosmos 2553 test satellite, which US and intelligence sources suggested could be a dummy run for the deployment of a nuclear weapon in space.

noticias.titulo: Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO
noticias.resumen: Chipmaker reverses decision it made to remove chief executive after reports of affairs including with alleged Chinese spy Business live – latest updates Nvidia has said it is reinstating Jensen Huang as chief executive, effective immediately, just weeks after his dramatic resignation after reports of extramarital affairs including with an alleged Chinese spy. Nvidia shares surged on the news, jumping more than 25% in premarket trading. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Nvidia has said it is reinstating Jensen Huang as chief executive, effective immediately, just weeks after his dramatic resignation after reports of extramarital affairs including with an alleged Chinese spy.
Nvidia shares surged on the news, jumping more than 25% in premarket trading.
The tech company’s move to bring Huang back marks a sharp reversal from its board’s decision just days earlier to rule out his return.
Huang built Nvidia from a video-game chip designer into the dominant supplier of AI processors, steering its roadmap, customer deals and Washington ties along the way.
He resigned on 12 November after revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with a businesswoman US authorities suspect of spying for China, an allegation Beijing denies.
The board said it was satisfied with Huang’s candour and leadership ability and, after receiving input from senior US government officials, saw no national security risk in his return.
Donald Trump called for Huang’s reinstatement overnight, posting on Truth Social: “I hope the Board of Nvidia rehires Jensen Huang. It would be the best thing for the Company, and also, for the U.S.A. President DONALD J. TRUMP.”
Reuters contributed to this report

Democrats are planning 12 presidential primary debates for what’s expected to be a crowded field of 2028 candidates, with the first scheduled for June, the Democratic National Committee has said.
The DNC’s announcement on Monday comes before major candidates have launched campaigns to succeed term-limited Republican president Donald Trump and follows the party’s convincing midterm performance, AP reported.
DNC chair Ken Martin said in a statement the party is aimed at staying united and helping the eventual nominee win the White House. “The DNC is keeping our foot on the gas as we head into the 2028 cycle,” he said.
Anticipating a large number of presidential hopefuls, the DNC said it will cap participation in each debate to 20 qualifying candidates over two nights, if needed.
The criteria for making the debate stage will be similar to 2020, when there was also a big field and a dozen debates, the DNC said, and will include meeting polling and other criteria such as grassroots fundraising.
More details are set to be announced in January, including specific times and locations for the debates, the DNC said, though the party confirmed that five debates will be in 2027 and seven in 2028. The final primary debate is planned for March 2028.
For the first time, candidates must pledge to reject dark money as a condition of making the debate stage. The new requirement is part of a DNC effort to curb the influence of outside groups that can spend unlimited amounts to support or oppose candidates without having to reveal funding sources.
The debate schedule is one of the most closely watched decisions the DNC makes, along with selecting the city for the 2028 convention. Earlier this year, the DNC narrowed the list of cities to Boston, Denver and Philadelphia.
In other developments:
Donald Trump has headlined his third cryptocurrency gala at his country club in Virginia, rewarding top holders of his own meme coin, as Democrats accuse the president of improperly profiting from his crypto ventures. The dinner, which took place at the Trump National golf club in Sterling, Virginia, included meet-and-greets with Trump supporters including the boxing champion Floyd Mayweather, the Shark Tank investor Kevin O’Leary, the NBA champion Tristan Thompson and the magician Lior Suchard, according to the event’s website.
Michigan US senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed on Sunday doubled down on naming healthcare reform legislation after Donald Trump as long as it meant the president would not impede its passage. “If he’s open to the conversation, I am open to it, too,” El-Sayed said of Trump on Sunday. “If the president is opening to signing that bill, let’s get it done.”
Jay Clayton, the US director of national intelligence, said he trusts Trump “completely” after the US president called Vladimir Putin “a friend” during their recent meeting in China. Clayton made the remarks on Sunday, where he was pressed during media appearances on Trump’s warm characterization of the Russian president – who is viewed as a chief US adversary – following his trilateral summit with Putin and China’s Xi Jinping.
Invoking Greek mythology, US senator John Kennedy has characterized former Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang’s reported affair with a suspected Chinese spy as “the most expensive sex since Helen of Troy”. The Louisiana Republican’s allusion to the legendary figure whose desirability was such that it caused the mythic Trojan war came during an interview on NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday.
Democrats have won their largest majority in the House in more than three decades after Chuck Hubbard defeated Republican representative Virginia Foxx in North Carolina on Sunday, extending the blue wave that swept the US midterms and increasing pressure on the party to deliver its promises to US voters. House Democrats have secured at least 258 seats in a midterm election sweep unseen since 1992, gaining 44 House seats so far, four more than the 40 they picked up in Donald Trump’s first midterm in 2018.
Here’s Trump’s full social media post, in which he also called Jensen Huang “a Great Patriot and National Treasure”.
The NVIDIA Board of Directors has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO. The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy. The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security. The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct. On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure. Separately, NVIDIA should continue its thorough internal investigation of the Company’s compliance with U.S. export controls in order to ensure that it is fulfilling its legal obligations and Patriotic Duty to protect U.S. National Security. Congratulations to Jensen, the NVIDIA Board, to the People of the United States — and, indeed, the World!
Trump insists US government has ‘no reason to believe’ Huang’s return to Nvidia poses a national security risk
In his post on Truth Social, Donald Trump also insisted that the US government has “no reason to believe” that JensenHuang’s return to Nvidia poses a national security risk.
“The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct,” Trump said of Huang.
As my colleague Graeme Wearden notes, in a hint to the political pressure put on the company, Nvidia added:
In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.
Two investigations into the company are still ongoing, one launched by Nvidia, which asked a leading US law firm to conduct a “thorough and independent” investigation into the relationship between CEO Huang, and an alleged Chinese spy.
The second, being conducted by the attorney general of California, will examine whether exports of Nvidia’s semiconductor chips ended up in China, contravening US restrictions.
Trump said in his post that Nvidia “should continue its thorough internal investigation of the Company’s compliance with U.S. export controls in order to ensure that it is fulfilling its legal obligations and Patriotic Duty to protect U.S. National Security”.
Graeme is covering the latest over on our business blog:
Trump praises Nvidia's reinstatement of Jensen Huang as CEO, calling it 'the correct and proper decision'
Donald Trump has praised the “correct and proper decision” of Nvidia’s board of directors to reinstate Jensen Huang as chief executive, saying both the company and the country “needs” Huang’s leadership.
Huang resigned on 12 November after revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with a businesswoman US authorities suspect of spying for China.
Days later, Huang offered to return. Nvidia chair Harvey Jones said last week that the company would not rehire him despite the growing pressure campaign from employees, shareholders and business partners, as well as Trump, for his reinstatement.
Trump called again for Huang to be reinstated over the weekend, saying “it would be the best thing for the Company” and the country.
Now, in an extraordinary reversal, Nvidia has announced that its board of directors voted unanimously to reinstate Huang as CEO, effective immediately.
“The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” Jones said in a statement on Monday.

The US Federal Aviation Administration’s grounding of all US flights last week, alongside separate outages affecting Microsoft services, caused widespread disruption across the country.

Many have directed their anger at the Trump administration, questioning its competence and calling for greater accountability and transparency about the systems millions of people rely on.

“I find it impossible to believe a single router brought the nation to its knees. There would have to be no redundancy or no contingency for backup plans. Is it possible for any government to run that way?” she said.
Berrier, who said the incident was making her “more reticent” about travelling, also expressed a broader distrust of the administration.
“I don’t believe anything this administration says. Not a day goes by without a lie, a grift exposed or some attempt to hide information from the public. What we get is propaganda that is intended to mislead and manipulate,” she added.

noticias.titulo: Over 100 writers from PEN America to form splinter group over Gaza tensions
noticias.resumen: Members of the free-expression literary and human rights group are forming a new chapter called PEN Writes US More than 100 well-known writers and members of the literary world are to form a splinter chapter of PEN America, the free-expression literary and human rights group, over tensions within the organization over Israel’s war in Gaza and other issues. noticias.texto:
More than 100 well-known writers and members of the literary world are to form a splinter chapter of PEN America, the free-expression literary and human rights group, over tensions within the organization over Israel’s war in Gaza and other issues.
Writers including Ta-Nehisi Coates, M Gessen and Jacqueline Woodson are among those who on Monday announced they are forming a new group called PEN Writes US that will be “guided by the PEN Charter’s vision of ‘one humanity, living in peace and equality in one world’”.
The group describes itself as an “aspiring PEN chapter founded by writers, translators, artists, editors, agents, and booksellers” from all over the US. The group says it is supported by PEN International while it aims “to build a new home for writers committed to free expression, and their range of backgrounds, languages, and perspectives is our greatest strength”.
“We seek to join more than 140 PEN Centers worldwide (and the many that have coexisted in the United States) in mobilizing writers at every stage of their career to defend free expression, support writers and artists at risk, and champion reading, translation, and literature,” it added.
PEN America told the Associated Press that it remains focused on “defending free expression as a universal right that must be protected regardless of viewpoint”.
Novelist Maaza Mengiste told the outlet that the new group does not seek to be a rival of PEN America and will probably share common ground about fighting censorship and oppression and encouraging discussions among writers.
Mengiste said that PEN Writes will differ in its structure and in some of its priorities, ideally becoming “a center where sustained and equal advocacy for all writers guides principles, rather than institutional caution”.
The formation of PEN Writes comes as PEN America has faced criticism from numerous writers and activists who say they are unhappy with the latter group’s response to Israel’s war in Gaza. Critics argue that PEN America has been reluctant to criticize Israel or to defend the rights of Palestinian writers with the same force it has advocated for writers elsewhere.
“I think there’s been a feeling for quite a while that PEN’s response to the war in Gaza has been inadequate,” says PEN Writes member Francine Prose, a former president of PEN America, according to the AP.
Fallout from the war in Gaza led PEN America to call off its annual awards show and World Voices festival in 2024 because so many participants dropped out.
Those events resumed. But in June, Dinaw Mengestu resigned as PEN America president after PEN published a report about obstacles and harassment faced by Israeli and Jewish writers since Israel began waging war in Gaza in 2023 in the wake of the 7 October attacks by Hamas that year.
Mengestu, a prize-winning novelist who is now a member of PEN Writes, at the time cited the report’s criticism of cultural boycotts. He expressed support for the Palestinian-led boycott, divestment and sanctions movement, or BDS.
Organizers advocated for economic and cultural pressure on Israel to end the country’s occupation of territories captured in the 1967 Middle East war, grant full equality to Arab citizens of Israel and promote the rights of Palestinian refugees to return.
PEN America says it “emphatically opposes any efforts to inhibit the free international exchange of literature, art, information, or knowledge, including academic and cultural boycotts”. The group says it also defends the rights of individuals to “be protected from retaliatory efforts” for participating in boycotts.
Mengiste told the AP that PEN Writes takes a broader view, supporting boycotts themselves.
In July, in the aftermath of Mengestu’s departure, PEN America issued a statement citing such initiatives as its direction of $500,000 in emergency aid to Palestinians in Gaza, its legal support for a pro-Palestinian activist threatened with deportation by Donald Trump’s administration, and a 2025 PEN report entitled All That Is Lost: The Cultural Destruction of Gaza.
The new group is aiming for recognition at the PEN International Congress in Montenegro in September 2027. The process includes forming a steering committee, establishing communication with the PEN International secretariat and “seeking interest from the full diversity of writers” in a given country, according to PEN International’s guidelines.
Other prominent members of PEN Writes include Pulitzer prize winner Percival Everett, literary agent Nicole Aragi and novelist Hannah Lillith Assadi, who on Wednesday won the National Book Award for fiction.
Mengiste said PEN Writes aims to be effective as a more stripped-down, egalitarian organization run entirely by writers on behalf of writers.
“I think writers know first-hand what self-censorship or lost contracts or de-platforming looks like,” she told the AP. “We know that what comes for one writer will very likely come for others. We are guardians of each other as much as we are stewards of literature. We do not work with a writers organization, we ARE writers, organized and mobilized to defend all writers.”
The Associated Press contributed reporting

noticias.titulo: Nine people shot at central California concert with one in critical condition
noticias.resumen: Authorities say they believe the Saturday night shooting at a concert in Strathmore ‘may be gang-related’ Nine people were shot at a concert in central California , leaving one person critically injured with a chest injury, the local sheriff said Sunday. The shooting broke out at about 7.30pm Saturday at a concert attended by about 150 people in Strathmore, a small town in Tulare county, a mountainous region in the center of the state, the local sheriff’s department said in a statement. noticias.texto:
Nine people were shot at a concert in central California, leaving one person critically injured with a chest injury, the local sheriff said Sunday.
The shooting broke out at about 7.30pm Saturday at a concert attended by about 150 people in Strathmore, a small town in Tulare county, a mountainous region in the center of the state, the local sheriff’s department said in a statement. An unspecified number of suspects opened fire on the crowd. No arrests were announced.
One 26-year-old man was shot in the chest and required surgery. He remained in critical condition, the sheriff’s department said. Two other victims ages 19 and 22 also required surgery, while six people sustained minor injuries.
Authorities said that they believe the shooting “may be gang-related” but didn’t elaborate. The show in the town of roughly 3,000 people featured rappers and performers from neighboring states, the department said.
The local Porterville Recorder news outlet reported Saturday’s shooting evidently occurred at a privately organized “norteño gang concert”. According to the outlet, “it was also reported investigators had not determined if there was security at the event”.
The department didn’t immediately respond to emailed questions seeking further details but said there was no longer any immediate threat to the public.
The concert headliner was Lazy Boy, a San Jose-based rap artist. Investigators believe the shooting may be gang-related.
As of Monday, there had been more than 420 mass shootings in the US so far for the year, according to the Gun Violence Archive. The archive, a nonpartisan resources, defines mass shootings as cases in which four or more victims are either wounded or killed.
High numbers of mass shootings reported annually in the US have prompted many to call for more substantial federal gun control. But Congress over the years has not passed such restrictions.
The Associated Press contributed reporting

noticias.titulo: Nvidia reinstates former CEO Jensen Huang despite China espionage scandal
noticias.resumen: Nvidia's board voted unanimously to bring back the disgraced CEO, who resigned this month amid news of his affairs. He's suspected of having had a relationship with a Chinese intelligence asset.
noticias.texto:
Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO despite China scandal
November 23, 2026
US tech company Nvidia said on Monday that it had resinstated Jensen Huang as its CNvidiaEO "effective immediately."
This follows just a matter of days after his resignation after admitting to extramarital affairs, reportedly including a dalliance with a woman who was a Chinese intelligence asset.
The board unanimously decided that his return was in the "best interests of the company," Nvidia said, adding that it was satisfied that Huang had demonstrated his "candor and ability to lead."
The decision was announced as trading started for the new week in New York.
The stock price of what investors deem the world's most valuable company has nosedived amid the scandal, with Nvidia's stock price falling from almost $220 (roughly €200) per share in late October to around $125 per share at the end of last week.

noticias.titulo: North Macedonia remains stalled on its EU path after 21 years as a candidate while Montenegro and Albania move closer to membership
noticias.resumen: EU enlargement has regained momentum, with Montenegro and Albania moving closer to membership. But North Macedonia, a candidate since 2005, remains stalled by a politically difficult dispute involving Bulgaria.
noticias.texto:
North Macedonia watches as EU enlargement moves on
November 23, 2026
The European Union's enlargement drive has regained momentum: Montenegro could become the bloc's 28th member in 2028, while Albania is rapidly advancing through accession talks and could complete accession negotiations by the end of 2027 if it maintains its current pace of reforms.
But North Macedonia, an EU candidate since 2005, remains stalled on the road to accession.
That contrast will be particularly evident at Wednesday's EU-Western Balkans summit in Brussels.
"The Western Balkans' future is in the European Union. Their accession is our priority, our shared ambition and a crucial geopolitical investment in these turbulent times," European Council President Antonio Costa said ahead of the meeting.
Prepared, but the handbrake is still on
North Macedonia formally opened accession talks with the EU in July 2022 but has yet to open the first of the EU's six negotiating clusters, the groups of policy areas through which candidates align their laws and institutions with EU standards.
But the lack of movement does not mean the country is unprepared for membership.
EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos said in November that North Macedonia was "among the countries with the highest level of preparedness" in aligning with EU law and had recently accelerated reforms under the EU Growth Plan.
However, she added, "the handbrake on its accession negotiations is still on."
Kos said that to release this handbrake and open the first cluster, North Macedonia must adopt the constitutional amendment agreed with the EU in 2022.
What's blocking N. Macedonia's EU progress?
The stalemate has deep roots.
For years, a dispute with Greece over the country's name blocked North Macedonia's progress along the EU accession path.
Although the 2018 Prespa Agreement resolved the dispute, and the country changed its constitutional name, clearing the way for NATO membership, a breakthrough on EU accession did not follow.
Bulgaria later blocked the process amid disputes over history, language and identity. A compromise brokered during the French EU presidency in 2022 lifted the veto but made further progress conditional on North Macedonia amending its constitution to explicitly include Bulgarians among the country's recognized communities.
The amendment requires a two-thirds majority in parliament, which has so far proved unattainable.
'Not blocked by a member state'
From the EU's perspective, this is no longer a Bulgarian veto, but a condition North Macedonia accepted as part of its negotiating framework.
"It [North Macedonia] is not blocked by a member state. It is blocked because it doesn't want to date to do what it knows needs to be done," Gert Jan Koopman, the European Commission's director-general for Neighbourhood and Enlargement Negotiations, recently told an Atlantic Council podcast.
North Macedonia's government sees the problem differently.
EU membership remains its declared strategic goal, but Skopje wants guarantees that amending its constitution will not simply pave the way for further demands from Sofia.
Those concerns are rooted partly in long-running disputes over identity and history: Bulgarian governments have challenged North Macedonia's interpretation of a centuries-old distinct Macedonian identity, while some Bulgarian politicians have gone further, describing Macedonian as a regional variant of Bulgarian, and Macedonians and Bulgarians as one people.
President Gordana Siljanovska-Davkova says North Macedonia is ready for talks with Bulgaria and the EU but wants certainty that one constitutional change will not simply be followed by demands for another.
"We only want certainty. We only want this not to be yet another amendment for the sake of an amendment, followed by another one," she said.
Strong support for membership, little appetite for compromise
After more than two decades of waiting, the deadlock has also become a domestic political problem in North Macedonia.
A nationally representative survey by the Institute for Democracy "Societas Civilis" illustrates the contradiction: 71% of respondents support EU membership, but only 24% back the constitutional amendments needed to advance the process. Among ethnic Macedonians, support for the amendments falls to just 11%.
Skopje-based political analyst Petar Arsovski describes the public mood as "passive-aggressive:" Strong support for joining the EU coexists with weak support for making the concession currently required to move forward.
That, he says, helps preserve the status quo.
High domestic political stakes
The dispute is now deeply embedded in domestic politics in both North Macedonia and Bulgaria, where retreat from established positions could easily be portrayed as a national defeat.
The political cost is particularly high in Skopje, where the current government came to power in part on a platform of opposition to constitutional changes under the existing conditions.
For North Macedonia's government, accepting the amendments without further guarantees carries considerable domestic political risks.
The EU, meanwhile, is not offering to reopen the negotiating framework.
The uncertainty is compounded by debate over how future EU enlargement should work. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron have proposed allowing candidates to gradually gain some benefits of membership before formally joining, while stressing that full membership remains the ultimate goal.
According to Arsovski, uncertainty over the future course of enlargement gives ammunition to Eurosceptic narratives and reduces the political incentive for a difficult compromise.
"If these overall conditions remain unchanged, the most likely scenario is that EU summits come and go, while political actors remain dug in, with no real convergence of positions and no genuine commitment to a substantive compromise," Arsovski told DW.

noticias.titulo: After Japan's APEC snub, what's ahead for China ties?
noticias.resumen: Japan has long-running concerns over Chinese military expansionism, and Beijing has bristled over Sanae Takaichi's comments on Taiwan. The frosty ties were on full display at last week's APEC summit.
noticias.texto:
After Japan's APEC snub, what's ahead for China ties?
November 23, 2026
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi received a cold shoulder from China during the recent Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in the tech hub of Shenzhen.
After Takaichi arrived in Shenzhen on November 18 for the two-day summit, there was an immediate issue when the mobile stairs to the door of her aircraft were some way short of the threshold, requiring her to hold on to the door frame to step down around 40 centimeters (about 15 inches) to the top step.
It may have been completely inadvertent, but upon safely reaching the airport tarmac, her official welcome was decidedly low-key. There were no musical performances, no cheering crowds or traditional dances, which were laid on for many other APEC leaders as they arrived.
Japan's Yomiuri newspaper reported on November 20 that when Takaichi met Chinese leader Xi Jinping at the dinner reception, "his reaction was cold." And while many other regional leaders managed at least a brief one-on-one with Xi on the sidelines of the main event, the Japanese delegation was not granted such access.
Frosty China-Japan ties on full display
"The level of frostiness from the Chinese side was on full display from the moment Takaichi's plane landed," said William Yang, a Taiwan-based analyst for the International Crisis Group.
"I cannot think that the issue with the plane steps was anything other than deliberate and there was a huge contrast between the welcome she received and virtually everyone else," he told DW.
Yang added the ice didn't break when Takaichi tried to speak to Xi at the dinner reception and the entire occasion "just reflects the state of bilateral relations."
China and Japan share a troubled history, marked by the Japanese invasion of China in the 1930s and the often brutal occupation of cities that were captured and subjugated.
Chinese schoolchildren learn about the horrors of the Nanjing Massacre and the use of chemical and biological weapons by Japanese forces.
Japan maintains that its repeated post-war apologies and massive economic aid that helped China to become the economic powerhouse it is today are overlooked amid the criticism.
Diplomatic relations were normalized in 1972 and Tokyo pursued a policy of engagement over the following decades, although that came to a halt in the mid-2000s, points out David Adebahr, a professor of international relations and Asia-Pacific security policy at Kobe University.
Japan's Taiwan comments open new rift with Beijing
"China's rising military spending, the breakdown of talks over the East China Sea in 2006, and a resurgence of nationalism raised concerns even among Japan's more China-friendly diplomats, while defence analysts noted an increase in Chinese submarine activity near Japanese waters," he told DW.
The nationalism on display during the 2008 Beijing Olympics, coupled with China's more assertive stance over the Senkaku Islands, which Japan has sovereignty over but which Beijing claims, accelerated this shift.
Ties took a sudden nosedive in November 2025 when Takaichi responded to a question in Japan's parliament, the Diet, by saying that any "contingency” involving Taiwan would also inevitably threaten the national security of Japan.
According to Adebahr, the Japanese leader was merely saying out loud what "had long been the internal logic of Japanese security planning." Nevertheless, Beijing has reacted with fury.
China has demanded that Takaichi retract the statement and raised pressure on Japan by restricting exports of rare earth minerals critical to Japanese industry, banning imports of Japanese seafood and telling tourists to take Japan off their destination list.
And while ruffled national feelings have been smoothed in the past with shows of reciprocal goodwill, China is standing firm on its demands this time.
"From Tokyo's perspective, it is clear that Beijing believes it holds more cards than in the past," said Adebahr.
"Today, Beijing has considerable leverage: Japan's dependence on Chinese rare earths; an increasingly visible military presence around Japan, sometimes in conjunction with Russia; and a US administration that has urged Tokyo to de-escalate rather than firmly backing it."
"This gives China little incentive to offer Takaichi a face-saving compromise," he said. "However, this approach comes at a cost to Beijing too: the more it relies on coercion, the more it pushes Japan towards increased defence spending and closer ties with other partners."
Japan's leadership faces the China test
Still, the Japanese leader finds herself in a difficult position, said analyst Yang.
As a committed conservative who has talked tough on Beijing's rapid military buildup, its seizure of islands and atolls in the South China Sea and the inexorable pressure on Taiwan to capitulate and become one with mainland China, Takaichi cannot give in to Xi's demands for fear of losing face with her hardline base.
"This is a major test of her abilities and wisdom as the nation's leader," Yang said. "She is walking a political tightrope between reducing tensions with China but, at the same time, preparing the nation and its allies for a potential contingency over Taiwan."
"I foresee China maintaining its current approach, continuing to step up the pressure by limiting targeted exports and amplifying the assertion with Russia and North Korea that Japan is embracing remilitarization," he said.
"I expect Japan to try to find areas where it can signal goodwill and seek to improve relations in return for small-scale compromises, but a reset in the dynamics will be determined by how the Trump administration shapes its foreign policy for the remaining years of his term," Yang added.
Analyst Adebahr said that while he expects diplomatic relations to remain frosty, there are too many interdependencies for a full decoupling between China and Japan.
"I would not be too pessimistic about the relationship, because in the medium term, trade, technology and critical minerals are now seen as security issues," he added. "Therefore, complex interdependence will prevent a return to the old pattern of keeping politics and economics separate."
"While economic interdependence alone will not be enough to stabilize the relationship, full decoupling is highly unlikely, as transaction costs would be far too high for both sides."

noticias.titulo: A reset for climate diplomacy?
noticias.resumen: COP31 has been branded a failure after countries couldn't reach a deal. But was the decision to walk away from what would have been a step back actually a show of strength? What the result means for the world.
noticias.texto:
A reset for climate diplomacy?
November 23, 2026
The longest-running climate talks in history came to a disappointing conclusion on Sunday as negotiators failed to come to an agreement on a shared political direction on climate change.
After two days of extended talks, representatives from country after country, tiredness etched into each face, voiced their opposition to the so-called "Antalya Pact."
"I understand that there is no agreement on this text. For that reason, these decisions have not been adopted," said Murat Kurum, Turkish president of the COP31 climate summit.
'Fossil fuels' as one of main sticking points
One of the main sticking points: the words "fossil fuels." While some nations, including petrostates like Saudi Arabia and Russia, wanted them omitted from the text, others saw it as a "step backwards" not to include them.
Around 130 parties — among them vulnerable island nations, developing countries and richer EU members — called for the reintroduction of the two words into the text, to no avail. And so many refused to support the adoption of the final COP agreement.
The deadlock signals a failure for the UN process. But the number of countries willing to walk away from what they saw as a weak text was, arguably, a show of strength, and one that had been long coming.
The phrase "fossil fuels" first appeared three years ago in the closing decision of COP28 in Dubai with the promise of "transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems, in just, orderly and equitable manner." But it has been omitted from every decision since.
More extreme weather as climate change accelerates
Yet this year's climate summit was the first to acknowledge that the world will breach the critical 1.5-degree Celsius (2.7-degree Fahrenheit) threshold that scientists said would safeguard the world from the worst impacts of planetary heating.
And so, the pressure was on for progress; to turn pledges from previous years into concrete action. But that progress didn't come.
"We don't celebrate the deep divisions exposed or the lack of a political signal from COP31 capable of driving climate action in line with science, equity and the law," said Nikki Reisch, director of the climate and energy program at the Center for International Environmental Law.
"But the rejected text would have done more harm than good," she added.
Financing climate action in the Global South
The lack of agreement was not solely about fossil fuels; moneyalso played a part.
Developing nations have long argued that they need additional financing, both as a means for them to move away from coal, oil and gas, but also to help them cope with the consequences of rising temperatures.
