Countries all over the world are being battered by extreme weather events. Catastrophes like flooding, drought and wildfires have been fueled and worsened by rising global temperatures. Often the worst hit are poorer countries with low rates of greenhouse gas emissions.
And yet, richer states behind much of the historical emissions are increasingly unwilling to foot the bill. Dissatisfaction at home due to higher food and fuel prices has left many governments loathe to pay more to finance climate action abroad.
With the United States — the world's biggest historical emitter — now absent from negotiations and on the verge of leaving the United Nation's Framework Convention on Climate Change, the European Union was portrayed as this year's villain with some observers accusing the EU of hypocrisy.
"You can't demand action and then block the finance that makes this possible," Fanny Petitbon, policy analyst at 350.org, said in a statement.
As the world's largest provider of climate finance, the EU reportedly refused to negotiate on providing additional finance and has repeatedly called for other nations to step up.
Moving forward on climate action beyond climate summits
The failure to find an agreement is a particularly bitter turn of events for countries that face ever worsening impacts of climate change, like the island states that are being confronted by a reality that could see their countries wiped off the map as sea levels rise.
But things are not all bad.
Although the Turkey-led electrification agenda calling for an increase in global electricity consumption to 35% by 2035 was not formally adopted as it made up part of the rejected final agreement, more than 90 countries pledged to move forward regardless.
It's not a silver bullet. There was no agreement on ensuring the increase was forged only through clean, renewable energy. But it would still signal forward momentum — momentum that is also being driven by economic forces and a need for home-grown energy security.
And there are other hopes. The second conference on the Just Transition Away from Fossil Fuels will take place in Tuvalu in July 2027. Initiated at the COP30 conference last year in Belem, Brazil, it has seen increasing support from countries putting together concrete roadmaps for abandoning coal, oil and gas.
Who's responsible?
There has been much talk of blame and who is responsible for the breakdown and collapse of talks. What is clear is that the UN climate summits need reform. Progress, when it does happen, is slow. While currently based on consensus, with all countries having to agree on every measure, there have been many calls for majority-rule decision making. That could force the inclusion of language like "fossil fuels" into the text.
But ultimately, this is not the time to focus on fault. As the climate crisis accelerates, governments need to reflect — and quickly — on what can be done outside of these UN processes, within their nations, to speed up climate action.
"The take-home message from COP31 is clear: the world must do much more to confront the climate crisis — and it must do it now," said UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres in a statement.

noticias.titulo: German police respond to multiple school bomb threats
noticias.resumen: Police in Germany are responding to bomb threats against a series of schools, but say that at present they don't believe them to be credible. Danish authorities are reporting a similar series of apparent hoaxes.
noticias.texto:
German police respond to multiple school bomb threats
November 23, 2026
Police in several locations across Germany reported large numbers of bomb threats targeting schools.
They said that while they were investigating the claims, they did not initially have reason to treat them as credible threats.
More than 400 schools in the southwestern state of Baden Württemberg received threats, and more than 250 in Saxony-Anhalt received the emails, with several other regions also targeted on Monday morning.
What did police say about the bomb threats?
Police in Erfurt in Thuringia were among the first to issue a statement on the threats, saying they were responding to threats at "multiple schools" after morning warnings, including in Jena, Erfurt, Mühlhausen, Zella-Mehlis, Nordhausen, Gotha, Rudolstadt and Greiz.
"The same word-for-word threats were received this morning at the various eductional institutes," police wrote in a press release. "Based on preliminary findings other federal states are also affected by the threatening messages."
Police said they had no information yet on the potential author or sender of the emails. They were investigating breach of the peace-based crimes via the threat of criminal activity.
"At present the police is not working on the assumption of the bomb threats being serious and recommends that schools do not implement evacuation measures and continue their normal operations," they said.
Police in Freiburg in the southwest and authorities to the north in Hanover also said they were responding to emailed bomb threats directed against schools.
Similar reports are emerging to the north of Germany in Denmark.
As in Germany, Danish police said they did not believe the threats were credible, "but they understandably create insecurity locally at the schools."
Various disruptive incidents targeting Europe in recent weeks
This follows other recent cases of coordinated bomb threats against multiple schools that turned out to be hoaxes in Italy earlier in the month.
It also comes amid various apparent bids to create disruption within Europe in recent weeks, such as multiple bomb threats targeting commercial airlines, or hacking into supermarket refrigeration systems to spoil produce en masse.

noticias.titulo: 'I've lost her forever' — Why German voice actors are refusing to sign Netflix's AI contract
noticias.resumen: For decades, Germans have known Hollywood's biggest stars through the same familiar voices. Now an AI clause in Netflix contracts is splitting the industry over whether it protects performers or exposes them.
noticias.texto:
AI dispute divides Germany's dubbing industry
November 23, 2026
When does Cameron Diaz not sound like Cameron Diaz? When you're in a German cinema.
For more than 30 years, whenever the Oscar-winning actor has appeared on German screens, she has spoken with the voice of Katrin Fröhlich.
The same goes for all other famous actors. In Germany's €125-million ($138-million) voiceover industry, Hollywood's up-and-comers are "adopted" by a voice actor who provides their German voice — often for decades — ensuring continuity and a certain relationship to the stars for audiences.
But on Netflix, and perhaps elsewhere, many of those voices might be about to change.
Netflix contract sparks AI dispute
Recently, Fröhlich and fellow voice actors Anne Helm (Margot Robbie) and Luise Helm (Scarlett Johansson) published a video on social media, letting their followers know they wouldn't provide their voices anymore.
The reason? They refuse to sign Netflix's contract, seen by DW, which contains a clause that lets the American entertainment giant use their voices for training its AI.
They're not the first voiceover artists to speak out on the topic. But they are the first ones to go viral.
"It was unexpected, completely," Fröhlich said. "For whatever reason, we managed to reach people, perhaps because … we are three well-known women in the voiceover industry."
"Over the years, we've managed to make good names for ourselves. It seems to have touched people that we made this statement together," she said.
Union says deal offers legal safeguards
The new AI clause has been in Netflix's contracts since January 2026. Voice actors sign one ahead of every production. It was negotiated by BFFS, Germany's union for film and television actors.
Fröhlich, like a significant number of voice actors, is not a member and feels as though the union went over their heads. However, BFFS says the deal gives them protection they wouldn't otherwise have.
Till Völger, an attorney and member of the union's board, says previous contracts and those with other streaming services are silent on AI or contain sweeping AI permissions.
If an AI-generated voice doesn't sound like a particular person, companies are free to use the data they have gathered as they wish. Training can take place in other jurisdictions and may not require the actor's consent at all, he pointed out.
"We have a massive, massive protection gap," Völger told DW.
Against that backdrop, BFFS argues the deal with Netflix is a step forward. It allows the company to train its own systems with recordings, but voice actors must give separate, explicit consent before their recordings are used to create actual AI-generated voices, even if the voice isn't recognizable as theirs.
"We've created a contractual right that the law doesn't provide," said Völger. "Is the situation perfect? No. Is it better than before? Yes."
He would like to see other streaming services agree to the same conditions that Netflix has. In his view, only legislation could create the necessary protections voice actors are seeking.
Netflix says human performance "is and remains important to us," in statement provided to DW.
"In recent years, we have commissioned thousands of hours of German dubbing, and we intend to continue supporting a similar volume of work and the use of human voices," the statement continued.
Voice actor plans legal challenge
Matti Klemm, the voice of Jason Momoa and beloved children's cartoon elephant Benjamin Blümchen, sees things differently. Like Fröhlich, he is refusing to sign the new contract.
"In short, it says: as soon as I record something for Netflix, I'm automatically training their AI, for free," he told DW. "My job is to create a German original, a dubbed version with my performance, not to train the computer systems of some tech companies."
He is taking Netflix to court, backed by the Society for Civil Rights (GFF), to find out how his voice has been used for training in previous projects.
According to Davy Wang, who is coordinating the case for Klemm and GFF, the lawsuit will seek to stop Netflix using his recordings for training, disclose how previous data was used and establish whether Klemm is entitled to any damages.
The suit will be filed at the end of the year or in early 2027. Supporters donated more than €50,000 to the legal fund in the first week following its announcement.
For Klemm, what is at stake goes beyond training. "It's not about our voice, it's about our soul, our performance, the way we are," he said. "How far have we come when AI training matters more than my actual work?"
Netflix said it cannot comment on a case that has not yet been filed.
Industry fears growing AI impact
For a multimillion-euro industry, the outcome of the case could reach well beyond Netflix and other companies and creative branches are watching. But no matter what the outcome of the lawsuit or contract agreements, voice actors' fears for their future run deep.
Those who don't sign contracts can't work, and streaming companies can make up a significant part of their income.
"Many say: I've held out for 10 months, but I can't anymore. I have to sign this contract, I have to pay my rent, I have to feed my children," explained Fröhlich.
Beyond that, many fear the future of their industry and the connections they have formed with stars and audiences.
"For a many people I'm connected with Cameron Diaz and I evoke something within them," said Fröhlich.
But if Diaz is involved in more Netflix projects, "then I've basically lost her," she concluded. "I'll never be her voice again."
Edited by: Tim Rooks

noticias.titulo: Budget cuts threaten Germany's fight against antisemitism and racism
noticias.resumen: Numerous grassroots initiatives in Germany are facing funding cuts. Affected organizations are sounding the alarm, pointing to growing challenges posed by far-right extremism.
noticias.texto:
Budget cuts threaten Germany's fight against antisemitism and racism
November 23, 2026
Initiatives and organizations in Germany are speaking out against planned budget cuts to the work of strengthening democracy and fighting racism and antisemitism. Berlin is planning drastic savings measures in its draft federal budget for 2027, which is to be debated in parliament this Friday.
The "Living democracy" (Demokratie Leben) program from the Ministry for Family Affairs is set to receive a total of €170 million ($187 million). That is about €20 million less than the current year's budget allocation.
The draft was agreed upon by Germany's governing coalition of the conservative Union – of the Christian Democrats (CDU) and its Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union (CSU) – and the center-left Social Democrats.
Numerous organizations consider the cuts a dire signal. Tahera Ameer from the Amadeu Antonio Foundation, a Berlin-based NGO which campaigns against right-wing extremism and discrimination, sees many initiatives in Germany under existential threat.
"In view of the antisemitic agitation, the open violence and the ever-increasing legitimization of its normalization, it is concerning that the very structures and grants which do something to oppose them are now standing on the verge of collapse," Ameer explained during a media briefing alongside other like-minded organizations.
Lasting damage to democracy in Germany?
According to the initiatives, the work to strengthen democratic civil society could suffer lasting damage, because long-established structures cannot simply be rebuilt after they have been destroyed.
The thing that outraged many organizations: The cuts come at a time when the extreme right is celebrating numerous election victories in Germany.
The Alternative for Germany (AfD), parts of which are considered far-right extremist, achieved record-high results in several elections in 2026, most notably in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt. "Especially in view of the AfD possibly coming into government in Saxony-Anhalt, we need these structures more urgently than ever," urged Tahera Ameer.
The promotion of democratic civil society in Germany has been controversial for years. While initiatives and associations regularly appeal for more money, some conservative politicians repeatedly criticize an alleged one-sidedness in the allocation of public funds.
During the federal parliamentary debate on the funding program in March 2025, Christian Democrat politician Marvin Schulz supported the planned changes, which were put forward by German Families Minister Karin Prien, also of the CDU: "We need new areas of focus," he said. Projects working against extreme Islamism and antisemitism were underrepresented, he said.
But initiatives to combat antisemitism will also receive less funding in the future. The Central Committee of German Catholics (ZdK) criticized cuts to the Federal Association of Departments for Research and Information on Antisemitism (RIAS), the nationwide OFEK counselling center for people affected by antisemitic violence and discrimination, and the German Alliance against Islamophobia and discrimination against Muslims, (CLAIM).
The ZdK called on the German government to continue its advocacy for the protection of Jewish and Muslim life and secure this structurally and financially. They say planned cuts achieve the opposite and are a fatal signal to a diverse and democratic society.
AfD: 'Program to secure power by the Left'
The AfD went further in its criticism: The party called for the funding to be stopped entirely, calling the initiatives a "program for the Left to secure power for itself."
If the AfD governs in Saxony-Anhalt, it wants wide-ranging cuts. The party wants to completely abolish the renowned State Center for Civic Education and cut state funding from numerous other organizations.
In December, the AfD, which has been classified as right-wing extremist in Saxony-Anhalt, wants its lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund to be the first AfD state premier to head a state government.
A spokesperson from the federal government's Family Affairs Ministry responded to questions from DW by referring to the need for the government to consolidate its budget. The goal was that funding programs "reliably continue, also in 2027, and make the biggest and widest impact possible with the means available."
However, an alliance of several organizations does not want to give up and is calling for a complete reversal of the decision: Instead of implementing the cuts, the organizations want the government to boost the funding pool by €50 million.
How is democratic civil society prioritized?
"Work to strengthen democracy must be funded," urged Tahera Ameer from the Amadeu Antonio Foundation. "That is a priority that we are currently not seeing. And that is very unsettling."
Many organizations point out that the consequences of the cuts will not remain abstract. They will have very real effects on people who experience discrimination in Germany, Lina Mitschke fears. She leads the Berlin association "Each One Teach One" (EOTO), an education and empowerment organization for people of color.
"The needs haven't gone away. But from January, people coming in have nobody to properly speak with; the phone will no longer be picked up; emails will go unanswered if someone needs support," she said.
For organizations such as EOTO, the planned cuts are a bitter setback. In past years, they had managed to raise awareness of the lived reality of Black people in Germany. "The experiences of more than a million Black people in Germany would be negated with the cuts," Mitschke said.
The associations want to fight until the very end to reverse the decision. They say work to promote and support democracy is what holds society together.
This article was originally written in German.

noticias.titulo: Rembrandt's 'The Night Watch' is more alive than you'd expect
noticias.resumen: A new project and exhibition, "The Night Watch Lives," lifts the veil on the hidden world of microbes covering one of the most famous paintings of the Dutch Golden Age.
noticias.texto:
Rembrandt's 'The Night Watch' is more alive than you'd expect
November 23, 2026
Rembrandt van Rijn's "The Night Watch" is one of the most famous paintings of the Dutch Golden Age. Amsterdam's Rijksmuseum, where the work is on display, hails the artist's 1642 masterpiece as "the turning point in his career and as the superlative example of his creative genius."
In the painting, Rembrandt made dramatic use of light and shadow to guide the viewer's eye to key figures. And unlike static group portraits typical of his era, the artist depicted Amsterdam's civic guards in mid-action, as they prepare to march out.
Beyond the sense of movement featured in "The Night Watch," the painting itself is also alive in a way that's rarely taken into consideration — through the microscopic organisms living on the canvas.
The research project "The Night Watch Lives" explores exactly that question: What kinds of life forms inhabit the surface of the famous painting?
The study is a collaborative scientific and exhibition project between the Rijksmuseum and ARTIS-Micropia — an Amsterdam museum dedicated to the world of microorganisms.
It's part of the broader "Operation Night Watch" restoration and research project described as the "biggest and most wide-ranging ever study and restoration of Rembrandt's most famous painting," started in 2019. Conservators and scientists in this project have been examining every aspect of Rembrandt's masterpiece using cutting-edge technology, seeking new insights into its materials, condition and history — and now, its microbiome.
Putting microbes in the spotlight
The idea behind "The Night Watch Lives" was to "put microbes in a positive spotlight," Eline van Bloois, who led the research, told DW. "Honestly, if you're asking me — I'm a microbiologist, so I'm biased of course — but they really deserve more positive attention."
Over a period of six months, van Bloois will be taking samples once a month directly from the famous painting at the Rijksmuseum, accompanied by the people working on the restoration of "The Night Watch."
Using small sterile discs gently pressed against selected areas of the painting, the samples collect microscopic material from both varnished and unvarnished sections.
These samples are then cultivated in laboratories, allowing previously invisible microbes to grow into visible colonies that can be studied and identified.
At the "The Night Watch Lives" exhibition, visitors can view Petri dishes containing the cultivated microbial colonies. A life-size reproduction of Rembrandt's masterpiece also shows where the samples were taken, and which microorganisms were found there.
A study in progress
At the exhibition's opening on November 11, the installation included the findings of two of van Bloois' sampling sessions. Four more will be added over the coming months, allowing the museum's visitors to follow the results of the study as it unfolds.
That means the exhibition's visitors "will be figuring out what I've found as I'm figuring it out myself," explains the microbiologist. "We really take them through that journey with us."
People often fear microbes or associate them with disease, even though the vast majority of these microscopic organisms are actually harmless or vital to human survival.
Some of the organisms found on the painting "are very commonly found on human skin, for instance, and they're a healthy part of the microbiome; most humans actually have these bacteria with them," says van Bloois, adding that the presence of these microbes on the painting made sense, since humans are often near the work.
But another bacterium stood out in the samples: Microbacterium saccharophilum, a species first identified at a sugar refinery in Japan in 2013. How this microorganism ended up on the Dutch "Night Watch," or when, is a guessing game.
"It's part of the fun and part of the frustration in microbiology. You cannot ask the microbes where they originate from," says van Bloois. "It would make our lives a bit easier, but it's also fun to have a little bit of a mystery."
The samples also revealed bacteria from soil, often found in plant roots. Could these organisms somehow harm the painting? Could plants start growing on the work?
Van Bloois explains why this is highly unlikely: On the painting, the bacteria can form inactive spores, but for the study, the researcher "provided them with all the nutrients and the right temperature and the right humidity that allowed them to grow again."
Still, studying these organisms may eventually contribute to understanding how paintings age, how environmental conditions affect cultural heritage, and how museums can better preserve priceless works of art.
As to whether the microorganisms could date back to Rembrandt's time, the microbiologist says that's also "highly unlikely" — but here again, microbes cannot reveal their origin story.
When art and science meet
As part of the larger "Operation Night Watch" team, van Bloois is definitely inspired by this "group effort where everyone is just really enthusiastic about telling these stories and adding to the knowledge surrounding 'The Night Watch.'"
The microbiological samples revealed by the laboratory process resemble abstract art in miniature: colorful clusters, delicate textures and intricate patterns created by living organisms.
And as the study is unfolding publicly, it also feels like an artistic performance of its own.
The project also perfectly embodies the full name of the museum where the exhibition is held: Natura Artis Magistra, a Latin phrase that translates to "nature is the teacher of art and science," as the microbiologist points out: "It's really cool to see science and art all come together in this project."
The exhibition "The Night Watch Lives" runs at ARTIS-Micropia in Amsterdam until the end of May 2027.

noticias.titulo: Germany's Early Start Pension: Can child investment accounts help?
noticias.resumen: Germany plans to pay €10 a month into investment accounts for children to encourage long-term retirement saving. Economists say the measure may help build wealth but won't solve the country's pension funding challenge.
noticias.texto:
Germany's Early Start Pension: Can child investment accounts help?
November 23, 2026
Germany's pension system is under growing strain as demographic change leaves a shrinking workforce funding the pensions of an increasing number of retirees.
In the 1960s, for instance, six workers contributed to the pay-as-you-go public retirement system for each pensioner. Today, that figure has fallen to just two contributors per retiree.
According to the Federal Statistical Office, Germany's fertility rate is currently 1.32 children per woman,and has remained below the 2.1 needed to maintain a stable population since the 1970s.
As a large cohort of baby boomers reaches retirement age, fewer young people are entering the workforce. Germany's working-age population is shrinking by around 1% each year due to demographic change alone, according to the German bank LBBW.
To keep up, nearly a quarter of the federal budget, over €123 billion ($135 billion), is transferred to the statutory pension system each year to help finance pension payments.
Now to help ease the pressure on the pension system, Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government plans to implement a raft of reforms, including a supplementary, capital-funded savings scheme known as the Frühstartrente, or Early Start Pension.
How does the Early Start Pension work?
Under the plan, the state would pay €10 per month into an investment account for every child and teenager aged six to 18.
Beneficiaries would not be able to access the money until they reach retirement age, though current plans would allow the funds to be transferred into private retirement accounts. Investment returns would be tax-free during the accumulation phase and taxed only when funds are withdrawn.
Assuming an average annual return of 7%, the €1,440 contributed by the government over 12 years would grow to around €53,000 by retirement, according to government projections.
Parents and relatives would be able to make additional contributions. If they invest an extra €50 per month, the account could grow to as much as €300,000 by retirement.
Starting to save early makes sense because of the power of compound interest, Axel Börsch-Supan, a professor of economics at the Technical University of Munich, told DW.
"But it will not solve Germany's pension problems, which stem from the pay-as-you-go system and costly policies such as the pension level guarantee and retirement at 63," he added, referring to a provision that allows workers with at least 45 years of pension contributions to retire at age 63 with a full pension.
Börsch-Supan argues that government subsidies under the program are likely to benefit higher-income families more than lower-income households.
"That's a waste of taxpayer money, because higher-income individuals are already well-positioned to provide for their own retirement and that of their children," he said.
The Ifo Institute, one of Germany's leading economic think tanks, shares a similar assessment.
It argues that the scheme effectively means "the government hands out money indiscriminately, only to reclaim it through taxes from the same citizens."
What does the government say?
The government, however, argues that the plan gives every child a head start in the capital markets regardless of their family's financial circumstances and helps them build retirement savings and long-term wealth.
Similar capital market-based savings and investment accounts for children exist in several countries, including the United Kingdom, Israel, Canada and Singapore.
Many of these programs include government contributions, matching payments or tax incentives designed to encourage long-term saving and asset accumulation from an early age.
But Germany's plan differs slightly as it links state-funded childhood investment accounts directly to retirement provision.
The government also hopes the program will boost financial literacy among children and young adults by familiarizing them with investing, saving and capital markets.
Can the scheme encourage long-term investing?
Johannes Geyer, deputy head of the department of public economics at the German Institute for Economic Research (DIW Berlin), says there is little evidence the Early Start Pension will fundamentally change how people engage with financial markets.
"The idea is that people will develop a connection to the capital markets through their experiences with their investment portfolios," he told DW. "But this is not very convincing. We neither know what experiences the future will bring nor what conclusions people will draw from them."
Geyer stresses that the program's impact will not be visible for decades because participants cannot access the funds until retirement.
"If we start now with the 2020 and 2021 cohorts, we're talking about the 2080s. That's a bit too far in the future to be able to draw meaningful conclusions."
In the meantime, he says, the scheme's most immediate effect may be to strengthen ties between families and financial institutions, particularly if account holders make additional contributions.
Opposition parties, including the Greens and the Left Party, have criticized the plan, arguing it would reinforce social disparities and boost inequality since better-off parents could pay more into accounts.
Yet Geyer says the measure won't increase inequality per se. "Sure, wealthy families are more likely to top up their contributions more substantially. But they probably would have done that anyway," he underscored.
"A more interesting question is whether the measure can also encourage people with limited financial means to invest in stocks," he said.
What else should be done to stabilize the pension system?
Geyer points out that Germany cannot entirely escape the costs of demographic decline and an aging society.
To address the challenge, he calls for a moderate increase in pension contributions, a broader contributor base that includes groups such as the self-employed, and policies aimed at attracting more qualified workers to the labor market.
Börsch-Supan, who specializes in the economics of aging, says the government's primary goal should be to stabilize the pay-as-you-go statutory pension system.
"A transition to a fully funded pension system would actually be desirable, but it would initially place a heavy double burden on the younger generation, because they would have to save for themselves while also paying contributions for their parents," he explained.
The expert also suggests other measures like restoring the sustainability factor, which is designed to link annual pension hikes to demographic shifts, and linking the retirement age to life expectancy.

noticias.titulo: NATO Parliamentary Assembly convenes amid Russian airspace violations
noticias.resumen: Ukrainian President Zelenskyy and German Foreign Minister Wadephul are set to address the NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin while NATO representatives discuss Russian airspace violations in Brussels. DW has more.
noticias.texto:
NATO Parliamentary Assembly convenes amid Russian airspace violations
Published November 23, 2026last updated November 23, 2026
What you need to know
- 72nd NATO Parliamentary Assembly continues in Berlin
- Germany's Wadephul: 'We will defend every centimeter of NATO territory'
- NATO members to discuss Russian airspace violations in Brussels
Follow below for developments from the NATO Parliamentary Assembly on Monday, November 23:
Zelenskyy calls for talks with Russia 'as soon as possible'
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called on Monday for fresh four-way negotiations with Russia – and involving European countries – to begin as soon as possible.
"We must do everything to make sure that the four-party meeting – Ukraine, Europe, America and Russia – happens as soon as possible," he told the 72nd NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin via video link.
"We have heard from our partners that they want to try to make it happen before Christmas," he said. "We hope it happens sooner. We are ready to do this literally tomorrow."
Poland to summon Russian ambassador over airspace violation
The Polish government intends to summon the Russian ambassador in response to a violation of its airspace which saw three Russian cruise missiles crash on its territory on Friday, the Polish Foreign Ministry said on Monday.
The security authorities and the military must first complete their investigations into the incident, a ministry spokesman told the Polish Press Agency (PAP).
On Saturday, Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski stated that Warsaw would convey its "strongest displeasure" to the Russians over the violation of Polish airspace.
Following examination of debris found in southeastern Poland, state prosecutors said that all three were Russian CH-101 cruise missiles.
The missiles are believed to have been manufactured in the fourth quarter of this year at an arms factory in Dubna, approximately 140 kilometers north of Moscow.
Rutte: NATO yet to assess if airspace violation was intentional
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said on Monday that Poland and allied countries were still working to establish whether the crossing of Russian missiles into Polish territory on Friday was intentional or not.
"It is clear that this is a dangerous incident," he told a meeting of the alliance's parliamentary assembly in Berlin.
"Whether it is intentional or not has to be decided, of course, by authorities," he noted, adding he would only be able to comment once Poland and NATO allies had assessed what exactly had happened.
"I will never speculate," he said.
Reports: Russia planning to station nuclear weapon in space
Western military intelligence services believe Russia is planning to station a nuclear weapon in space by the end of this year, German media reported on Monday morning.
According to public broadcasters NDR and WDR, as well as the Süddeutsche Zeitung broadsheet, intelligence chiefs believe Moscow intends to fire a satellite armed with a nuclear warhead into orbit.
Intelligence regarding the plans was reportedly shared among NATO member states recently and German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius is said to have been informed by experts from Germany's armed forces, the Bundeswehr.
A Bundeswehr spokesman reportedly declined to comment on the reports, acknowledging only that Russia does possess such capabilities and warning that a nuclear explosion in space would have devastating consequences for global satellite communications.
"It would effectively mean: back to the stone age," he said.
The German Ministry of Defense said only that it was continuously observing global developments in space while the Russian embassy in Berlin said it had no information regarding such plans.
The United States Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) warned in October that Russia was developing a satellite capable of transporting a nuclear weapon and, according to the new report, a satellite codenamed "Sputnik-S" is believed to have been in storage in the Moscow area for several years.
Back in February 2022, the same month as the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russia launched its "Kosmos-2552" satellite into orbit, considered by western intelligence at the time to be a test designed to measure the effects of radiation in space.
Should Moscow indeed launch a nuclear weapon into space, it would constitute a breach of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty which prohibits the stationing of weapons of mass destructions in Earth orbit. Russia agreed to a continuation of the treaty at the United Nations General Assembly in December 2024.
Space is nevertheless becoming increasingly militarized, with the United States admitting in September 2025 that it had positioned offensive non-nuclear weapons in orbit.
WATCH: Was Moscow testing Europe with airspace violations?
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the latest violation of NATO airspace on Friday an "intentional provocation."
The incident occurred as Russia was carrying out a wide-ranging attack on Ukraine.
But it also coincided with European military drills in Poland, intensifying concerns about Moscow's intentions.
Wadephul: 'We will defend every centimeter of NATO territory'
Following the most recent violations of Polish airspace by Russian weapons, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has emphasized NATO's determination to defend itself.
"We will defend every centimeter of NATO territory," he said on Monday as the 72nd NATO Parliamentary Assembly continued in Berlin.
Addressing Russian President Vladimir Putin, he added: "Don't be deceived: we may be a defensive alliance but we are prepared to defend our countries and our alliance."
According to Polish state prosecutors, the three objects which crashed in southeastern Poland on Friday were Russian CH-101 cruise missiles.
Wadephul said he was in close contact with Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski and assured Warsaw of his full solidarity.
Later, at approximately midday local time, NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte is expected to address the assembly before heading to an official reception with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in the afternoon.
NATO to discuss Russian violations of Polish airspace
Parallel to the continuing NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin, representatives of the alliance's member states are also set to convene in Brussels on Monday to discuss the recent violations of Polish airspace by Russia.
Russian drones and missiles have frequently penetrated the sovereign airspace of Poland, a European Union and NATO member, in the course of air strikes against neighboring Ukraine over the past four years.
According to the Polish government, three Russian missiles entered Polish airspace on Friday, crashing in the south-east of the country.
Airspace violations have also been reported in other NATO and EU countries including Romania, Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia.
On Saturday, Finland reported a suspected airspace violation by a manned Russian military helicopter near the southeastern town of Loviisa.
Moldova, which is not in the EU or NATO, has also reported airspace violations, most recently this weekend.
Welcome to DW's coverage
Hello and welcome to DW's coverage of the 72nd NATO Parliamentary Assembly which continues in Berlin on Monday.
Speakers in the German capital are set to include NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, joining by video link.
Later, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is to officially receive Rutte at the Chancellery in Berlin.
Meanwhile, in Brussels, representatives of the 32 NATO member states are due to discuss the recent violations of Polish airspace by Russia.

noticias.titulo: Ukraine updates: Kyiv claims strike that sank Russian ship off Libya
noticias.resumen: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the attack was carried out with Ukrainian-made naval drones. Meanwhile, NATO members are meeting to discuss an alleged Russian violation of Polish airspace. DW has more.
noticias.texto:
Ukraine updates: Kyiv claims strike that sank Russian ship off Libya
Published November 23, 2026last updated November 23, 2026
What you need to know
- Ukraine has claimed responsibility for an attack that sank a Russian ship off Libya
- Russian strikes on Kyiv region kill several Ukrainian civilians
- NATO to discuss Russian violations of Polish airspace
- Interfax reports Ukrainian drones attack oil storage facilities in Russia's Tatarstan
Below are the update on Russia's war in Ukraine on Monday, November 23:
Over 350,000 homes without power, Ukrainian energy company says
Some 353,000 homes have been left without power after Russia attacked four energy facilities repeatedly in Ukraine's Dnipropetrovsk region, the private energy company DTEK reported in a post on Telegram.
The company said repairs were ongoing, but with priority being given to critical infrastructure facilities.
Russia has repeatedly targeted Ukrainian energy facilities, especially with the cold of winter approaching.
NATO assessing intentionality of Russian violation of Polish airpsace, Rutte says
NATO allies are meeting to discuss the violation of Polish airspace by Russian missiles last week.
The alliance chief, Mark Rutte, said they were still assessing whether this was an intentional act by Moscow or not.
"It is clear that this is a dangerous incident. It comes from Russia," Rutte said.
"Whether it is intentional or not has to be decided, of course, by authorities. I will never speculate," he added.
He said a full comment would only come once Poland and NATO had fully assessed what had happened.
Realistic? President Trump pushes a year-end Ukraine peace deal
Days after warmly shaking hands with Russian President Vladimir Putin, US President Donald Trump reportedly proposed ending the war in Ukraine by the end of the year. The news has raised concerns that Trump aims to end the war on terms highly favorable to Moscow.
DW's Alex Forrest Whiting spoke to former US official Tyson Barker of the Atlantic Council, Domitilla Sagramoso of King's College London, and Ukrainian MP Kira Rudik about the obstacles to peace, the pressures facing Washington, and why Putin may see little reason to rush into a deal:
Russia warns against conflict expanding in Baltic Sea
Following a drone attack on a Russian cargo ship over the weekend, Moscow has warned against a an "escalation fo tension" in the region.
"It is indeed a very dangerous trend, the expansion of terrorist activity in the Baltic region... This is very dangerous. It is, of course, leading to an escalation of tensions in the region," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said.
Finland said the cargo ship strike had been carried out by Ukraine.
Peskov declined to comment on the drone strike that sunk a Russian ship off the coast of Libya which Ukraine claimed responsibility for on Monday.
Oil refinery in southern Russia suspends operations after attack
The Novoshakhtinsk in the Russian state of Rostov has suspended its operations after a barrage of attacks overnight, the state governort Yuri Slyusar said on Telegram.
Slyusar said the attack, which involved both drones and missiles, lasted over six hours.
He added that emergency services were working to contain the aftermath.
Ukraine has repeatedly targeted Russian refineries as a means to hamper the Russian economy.
The Novoshakhtinsk refinery lies close to Ukraine's eastern border with Russia. It mainly refines oil for export and has a capacity of 100,000 barrels per day.
UN calls for investigation into attack on Russian ship off Libya
The UN Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL) has expressed concern over the Ukrainian attack that sunk a Russian ship off the coast of Libya, saying in a post on X: "Libya’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and the security of its citizens and assets must be fully respected."
"UNSMIL calls for an immediate, independent and transparent investigation to establish the facts and hold those responsible to account," it added.
Libya has been split between two competing powers claiming to be the sovereign government of the country for several years.
"UNSMIL calls on all actors to act responsibly to preserve the country’s stability and build on the hard-won gains in the political process towards a durable settlement," the statement said.
WATCH: Is Germany's army ready for a war with Russia?
Germany is preparing for a war it hopes will never happen. The Bundeswehr has begun testing single-use — so-called 'kamikaze drones' — and AI-assisted targeting technology during its largest military exercise yet in Lithuania, close to Russia's ally Belarus.
The drills come as Germany builds up a permanent combat brigade of around 5,000 troops on NATO's eastern flank. But after years of debate over armed drones, is the German military adapting fast enough to the lessons of Russia's war in Ukraine?
Defense journalist Thomas Wiegold, who observed the exercises in Lithuania, tells DW that Western militaries have been slow to integrate drones. He explains how AI and software are changing warfare, and why Germany's deterrence depends on the readiness of its troops.
Watch the full report here:
Ukrainian attack kills 1 in Russia's Perm, governor says
The governor of Russia's Perm region, Dmitry Makhonin, said one person was killed in a Ukrainian drone attack that hit and damaged several industrial sites.
Two others were injured by shrapnel, Makhonin said in a post on Telegram.
The governor said 56 drones had been shot down. It wasn't clear how many drones were involved in the attack.
Perm lies some 1,700 km (1,050 miles) from Ukrainian-held territory and is home to an oil refinery that has repeatedly come under attack.
Zelenskyy says Ukraine drones sunk Russian ship off Libya
Ukraine on Monday claimed attacks on Russian vessels off the coast of Libya, with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy lauding the nation's defense forces for the "exemplary Ukrainian operation."
"Our warriors deployed seven Ukrainian-made naval drones. Despite all the enemy's efforts to counter the attack, the Russian corvette Merkury was sunk. It's one of their newest ships, commissioned in 2023, during the full-scale war," Zelenskyy said in a post on X.
"A Ka-27 combat helicopter was also destroyed along with the corvette. Our second target was the Russian dry cargo vessel MV ANGARA, which the enemy used to transport weapons. Result: target hit," he said.
This comes a day after a Russian vessel, docked at the Libyan port of Benghazi, was attacked by a suspected drone.
Zelenskyy further said Ukraine was continuing "operations in designated Waters," adding that it was in response to Russia's aggressions.
Ukrainian drones attack Russian oil facilities, reports
Ukrainian drones attacked oil storage facilities in Russia's Tatarstan region, Russian news agency Interfax reported on Monday, citing local authorities.
As per the report, the strikes damaged several facilities but did not lead to any deaths or injuries.
Russia's oil industry is particularly important to its economy and generates revenue that helps fund its war in Ukraine.
Russia and Ukraine have been regularly targeting each other's energy infrastructure. Russian oil is especially key to the warring nation's economy and supports much of its military operations in Ukraine.
UN urges probe after Russian ship attacked at Libyan port
The United Nations on Monday called for an independent probe into suspected drone attacks on two ships off the coast of Libya, in what could be spillover from the war in Ukraine. One of the two vessels was Russian while the other was sailing under a Maltese flag.
The UN mission in Libya expressed "serious concern" over the attacks, calling for "an immediate, independent and transparent investigation".
"Libya cannot afford, and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts," the UNSMIL wrote on X.
Libya's eastern administration did not identify who was behind Sunday's attack but said Libya was "not a party to the Russian-Ukrainian war".
NATO to discuss Russian violation of Polish airspace
Representatives of NATO's 32 member states are set to discuss the recent Russian violations of Polish airspace on Monday in Brussels.
No special meeting has been called for this purpose and the discussion will take place during regular consultations, a spokesperson said.
Three Russian missiles entered the Polish airspace on Friday during airstrikes on Ukraine, the Polish government has said. They crashed in the southeast of Poland which is both a member of NATO and the European Union.
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte, who is currently in Berlin for the 72nd annual session of the NATO Parliamentary Assembly, earlier said Europe would do everything possible to identify where the risks to Western deterrence and defense systems lie.
Russian strikes kill at least 14 in Ukraine
At least 14 people were killed as Russia pounded Ukraine's Kyiv region with airstrikes overnight, local authorities said.
In Dymer, at least 11 people died after a Russian strike hit a five-storey building, regional official Tymur Tkachenko said over messaging app Telegram. "Search and rescue operation is ongoing," he said.
Ukraine's State Emergency Service had earlier said that the dead included a teenager and a woman in her forties. Before that, it said rescuers were searching for 11 people, including two children, who were "not responding or cannot be reached."
It is not yet clear how many people remain trapped in the rubble of the collapsed building.
In the city of Vyshneve, a Russian strike hit a supermarket, killing three people, Mayor Illya Dikov wrote on Facebook.
Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets called the attack in Dymer part of "Russia's genocidal war against Ukraine....The world must stop looking away. Condemn this terror, hold Russia accountable, and act now to stop the killing of innocent Ukrainians."
Moscow has been pummeling Ukraine with nightly aerial barrages as the war-torn country braces for another winter, as the invasion grinds through its fifth year.
Welcome to our coverage
Hello and welcome to DW's coverage of Russia's war in Ukraine.
Overnight Russian strikes on Ukraine have killed several residents in the Kyiv region, local authorities said on Monday morning. The strikes hit a residential building in Dymer where search and rescue operations are still ongoing, and a supermarket in Vyshneve.
This comes after Russian President Vladimir Putin, last week, vowed a "painful" response to Ukrainian strikes on Russia's Crimea bridge, right after holding a meeting with US counterpart Donald Trump and China's Xi Jinping.
Meanwhile, Russian media reported Ukrainian drone strikes on the country's oil facilities.
As the war rages on, NATO member states are set to discuss Russian violations of Polish airspace in a regular scheduled meeting on Monday.
Stay tuned for all of this and more.

noticias.titulo: Germany news: Metalworkers go on strike as pay dispute heats up
noticias.resumen: Germany's biggest union is calling for more strikes over heated pay disputes with car makers like Mercedes and shipyards among the companies impacted. Meanwhile, a Berlin hospital fire leaves many injured. Follow DW.
noticias.texto:
Germany news: Metalworkers go on strike as pay dispute heats up
Published November 23, 2026last updated November 23, 2026
What you need to know
- Germany's biggest union IG Metall is calling for metal workers to go on strike, affecting factories across much of northern Germany. It centers around a pay dispute that's been heating up for weeks
- German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier heads to several African countries for a 4 day visit focusing on economic cooperation and the training of skilled workers
- A fire at a Berlin hospital has left at least 15 people injured with the police suspecting arson
- A key survey is expected to give insights into how Germans are thinking about foreign policy issues at a time of intense geopolitical tensions
Read below for more on these stories and all other things Germany on Monday, November 23.
Free Voters party chooses chairman following Aiwanger death
Germany's Freie Wähler (Free Voters) party have chosen a new chairman, weeks after their former front man Hubert Aiwanger unexpectedly passed away on November 4.
The party announced on Monday that Bavaria's Digital Affairs Fabian Mehring is to succeed Aiwanger both as party leader on the federal level and as one of two co-chairs of the Bavaria section of they party. The second state co-chair still needs to be decided.
Aiwanger was found dead in a Berlin hotel room at the age of 55 with no foul play suspected. He's been the party's defining figure for almost four decades, having led the Free Voters to substantial success, especially in Bavaria.
The Free Voters are originally a grass roots party in Bavaria and sit on the conservative edge of the political spectrum. They've been in government in Bavaria as junior coaltion partners of the Christian Social Union (CSU), sister party to Chancellor Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU).
There are also changes in the Bavarian state government. Tobias Gotthardt is to take over as economy minister, while Environment Minister Thorsten Glauber is set to become deputy premier behind Bavaria state Premier Markus Söder. The appointments still require formal approval by party conventions.
German foreign minister says NATO 'will defend every inch of territory'
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has inisted that NATO was ready to defend itself in the face of potential Russian threats against any of its member states.
"We will always defend every inch of our NATO territory," Wadephul said at the NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin.
His comments come after three Russian projectiles violated Polish airspace on Friday and crashed in the southeast of the country.
Wadephul is attending the NATO assembly in Berlin and DW has a dedicated blog on those talks where you can read all about how Russia's war in Ukraine is taking center stage for the defense alliance.
Strikes at car makers and other manufacturing in full swing
A massive strike is underway in Germany hitting major car brands another manufacturing factors. Metal and electrical workers are demanding better pay ahead of upcoming wage talks later this week. The strike has been initiated by IG Metall, Germany’s biggest and most powerful union.
Famous car brands Mercedes and BMW were affected as was an Opel plant, which is part of the international Stellantis group.
The strikes began on Friday and are due to continue until Tuesday. Wage negotiations are then set to continue on Wednesday with another round of collective bargaining for some 3.7 million workers across the sector.
The union is demanding a pay rise of 5% over one year while the employers association, Gesamtmetall, has offered a one-time payment and a pay increase of 1.3%.
The tough struggle over wages comes as especially the German car industry is facing serious headwinds because of higher energy prices, US tariffs and mounting Chinese competition.
Report claims Russia 'could' soon launch nuclear-armed satellite
A German investigative media report published on Monday claims that Russia would be able to launch a nuclear-armed satellite, called Sputnik-S, into orbit within the space of about 60 days if it wished.
The report from public broadcasters WDR, NDR and the Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper, cites a warning from German and other western intelligence agencies that it says was circulated at the start of November.
It said that a launch "could" take place by December, without quoting the document or clarifying whether it was talking only about a Russian capability, or a more firm intention.
The report said the satellite itself had been built several years ago and was being stored in the Moscow area.
German authorities did not respond to requests for comment on the record while the Russian Embassy in Berlin said the claims were part of a "propaganda" campaign.
The report matches longstanding warnings, mainly but not exclusively from the US, that Russia could be preparing a nuclear strike in Earth orbit designed to take out a large number of satellites.
This could have a severe impact on intelligence, communications, logisticts, navigation and other key services.
Russia's war in Ukraine, and the Ukrainian military's reliance on the Starlink satellite internet service, has provided an additional reminder of the strategic significance of satellites in orbit.
German exports to Africa see second year of growth
German exports to Africa have reached a new record. That’s according to a fresh study just as the country's president embarks on a trip to several African countries.
Exports are expected to rise by 6% in 2026 to reach about 30 billion euros ($33bn).
What’s behind the growing demand are especially orders from South Africa, Egypt, Tunisia, Nigeria, Angola and Kenya — countries where inflation has been dropping and exchange rates are more stable.
The biggest single export at the moment is a high-speed train network to Egypt. Other main exports include electrical equipment, optical instruments, plastics and pharmaceuticals, as well as food products, including dairy goods, cereals and baked goods.
The data is being reported by the Reuters news agency, based on the government-owned agency Germany Trade & Invest (GTAI), which promotes foreign trade and investment in Germany.
In 2025, exports to Africa had risen by 8% while in 2024 it had gone down.
Germany criticises oil states over failure to adopt climate resolution
The Germangovernment has blamed oil and gas-producing nations for the COP climate conference ending without an agreement.
"The oil and gas industry is still dragging its feet," German Environment Minister Carsten Schneider said after the UN climate talks had failed on Sunday. "Some oil-producing nations realize that the situation is becoming serious for them — that is why they are blocking it so vehemently," saidSchneider.
Almost two days into overtime, the COP31 climate talks in Turkey ended on Sunday as many countries, including the EU, rejected a final declaration.
Major sticking points at the summit included a commitment to accelerate global electrification and whether or not to explicitly mention plans to phase out fossil fuels. The suggested final declaration put forward by the COP presidency did not mention fossil fuels and according to critics would have undermined the shift away from fossil fuels.
"I understand that this poses a threat to the business model of those countries that sell us oil and gas. But electrification will make the world a more peaceful and stable place," Schneider said.
The inability to agree on a final declaration comes as climate change is increasingly linked to worsening heatwaves, floods and other natural catastrophes.
German President Steinmeier starts Africa trip
German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier begins a five-day trip to Africa that will take him to Ivory Coast, Ghana and Kenya with a focus on economic cooperation and the training of skilled workers.
He begins in Abidjan, where he is due to meet Ivorian President Alassane Ouattara. Steinmeier will also visit a vocational college and the International Academy for Counter-Terrorism before travelling on to Ghana.
In the capital Accra on Tuesday, he is set to open the German-African Business Summit, which according to its website, "brings together senior business executives, policymakers, investors, and industry leaders from across Germany and Africa."
His final stop will be Kenya, where he will meet President William Ruto in Nairobi on Wednesday.
The German president is traveling with a German business delegation and wants to encourage closer economic ties and greater investment in Africa.
The trip is his 11th to sub-Saharan Africa and his final one as president as his term in office due to end next March.
Patient suspected of starting fire in Berlin hospital
Police are investigating a suspected case of aggravated arson after a fire broke out at a hospital in Berlin.
Investigators believe a patient set fire to his bed in a room on the first floor of one of the hospital buildings in the Lichtenberg district on Sunday evening.
One nurse and the suspected arsonist suffered smoke inhalation and had to be treated in hospital. Overall, 15 people were injured with another 13 suffering from minor injuries.
While firefighters managed to put out the flames, smoke spread to other parts of the hospital which then had to be evacuated.
Widespread strikes expected across Germany
The country's largest and most powerful union, the IG Metall, has called for a strike this Monday over an ongoing pay dispute.
The union has called on some 23,000 workers to down tools in as many as 19 factories in northern Germany. Among the companies affected likely to be impacted are Siemens, Mercedes Benz, and shipyard Meyer Werft.
At a similar strike on Friday, more than 12,000 workers had taken part.
IG Metall hopes that the strikes will increase pressure on employers to yield to its demands, which include a 5% wage increase.
Employers have so far offered a one-off payment next year and a 1.3% wage increase from July 2028.
Welcome to our coverage
Welcome and guten Morgen from the DW newsroom in Bonn!
Another busy week is kicking off and in large parts of Germany it starts with workers are walking off the job today in what is becoming a very heated dispute over pay. Factories from Mercedes Benz to the large shipmakers will likely be affected.
Berlin woke up this morning to news of a fire in the Lichtenberg part of the city, leaving at least 15 people injured. Police have described it as a serious case of arson.
And the country's president, Frank-Walter Steinmeier, is off for a trip to Africa which over the next few days that will take him to Ivory Coast, Ghana and Kenya.
We'll cover all those stories and whatever else hits the headlines across Germany so stay tuned.

noticias.titulo: Rule-breaking is contagious — and good examples barely help
noticias.resumen: Seeing someone break a rule makes people more likely to break it too, a new study finds, especially when the rule-breaker is on their side politically. Watching others behave well barely made a difference.
noticias.texto:
Rule-breaking is contagious — and good examples barely help
November 23, 2026
Most people stop at a red light, even when the road is empty. But what happens when the person next to them walks straight across?
A new study suggests they become more likely to follow. In an online experiment led by researchers at the University of Amsterdam, people who saw someone from their own political camp break a rule outright were nearly twice as likely to do the same. Seeing someone follow the rule barely made a difference.
A small number did more than copy. They broke the rule by more than the person they had watched. According to Lucas Molleman, an assistant professor of developmental psychology at the University of Amsterdam who led the research, a few bad actors like these can "basically take off the guardrails of the group."
How was the study done, and what are its limits?
The researchers wanted to know how seeing other people's choices affects whether someone sticks to a rule. They recruited 750 adults in the United States, roughly half Democrats and half Republicans, a week before the 2024 presidential election.
Participants watched an animated shooting star cross a row of 100 squares and were told to click the square where it shone brightest, which was always near the middle. Squares further to the right paid more money, so there was a reason to cheat.
Each person chose first on their own. They were then shown what a previous participant had done, whether that person had followed the rule, bent it or broken it outright, and which party they supported. Then they could change their answer. The task was repeated six times.
The experiment had no real-world stakes, and nobody was punished for cheating. Other researchers say that matters. "That's not how the world works," Eugen Dimant, a behavioral economist at the University of Pennsylvania who was not involved in the study, told Science News. Punishment and social pressure, he argues, also shape whether rule-breaking spreads.
Is rule-breaking contagious?
Rule-breaking spread in the experiment. When people chose on their own, they picked the square furthest to the right, the most lucrative and most blatant violation, about 23% of the time. After seeing someone from their own party make that choice, they did so almost 40% of the time.
Small violations had only a small effect. Blatant ones had a much larger one.
Most people matched what they had seen or stayed below it. But just over 4% went further, breaking the rule by more than the person they had watched.
Do good role models make people follow rules?
Good examples had little effect. Seeing a previous participant stick to the rule rarely changed what others did, even when that person was from their own party.
People also differed. Some followed the rule every time and others broke it every time, whatever they saw. The rest shifted depending on what others had done.
Are people more likely to break rules when their own side does?
People were more likely to copy rule-breaking when it came from their own side. The effects were stronger when the person being watched shared the participant's political leanings.
Not everyone reads that as contagion. Stephen Reicher, a social psychologist at the University of St Andrews in Scotland who was not involved in the study, told The Guardian that if influence depends on who the other person is, it does not spread the way a disease does. He pointed out that people who see a riot often turn up afterwards to help clean up.
Can a few bad apples spoil the whole group?
To see how individual choices might add up, the researchers ran computer simulations. They created a digital version of each participant and placed them in groups of 100.
In some scenarios, the handful of people prone to escalating pushed the whole group towards heavy rule-breaking. But when the simulated groups contained the same share of committed rule followers as the real experiment, rule-breaking leveled off at a moderate level.
What does this mean in real life?
Molleman calls the work fundamental science and says the real world is far more complex. He sees possible links to situations such as drivers speeding together, or protests that turn violent.
He also says it challenges how people see themselves. In individualist cultures such as the Netherlands and the UK, he said that people tend to believe they make their own decisions. But "in many, many cases we are very much influenced by what others are doing."
This article is an excerpt from our podcast Science Unscripted.

noticias.titulo: EU takes aim at tech giants in tax proposal
noticias.resumen: European Council President Antonio Costa has proposed a smaller EU budget for 2028-2034, including a 3% tax on major digital firms to ease member states' contributions. France has already rejected the plan as inadequate.
noticias.texto:
EU takes aim at tech giants in tax proposal
November 21, 2026
European Council President Antonio Costa has proposed a new draft for the next EU budget.
Among other things, he is suggesting a tax on big tech firms to ease the contributions of member states, some of which strongly criticised earlier proposals.
The EU budget is theEuropean Union’s shared budget and it is used for things ranging from agricultural subsidies, infrastructure projects to border control and defence.
A first draft for the 2028 to 2034 budget was proposed by the EU Commission in 2025 but was criticised, especially by a group of northern European members including Germany who wanted the budget to be much smaller.
Following that criticism, the European Council President has now suggested a new draft, which is smaller by €204 billion.
But divisions among member states appear to remain, with France immediately coming out against Costa’s new draft, saying it was "deeply disappointing."
What’s the plan for the tech tax?
The proposal includes a string of new "revenue channels," explicitly intended to "to keep national contributions at a reasonable level," so that member state will have to contribute less than otherwise would be the case.
The biggest splash would likely come from a tax on companies with an annual turnover from digital activities of at least 50 million euros in the EU and 750 million euros worldwide.
Those firms would be subject to "an annual contribution corresponding to 3% of the annual net turnover from online advertising, digital intermediation services and user-generated data," according to Costa.
Aside from the tech tax, the "balanced basket of new own resources" also includes taxes on tobacco products and electronic waste.
What happens next?
Neither the EU Commission nor European Council President Costa will have the final word on the budget. Costa's plan will now be at the centre of hours of talks when EU leaders meet in Brussels next week.
"This is a realistic budget that addresses our new priorities while preserving our established policies," Costa wrote about his proposal. "I am confident that this proposal is a good basis for moving towards a final agreement."
But an initial reaction from France suggests that any final agreement might still be some way off.
The French presidency said the budget "falls well short of what is needed, particularly on the Common Agricultural Policy, notably to guarantee income support for farmers."
"As it stands, this proposal from the President of the European Council does not provide a basis for an agreement."
The EU was hoping to reach a general agreement on the budget by the end of 2026 with its formal adoption planned for 2027.

noticias.titulo: Democrats win House by largest margin in 50 years. And, COP31 ends with no deal
noticias.resumen: Democrats have currently flipped 47 House seats and could flip 49 total. And, climate change talks at COP31 ran two days longer than expected, becoming the longest conference in the summit's history.
noticias.texto:
Democrats win House by largest margin in 50 years. And, COP31 ends with no deal
AI Impact On Economy, Russia-Ukraine War Spills Into Poland, No Deal At COP31
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.
Today's top stories
Vote counts are concluding for the 2026 midterm elections, revealing a better picture of just how much Democrats dominated. Fifty-six percent of voters chose the Democrats in House races compared to 42% for Republicans. The 14-point gap is the largest margin won by Democrats in 50 years. The party has officially won the largest majority in Congress since the early 1990s. Take a look at NPR's breakdown of the U.S. House races, by the numbers.
Artificial intelligence is causing significant swings in the stock market as investors speculate about the future of the technology boom. While AI stocks have driven markets to record highs and bolstered the economy, concerns are growing about a potential bubble. Investors anticipated that AI giant Anthropic's stock market debut last week would lift markets, but instead Wall Street experienced one of its worst weeks in recent times.
- 🎧 The National Association for Business Economics released a survey asking firms about their AI experiences. NPR's Scott Horsley tells Up First that one in five reported measurable, widespread productivity gains, while about half said they saw some gains, but they weren't widespread. About 30% were either not using AI or felt it was too soon to assess its impact. Austan Goolsbee, head of the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago, pointed out that the significant investment in AI is already affecting the economy, contributing to inflation by increasing demand for construction materials and electronic components. Although proponents believe AI could eventually help lower costs and limit inflation, Goolsbee tells Horsley that the Federal Reserve must address inflation challenges right now.
Poland has called an emergency NATO session for today after Russia fired three cruise missiles into its territory. The incident highlights the stakes for European countries in Russia's war on Ukraine, prompting nations along NATO's eastern border to seek enhanced air defense support. Poland plans to present proposals to increase surveillance capabilities and deploy more F-35s to intercept incoming missiles and drones.
- 🎧 Anti-missile systems and NATO flights were activated successfully, but Polish authorities say that poor weather prevented them from intercepting the incoming Russian missiles, according to reporter Teri Schultz. No injuries or damage were reported. More than a year ago, NATO established the Eastern Sentry to enhance air defense after a significant drone swarm from Russia entered Poland. Experts are now scrutinizing potential gaps in this defense. If this attack was deliberate by Moscow, Russia is risking severe consequences by endangering the lives of people on the ground in a NATO country, Schultz says.
Delegates at COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, couldn't agree on a plan over the weekend to address fossil fuels, the main cause of climate change. The event ran two days longer than expected, making it the longest in the history of these summits. Nearly 200 nations failed to finalize targets for electrification and financial aid for developing countries, or to address the impacts of climate change. The European Union rejected any conclusion that didn't advocate for a transition away from fossil fuels, while oil-producing countries like Saudi Arabia opposed this position. Fossil fuels contribute about 73% of global emissions.
- 🎧 Ultimately, the EU decided that no COP deal was better than a deal that didn't address fossil fuels, NPR's Rachel Waldholz says. She adds that money was another major issue. Developing nations sought increased support to tackle climate change, noting that they've contributed very little to climate change but often deal with the worst impacts. Wealthy nations agreed to provide funding under the Paris Climate Agreement. The U.S. was absent from the discussions due to the Trump administration's withdrawal from international climate negotiations. Many smaller and developing nations are strong defenders of these talks, viewing them as a vital platform to ensure their voices are heard alongside larger countries, Waldholz says.
Books We Love
NPR's annual reading guide, Books We Love, is back with more than 380 new recommendations from staff and trusted critics. This year's picks span a range of genres, including fiction, cookbooks, children's reads, poetry and science fiction. Don't worry if it looks overwhelming; the interactive filters will help you narrow down your list and find your next great read. And why stop at this year's reads? The Books We Love archive has 14 years of recommendations, so you can discover more than 4,700 amazing books, all in one place. This year's edition of Books We Love is dedicated to Rose Friedman, who edited a dozen editions and worked at NPR for 15 years before her death this year at age 38. Friedman was one of the original founders of Books We Love, formerly known as The Book Concierge. In her honor, start exploring and find something wonderful to read today.
Behind the story
by Maria Godoy, senior science and health editor and correspondent
People had warned me it might be tough to get Amish people to talk to me as a journalist — and probably impossible to get their permission to record their voice. Not a great omen for compelling radio storytelling.
Yet as I headed off to Lancaster County, Pa., last month to report on the biggest and deadliest measles outbreak in the U.S. in decades, I knew I wanted to hear directly from the community hit hardest.
So I turned to some good old shoe-leather reporting. My producer and I mapped out Amish-owned businesses in and around Lancaster County and spent a day driving around from shop to shop. At every stop, we introduced ourselves and explained the focus of our story. We asked Amish people (easily identifiable by their traditional dress) about their views on the measles outbreak and vaccination. While some declined to talk, others opened up about how measles had affected their families and communities, and why they had or hadn't decided to get vaccinated. To my surprise, one woman even let me record her voice.
Outside a farm supply store in a rural town, I met an Amish woman who was visibly pregnant. Measles can have devastating consequences during pregnancy. She told me her husband and two children had gotten vaccinated to protect her and her unborn child. She declined to give me her name at first, then got in a car driven by her hired non-Amish driver. As they exited the parking lot, the driver stopped to ask us what media outlet we were with. "Oh, NPR!" the driver said when we replied. Then she turned to her Amish passenger and told her, "Don't worry, you can trust them."
Part of gaining trust is about showing up, showing respect and really listening. Word gets around that you're trustworthy. Public health officials in Pennsylvania have also been using a similar approach to win the trust of Amish people as they seek to boost vaccination rates in the current outbreak. You can read more about it here.
3 things to know before you go
- Bayer could pay up to $7.25 billion to settle lawsuits alleging that its weed-killer Roundup caused cancer. A Missouri judge gave final approval to the nationwide settlement.
- South Africa's grassroots program Read Alex is tackling a children's literacy crisis and inspiring kids to write. The initiative culminated in a book launch for an anthology titled From Gomora to the World, showcasing stories written by children.
- Orchestra Noir transforms 2000s hip-hop and R&B classics into high-energy, choreographed symphonic shows. Beyond delivering performances, the all-Black ensemble creates a cultural bridge through their post-show ritual, when musicians meet with their multigenerational audiences.
This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

noticias.titulo: Ukrainian drones hit a Russian warship at a naval base in Libya, Zelenskyy says
noticias.resumen: Ukraine carried out an attack on a Russian warship moored at a port in Libya, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, claiming that sea drones sank the navy vessel in a surprise assault.
noticias.texto:
Ukrainian drones hit a Russian warship at a naval base in Libya, Zelenskyy says
KYIV, Ukraine — Ukraine carried out an attack on a Russian warship moored at a port in Libya, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Monday, claiming that sea drones sank the navy vessel in a surprise assault the previous day.
Ukrainian forces deployed seven domestically made sea drones in the operation, which struck the Russian navy corvette in the Mediterranean, according to Zelenskyy. The ship was one of Russia's newest vessels, commissioned a year after Moscow launched the 2022 invasion of its neighbor, the Ukrainian leader said in a post on X.
Russian officials made no immediate comment.
The operation, conducted some 2,400 kilometers (1,500 miles) from the front line in Ukraine, was the latest daring long-range assault by Kyiv's forces.
Ukraine has at times blindsided Russia during the war with ingenious attacks that embarrass Moscow, such as Operation Spiderweb in June last year, when drones launched from trucks hit over 40 aircraft parked near air bases across Russia. Along the roughly 1,250-kilometer (almost 800-mile) front line snaking through eastern and southern Ukraine, Kyiv's cutting-edge drones and ground robots are helping hold back Russia's bigger army.
At the same time, Russia's strategic bombing of Ukraine has devastated the power grid ahead of winter and damaged civilian buildings.
A Russian strike on a five-story apartment block in a village near Kyiv killed 11 people, regional police said Monday. A 7-year-old child and a 79-year-old woman were pulled from the rubble after the Sunday morning attack, rescue services said.
Ukraine hits Russian assets from Siberia to Libya, Zelenskyy says
Zelenskyy described Sunday's attack as "exemplary" and said "the targets we set were achieved."
"We continue our operations in designated waters. We are responding to Russia's aggression. We are developing Ukrainian weapons," he said.
