Ukraine has hit Russian oil refineries as far away as western Siberia and Russian warships in the Mediterranean, Zelenskyy noted in a live video address Monday to a meeting of the NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin.
"We keep finding ways to get back on our feet after every Russian attack," Zelenskyy said.
Ukrainian forces also struck the Russian dry cargo ship MV Angara, which Zelenskyy said Moscow used to transport weapons, and destroyed a Ka-27 military helicopter in the attack, the Ukrainian leader said.
Ukrainian forces are operating in western Libya under a covert deal endorsed by the West, using the North African country's territory to strike a Russian tanker in the Mediterranean in March, according to Libyan officials.
The Ukrainian forces, most of them drone experts, were at the time operating mainly at an air base in the coastal city of Misrata, but also in other military facilities in the capital Tripoli and the coastal town of Zawiya, the officials told The Associated Press earlier this year.
Sunday's attack severely damaged the Russian corvette at the Benghazi Naval Base in eastern Libya, according to two Libyan officials.
Residents in Benghazi heard loud explosions and saw flames at the base early Sunday. Civil defense units rushed to the site and extinguished the fire, authorities in eastern Libya said.
The vessel had docked to refuel and take on supplies as part of a cooperation agreement between Russia and the eastern-based government in Libya, a statement said without providing details about the vessel or its cargo.
The government in eastern Libya sent a letter to U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres and the U.N. Security Council, calling for an international investigation into the potential use of western Libya to prepare and launch Sunday's attack.
Libyan officials say two sea drones hit Russian warship
Libyan officials who were briefed on the attack told The Associated Press that at least four drones were intercepted while two hit the corvette, which is designed to patrol coastal waters and escort other ships.
At least 10 people, including Libyan and Russian nationals, were wounded in the attack, one of the officials said.
The officials, affiliated with the self-styled Libyan National Army, which controls eastern and southern Libya, spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren't allowed to talk with reporters.
Ambrey, a U.K.-based maritime security and risk intelligence firm, said that some of the explosions at the Benghazi Naval Base were likely caused by the detonation of ammunition on board the Russian warship.
Hours after the warship attack, another sea drone strike hit a Maltese-flagged commercial vessel sailing off Benghazi, the Libyan coast guard said.
Russian cargo ship was sanctioned, Ukraine says
Ukraine's Security Service, or SBU, described the operation as "unique." It said the cargo ship MV Angara was sanctioned and used to transport Russian military equipment, and the multipurpose corvette Merkury regularly escorted Russian naval convoys, including guarding the MV Angara.
The drones were delivered to a designated location and launched from a so-called "mothership" near the target, the SBU said.
A Ka-27 helicopter was on board the corvette and also went under, the SBU added.
Russian defenses tried from air, sea and land to hit the attacking drones, it said.
"Ukraine's defense forces have once again shown that the Russian navy and its logistics have no safe routes, even far beyond the Black Sea," which borders both Russia and Ukraine, the SBU said.

noticias.titulo: Seniors embrace Tesla automated driving technology despite questions about safety
noticias.resumen: Older drivers are using Tesla's automated driving technology to stay on the road longer. But safety experts warn the company may be over-selling what its cars can do.
noticias.texto:
Seniors embrace Tesla automated driving technology despite questions about safety
EVERGREEN, Colo. — Joan Spalding has driven the steep, winding road that leads to her house outside Denver for more than 50 years. But these days, the 89-year-old barely touches the steering wheel or the pedals.
Instead she tells the car where she wants to go, and presses a button on the large touch-screen in the dashboard of her Tesla Model Y.
"I just get in and go," Spalding says.
For all practical purposes, the car appears to be driving itself, navigating confidently on twisting roads through postcard valleys full of juniper and ponderosa pine.
"Now this is probably one of the narrowest roads," Spalding says, as the car pulls onto a dirt track that can barely fit two cars side by side, with a steep drop off to one side.
The Tesla handles the tight turns gracefully, even stopping to let an SUV squeeze by in the other lane.
Spalding was skeptical at first of what Tesla officially calls Full-Self Driving (Supervised), often abbreviated as FSD. It's a subscription service that drivers pay for, usually $99 dollars per month.
That was, until she saw what it could do.
"When I was driving," Spalding said, "I saw that the kind of things that it did were safer than what I would do."
There are more older drivers on the road than ever, and families often struggle with the question of when it's time to stop driving. Now, seniors are using emerging technology to stay behind the wheel longer, specifically automated systems made by Tesla. But safety experts worry the company may be over-selling what its cars can do.
"It's not a technology that I would drive with. It's not a technology that I would suggest that my loved ones use. I think it has a few safety gaps that just make me uncomfortable," said Bryan Reimer, a research scientist at MIT, who studies how drivers interact with technology.
It's hard to know exactly how many seniors are using Tesla's automated driving system, but the numbers may be growing. Overall, Tesla says FSD has more than 1.7 million active subscriptions, an increase of 67% from a year ago. If the car-maker knows how many of those subscribers are seniors, it isn't saying.
Riding along with Joan Spalding, it's easy to understand the appeal for older drivers. The car gives her mobility and freedom that she wouldn't have otherwise.
Before she got her Tesla, Spalding had gotten into a number of minor fender benders. Then, two years ago, she was in a serious crash while she was trying to make a left turn.
"I made a wrong decision. I wasn't focusing on what I should be doing … I was lucky," she said. "But I realized then that my abilities were not where I wanted them to be."
Her son Mike Spalding had known for a while that his mother's driving was getting worse. He was already driving a Tesla, and it was his idea to get one for her.
"It would be safer for mom if she was in a wreck because it's got all kinds of safety features. And then safer for people around her if we didn't have any more crashes. I've been driving one for years, and so I'd experimented with the Full Self-Driving and saw what it could do," Spalding said. "It's better than me."
Tesla agrees. The company claims that FSD is up to nine times safer than human driving. Tesla doesn't release much data about FSD, so it's impossible to independently verify whether its safety claims are true, Reimer said. He concedes Tesla's technology is impressive and is getting better all the time, but says it's not a replacement for a human driver — at least, not yet.
"Tesla has continually over-promised and under-delivered," Reimer said. "Full self-driving is not full self-driving, but yet the name feels so real."
If you read the fine print, FSD is not fully autonomous. The company always uses its full title — FSD (Supervised) — in official communications, to underscore the point. The driver is supposed to be paying attention at all times, in case the car encounters a situation FSD can't handle.
The problem, according to safety experts, is that human drivers tend to get complacent.
"It's good enough, often enough, where people go, 'The next time I'm in this similar situation, I know how it's going to behave,'" said Alexandra Mueller, a senior research scientist at the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety, the nonprofit funded by the insurance industry.
But Mueller worries older drivers won't be ready or able to take control of the car in an emergency.
"This can be a huge problem," she said. "Ultimately it is very unsafe if you have drivers who are not fully competent due to age-related impairments or decline."
Tesla did not reply to requests for comment.
The company has not said exactly how many senior drivers are using FSD to stay on the road longer, or even if that's something Tesla is tracking. But the company's CEO, Elon Musk, has encouraged the practice.
In a recent post on his social media platform X, Musk said that "Tesla self-driving gives mobility to seniors." Several times, he's amplified a video from a YouTube channel called TFLEV, featuring a 98-year-old man, who just bought his first Tesla.
"It has not made a mistake. And I've been driving it probably two or three months and it's not made an error in its driving, " the driver, Larry Dimmock, said in the video. "In fact, the other day it stopped. A chipmunk was crossing the road and there was no other traffic and it did not run over the chipmunk."
Musk reposted the video last month, saying, "At Tesla, we even care about the chipmunks." The clip has been viewed more than 3.5 million times.
"My moment of fame, I guess," Dimmock joked in an interview with NPR.
Dimmock says he's owned dozens of cars in his life, starting with a Ford Model A. He says he's still a pretty good driver at 98 — but not as good as his Tesla.
"I feel safer riding with this auto system than I do driving or riding with anybody. It's just been flawless," Dimmock said. "I'll get in the car and go somewhere, otherwise, I probably wouldn't."
For Joan Spalding in Colorado, it's more than just a question of convenience. She says FSD is allowing her to live independently in the house that she and her late husband built more than 50 years ago.
"I love the solitude of being in that place and being by myself," she said.
Without the mobility that FSD gives her, Spalding said, she would likely have to find another place to live where she wouldn't need to drive.
"I'd have to move," she said. "This way, I think I can drive it for as long as I want to. I don't see any reason why not."

noticias.titulo: Mushroom supplements promise health benefits. What does the science say?
noticias.resumen: Wellness influencers say mushroom supplements can help with your gut health, focus and immune system. Here is where research suggests there are some links.
noticias.texto:
Mushroom supplements promise health benefits. What does the science say?
Growing up in the French Alps, Julie Daoust fell for mushrooms early in life.
"So as a kid, we'd go out and forage," she recalls. "We'd come across species like lion's mane or reishi. And I became more and more interested in those species."
Daoust went on to get a Ph.D. in chemistry, searching nature for novel pharmaceuticals. Her work ultimately led her back to mushrooms, a group of organisms to which humans are more closely related than plants. And yet, many of our modern medicines and therapeutics come from plants.
"Mushrooms share a lot more in terms of their biochemistry with us than plants do," says Daoust, which means "you have more chances of finding something that's going to have bioactivity in a human than you would with other source organisms."
Daoust is now vice president of science and innovation at Monterey Nutra, a company that specializes in the genetics and cultivation of mushrooms and sells fungal extracts and powders. Her team focuses not on the poisonous varieties, nor the psychedelic ones that contain psilocybin. Rather, they are interested in the functional or medicinal mushrooms that Daoust likens to tiny cauldrons of potentially useful molecules.
"We love to look for soft things that can't run away very fast," says Daoust, "because they typically produce really interesting chemistry to defend themselves or to communicate with others in their environment to survive."
The claim
Daoust says that certain types of fungi may have specific uses.
For instance, lion's mane — a soft chandelier of a fungus — may aid cognition. Reishi and turkey tail, which are mushrooms that grow as hard brown scales on decomposing trees, could bolster immune health.
And on social media, influencers and advertisers promise that medicinal mushrooms, taken as supplements, can slow aging and improve energy levels, focus and immune health.
The evidence
Robust clinical trials proving such connections — and their safety — are largely lacking, according to Abby Langer, a registered dietitian based in Toronto. "In my opinion, I don't think that there's much evidence for functional mushrooms as of now," she says.
Langer says mushrooms accumulate and concentrate the materials in the ground they're grown in, both good and bad — so one has to be cautious.
Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
She grants that in certain communities (in parts of Asia, for instance), mushrooms have been incorporated into their healing practices for generations. However, "just because something has been used for a long time doesn't mean that it's safe, that it's effective, that the dosing has been established," Langer says. "There are a lot of unknowns."
Still, she acknowledges that empirical support for the potential positive impacts of mushrooms is growing. "The clinical research on specific functional mushroom products is young," she says, "but it's accumulating fast and already includes some impressive results."
Mushrooms are a good source of vitamin D2 and antioxidants. Their cell walls contain beta-glucan, which has been linked to gut health, including a lower risk of Crohn's Disease, and immune response. Research into the effects of mushrooms on cognition have been mixed.
In addition, there's work out of Japan looking at how PSK, a purified extract from turkey tail, improved immune response in cancer patients. A meta-analysis considered 8,009 patients in eight randomized controlled trials who had undergone surgical removal of a gastric tumor and in almost all cases chemotherapy. Those who were also given PSK showed a 12% reduction in risk of death.
"This is not something that we brush off," says Santhosshi Narayanan, an integrative oncologist based at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center who recognizes the potential of PSK.
Even so, she admits that this "does not mean that PSK or any mushrooms alone cures cancer. It just shows to us that we need to pay attention to these natural products." Narayanan says there's still a lot to figure out with this particular extract, especially for populations outside Japan with different genetics or treatment regimes who might experience unwanted side effects.
"We need to do more research and understand how we can use it," she says. "Like which people, which type of patients benefit from which type of mushroom — because that itself is a whole science."
Narayanan and her colleagues also surveyed 2,349 studies examining the relationship between medicinal mushrooms and cancer, but only 39 were robust enough to be included in their 2023 analysis. Of that subset, "31 studies showed beneficial effects of the mushrooms, resulting in improved quality of life, reduced [side effect] profiles of different chemotherapeutic drugs, improved anti-inflammatory and anti-metastatic effects, and improved [disease-free survival] as well as [overall survival] in a few trials," according to the report.
Six studies didn't reveal any advantage and two highlighted worse outcomes. Overall, the analysis was unable to make clear conclusions about "the complex biological effects of mushrooms on the immune system in cancer."
The bottom line
In Narayanan's estimation, there's not yet enough evidence to support routine clinical use in cancer treatment.
And Langer recommends considering a few nutrition basics before introducing a supplement for gut health or cognition. "Take a closer look at what you're eating, how you're eating, when you're eating," she advises, "and see if there's any tweaks that you need to make."
Maybe it's possible to eat more fiber or protein, reduce consumption of alcohol or sugar-sweetened beverages, skip fewer meals, or eat out less often, she says.
"There's so many things that people can potentially improve on," Langer says, "before adding something else that's promised to be this panacea for everything that ails you."

noticias.titulo: Let's talk turkey: Here's how Thanksgiving meal costs have changed this year
noticias.resumen: Grocery costs have been on the rise, but food-price analysts say it's unclear if you'll spend more on the Thanksgiving meal this year. Some people are deciding not to host or are hosting fewer guests.
noticias.texto:
Let's talk turkey: Here's how Thanksgiving meal costs have changed this year
If you're planning to cook this Thanksgiving, you might not be so thankful for higher food prices.
Grocery costs have risen nearly 22% over the past five years, according to federal data. Wars in Ukraine and Iran, the Trump administration's tariffs and severe weather across the globe have pushed up the price of food.
Still, food-price experts say it's unclear whether you'll be spending more dough this Turkey Day — and, if so, by how much.
The American Farm Bureau Federation estimates that the cost of Thanksgiving will be up more than 6% compared with last year, with staples like cranberries and dinner rolls boosting the overall cost.
The Wells Fargo Agri-Food Institute found that drinks like sparkling water and wine have become more expensive but that the average Thanksgiving food bill will come in a little cheaper than last year, due in part to sales and promotions.
"But you have to be very disciplined," said Wells Fargo chief agricultural economist Michael Swanson. "You get the turkey at a great price, but then you might throw a bunch of stuff in the cart you didn't look at that carefully and find out you spent more money than you intended to."
Financial worries have pushed some people to shake up their Thanksgiving celebrations. In a recent survey by the website LendingTree, 53% of respondents said inflation was affecting their holiday plans or how much they expected to spend on the meal.
"They're doing everything from changing their food choices to couponing more and even cutting back on guests," said Matt Schulz, chief consumer finance analyst at LendingTree.
The survey also observed a drop in the percentage of people who said they might host Thanksgiving this year: 51% expect to have company over, down from 59% last year.
Shoppers say they still want to celebrate Thanksgiving, despite the price of groceries.
"It's too high," said Philadelphia resident Andre Andrews, who is retired. "Things are high, so much higher." Nevertheless, Andrews said he plans to smoke a turkey and a roast for the holiday, even though they cost him more than previously. "I can tell you this: I know it was more than it was last year," he said.
Schulz of LendingTree said those cooking on Thanksgiving can save money by sticking to a budget, shopping around for the best price and paring down the menu.
"Nobody wants to cut back on something as meaningful as a gathering of family and friends on Thanksgiving because it costs too much," he said, "but that's what a lot of people are facing right now."

noticias.titulo: K is for kindness, but families worry the world has less of it
noticias.resumen: A decade after first asking families about kindness, Sesame Workshop asked parents similar questions. They responded that their kids are getting kinder even as the wider world becomes less so.
noticias.texto:
K is for kindness, but families worry the world has less of it
Parents and caregivers of young children worry the world has become less kind, and they now value empathy in their children over good manners, compassion over confidence.
Those are just a few highlights from a new survey of families' views on kindness from Sesame Workshop, the education nonprofit behind Sesame Street.
"Caregivers see the world as much more unkind to their young children than they did in 2016," says Kim Foulds, vice president of research and evaluation at Sesame Workshop, "but the reason to hope is that parents see their children as more kind, more empathetic, more resilient than they did in 2016."
The new "K is for Kind Study 2026" comes 10 years after the original "K is for Kind: A National Survey on Kindness and Kids," and it offers a remarkable glimpse at how families' feelings about kindness have shifted, in some cases dramatically, over a decade defined by the rise of social media and bitter political polarization.
Monday's release also coincides with the debut of Sesame Street's 57th season, which will focus on kindness and compassion in action.
Let's start with that bad news: Compared to survey results from 2016, caregivers today have a much darker view of the world:
- About 80% often worry the world is an unkind place for children. That's a nearly 11-percentage-point increase since 2016;
- Fifty-four percent say kindness is not a priority for most people, a 10-point increase since 2016; and
- On a scale of 1 to 5, caregivers give the average American a 2.8 for kindness.
Taken together, the data shows a worrying shift in the way families perceive the world — as a place with more rough edges that is less attuned to the needs of their young children. To draw these conclusions, Sesame Workshop conducted 2,080 interviews in October with a nationally representative sample of caregivers of children ages 3-8 years old across all 50 states.
The good news, Foulds says, is that, while caregivers "are concerned about the division and unkindness they see in the wider world, their experience of their own children is much more immediate and hopeful."
Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.
This manifests in a few key ways. First, in parents' own values for their children:
- Caregivers say they value their child being considerate (68%) over being smart (32%);
- They value compassion (56%) over confidence (44%), a big swing of 8 percentage points compared to when the same question was asked in the 2016 survey; and
- They value empathy (64%) over manners (36%) — an even bigger swing of 24 points compared to a decade ago.
In short, parents and caregivers say their values are shifting toward kindness. That shift, in turn, is showing up in the behaviors families say they're seeing from their kids.
- A whopping 92% of caregivers rate their child highly for kindness, a 5-percentage point increase since 2016;
- Some 74% of caregivers rate their child highly for resilience, a 12-point increase;
- And 56% gave their child a low anxiety rating, an 8-point improvement over 2016.
And that leads to what Foulds says was one of the most startling — and hopeful — results from the survey: 94% of caregivers said, when their child does something kind, they do it on their own, without encouragement or nudging.
"The child was seeing the opportunity to be kind themselves," Foulds says. "And I thought that was an incredibly beautiful, incredibly powerful finding to see how kindness is showing up in action in young children's lives."
These encouraging numbers come with one grain of salt: It's not unusual for caregivers to have a rosier view of their own children or their own local circumstances than of the wider world. In fact, this is a common phenomenon in education research, for example, where families often give America's schools low marks but high marks to their child's school and their child's teacher.
While this phenomenon likely influenced today's results, too, Sesame's twin surveys still offer a remarkable view of how caregivers' own views have shifted over the past decade.
What is kindness? The survey offers answers there, too. Caregivers talk about their children sharing in a way that requires them to give something up, connecting across languages and culture, making room for different abilities and including children who have been left out.
The survey also includes caregiver testimonials.
The parent of a 4-year-old told researchers, "He has a child in his class that is neurodivergent, which is different than him, and he is always helpful, always kind, always says 'Hi' whenever he sees this child for class and tries to be a good friend."
The parent of a 6-year-old told researchers, "My child was friends with an autistic child who is nonverbal. My child figured out a way to communicate with him, even though he could not express himself with words."
In the new survey, 85% of caregivers say it's "extremely important" to promote kindness, which is what Sesame Street's latest season will do when it debuts today on both Netflix and PBS KIDS.
"Each story really focuses on kindness, compassion, big feelings, and it's really designed to inspire children to carry the lessons beyond the screen," Foulds says. "We want the viewing to be the beginning of something, not the beginning and end."
In one scene from the new season, Muppets Elmo and Abby realize their choices have made a playmate feel left out and alone. They feel badly and decide to comfort and include him.
As one of the show's grown-ups reminds them, "One little help is all it takes."
Edited by Nirvi Shah and Nicole Cohen

noticias.titulo: Badenoch: Rejoining EU won’t fix Britain’s economic woes
noticias.resumen: Renewed membership of the EU "is not going to solve our recurring problems," Tory leader told business chiefs.
noticias.texto: LONDON — Britain’s economy needs a reboot and reopening the debate on its relationship with the European Union won’t solve it, Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch told business chiefs Monday. Speaking just a few days after Andy Burnham’s government reached a series of deals with the EU in a landmark summit, Badenoch accused the British prime minister of choosing to “look backwards” on a topic which creates uncertainty and prevents politicians from focusing on economic growth. “I know I speak for the majority of people when I say reopening the Brexit debate is the last thing our country needs right now. There are many more urgent priorities,” Badenoch told the Confederation of British Industry’s annual conference in London Monday. “The last thing this country needs is another five years of division, distraction and arguments about Brexit,” she added. The Tory leader echoed several former prime ministers, including Tony Blair and Theresa May, who in recent days cautioned Burnham over reopening Brexit. Badenoch said Burnham is opening a “Pandora’s box” and noted that “five prime ministers, not just Conservative ones … have told him that the rejoining the EU conversation he’s opening is not the right one.” Friday’s discussions with the EU focused on deals on food and drink, emissions trading and a youth visas scheme. Burnham has said he wants Britain to rejoin the EU in his lifetime but has not committed his government to pursuing membership. Badenoch said the U.K. should work with the EU on issues including defense, security and trade, but argued renewed membership of the EU “is not going to solve our recurring problems,” including lower projected growth and the government spending more than £100 billion servicing its debt. “Something bad is happening in our economy, and rejoining the EU is not going to fix it. Nor will staying outside the EU automatically fix it either. Britain needs to be more ambitious than just changing our relationship with Brussels,” she said. Instead, Badenoch said the U.K. should continue looking to the rest of the world rather than “locking yourself into one market,” adding that “Europe will always remain an important market, but it is not the market of the future.” Manifesto The Conservative leader’s speech came after First Secretary of State Louise Haigh dodged questions about her personal view on Britain rejoining the EU. “We’ll come back to what that might look like at the manifesto,” she told the same conference Monday. But she earlier cautioned Britain needs to consider the growth created from diverging with the EU on AI and financial services regulations. “I really note Tony Blair’s caution around AI, because we have diverged on AI and financial services, and that has driven growth in our economy,” she said of warnings from the ex-prime minister that Brussels must reform and allow more innovation on technology if Britain is to rejoin. “So we need to consider these things when we consider our next steps in the relationship with the EU,” Haigh said. Speaking to broadcasters on Monday morning, Burnham dismissed the warnings from former prime ministers May, as well as David Cameron and Rishi Sunak, on reopening Brexit talks. “I’m not a prime minister that’s going to be stuck in the past,” Burnham said. “I want to lead Britain forward to a more hopeful future, get the economy growing again, get cost of living down for people, lower energy bills.”

noticias.titulo: Macron moves to ‘trap’ successors with new budget rule
noticias.resumen: The French president's opponents and allies aren't buying his rationale for new deficit spending legislation.
noticias.texto: PARIS — French President Emmanuel Macron is pushing to enshrine strict rules on deficit spending in his country’s constitution before leaving office in May. An adviser to Macron, who was granted anonymity to discuss the plan like others quoted in this report, confirmed that the Elysée is looking at adopting a so-called golden rule in the constitution to “demonstrate the country’s ability to maintain sound public finances over the long term.” France is saddled with nearly €3.6 trillion in debt amounting to 119% of gross domestic product and a stubbornly high budget deficit projected to come in at 5.4% of GDP this year. But Macron’s opponents — and even some of his allies — aren’t buying that logic. “The fact that Emmanuel Macron waited until his tenth budget with a massive deficit under his presidency to consider this tells a lot about a president who waited until he had emptied the coffers before deciding to lock them up,” conservative candidate Bruno Retailleau wrote on X . “It’s as if he were saying, I pursued a policy that led to deficits, but now I want to pressure my successor to follow a rule that I didn’t accept,” said an adviser to a lawmaker from Macron’s party. An unofficial adviser who speaks regularly with Macron said the French leader is “trying to trap” presidential candidates who have floated their own constitutional spending limits — like far-right leader Marine Le Pen and center-right former PM Edouard Philippe — by forcing them to pick a side in a potential vote. The first Macron adviser quoted above said the model for their proposal would be a measure adopted in 2011 but never formally enacted that would have required governments to lay out their deficit trajectory for three years — not the “golden rule” of government spending as it’s normally understood. The rule is typically defined as a fiscal policy in which governments only borrow to invest , but in French public discourse the phrase is often used to refer to constitutionally mandated deficit targets like those in place in Germany and Italy. In France, constitutional reforms can only be adopted by referendum or in a vote that receives a three-fifths majority of the country’s two chambers of parliament. A former aide to an MP who still advises on parliamentary procedure said such a measure could pass, possibly by as many as 20 votes if all centrists and conservatives backed it and Le Pen’s far-right National Rally abstained. Le Pen, the front-runner in the race to succeed Macron next spring, said Sunday that she was waiting to see details on Macron’s plan before deciding whether to back it. Retailleau backed the idea while questioning its timing. Philippe, who was once seen as the best-placed moderate to beat Le Pen but is struggling in the polls, said last year he supported holding a referendum on constitutional budget restrictions. Far-left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who polls show is on track to face Le Pen in the presidential election runoff, is likely to oppose the measure. Lawmaker Eric Coquerel, a prominent member of Mélenchon’s party who chairs the National Assembly’s finance committee, said the proposal would amount to the “constitutionalization of the neoliberal nightmare.”

noticias.titulo: EU Commission confirms personal data leak after cyberattack, warns of further disruption
noticias.resumen: Names and email addresses were leaked in the cyberattack, according to one EU official, who warned that the full extent of the breach remains unclear.
noticias.texto: BRUSSELS — The European Commission said its EU Academy platform, which allows external users to take courses on EU policies, was compromised in the cyberattack first reported by POLITICO last week . “We can confirm that the EU Academy platform has been affected by the detected cyber campaign against the Commission,” spokesperson Thomas Regnier told reporters Monday. “This resulted in a leak of personal data of EU Academy users.” Names and email addresses were leaked, according to one EU official, who warned that the full extent of the data breach remains unclear. “It’s not over yet,” said the official, who was granted anonymity to speak freely. The exact scale of the breach remains under investigation, Regnier said, adding that public access to the EU Academy platform had been disabled as a precaution while additional security measures were put in place. The Commission has not contacted affected users individually by email, instead publishing a general notice on the EU Academy website. “There was no reach-out to individual users, but rather a general message to all users on the website out of transparency,” Regnier said, saying the message included ways for users to seek assistance. The European Data Protection Supervisor has been informed of the breach, he said. The admission came as two senior European commissioners warned staff to expect further interruptions to internal systems following the cyberattack, which left officials unable to input salary and leave information, and raised concerns that large amounts of personal data may have been compromised. In an internal note sent Monday and seen by POLITICO, Commission Executive Vice President for Tech Sovereignty and Security Henna Virkkunen and Budget Commissioner Piotr Serafin told staff to expect “further temporary interruptions” while security upgrades and updates are rolled out. “When interruptions happen, it is to protect our systems and our data,” the pair wrote. “We understand the disruption this can cause, but protecting our systems and data must remain the priority.” The note follows complaints from a staff union that employees had been kept in the dark about the attack and its potential consequences. Asked Monday whether the cyberattack was now fully contained, Regnier declined to give assurances. “As long as the investigation is ongoing, I will not make any conclusive statements at this stage,” he said. The Commission has confirmed that the cyber campaign involved an AI-assisted tool but has yet to establish who was behind it. Regnier said investigators would need to conclude their work before the institution could attribute responsibility. The attack comes as governments, critical infrastructure operators and businesses worldwide grapple with increasingly sophisticated cyber threats, including those involving artificial intelligence. “These last few weeks confirm a lesson we must act on,” Virkkunen and Serafin wrote in their note to staff. “When attackers operate at machine speed, we cannot respond at human speed.” The Commission is turning to AI tools to detect cybersecurity vulnerabilities. EU cybersecurity agency ENISA and the bloc’s internal cyber defense team CERT-EU have been probing EU systems for weaknesses using artificial intelligence in recent months.

noticias.titulo: Grand Theft Auto VI backlash engulfs Greek leader Mitsotakis
noticias.resumen: Opposition chiefs hit out at Greece's prime minister after he suggested that pensioners buy their grandchildren the violent video game.
noticias.texto: ATHENS — Greece’s opposition on Monday attacked Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis for his quip that elderly people could use a state payment to buy video game Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA) for their grandchildren. “Grandparents, don’t listen to nonsense and stand your ground,” said Alexis Tsipras, former prime minister and leader of the left-wing Elas party, warning that the game contains violence and is unsuitable for children. “They heard ‘Grand Theft’ and couldn’t hide their excitement,” Tsipras added, alluding to allegations of fraud and corruption that have bedeviled Mitsotakis’ center-right New Democracy party. The latest installment of the GTA video game series, released last Thursday , was billed as the most anticipated digital entertainment launch in history. In a social media video posted Friday, marking a one-off bonus payment of €400 to around 2 million Greek pensioners, Mitsotakis asked: “Which of you will be asked by your grandchildren for Grand Theft Auto VI as a Christmas present? We all know how much grandparents enjoy spoiling their grandchildren.” The video featured music and scenes from the popular game in the background. The socialist Pasok party also lashed out at Mitsotakis in a statement, accusing him of hypocrisy as the government recently voted for a social media ban for under-15s — but appeared to promote a game that regulators don’t recommend for anyone under 18 due to violence, profanity and drug use. “We didn’t need proof regarding how shallow the government policy is … Communication is always more important than substance for New Democracy and Mitsotakis,” the party said.

noticias.titulo: De Wever sets year-end deadline for Belgian budget deal
noticias.resumen: The five-party coalition government is deadlocked over how to shrink the deficit.
noticias.texto: BRUSSELS — Belgium’s Prime Minister Bart De Wever on Monday set an end-of-year deadline for his five-party coalition government to reach a budget agreement. De Wever is seeking to overcome a major political deadlock between his coalition partners — notably between the Dutch-speaking socialist party on one side and centrist to center-right partners on the other. At stake is a budget deal aimed at shrinking Belgium’s deepening deficit by €10 billion. Belgium is facing a deficit of 5.2 % of GDP in 2025 — well over its EU obligations — and the gap is expected to rise further next year. De Wever, a Flemish nationalist politician who previously served as mayor of northern powerhouse Antwerp, sought to overcome differences Monday morning but a two-hour meeting failed to result in an agreement, after which he briefed Belgium’s King Philippe on the lack of progress. The prime minister is now shifting gear and will turn to party leaders of the coalition parties in coming weeks to “gauge whether and how there is a willingness to find a solution,” his office said in a statement shared with local media . If government parties fail to conclude a deal before Christmas, “the government can de facto no longer govern” and will fall, the statement said. The royal palace said in a statement that the prime minister will continue to report on progress to the king in weekly meetings. De Wever previously offered his resignation at the start of November, but the king gave the prime minister more time to find agreement among his coalition partners. Monday’s trip was the third visit by De Wever to the palace in less than a month. This report has been updated.

noticias.titulo: UK appoints energy boss to drive reindustrialization
noticias.resumen: LONDON — Great British Energy Chair Jürgen Maier has been appointed the government’s new northern economy and reindustrialisation commissioner, in a move aimed at attracting private investment and accelerating growth across the North. The appointment was announced by First Secretary of State Louise Haigh during her keynote address to the CBI annual conference Monday, where […]
noticias.texto: LONDON — Great British Energy Chair Jürgen Maier has been appointed the government’s new northern economy and reindustrialisation commissioner, in a move aimed at attracting private investment and accelerating growth across the North. The appointment was announced by First Secretary of State Louise Haigh during her keynote address to the CBI annual conference Monday, where she set out plans for a stronger partnership with business to drive reindustrialization. The former Siemens UK boss, who has led the publicly owned clean investment company Great British Energy since 2024, will be based at No. 10 North and will report to the Business and Trade Secretary Jonathan Reynolds. A government official confirmed Maier will be leaving his role at GB Energy to take up the new position. Announcing Maier’s appointment, Haigh said the role of the private sector was “essential” to creating good jobs in Britain’s industrial heartlands. As northern economy and reindustrialization commissioner, Maier will be tasked with implementing the government’s reindustrialization agenda and using his “extensive expertise to link with business and leverage private capital,” Haigh added.

noticias.titulo: EU opens antitrust probe into Coca-Cola bottler
noticias.resumen: Competition czar Teresa Ribera says Europeans “should not have to pay more simply because they live in one EU country rather than another.”
noticias.texto: BRUSSELS — The European Commission opened an antitrust investigation on Monday into one of Coca-Cola’s European bottlers over concerns it prevented retailers from buying its drinks at cheaper prices in other EU countries. The EU executive suspects that the bottler offered supermarkets and other retailers discounts on the condition that they didn’t sell the drinks on in other EU countries. The Commission will also examine whether the company changed bottle and can sizes from country to country to make cross-border trade harder, and whether it paid retailers to limit soft drink imports into Spain. Brussels is also looking into claims that the U.K.-based bottler refused to let retailers negotiate a single supply deal covering several countries, forcing them to strike separate deals country by country. “People across Europe enjoy soft drinks every day. But they should not have to pay more simply because they live in one EU country rather than another,” EU competition chief Teresa Ribera said in a statement . Coca-Cola Europacific Partners is a distinct, publicly listed company that bottles and sells Coca-Cola drinks under licence from The Coca-Cola Company, which owns a 17% share in the firm. The case comes as the Commission prepares new rules on so-called territorial supply constraints, the practice of big brands stopping retailers from buying goods in one EU country to resell in another. Brussels has already targeted the practice under its antitrust rules. It fined Mondelez €337.5 million in 2024 for restricting cross-border sales of its snacks, and raided Ferrero in April. The Commission raided CCEP’s offices in several countries in March 2025. The company could face a fine of up to 10% of its global annual turnover if the case is proven. There is no deadline for the investigation to finish. CCEP said in a statement that it takes competition law “very seriously” and will “continue to engage fully” with the Commission’s inquiries, but declined to comment further on the investigation. This report has been updated.

noticias.titulo: How industrial cooperation strengthens Europe’s defense readiness
noticias.resumen: European and North American defense companies are strengthening industrial cooperation through the Patriot® program, supporting manufacturing capacity, technical expertise, and long-term defense readiness across Europe.
noticias.texto: Europe’s defense industrial sector is evolving as governments, manufacturers and suppliers work together to strengthen production capacity, technical expertise and long-term resilience. Across the continent, collaboration between European and North American industry is helping expand manufacturing networks, support highly skilled jobs and develop the capabilities needed to sustain critical defense programs over time. As policymakers focus on readiness, industrial resilience and security, cooperation across borders is becoming increasingly important. Advanced manufacturing, engineering expertise and long-term investment depend on extensive networks of suppliers and technology partners working together to support shared objectives. One example of this cooperation can be seen in the Patriot program, led by Raytheon, an RTX business. Patriot brings together a broad network of industrial partners across Europe and supports collaboration among companies that contribute specialized expertise and capabilities from across the continent. Maintaining and producing Patriot technology in Germany through this partnership is an excellent contribution to support Germany and NATO partners while strengthening industrial capabilities across Europe. ” Developing, delivering and deploying truly integrated air and missile defense systems depends on Europe’s aerospace and defense engineers, suppliers and production facilities. Technological interoperability and availability among European and NATO partners rely on shared engineering standards, coordinated production processes and aligned sustainment pathways. With the support of 24 European suppliers, Raytheon is not doing this alone. A cornerstone of this expansion is COMLOG, Raytheon’s joint venture with MBDA Deutschland, which will begin production in Germany by 2027. This initiative will boost output, increase in-region sustainment capacity and further anchor production within Europe and expedite deliveries on both sides of the Atlantic. “Maintaining and producing Patriot technology in Germany through this partnership is an excellent contribution to support Germany and NATO partners while strengthening industrial capabilities across Europe,” explains Jürgen Koneczny, Vice President Program Patriot at MBDA Deutschland GmbH and Managing Director of COMLOG GmbH. “This collaboration strengthens industrial and military capabilities in Europe, creates jobs in Germany and strengthens supply chains that benefit European partner nations.” Expanding industrial capacity and strengthening supply-chain resilience are becoming increasingly important priorities across Europe. Bayern Chemie, a key German supplier supporting the Patriot program, plays an essential role in building manufacturing capacity and diversifying sources of critical components. “Our partnership with RTX’s Raytheon is a strong example of how U.S. and German industrial cooperation can accelerate innovation, deepen co-production and reinforce the technological strength of the Western defense industrial base,” says Dr. Wolfgang Rieck, Managing Director of Bayern Chemie GmbH. “By bringing together complementary expertise, advanced technologies and shared industrial capabilities, we are well positioned to support evolving defense and security requirements across Europe and for customers worldwide.” Europe’s defense readiness depends on the ability to sustain critical systems throughout their operational life. ” Beyond production, European governments are increasingly focusing on sustainment, the maintenance and modernization capacity that keeps systems operational over decades. In the Netherlands, Fokker Techniek provides specialized maintenance, repair and overhaul support for Patriot units. In Poland, Wojskowe Zakłady Elektroniczne (WZE) delivers electronics modernization and testing capabilities that help improve readiness and expand national industrial expertise. “Europe’s defense readiness depends on the ability to sustain critical systems throughout their operational life,” says Roland van Dijk, CEO of Fokker Techniek. “Through our partnership with Raytheon, Fokker Techniek brings decades of Dutch MRO expertise to help ensure long-term readiness, reliability and availability. Together, we are strengthening the resilience of Europe’s defense industrial base while supporting the security and operational readiness of The Netherlands, NATO and its allies.” For WZE, participation in the Patriot program represents both industrial growth and strategic value: “Our cooperation with Raytheon represents an important opportunity for Wojskowe Zakłady Elektroniczne to further develop its technological and industrial capabilities. Through our participation in an international supply chain, we have strengthened specialized expertise, contributed to the growth of Poland’s defense industrial base and supported the development of modern capabilities for Poland and allied nations. This collaboration demonstrates the value of long-term industrial partnerships in fostering innovation, strengthening industrial resilience and enhancing collective security across the Alliance,” says Damian Gorzelany, WZE President. Today, 24 European partners support Patriot-related work, making the system an increasingly co-produced and co-maintained asset built in Europe for Europe.” Together, these partnerships reflect a broader shift in Europe – a move toward more distributed production, resilient supply chain and deeper industrial cooperation among allies. With 21,000 employees across 65 locations and 13,500 suppliers in Europe, RTX is woven into this ecosystem. Today, 24 European partners support Patriot-related work, making the system an increasingly co-produced and co-maintained asset built in Europe for Europe. For companies across Europe, these collaborations are about more than production. They help sustain specialized expertise, create high-value employment opportunities and reinforce the interconnected industrial ecosystem that supports security, innovation and economic growth across the region.

noticias.titulo: Ukraine sank Russian warship off Libya, Zelenskyy says
noticias.resumen: Kyiv said seven sea drones sank the corvette and hit a cargo ship, as Ukraine's war at sea spreads from the Baltic to the Mediterranean.
noticias.texto: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Monday credited his intelligence services with sinking a Russian warship in the Libyan port of Benghazi, calling it “an exemplary Ukrainian operation in response to the Russian war.” Libya’s eastern-based administration said Sunday that a suspected drone attack had caused an explosion on a Russian ship docked in Benghazi, and that a second vessel was hit off the city’s coast that evening. Satellite images, published by Vantor and distributed by AP , showed the corvette Merkury capsized in port. “Despite all the enemy’s attempts to counter them, the Russian corvette Merkury was sunk,” Zelenskyy wrote on Telegram. According to his post, a Ka-27 combat helicopter was also destroyed along with the ship. The operation used seven Ukrainian-made sea drones and also hit the cargo ship MV Angara, which Kyiv accuses Moscow of using to carry weapons. Moscow has not yet commented. The U.N. mission in Libya called for an independent investigation . In March, Russia accused Ukraine of launching sea drones from Libya against the Arctic Metagaz, a sanctioned LNG tanker that was hit around 240 kilometers north of the Libyan port of Sirte and left damaged and drifting in the Mediterranean. The Libyan strikes occurred a day after a drone hit the Russian cargo ship Sparta II in the Gulf of Finland. Finland’s defense forces said Ukraine was likely behind that attack. “War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity,” Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo wrote on X on Saturday. “Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor.” Overnight, Russia launched 153 drones at Ukraine, the air force said. In the Kharkiv region, eight people were injured when drones hit a kindergarten and a hotel, regional officials said .

noticias.titulo: Kaliningrad is the Achilles’ heel of Putin in the Baltic Sea
noticias.resumen: With Kaliningrad’s residents now hearing air-raid sirens and Crimea’s lifelines under fire, Russian “trophy territories” risk turning into winter pressure cookers for both Moscow and the civilians trapped inside.
noticias.texto: “Hm, Kaliningrad,” said the senior military officer, when I told him about my forthcoming research project, “that may turn out to be rather topical”. He didn’t give details. Indeed, he gave the impression that he might have said too much. But he was right. Our chat, at a well-lubricated party, was followed by one of the most intense weeks of news I can remember. To refresh your memory: Poland released details of a planned sabotage operation involving a Russian attack on the border, which was to be blamed on Ukrainians. The Warsaw authorities deployed special forces to deter the false-flag stunt; two Russian missiles and a jet-powered drone hit Polish territory , an accident, perhaps; Ukrainian drones destroyed the Russian naval corvette Merkury in the Libyan port of Benghazi and hit the cargo ship Ascalon, both of which had sailed there from Kaliningrad; a Russian cargo ship heading to Kaliningrad was hit by a drone attack, presumably Ukrainian; fears of a drone strike at the Kaliningrad naval base, Baltiysk, prompted air-raid warnings (perhaps the first in the territory’s history, and certainly a useful bit of psychological warfare); Ukraine destroyed the Kerch bridge roadway, a vital supply line for Russian-occupied Crimea. This non-exhaustive selection highlights an emerging trend in Europe’s response to Russia’s war in Ukraine. A new focus is Kaliningrad . Read more Russia is losing its grip on Kaliningrad, despite using the exclave for anti-Nato scare stories For the first years of the war, an unstated taboo prevented Ukrainian attacks on Russia’s trophy territory (many were planned; none happened). Not any more. It is not clear yet whether Ukrainian drones flew there via Russia, (a long way round) or headed over Belarus, or were perhaps launched from somewhere closer. What is clear is that the 1 million residents of Kaliningrad now have to worry about sirens, alarms, and, quite possibly, explosions. Attacks on Russian merchant shipping in the Baltic Sea have exposed the fragility of the territory’s supply lines by sea, while the drone scare disrupted vital air links to Russia. And it’s not only Kaliningrad. Russia’s other trophy territory, Crimea, is also proving to be a hostage. Read more Nato’s Achilles heel? The Suwałki Gap, and Lithuania’s fears of a Russian attack Squeezing Crimea How will the population there feel as winter bites and Ukraine throttles their food and fuel supplies? The Russian forces along the far west of the front are looking vulnerable too. This article continues, but the full version is available only to EUobserver.com subscribers. noticias.titulo: Listen: Could Czech public media lose their independence?
noticias.resumen: 205 crowns, or 8.20 euros, is what Czech households pay each month to fund their public broadcasting service. But this licence fee could soon be abolished. This decision is causing concern both within and outside the country. To the point that the European Commission has sent warnings about it.
noticias.texto: Production: By Europod , in co-production with Sphera Network . EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms . Find the full transcript below : 205 crowns, or €8.20, is what Czech households pay each month to fund their public broadcasting service. But this licence fee could soon be abolished. This decision is causing concern both within and outside the country. To the point that the European Commission has sent warnings about it. How can we ensure that Czech television and radio remain independent? It was the largest demonstration in the Czech Republic since the fall of communism. Last Sunday, around 400,000 people gathered in central Prague. They came to protest against a plan to reform the funding of public broadcasting, which they see as an attack on press freedom. Since 1995, Czech public service media have been funded by the public through a mandatory monthly licence fee. This is the case in 13 other EU member states, out of the 27. In the case of the Czech Republic, only the poorest households, and people with no device able to receive the programmes, smartphones included, are exempt. However, on 24 October, the chamber of deputies passed, at first reading, a bill aimed at replacing the licence fee with direct state funding. Why has this decision sparked such strong public opposition? Read more ‘He who pays the piper calls the tune’: Czech media-freedom attack is part of wider EU malaise, ex-commissioner Věra Jourová says Many fear the government could interfere with the impartial and independent running of Czech Television and Czech Radio, as our colleagues at the Hungarian outlet 444, a member of Sphera Network, explain . For a simple reason: without robust safeguards, funding allocated directly from the state budget may be easier to cut and to use as political leverage. With this new system, state support would also be far lower than under the current system. It is estimated that the reform would cut funding for public television and radio by 15 percent . Weaker finances could again leave the broadcasters more exposed to direct political pressure and put their independence at risk. So are these fears justified? Though prime minister Andrej Babiš claimed that “nobody wants to take control of public service media or nationalise them,” his critics are afraid the country is going down the same road as its neighbour, Slovakia. The licence fee was abolished there in 2023 and replaced by state funding. The government had initially set this funding at 0.17 percent of GDP, but upon his return to power, the populist prime minister Robert Fico reduced this percentage to 0.12 percent, representing a 30 percent cut to the budget for Slovak public broadcasting. He then abolished the public broadcaster RTVS, which he criticised for “not being objective enough.”, and replaced it with a new body on which the state has more control. Concerns about the possibility of a similar scenario unfolding in the Czech Republic are not confined to within the country. On 3 November, the European commission stated that it had sent an official letter to the Czech authorities regarding the reform. On 11 November, in Brussels, the commissioner for justice, Michael McGrath, stated that Brussels stood ready to use “all relevant tools” to defend media freedom and independence. Read more EU commissioner vows to use ‘all relevant tools’ to protect media freedom as Babiš public broadcasting bill alarms MEPs What does that mean? Michael McGrath is probably referring to the European Media Freedom Act. This legislation requires member states to implement a new set of rules to protect media pluralism and independence from August 2025. In the commission’s view, what is at stake in the Czech reform is not the change in the funding mechanism itself. The Media Freedom Act does not require member states to retain licence fees. For example France abolished its licence fee in 2022, and several Nordic countries, such as Finland, Sweden and Denmark, have opted for funding through various taxes, without the independence of their public service broadcasters being called into question. However, Article 5 of the Media Freedom Act clearly states that member states must use transparent, objective funding procedures established in advance and guarantee adequate, sustainable and predictable resources. It favours multi-year funding to reduce political influence through annual negotiations. So what will happen next? If Babiš does not give in to protesters’ pressure, the draft bill is due to be debated again in the Czech parliament in mid-January. The EU’s ability to enforce these rules will then be put to the test, as other political parties, mainly on the far right, such as the AfD in Germany, are considering similar reforms should they come to power.

noticias.titulo: Hundreds of methane leaks uncovered in Europe, as Brussels delays monitoring crackdown
noticias.resumen: Infrared cameras exposed hundreds of methane leaks across seven EU countries, as capitals lag on enforcing the rules and the EU prepares to delay them.
noticias.texto: A massive methane leak at a gas export station on the Dutch-German border went unnoticed until campaigners pointed an infrared camera at it, one of hundreds they have uncovered across Europe as the EU moves to delay rules meant to catch such leaks. Gasunie, the state-owned grid operator, at first denied there was a leak, but when confronted with the evidence quickly had it repaired. It is just one of hundreds of cases documented by environmental groups in seven EU countries in the past year using handheld infrared cameras. The coalition, led by climate non-profit Clean Air Task Force (CATF) and US group Earthworks, published their findings together on Monday (23 November), as MEPs prepare to vote this week on delaying parts of the EU’s methane law by two years, on the grounds that the rules threaten gas supply. Read more EU gives oil and gas importers until 2029 on methane checks, closes easy route to more delay No checks, no penalties “Without inspections and penalties that bite, this pattern will continue,” said Mihai Stoica of Romanian group 2Celsius. But many member states have yet to appoint the inspectors the EU rules required them to have in place already last year. When the Dutch campaign group Fossielvrij filed a complaint with the regulator, they were told that as long as it had not been officially appointed to enforce the EU’s methane rules, it did not have to supervise, and would not act on their findings. The necessary Dutch legislation is not expected until next year. Until then, Gasunie relies on “self-regulation”, the campaigners were told. CATF found methane leaks or venting taking place at 192 of the 275 sites it inspected this year in France, Romania, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, and Greece. Earthworks, which surveyed sites in the Netherlands and Germany, recorded emissions at 13 of the 44 facilities they visited. In Slovakia, CATF found a leak at a site run by pipeline operator Eustream that was so large they judged it a possible safety risk, not just a climate problem, and called the emergency hotline. In Romania, campaigners found yellow tags on equipment where company engineers had already flagged leaks, but which were left unrepaired. In Germany, many states have yet to appoint the authorities meant to enforce the rules, including North Rhine-Westphalia, where the responsible authorities have “not yet been determined”, the state government says on its website . There were also signs of progress. In France and Slovakia, routine venting — the deliberate release of gas into the air — was seen less often than in previous years. In Romania, some operators had installed equipment to capture gas on installations that used to release gas straight into the air. “These are practical steps, and they show that implementation is possible,” said Théophile Humann-Guilleminot of CATF. Read more [Investigation] TotalEnergies official coordinated with Trump to delay EU methane rules Poor cooperation The deal, which MEPs and member states reached last week, pushes back monitoring and reporting rules for oil, gas and coal importers from January 2027 to January 2029. noticias.titulo: THIS WEEK: EU leaders clash over budget cuts, Sánchez risks losing power, and Putin invites EU to dinner
noticias.resumen: Thursday's EU summit could be the last one for Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez, as his socialist PSOE party polls behind the centre-right PP ahead of snap elections on Sunday.
noticias.texto: This week, EU leaders will discuss massive cuts in future spending, as Spain prepares to hand over power to a rightwing government, and Russia invites Europe to peace talks. EU Council president António Costa unveiled proposed cuts to the bloc’s €1.8 trillion draft budget on Saturday (21 November), covering the 2028 to 2034 period, as well as plans for a new digital levy on US tech firms. And the 27 EU leaders will flock to Brussels for two days of haggling on Thursday (26 November) and Friday, as poorer states fret over losing “cohesion” funds, while wealthier ones seek to protect historical farm subsidies. Read more Costa’s EU budget plan for 10 percent cuts pits ‘frugals’ against ‘cohesion’ group ahead of crunch summit Leaders will also discuss a new €45bn loan for Kyiv, covering 2027, after Germany threatened to slow-walk cohesion funding if Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Hungary, and Slovakia did not drop their opt-outs to Ukraine assistance. French president Emmanuel Macron and German chancellor Friedrich Merz will be under pressure to drive a hard bargain in Brussels, with the French Senate and German Bundestag also to debate national budgets this week, as eurosceptic parties snap at Macron and Merz’s heels. And after Hungarian prime minister Péter Magyar secured the unfreezing of €10bn in EU funds, MEPs will debate Hungary’s compliance with rule-of-law benchmarks in a plenary debate in Strasbourg on Tuesday (24 November), some 200 days into Magyar’s post-election reforms. Read more Pedro Sánchez: EU hero or Spanish problem? Sánchez swan song? Meanwhile, this EU summit could be the last for Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez, as his socialist PSOE party polls behind the centre-right PP ahead of snap elections on Sunday (29 November), with voting to close at 8PM. noticias.titulo: El CIS estima que el PSOE ganará las elecciones con casi diez puntos de ventaja sobre el PP
noticias.texto:
El CIS estima que el PSOE ganará las elecciones con casi diez puntos de ventaja sobre el PP
- El PSOE tendría el 34,4% del voto, por encima de su resultado en 2023, según el barómetro de noviembre
- El PP bajaría al 24,7% del voto, en una encuesta a la contra del resto de sondeos electorales
En el día en que termina el plazo legal para publicar encuestas, y a seis días de la cita con las urnas, el CIS estima que el PSOE sería el partido más votado si se celebrasen hoy las elecciones generales, con un 34,4% de los votos, casi diez puntos por delante del PP (24,7%), con Vox en tercer lugar (15,6%) y Frente Amplio en cuarta posición, con un 5,7%. La suma de PP y Vox se quedaría en el 40,3% del apoyo, lejos de las estimaciones de la mayoría de las encuestas.
En cambio, el PSOE y otras formaciones de izquierda (Compromís:Front Valencià, 1,8%; Adelante Andalucía, 1,8%; Podemos, 0,8%; Unidad del Pueblo Canario, 0,4%; y Aramés-Front Ampli, 0,3%) se irían en conjunto al 44,3%, sin contar el potencial apoyo de ERC, EH Bildu o BNG a una eventual investidura de Pedro Sánchez. De nuevo, la estimación del CIS va en sentido contrario al resto de principales sondeos en España.
Es la estimación electoral del barómetro de noviembre (ver en pdf) que publica el Centro de Investigaciones Sociológicas, y que sigue la senda de la macroencuesta electoral que la institución presidida por José Félix Tezanos difundió la víspera de iniciarse la campaña, el 12 de noviembre.
Entonces, también apuntaba que el PSOE sería la fuerza más votada en las elecciones generales del 29 de noviembre con un 33,3% de los votos, que le reportarían entre 134 y 143 escaños, con una ventaja de casi ocho puntos respecto al PP (25,5% del voto y 98-106 escaños), una ventaja que ahora se habría ampliado casi otros dos puntos en apenas diez días, ya que el PSOE sube 1,1 y el PP baja 0,8; Vox perdería 2,8 respecto a la macroencuesta y Frente Amplio bajaría un punto.
Respecto al barómetro de octubre, que tuvo una muestra de 5.025 entrevistas, el PSOE sube cuatro décimas y el PP 2,5 puntos, mientras que Vox cae 1,5 puntos y Frente Amplio 0,4, como puede consultarse en el siguiente gráfico.
El CIS elaboró la encuesta de este barómetro mediante 8.034 entrevistas telefónicas realizadas entre el 10 y el 17 de noviembre, con un margen de error de ±1,1% para el conjunto de la muestra. El trabajo de campo se realizó, pues, en plena campaña electoral, y contempla el accidente ferroviario de Urda y la posterior dimisión del ministro Óscar Puente y la huelga general del 11 de noviembre, pero se terminó antes del debate cara a cara televisado entre los candidatos del PSOE y el PP, Pedro Sánchez y Alberto Núñez Feijóo.
Una encuesta contraria al resto de sondeos electorales
El CIS es la institución que realiza los sondeos más grandes de España, y es también la única de las principales casas encuestadoras, junto a SW Demoscopia (que realiza sondeos para la cadena de televisión La Séptima), que de forma regular pronostica que el PSOE será el partido más votado en las próximas elecciones generales y que la derecha formada por PP y Vox no alcanzará la mayoría absoluta.
Una estimación contraria a la del resto de sondeos, así como al promedio de DatosRTVE, calculado a partir del conjunto de encuestas publicadas, que señalan que el PP alcanzará la mayoría absoluta de manera holgada junto a Vox. Ninguna encuesta estima para los socialistas un porcentaje de voto tan alto ni uno tan bajo para los 'populares' como los que difunde el CIS.
Como ha pasado en encuestas anteriores del CIS y se ha venido señalando, en la encuesta del CIS hay una sobrerrepresentación de votantes del PSOE, de dos por cada votante del PP (39,8% frente a 20,4%), cuando los 'populares' fueron la primera fuerza en 2023 (33,1% frente al 31,7% de los socialistas).
Sánchez sería el presidente preferido, pero ganará el PP
Como presidente de gobierno, Pedro Sánchez se mantiene como la opción favorita para un 42,4% de los encuestados, lo que supone una ventaja de 19,1 puntos sobre Alberto Núñez Feijóo, que es preferido por el 23,2%. Santiago Abascal sería el presidente preferido por el 13,2% de los encuestados y Ada Colau por el 5%.
Sin embargo, uno de cada dos españoles (55,4%) cree que será el PP el partido que gane las elecciones, duplicando a quienes creen que ganará el PSOE. De hecho, entre quienes afirman que votaron al PSOE en 2023, hay tantos encuestados que creen que ganará el PP (42,9%) como los que creen que ganará el PSOE (43%), y entre los antiguos votantes de Sumar son más los que creen que el PP será el más votado (48% frente al 38,9% que cree que la primera fuerza será el PSOE).
Más de un 20% decidirá su voto esta semana
Dos de cada tres encuestados (65,9%) afirman que votarían lo mismo que en las pasadas elecciones generales si se celebrasen ahora las elecciones, mientras que un 28% dice que no votaría lo mismo y un 5,3% aún no lo sabe. Del mismo modo, un 63,3% afirma que decide su voto "mucho antes del inicio de la campaña electoral", y un 11,2% lo decide "al comienzo de la campaña".
Así las cosas, habría casi un 22% de ciudadanos que aún están pendientes de decidir a quién votar. El 12,7% afirma que toma su decisión en la última semana de campaña electoral, un 43,3% dice que toma la decisión durante la jornada de reflexión, y un 4,9% afirma que lo decide el mismo día de las elecciones.
La proporción de quienes están pendientes de decidirse es menor en la derecha: el 14% de quienes votaron al PP en 2023 y el 12% de quienes votaron a Vox dejan su decisión para algún momento de esta última semana, porcentaje que sube al 18% entre quienes dicen que votaron al PSOE en 2023 y al 24% entre quienes fueron votantes de Sumar.
La preocupación por la vivienda marca nuevo récord
Como en cada barómetro, el CIS pregunta a los ciudadanos por los temas que más les preocupan, y en la antesala de las elecciones generales, la preocupación por la vivienda marca nuevo récord, al ser señalada por el 59,5% de los encuestados como uno de los tres principales problemas que existen actualmente en España, cuando el mes anterior era del 55,7%. El adelanto electoral y la huelga general del pasado 11 de noviembre vinieron motivados por las dificultades crecientes para acceder a una vivienda y por unos salarios dignos.
Como segunda preocupación, aparecen los problemas económicos (24,7%), su porcentaje más alto desde abril y, en tercer lugar, la calidad del empleo (23,9%), que también marca su máximo este mes y sigue en tendencia ascendente.

noticias.titulo: Ocho portavoces parlamentarios debaten en RTVE sobre vivienda, migración, Ceuta y pactos para el 29N
noticias.texto:
Ocho portavoces parlamentarios debaten en RTVE sobre vivienda, migración, Ceuta y pactos para el 29N
- Xabier Fortes modera el encuentro este lunes entre los partidos con grupo propio a las 22:00
- Ester Muñoz (PP), Patxi López (PSOE), Pepa Millán (Vox), Emilio Delgado (Frente Amplio), Gabriel Rufián (ERC), Miriam Nogueras (Junts), Oskar Matute (EH Bildu) y Maribel Vaquero (EAJ-PNV)
Tras el decisivo cara a cara entre Pedro Sánchez y Alberto Núñez Feijóo, este lunes 23 de noviembre llega el turno de los portavoces parlamentarios. A seis días de las elecciones generales, RTVE reúne a las ocho formaciones con grupo propio en el Congreso. Los partidos expondrán sus propuestas sobre vivienda y servicios públicos o migración. También tendrán ocasión de aclarar con quién estarían dispuestos a pactar tras el 29-N, los posibles acuerdos estarán en el centro de la conversación.
De este modo, Ester Muñoz (PP), Patxi López (PSOE), Pepa Rodríguez de Millán (Vox), Emilio Delgado (Frente Amplio), Gabriel Rufián (ERC), Míriam Nogueras (Junts), Oskar Matute (EH Bildu) y Maribel Vaquero (EAJ-PNV) confrontarán sus programas y propuestas durante una hora y media, en un debate moderado por el periodista de RTVE, Xabier Fortes, .
El encuentro comenzará a las 22:00 horas y se podrá seguir a través de La 1, el Canal 24 horas, Radio 5, RTVE Noticias y RTVE Play. Desde las 20:45, Pepa Bueno presentará el programa especial, La gran decisión, que repasará las posiciones de los partidos antes del debate y analizará después las intervenciones de los ocho portavoces.
Tres bloques temáticos y el 'minuto de oro'
Los grandes temas que han acordado los partidos serán tres repartidos en bloques a lo largo de 90 minutos en total. Los dos primeros bloques durarán 28 minutos cada uno, mientras que el tercero y último durará 24 minutos.
Abrirán la discusión hablando sobre vivienda y estado del bienestar, temas que están vertebrando la campaña electoral de todos los partidos políticos. Hasta el momento, la gran mayoría ha coincidido en propuestas como la construcción de nueva vivienda, mientras que la regulación del mercado o los impuestos —generalmente propuestos por las formaciones de izquierdas— han sido punto habitual de fricción. Más allá de esto, otros asuntos que centrarán la conversación serán la salud y la educación pública, pero también la migración, con la crisis de Ceuta como telón de fondo.
Continuarán el debate con el bloque de economía, empleo e infraestructuras, donde deberán desgranar sus recetas para la próxima legislatura. Temas como la subida de salarios, las pensiones, la energía o el mantenimiento de los trenes, con los accidentes de Adamuz y Urda como telón de fondo, se convertirán en grandes protagonistas, como ya ocurrió en el cara a cara entre Feijóo y Sánchez.
Por último y como cierre al debate a ocho llegará el bloque sobre clima sociopolítico y pactos, en el que tendrán que dejar claras sus posiciones respecto al resto de partidos, especialmente ante los pronósticos electorales que auguran un parlamento muy fragmentado y en el que los acuerdos serán necesarios para sacar adelante los proyectos legislativos. Es probable que la polarización política cope parte de las intervenciones de los portavoces, ya que ha sido otro de los grandes temas de esta campaña.
Como broche final, los participantes tendrán el conocido como 'minuto de oro' para cerrar sus intervenciones y pedir el voto a los ciudadanos.
Asimismo, se ha sorteado tanto la apertura y cierre de los bloques como las llegadas y salidas del estudio. De este modo, se organizarán por representación parlamentaria de menor a mayor: PNV, EH Bildu, Junts, ERC, Frente Amplio, Vox, PSOE y PP.
Un fin de semana repleto de entrevistas y actos
Al contrario que Feijóo y Sánchez, que optaron por despejar sus agendas para poder preparar el debate con tranquilidad, la mayor parte de los portavoces ha mantenido este fin de semana su intensa actividad electoral, ya sea participando en mítines o dando entrevistas.
En el caso de Ester Muñoz, intervino el domingo en un acto junto a la presidenta del PP de la Comunidad de Madrid, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, en Alcalá de Henares. Por su parte, Patxi López intervino el sábado en acto político celebrado en Ermua (Vizcaya).
Emilio Delgado estuvo el sábado en Barcelona en el acto central de su partido, junto a la candidata Ada Colau y los ministros Yolanda Díaz y Ernest Urtasun. En la misma ciudad estuvo el domingo el republicano Gabriel Rufián, que compartió mitin con la 'número uno' de Podemos, Irene Montero. Ese mismo día, Miriam Nogueras estuvo en Castelldefels (Barcelona) junto a los expresidentes Artur Mas y Jordi Pujol y, por videoconferencia, Carles Puigdemont. El día anterior, participó en otro acto de Junts en Vic (Barcelona).
En Euskadi, Maribel Vaquero ha hecho doblete: el sábado participó en un mitin en Eibar y el domingo en la ofrenda floral al fundador del PNV, Sabino Arana, y en un acto político. Por su parte, Oskar Matute no ha participado en actos en los últimos dos días, pero sí ha concedido varias entrevistas a diferentes medios nacionales. Caso parecido el de Pepa Millán, que ha mantenido un perfil más bajo a lo largo del fin de semana.
El debate de 2023
El antecedente de un debate de estas características lo tenemos en las elecciones de 2023, cuando RTVE lo organizó con siete portavoces: Patxi López (PSOE), Cuca Gamarra (PP), Iván Espinosa de los Monteros (VOX), Aina Vidal (Sumar), Gabriel Rufián (ERC), Aitor Esteban (PNV) y Oskar Matute (EH Bildu). Junts es el único partido con grupo parlamentario propio que no participó en el debate de 2023 y que sí lo hará esta vez. Sus siete votos permitieron entonces a Sánchez alcanzar la mayoría absoluta en la primera votación de investidura.
En aquel encuentro, menos bronco que el cara a cara que protagonizaron Sánchez y Feijóo días antes, se pudo ver con claridad las que serían las futuras alianzas de cara a la posterior investidura del líder del PSOE. El portavoz socialista y la de Sumar mostraron su disposición a reeditar la coalición de gobierno progresista, mientras que ERC, PNV y EH Bildu se posicionaron en contra de cualquier pacto con Vox —tal y como plantean ahora de cara al 29N— y pidieron defender sus respectivos territorios.
Desde el PP, en cambio, se mostraron convencidos de un gobierno "en solitario" y defendieron que fuera la lista más votada quien gobernara, algo que finalmente no pasó. Y Vox reclamó el apoyo de los ciudadanos para construir una "alternativa" y ofrecer una "solución que no sea tibia".
En cuanto a los temas que más interés suscitaron en aquel debate, estuvieron las alianzas del PP y Vox en varias comunidades autónomas, la polémica ley del 'solo sí es sí', Cataluña y el independentismo, ETA y la situación económica.
Algunas caras han cambiado desde el encuentro a siete de 2023, solo repiten tres portavoces: el socialista Patxi López, el portavoz de ERC, Gabriel Rufián, y el de EH Bildu, Oskar Matute. Tres mujeres se estrenan.
