noticias.texto:
It is harvest time in rural Wisconsin, and the Badger state’s most vibrant crop is painting the rolling countryside a brilliant, unmistakable red.
For nearly three decades, Nicole Hansen has been farming cranberries here. Wisconsin produces more than 60% of the nation’s supply. On a crisp fall morning, we waded into a marsh with her to round up the floating harvest.
“We need to corral all these berries,” she said.
Cranberries are one of the few fruits native to North America. Contrary to popular belief, they do not grow submerged in water; instead, they thrive on low-lying vines in dry soil. But when harvest time arrives, the growing beds are flooded. Specialized machines shake the fruit loose, and the buoyant berries rise to the surface.
Growing and harvesting cranberries relies on a highly choreographed combination of machines and manual labor, but the process is ultimately driven by Mother Nature. “So we are checking the weather, I don’t know, five to 10 times a day because everything we do is controlled by the weather,” Hansen said.
Across the US, that weather is growing increasingly erratic, due in large part to the human-caused climate crisis.
Shifting seasons and unpredictable extremes
In cranberry-producing states such as Massachusetts and New Jersey, record-breaking summer heatwaves frequently trigger fruit scalding, in which berries literally bake on the vine before they can be harvested. At the same time, increasingly humid conditions and heavy rainfall during the growing season create stagnant, moisture-rich environments that invite fungal pathogens, resulting in devastating crop rots.
In Wisconsin, the threats often emerge after the harvest is done. To protect the plants from winter’s bitter cold and damaging winds, growers spray water over the vines, building up several inches of ice that act as a natural thermal blanket.
“So if you don’t protect them, they do get cold damage,” Amaya Atucha, a fruit scientist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, explained.
Atucha spends a lot of time thinking about cranberries and the changing climate affecting them. Data from Climate Central shows that winters in the upper midwest are among the fastest-warming in the nation. Cranberry-growing regions now experience an average of 14 more warm winter days than they did in 1970, triggering erratic cycles of thawing and freezing.
“We know for certain the climate is changing,” Atucha said. She pointed to recent years in which unusually warm February temperatures melted protective ice sheets prematurely, leaving vulnerable vines exposed to sudden deep freezes.
Innovation in the bogs
To keep this seasonal favorite on holiday tables, scientists and growers are racing to adapt. Researchers are leveraging artificial intelligence to identify and breed new, resilient crop varieties capable of withstanding extreme weather and disease. Meanwhile, growers are integrating advanced technology into their daily operations, utilizing drones to precisely apply fertilizers and monitor temperatures across their marshes and bogs.
“When you have a system that works and then out of nowhere you change the rules of the game, then you need to adjust,” Atucha said.
Adapting to change is simply part of the job description for modern farmers. And on a perfect autumn morning, surrounded by glassy waters and floating red cranberries, Hansen acknowledged the pull of this crimson tide.
“It’s amazing,” she told us. “It’s a great way to raise a family.”
- Climate Central is an independent group of scientists and communicators that researches and reports the facts about our changing climate and how it affects people’s lives

noticias.titulo: US and UK to host Women's World Cups in 2031 and 2035
noticias.resumen: FIFA has confirmed the United States, alongside Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica, will host the 2031 Women's World Cup — the first to feature 48 teams. The UK will stage the 2035 edition, its first World Cup since 1966.
noticias.texto:
US and UK to host Women's World Cups in 2031 and 2035
November 23, 2026
FIFA have confirmed the hosts for the 2031 and 2035 Women's World Cup.
The United States, along with Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica, was the only candidate to host in 2031, the first tournament that will feature 48 teams — as is the case with the men — for the first time. The US has hosted the tournamnent twice before, in 2003 and 1999, and is also the most successful country in World Cup history having won it four times.
After FIFA announced its revenue for the 2026 men's World Cup that finished just last summer was around $15 billionn (€13.7 billion), it is clear that US Soccer feels empowered that hosting the women's tournament is the next move forward. With the women's domestic league (NWSL) considered the strongest in the world and the US national team so strong, it is clear that securing the tournament in 2031 is a further sign of the US' committment to women's football.
"We expect and plan for the 2031 Women’s World Cup to be the largest women’s sporting event in history," Emily Cosler, US Soccer’s vice-president of strategy told The Guardian.
Two tournaments in seven years for the UK
The 2035 tournament was also awarded to the sole bidders, England, Scotland, Northern Ireland and Wales. This sees the World Cup return to the United Kingdom for the first time since 1966, the only time England's men's team won the competition. The women lost the 2023 final to Spain. It also means that the UK will host two major tournaments in relatively quick succession, with the men's 2028 European Championships also set to be held in England, Scotland and Wales and the Republic of Ireland.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the tournament would bring "visitors, investment and jobs to every part of the country."
Given that FIFA President Gianni Infantino had revealed last year that both bids were unchallenged, this news comes as little surprise. Nevertheless, with the hosts now official, a 48-team tournament marks a remarkable growth for the women's game. For reference, the 2011 World Cup in Germany had just 16 teams.
The next World Cup will be in Brazil next year. Eighteen of the 32 teams have already secured qualification, including Germany, for the tournament, which runs from June 24 to July 25.

noticias.titulo: Turkey: Authorities search for lioness on the loose in Istanbul
noticias.resumen: A lioness was on the loose in northern Istanbul, with wildlife advocates demanding answers over how the animal entered the country and who was keeping it in captivity.
noticias.texto:
Turkey: Authorities search for lioness on the loose in Istanbul
November 23, 2026
Turkish security forces and wildlife authorities were searching woods in the north of Istanbul on Monday for an animal believed to be a lion that was reportedly roaming free, the national parks authority said.
In an online statement, the parks authority said police officers in the Zekeriyakoy area, north of Istanbul's European side, reported spotting "an animal resembling a lion" on surveillance cameras at around 9 p.m. (18:00 GMT) on Sunday.
Grainy images published by the Turkish media showed the lioness walking through a grassy area. It was unclear where the animal came from, though some media reports suggested it had escaped from a nearby home. The Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor's Office said it launched investigation focused on identifying its owner.
Istanbul governor's office said in an online post, the location of the lion has been identified and the efforts to capture it were underway.
According to park authority, the search is still underway, with specialist veterinarians also involved in the operation to capture the animal.
Outcry among activists
Last year, a lion that escaped from a "theme park" near the southern city of Antalya was shot dead after attacking a man. It remains unclear where the Istanbul lion escaped from but it sparked an outrage among activists and advocates.
Northern Forests Defense, an independent ecology advocacy movement, called for "the individuals who illegally held this lion captive to be identified and brought to justice."
"Removing wild animals from their natural habitats and keeping them in captivity in villas is a crime," it said on X.
Wildlife conservationist Gokce Coskun said on X that "there are thousands of people keeping lions illegally in Turkey" and "licensed 'lion parks' have sprung up everywhere."
Doganay Tolunay, an ecology professor at Istanbul University, said questions must be raised about how a globally threatened species was brought into Turkey, how it passed through customs and why those keeping it have not been identified.
Although keeping wild animals as pets are forbidden in Turkey, it has become a hub for the illegal trade in wild animals as traffickers exploit its air links to Africa and Asia.
In December 2024, a young gorilla was rescued after being discovered at Istanbul Airport on a flight from Nigeria to Thailand.

noticias.titulo: After Japan's APEC snub, what's next for its China ties?
noticias.resumen: Japan has long-running concerns over Chinese military expansionism, and Beijing has bristled at Sanae Takaichi's comments on Taiwan. The frosty ties were on full display at the APEC summit.
noticias.texto:
After Japan's APEC snub, what's next for its China ties?
November 23, 2026
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi received a cold shoulder from China during the recent Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in the tech hub of Shenzhen.
After Takaichi arrived in Shenzhen on November 18 for the two-day summit, there was an immediate issue when the mobile stairs to the door of her aircraft were some way short of the threshold, requiring her to hold on to the door frame to step down around 40 centimeters (about 15 inches) to the top step.
It may have been completely inadvertent, but upon safely reaching the airport tarmac, her official welcome was decidedly low-key. There were no musical performances, no cheering crowds or traditional dances, which were laid on for many other APEC leaders as they arrived.
Japan's Yomiuri newspaper reported on November 20 that when Takaichi met Chinese leader Xi Jinping at the dinner reception, "his reaction was cold." And while many other regional leaders managed at least a brief one-on-one with Xi on the sidelines of the main event, the Japanese delegation was not granted such access.
Frosty China-Japan ties on full display
"The level of frostiness from the Chinese side was on full display from the moment Takaichi's plane landed," said William Yang, a Taiwan-based analyst for the International Crisis Group.
"I cannot think that the issue with the plane steps was anything other than deliberate and there was a huge contrast between the welcome she received and virtually everyone else," he told DW.
Yang added that the ice didn't break when Takaichi tried to speak to Xi at the dinner reception and the entire occasion "just reflects the state of bilateral relations."
China and Japan share a troubled history, marked by the Japanese invasion of China in the 1930s and the often brutal occupation of cities that were captured and subjugated.
Chinese schoolchildren learn about the horrors of the Nanjing Massacre and the use of chemical and biological weapons by Japanese forces.
Japan maintains that its repeated post-war apologies and massive economic aid that helped China to become the economic powerhouse it is today are overlooked amid the criticism.
Diplomatic relations were normalized in 1972 and Tokyo pursued a policy of engagement over the following decades, although that came to a halt in the mid-2000s, points out David Adebahr, a professor of international relations and Asia-Pacific security policy at Kobe University.
Japan's Taiwan comments open new rift with Beijing
"China's rising military spending, the breakdown of talks over the East China Sea in 2006, and a resurgence of nationalism raised concerns even among Japan's more China-friendly diplomats, while defence analysts noted an increase in Chinese submarine activity near Japanese waters," he told DW.
The nationalism on display during the 2008 Beijing Olympics, coupled with China's more assertive stance over the Senkaku Islands, which Japan has sovereignty over but which Beijing claims, accelerated this shift.
Ties took a sudden nosedive in November 2025 when Takaichi responded to a question in Japan's parliament, the Diet, by saying that any "contingency” involving Taiwan would also inevitably threaten the national security of Japan.
According to Adebahr, the Japanese leader was merely saying out loud what "had long been the internal logic of Japanese security planning." Nevertheless, Beijing has reacted with fury.
China has demanded that Takaichi retract the statement and raised pressure on Japan by restricting exports of rare earth minerals critical to Japanese industry, banning imports of Japanese seafood and telling tourists to take Japan off their destination list.
And while ruffled national feelings have been smoothed in the past with shows of reciprocal goodwill, China is standing firm on its demands this time.
"From Tokyo's perspective, it is clear that Beijing believes it holds more cards than in the past," said Adebahr.
"Today, Beijing has considerable leverage: Japan's dependence on Chinese rare earths; an increasingly visible military presence around Japan, sometimes in conjunction with Russia; and a US administration that has urged Tokyo to de-escalate rather than firmly backing it."
Adebahr added that this left China with little incentive to offer Takaichi a face-saving compromise. However, he pointed out that Beijing's reliance on coercion could backfire by prompting Japan to increase defence spending and seek closer ties with other partners.
Japan's leadership faces the China test
Still, the Japanese leader finds herself in a difficult position, said analyst Yang.
As a committed conservative who has talked tough on Beijing's rapid military buildup, its seizure of islands and atolls in the South China Sea and the inexorable pressure on Taiwan to capitulate and become one with mainland China, Takaichi cannot give in to Xi's demands for fear of losing face with her hardline base.
"This is a major test of her abilities and wisdom as the nation's leader," Yang said. "She is walking a political tightrope between reducing tensions with China but, at the same time, preparing the nation and its allies for a potential contingency over Taiwan."
"I foresee China maintaining its current approach, continuing to step up the pressure by limiting targeted exports and amplifying the assertion with Russia and North Korea that Japan is embracing remilitarization," he said.
Yang added that Japan was likely to seek opportunities to signal goodwill and improve relations "in return for small-scale compromises." However, he said that a reset in the dynamics would depend on how the Trump administration shaped its foreign policy for the remainder of his presidency.
Analyst Adebahr said that while he expects diplomatic relations to remain frosty, there are too many interdependencies for a full decoupling between China and Japan.
"I would not be too pessimistic about the relationship, because in the medium term, trade, technology and critical minerals are now seen as security issues," he added. "Therefore, complex interdependence will prevent a return to the old pattern of keeping politics and economics separate."
"While economic interdependence alone will not be enough to stabilize the relationship, full decoupling is highly unlikely, as transaction costs would be far too high for both sides," he said.

noticias.titulo: Gukesh to defend chess crown against rising star Sindarov
noticias.resumen: As the World Chess championship gets underway, it's no coincidence that the titleholder, Gukesh Dommaraju, and his challenger, Jakhovir Sindarov, are both from Asia.
noticias.texto:
Gukesh to defend chess crown against rising star Sindarov
November 23, 2026
When India's world chess champion, Dommaraju Gukesh, faced reporters at the pre-tournament press conference in Geneva on Sunday, there was no sign of the youthful, carefree energy one might expect from a 20-year-old.
"I don't think I'm here to defend anything—I'm here to win it all over again," he said.
Starting November 24, Gukesh will be facing challenger Jakhovir Sindarov of Uzbekistan for a purse of $2.5 million (€2.3m) in the World Chess Championship.
Gukesh captured the title in 2024, making him the youngest-ever world champion at just 18. Since then, however, things have not as gone well for the player known for his exceptional calculation skills and a penchant for risky moves. He currently languishes in 26th place in the FIDE world rankings.
The challenger as the favorite
Sindarov, who has climbed to number four in the world, told reporters that he only began training "seriously" last year and has learned a lot from observing the reigning world champion.
"He has a very good strength in typical positions, his calculation is very good, and Gukesh can fight until the end," Sindarov said.
Former world champion Viswanathan Anand, who was also one of the world's best players as a teenager, is not completely surprised by Gukesh's lack of form over the past two years.
"He became the world champion (very young). So suddenly the responsibility is shifted onto you and even expectations," Anand told DW.
"Clearly he has deficiencies in his chess as is normal for someone who's 20, he's not had time to experience a lot."
By the time he became India's first world champion, Anand was 37 – ancient by the age-standards of today's top players.
The computer generation
"With powerful chess software and global connectivity, it is easier for young players today to reach the top level," Jan Gustafsson, coach of Germany's national chess team, told DW.
"Online chess provides many more learning opportunities for talented players," added Gustafsson, who sees the recent movement at the top of the rankings as a "generational shift."
While Norway's Magnus Carlsen, long considered the greatest player of all time, remains number one in the world rankings, he rarely plays classical chess anymore and gave up his world championship title after declining to defend it in 2023.
Now, young players—particularly from Asia—are pushing to the forefront. Alongside Gukesh and Sindarov, players such as Rameshbabu Praggnanandhaa from India and Nodirbek Abdusattorov of Uzbekistan—an emerging chess powerhouse—are considered contenders to win a world championship in the not-too-distant future.
"Broad social acceptance and state support ensure that children can focus on chess at a very early stage," Gustafsson said.
Another contender is Germany's Vincent Keymer, who at 22 is number nine in the world and well established among the world's elite. Most recently, Keymer and his teammates won a bronze medal at the World Team Championship, often referred to as the "Chess Olympiad."
Additional reporting by: Thomas Lemmer

noticias.titulo: Nepal's new PM eyes closer ties with India amid lingering disputes
noticias.resumen: On his first foreign bilateral visit, rapper-turned-Prime Minister Balendra Shah sought deeper ties with Nepal's neighbor and largest trading partner, while steering clear of sticky territorial issues.
noticias.texto:
Nepal's new PM eyes closer ties with India amid lingering disputes
November 23, 2026
For years, Nepal's relationship with India was shaped by familiar faces, as leaders of the Himalayan country's erstwhile three major parties took turns in the prime minister's office through revolving coalition governments.
This week's state visit to India by Balendra Shah, a 36-year-old rapper-turned-politician, marked a clear break from that pattern.
As a young, first-time prime minister with a strong electoral mandate , Shah represents a new political force in Kathmandu.
But long-standing economic strain, along with August's devastating flash floods and the Nepalese public's high hopes for more jobs, investment and better governance at home, have made Shah's first bilateral visit abroad more than a mere diplomatic box-ticking exercise.
To safeguard Nepal's flood recovery and development, Shah needs to get off on the right foot with India, his country's southern neighbor and largest trading partner, and its long-standing prime minister, Narendra Modi.
While Nepal and India share an open border as well as deep cultural and historical ties, their relationship has also been marked by territorial disputes and a desire in Nepal to be seen as an equal by its much larger and more powerful neighbor.
Constantino Xavier, a senior fellow at the Center for Social and Economic Progress in New Delhi, however, cautioned against expecting too much from a single visit.
"We need a big, long-term ambition coupled with small, short-term steps," he told DW, arguing that economic cooperation should remain the central focus of relations because it directly contributes to the socioeconomic development of both countries.
Economic cooperation takes center stage
The young prime minister's test is to turn a strong domestic electoral mandate and political goodwill with New Delhi into tangible economic gain, as well as to address longstanding border disputes and a massive trade imbalance.
Shah's administration sees diplomacy as key to addressing the country's development aspirations, which was reflected in bilateral talks with Modi on Monday.
Economic cooperation featured prominently during the talks as both sides sought engagements in trade, investment, connectivity and infrastructure development.
Kathmandu's priority was securing Indian financial support for reconstruction following the August disaster that claimed the lives of more than 1,450 people, while 5,745 are missing or unaccounted for.
The floods swept away roads, bridges, hydropower projects and settlements, with reconstruction bills estimated at around $4.8 billion (about €4.4 billion)
At a joint press briefing after their talks in New Delhi, Modi announced a package of $1.63 billion to help rebuild flood-hit areas and upgrade other infrastructure projects — around $380 million as a grant, with the rest as a concessional loan.
The South Asian neighbors also agreed to deepen cooperation across a wide range of areas, including trade, investment, connectivity and people-to-people ties, and launched a new long-term vision aimed at strengthening economic integration and development.
The talks also yielded commitments to broaden educational and innovation partnerships, boost energy and infrastructure cooperation, improve market access and trade links, and enhance landlocked Nepal's connectivity through additional air and port access via India.
Bilateral trust and unresolved differences
Shah's visit offered an opportunity to break the ice in a high-level exchange visit and improve a relationship periodically strained by political mistrust, territorial disputes and differing strategic interests.
Nepal and India both have competing territorial claims over Kalapani, Lipulekh and Limpiyadhura, a strategic Himalayan territory in northwestern Nepal.
As mayor of Kathmandu, Shah raised the border disputes with India, which helped boost his nationalist image and set his broader political agenda. However, his India visit steered clear of such contentious issues.
Bimala Rai Paudyal, a former Foreign Minister of Nepal, said Shah avoided tricky bilateral issues to focus on his administration's economic agenda.
"This visit could be a good starting point towards resolving the border issues that have been the key strain in our relations," she told DW. "But the new government didn't show interest or the guts to address this."
Ashok Swain, head of the Department of Peace and Conflict Research at Sweden's Uppsala University, said the visit's success should be measured by whether the two countries can establish a predictable and mutually beneficial relationship.
"Nepal's territorial disputes, concerns over the 1950 Treaty of Peace and Friendship and its economic and transit dependence on India need to be addressed," Swain told DW.
"Shah's biggest opportunity is to transform Nepal's geographical location between India and China from a strategic vulnerability into an economic and diplomatic asset," he added, arguing that Nepal should not be forced to choose between its two neighbors.
Whether the visit marks a tangible reset on the economic front will ultimately depend not on the number of agreements announced, but on how they are implemented and whether the two governments are willing to address the disputes that have long strained ties.

noticias.titulo: COP deadlock prompts calls for a reset of climate diplomacy
noticias.resumen: COP31 has been branded a failure after countries couldn't reach a final agreement, divided over a reference to "fossil fuels." But was the decision to walk away from a watered-down text actually a show of strength?
noticias.texto:
COP deadlock prompts calls for a reset of climate diplomacy
November 23, 2026
The longest-running climate talks in history came to a disappointing conclusion on Sunday as negotiators failed to come to an agreement on a shared political direction on climate change.
After two days of extended talks, representatives from country after country, tiredness etched into each face, voiced their opposition to the so-called "Antalya Pact."
"I understand that there is no agreement on this text. For that reason, these decisions have not been adopted," said Murat Kurum, Turkish president of the COP31 climate summit.
'Fossil fuels' as one of main sticking points
One of the main sticking points: the words "fossil fuels." While some nations, including petrostates like Saudi Arabia and Russia, wanted them omitted from the text, others saw it as a "step backwards" not to include them.
Around 130 parties — among them vulnerable island nations, developing countries and richer EU members — called for the reintroduction of the two words into the text, to no avail. And so many refused to support the adoption of the final COP agreement.
The deadlock signals a failure for the UN process. But the number of countries willing to walk away from what they saw as a weak text was, arguably, a show of strength, and one that had been long coming.
The phrase "fossil fuels" first appeared three years ago in the closing decision of COP28 in Dubai with the promise of "transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems, in just, orderly and equitable manner." But it has been omitted from every text since.
More extreme weather as climate change accelerates
Yet this year's climate summit was the first to acknowledge that the world will breach the critical 1.5-degree Celsius (2.7-degree Fahrenheit) threshold that scientists said would safeguard the world from the worst impacts of planetary heating.
And so, the pressure was on for progress; to turn pledges from previous years into concrete action. But that progress didn't come.
"We don't celebrate the deep divisions exposed or the lack of a political signal from COP31 capable of driving climate action in line with science, equity and the law," said Nikki Reisch, director of the climate and energy program at the Center for International Environmental Law.
"But the rejected text would have done more harm than good."
Financing climate action in the Global South
The lack of agreement was not solely about fossil fuels; money also played a part.
Developing nations have long argued that they need additional financing, both as a means for them to move away from coal, oil and gas, but also to help them cope with the consequences of rising temperatures.
Countries all over the world are being battered by extreme weather events. Catastrophes like flooding, drought and wildfires have been fueled and worsened by rising global temperatures. Often the worst hit are poorer countries with low rates of greenhouse gas emissions.
And yet, richer states behind much of the historical emissions are increasingly unwilling to foot the bill. Dissatisfaction at home due to higher food and fuel prices has left many governments loathe to pay more to finance climate action abroad.
With the United States — the world's biggest historical emitter — now absent from negotiations and on the verge of leaving the United Nation's Framework Convention on Climate Change, the European Union was portrayed as this year's villain with some observers accusing the EU of hypocrisy.
"You can't demand action and then block the finance that makes this possible," Fanny Petitbon, policy analyst at 350.org, said in a statement.
As the world's largest provider of climate finance, the EU reportedly refused to negotiate on providing additional finance and has repeatedly called for other nations to step up.
Moving forward on climate action beyond climate summits
The failure to find an agreement is a particularly bitter turn of events for countries that face ever worsening impacts of climate change, like the island states that are being confronted by a reality that could see their countries wiped off the map as sea levels rise.
But things are not all bad.
Although the Turkey-led electrification agenda calling for an increase in global electricity consumption to 35% by 2035 was not formally adopted — it made up part of the rejected final agreement — more than 90 countries pledged to move forward regardless.
It's not a silver bullet. There was no agreement on ensuring the increase was forged only through clean, renewable energy. But it would still signal forward momentum, driven by economic forces and a need for home-grown energy security.
And there are other hopes. The second conference on the Just Transition Away from Fossil Fuels will take place in Tuvalu in July 2027. Initiated at the COP30 conference last year in Belem, Brazil, it has seen increasing support from countries putting together concrete roadmaps for abandoning coal, oil and gas.
Who's responsible?
There has been much talk of blame and who is responsible for the breakdown and collapse of talks. What is clear is that the UN climate summits need reform. Progress, when it does happen, is slow. The present model, based on consensus, requires all countries to agree on every measure. There have been many calls for majority-rule decision making, which might have forced the inclusion of language like "fossil fuels" into the text.
But ultimately, this is not the time to focus on fault. As the climate crisis accelerates, governments need to reflect — and quickly — on what can be done outside of these UN processes, within their nations, to speed up climate action.
"The take-home message from COP31 is clear: the world must do much more to confront the climate crisis — and it must do it now," said UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres in a statement.

noticias.titulo: 'Medicare for all' is back on the drawing board. Does it stand a better chance this time?
noticias.resumen: Several newly elected Democratic U.S. senators campaigned on Medicare for All. Could this be the time it actually gets traction?
noticias.texto:
'Medicare for all' is back on the drawing board. Does it stand a better chance this time?
Check out the NPR Politics Podcast for daily analysis of the biggest news out of Washington, D.C.
History doesn't repeat itself, but it does rhyme, as the saying goes. That's certainly true of the coming fight over "Medicare for All."
The midterm elections resulted in victories for several candidates who made universal, government-funded health coverage, or some variation thereof, a central pillar of their campaigns, including new Democratic U.S. senators-elect from Michigan, Maine, Iowa, and Texas. They — and many of their soon-to-be colleagues — say they will push the new Democratic majorities in the House and Senate to finally solve the healthcare affordability problem, which so many voters complained about on the campaign trail.
But while virtually every elected official supports making healthcare available and affordable for all Americans, the details of getting there cleaved the Democratic Party the last several times healthcare topped the national agenda. The Clinton health reform effort in 1993-94 fractured over differences within the Democratic majority, as those who wanted a dramatic overhaul like Medicare for All argued with those who saw incremental changes — such as a public option — as more politically feasible. The Affordable Care Act, which despite incendiary politics made incremental reforms, barely squeaked into law in 2010 after similar disputes..
And, so far, it appears history is about to write another stanza of this epic poem.
"It's cosplay"
So why is something so popular in the abstract so hard to accomplish?
For one thing, most Americans have no real idea what the phrase "Medicare for All" actually means. "It's cosplay," said Nicholas Bagley, a law professor at the University of Michigan who has written about health policy for years. "When you say 'Medicare for All,' people think 'Healthcare — good. We should have more of it.'"
Mollyann Brodie — who oversees KFF's public opinion and survey research program as executive vice president and chief operating officer of the health information nonprofit — points out that in the long history of Medicare for All, support rises and falls dramatically depending on how the policy is described to voters.
"I can move it up to three-quarters [percent approval] if I talk about it being a guaranteed right to healthcare or eliminating insurance premiums and reducing out-of-pocket costs," she said of survey respondents' support, on a recent episode of the What the Health? From KFF Health News podcast. "I can plummet that support down to the 20s if I talk about it requiring people to pay more in taxes or threatening the current Medicare program."
Medicare faces headwinds
A second problem Democrats face is that the Medicare program itself, which covers adults 65 and older and some people with disabilities, is on less-than-firm financial footing. As of this year, the trust fund that underpins the hospital insurance part of the program is projected to become insolvent in 2033.
Costs are rising for Medicare beneficiaries as well. The program requires significant out-of-pocket spending on premiums, deductibles, and coinsurance. At the same time, traditional Medicare fails to cover much-needed services such as dental, vision, hearing, and, most expensively, long-term care. Beefing up Medicare benefits would be expensive and likely require large tax increases, according to most outside estimates.
The new Democratic majorities in Congress will have to decide whether their priority is to reverse the spending cuts made by the Trump administration — both to the Medicaid program for low-income and disabled people and to Affordable Care Act health plans — or to expand coverage and lower costs, turning back time to before President Donald Trump's second term began.
"Expectations are super high among voters right now, and they are demanding action on healthcare costs," Brodie said.
There are already indications that Democratic leaders are listening to the Medicare-for-All wing of their party. A day before being officially nominated as the next speaker of the House, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York voiced support for expanding government-funded coverage, including by lowering the age of Medicare eligibility and covering all children.
Of course, even if Democrats can pass legislation to restore what was cut by the GOP, there is every expectation that Trump — who has referred to Medicare for All in the past as "a socialist takeover of our healthcare system" — would veto those efforts. And the new majorities, while large, are not veto-proof.
Finally, Democrats must face a reality that both parties often forget: The larger your majority, the more ideologically diverse it will be. While the next Congress will include more progressives pursuing Medicare for All, it will also have plenty more moderate members from swing districts currently represented by Republicans. It's the reverse of the splits that plagued the GOP in the current Congress, with conservatives from safe red districts pitted against moderates from purplish ones.
A deeper dissatisfaction?
There is one big difference in the coming Democrat-on-Democrat debates compared with those in 1993 and 2009. One thing that has hamstrung Democrats trying to fix the health system is resistance from a plurality, if not a majority, of Americans who are relatively satisfied with their current health coverage. During the Clinton-era health reform debate, those people were represented in the famous "Harry and Louise" ads sponsored by the health insurance industry, featuring a couple at their kitchen table worrying that proposed changes would leave them worse off financially.
KFF's September tracking poll found instead that not only was the professed support for Medicare for All at its highest since the organization started regularly asking about it, but also a majority of respondents said they would support the policy even if it meant eliminating the private insurance industry. That's a first, and a significant change at that. It suggests the public is so fed up with the status quo that they'd rather risk something completely new than stick with what they have.
Of course, that sentiment could change fast when industry opposition revs up its counter-campaign. Still, the survey results suggest the next health reform debate could start with a public ready for something bigger. Now it's up to the people who could make it happen to get on the same page.
HealthBent, a regular feature of KFF Health News, offers insight into and analysis of policies and politics from KFF Health News chief Washington correspondent Julie Rovner, who has covered health care for more than 40 years.
KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

noticias.titulo: Nvidia's board of directors brings Jensen Huang back as CEO
noticias.resumen: President Trump endorsed the announcement, calling it essential for the success of the company and the economy. He added that the government does not see Jensen's return as a national security risk.
noticias.texto:
Nvidia's board of directors brings Jensen Huang back as CEO
Nvidia says it is bringing back co-founder Jensen Huang to be its CEO, president and board director. In a statement, the company says the board voted unanimously in favor of reinstating Huang after a series of conversations and meetings, as well as input from people at "senior levels of the United States government."
"I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution," Huang said in the statement. "I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment."
President Trump endorsed the move, calling it the "correct and proper decision." He said Huang's leadership was needed "in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy."
Nvidia shares jumped sharply on the news Monday morning, as did the broader stock market.
Trump added that the government has "no reason to believe that Jensen's return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security," and that Attorney General Todd Blanche says the U.S. "does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct."
Huang resigned from Nvidia less than two weeks ago, following reports that he had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. The board said as recently as Nov. 17 that it did not intend to reinstate Huang, though Huang publicly said he would return if the board allowed it.
The company's internal investigation into Huang continues, but the board says the turnaround followed a series of meetings with Huang that left them satisfied with his candor and ability to lead the company. Trump said Nvidia should continue looking to its own compliance with U.S. export controls as well.
Huang is expected to testify before congressional committees next week.

noticias.titulo: EU to target Russian ex-soldiers, banks and sports in new sanctions push
noticias.resumen: Brussels wants to restrict visas for former Russian soldiers, target banks and crypto platforms and bar Russian athletes from competing in the EU.
noticias.texto: BRUSSELS — The EU wants to target former Russian soldiers, banks, crypto platforms and sports teams in its 22nd sanctions package against Moscow since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced on Monday. “We’re giving Ukraine the strength to secure a peace. And Russia, every reason to choose it,” von der Leyen said in a prerecorded video message launching the package. The Commission’s proposals will now be negotiated by EU countries, with several diplomats telling POLITICO that they aim to reach an agreement by the end of the year. One major measure would restrict visas for former Russian soldiers. The EU agreed on a legal framework for the restrictions in its previous sanctions package over the summer but has yet to put them into effect. “Russian ex-combatants pose a security risk to Europe. They cannot be allowed to wander freely across our countries,” von der Leyen said, citing a recent escalation in covert Russian operations in Europe. The Commission also wants to add 70 vessels to its sanctions list targeting Russia’s so-called shadow fleet, which Moscow uses to export oil and other commodities. European companies would also be barred from repairing Russian refineries damaged by Ukrainian drone attacks. EU citizens would no longer be allowed to sit on the boards of Russian companies. On sports, the Commission is proposing to bar Russian teams and athletes from competing in the bloc, a move that would prevent Russia from returning to next year’s ice hockey world championship in Germany. “We propose to ban the display of official Russian symbols. We will also restrict financial flows from Russian sponsors to European based sports and cultural associations,” von der Leyen said. An arbitration court had ruled that the International Ice Hockey Federation lacked sufficient grounds to exclude Russia from the tournament. Closing sanctions loopholes and cracking down on shadow finance is another focus of the package. The Commission wants to disconnect 60 more banks from international payment systems and target cryptocurrency and payment networks used to circumvent sanctions. “We will focus on Russia, but also include third countries that help Russia to evade our sanctions,” von der Leyen said. The EU has previously been cautious about directly targeting third countries, but von der Leyen said the new measures would help “align with international partners.” The latest proposals follow a difficult year for EU sanctions policy. A previous package was held up for weeks over restrictions on liquefied natural gas shipments, while France delayed the renewal of an existing sanctions framework over a national security dispute, demanding the removal of two Russian billionaires from the sanctions list. Last week, the Commission announced the creation of a dedicated sanctions office to oversee the design, drafting and coordination of restrictive measures.

noticias.titulo: Ukraine takes the war against Russia far from its borders
noticias.resumen: It's the first time Kyiv has admitted to striking Russian ships so far from home.
noticias.texto: KYIV — Ukraine regularly hits targets deep inside Russia; now it’s admitting to an attack far beyond the war zone in North Africa. The attack — an effort to harm Russia’s ability to project power into distant regions—highlights Ukraine’s growing technological prowess but it also carries the risk of diplomatic blowback against Kyiv. The Security Service of Ukraine, or SBU, said its forces on Sunday sank the Russian corvette Merkury anchored in the Libyan port of Benghazi. Also hit was the Angara, a Russian dry cargo vessel that Kyiv claimed was being used to transport weapons. In another attack, a cargo ship sailing under the Russian flag was damaged by a drone attack in the Gulf of Finland on Saturday morning, the defense ministry in Helsinki said . Finnish authorities said that Ukraine carried out the attack in international waters; however, Ukraine has not admitted responsibility. Ukraine has expanded its attacks against Russian targets well outside the war zone in an effort to exert more pain on Moscow, said Mykola Bielieskov, research fellow at the Ukrainian National Institute for Strategic Studies. “Given the fact that frontline operations and strikes against oil refineries and the defense-industrial complex are insufficient to compel the enemy to end the war immediately and unconditionally, Ukraine is seeking additional tools of pressure,” he said. The Libya operation is the first time Ukraine has claimed credit for such a distant strike, but there was little point in denying it after the Benghazi government posted videos of the attacks. There are also accusations that Ukrainian forces have long been active in other theaters. Earlier this year, Greece said it would launch an investigation after a naval drone carrying explosives was discovered in the Ionian Sea. Greek and Ukrainian media identified it as likely a Ukrainian-made Magura drone. Sudan, Mali and Niger have accused Ukrainian special operatives of getting involved in their internal affairs; Russia’s mercenary troops are present in all three countries. Kyiv has strongly denied those accusations. “These operations have demonstrated the remarkable agility and boldness of Kyiv’s intelligence services in attacking vulnerable parts of the Kremlin’s sprawling security apparatus and its global footprint,” said the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace in a report issued last year , adding: “The persistence of such attacks suggests that Kyiv will continue to look for ways to punish Russia beyond the front line.” Libyan anger After Sunday’s attacks, local Libyan authorities filed a complaint to the United Nations and demanded an investigation. “We call on Ukraine to provide an official explanation of its military activities in Libya,” said Osama Hammad, the head of Libya’s parliament-appointed government. Ukraine said the operation was carried out from the sea. A so-called mothership transported seven Ukrainian-made sea drones to the area and launched them, the SBU said. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov on Monday denounced the Gulf of Finland attack . “All coastal countries are undoubtedly concerned about this. It is very dangerous. It is escalating tensions in the region,” he said, adding: “Of course, we hope that the Baltic states will use their influence to dissuade the Kyiv regime from continuing these dangerous terrorist practices.” On the Libya attacks, Peskov said the Kremlin has “noticed [Ukrainian President Volodymyr] Zelenskyy’s statement on ship destruction,” but refused to issue any further comments. While there is no debate that the Merkury is a military vessel, Kyiv said that the cargo vessel was also a legitimate target. “The Defense Forces of Ukraine have once again demonstrated that the Russian military fleet and its logistics have no safe routes, even far beyond the Black Sea,” the SBU said. “Such unique special operations disrupt the enemy’s logistical capabilities and force Russia to pay for its aggression, even at a strategic distance from Ukraine.” Ukraine has not claimed credit for the March sinking of the Russian-flagged Arctic Metagaz LNG tanker sailing between Libya and Malta, said Igor Semyvolos, executive director of the Association of Middle East Studies think tank. Moscow says Kyiv was to blame. “A tanker is a civilian vessel; striking one would raise environmental concerns and lead to complaints with the International Maritime Organization. A corvette, by contrast, is an aggressor’s warship — a legitimate military target. It is safe to claim responsibility for such a strike,” Semyvolos said. The sinking of the Metagaz did send a cautionary signal to Moscow, said Sebastian Rötters, sanctions campaigner at Urgewald, an NGO, forcing Russia to ship its LNG “onto longer and more expensive routes.” “The latest strikes near Benghazi show that risks have not disappeared,” he said. Zelenskyy underscored on Monday that the Libyan attacks were part of a broader campaign aimed at getting Moscow to end the war. “Russia can feel our response all the way from western Siberia, where its oil refineries are burning, to the coast of Libya, where its warships are sinking,” he said. “And we have offered Russia steps to reduce the fighting dozens, dozens of times. And we have never been the ones to raise the stakes.” Martina Sapio contributed to this report.

noticias.titulo: From protest to power: Serbia’s student movement prepares to dismantle Vučić’s regime
noticias.resumen: Serbia’s student movement has secured a historic parliamentary victory, ending Aleksandar Vučić’s 14-year grip on power. With 140 seats in the 250-seat assembly, the movement now faces the challenge of forming a government, tackling corruption and delivering domestic reforms. But its diverse political factions remain divided over Serbia’s future relationship with the EU and Russia.
noticias.texto: First published in Deník N. Belgrade convened the first session of its newly elected parliament following the ousting of Aleksandar Vučić. After 14 years in power, the former Serbian leader took his place on the opposition benches, as candidates from the Student List entered parliament following their victory in October’s elections. The student movement holds 140 seats in the 250-seat National Assembly, while Vučić’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) holds 103, and the remaining seats belong to ethnic minority parties. Following parliament’s inauguration on Tuesday (17 November), the movement has three months to appoint a new prime minister, present its programme, and form a government. Read more Serbia’s Student List has been inspirational, but the big test will be forming a stable anti-corruption government No mercy for Vučić Outside the National Assembly in Belgrade, supporters of the student movement gathered in Pioneer Park. It had previously been closed to the public for over a year; after anti-government protests began, Vučić supporters took the park over, pitched tents and fenced it off. On the night of 25 October, when Vučić acknowledged his election defeat, their camp was dismantled. Before new parliamentarians began arriving on Tuesday, people danced the Serbian kolo in the park, celebrating. Neki normalan svet u Pionirskom parku i ispred Skupštine! Konačno nakon 2 godine! 👏👏👏 pic.twitter.com/JQtdjKNwhV — Dr@go (@tojedrago) November 17, 2026 And judging by signs waved by those present, it appeared unlikely they would forgive Vučić and his most loyal colleagues. One placard even suggested that former SNS ministers should “end up like Elena and Nicolae Ceaușescu” (a Romanian dictatorial couple hastily executed in 1989 when the communist regime was overthrown). noticias.titulo: Fighting at sea escalates sharply: Russian ships are burning in the Baltic and Mediterranean (Ukraine Battlefield update, Day 1,733)
noticias.resumen: Ukrainian drones torch a prized Russian warship in Libya and a military cargo vessel in the Baltic, while commanders in Moscow and Helsinki alike are suddenly forced to rethink how close this war has come to their own shores.
noticias.texto: The Russians ceremonially launched the Merkur corvette in March 2020; it has now sunk to the bottom of the port in Benghazi. Drones set fire to the Sparta II cargo ship, which serves the Russian army; the Finns extinguished the fire and allowed the Russians to tow it to safety. A Ukrainian counteroffensive is under way in the Sumy region, according mainly to Russian claims. Bear trap: this Ukrainian counteroffensive remains highly disputed. Our precision weapons are not precise enough, Russians write. Maps of the day: Ukrainian counteroffensive in the Sumy region ; Kharkiv region Videos of the day: attacks on ships in the Baltic and Mediterranean seas; an attack on a railway station in Lviv; a sailor aboard a Russian shadow fleet ship recorded a Ukrainian drone attack; a Mirage 2000 shot down a drone; Russians killed 11 residents of an apartment block in Dymer; an attack on a tanker on the R-280 road The Merkur corvette was ceremonially launched in March 2020; it has now sunk to the bottom of the port in Benghazi. There have previously been isolated attacks on Russian ships outside the Black and Azov seas. But never before have there been such concentrated attacks on the Russian navy in other seas as during this weekend. All indications suggest that the war at sea is thus taking on new dimensions. It had already been intensifying. As we wrote last week, Russian drones began systematically attacking ships off the coasts of Bulgaria and Romania. The Russians are semi-officially but clearly acknowledging the attacks near Nato shores on ships carrying goods from Ukraine. For example, the influential Rybar commented approvingly on Sunday evening on the very weak response: “A year ago, such a move would have seemed too bold, but now we have an example of an effective campaign against Ukrainian shipping. Nato countries’ response to what is happening near their own territorial waters has been rather lukewarm, including in terms of public comments.” The way Ukrainians have expanded the scope of the naval war has now alarmed the Russians, who are calling for the same kind of retaliation. It is highly likely that the seas around Europe will cease to be safe for Russian and Ukrainian ships in the long term. The Russians felt this particularly painfully off the Libyan coast at Benghazi on Saturday. One of the Russian navy’s most modern ships, the Merkur corvette, was moored at the port quay. Its destruction demonstrates the Ukrainian army’s expanding capabilities to weaken Russian influence around the world not through sabotage, but through direct military operations. noticias.titulo: [Interview] ‘There is nothing soft about Russian soft power’: Ukraine institute director on the battle to re-name streets honouring Pushkin and other Russian figures
noticias.resumen: Should Russian cultural figures continue to be celebrated in European public spaces? Should streets named after Pushkin be renamed? Where do we draw the line between rejecting Russian imperialism and preserving Russian cultural heritage? These are some of the questions director general of the Ukrainian Institute Volodymyr Sheiko discusses with EUobserver.
noticias.texto: Far from the Ukrainian front, Russia continues to enjoy a privileged place in European public life. In schools, museums and cultural institutions, Europeans encounter its renowned writers, artists and historical figures – Tolstoy, Pushkin, Soviet general Ivan Konev … and many others. Yet something that might seem distant from the realities of war, something as abstract as art and culture, is in reality another front in this conflict. As Ukraine fights for its very existence, it is also fighting over its identity: how it sees itself, how it defines its history, and how it understands the identity of its enemy – Russia. Should Russian cultural figures continue to be celebrated in European public spaces? Should streets named after Pushkin be renamed? Where do we draw the line between rejecting Russian imperialism and preserving Russian cultural heritage? These are some of the questions director general of the Ukrainian Institute Volodymyr Sheiko discusses in the following interview. Russian culture is frequently used in public discourse. Suppose the leader of a major EU country began a speech with the line, “Happy families are all alike; every unhappy family is unhappy in its own way”, the opening sentence of Tolstoy’s Anna Karenina . Would that be problematic for you? It would trouble me, yes. Not because I believe Tolstoy should never be quoted, but because we need to ask what that quotation is doing at this particular moment. When an EU leader opens a major speech with Tolstoy while Russia is bombing Ukrainian cities, the choice is not entirely neutral. It reinforces the idea that Russian culture is still the natural source of universal wisdom, something every European is expected to recognise and admire. And I think we need to question that reflex. For generations, Russian culture was presented as universal, while Ukrainian, Georgian or Crimean Tatar cultures were treated as regional or secondary. Russia was the centre; everyone else was the periphery. So, my first response would be: why Tolstoy? Why not Lesia Ukrainka ? Her Cassandra , a masterpiece of literary modernism, is about someone who understands the truth but cannot persuade others to act before catastrophe arrives. That seems painfully relevant to European politics today. The work is now available in a contemporary English translation and is increasingly recognised for its treatment of political blindness, colonial subjugation and the isolation of the person who voices an inconvenient truth. Or take Taras Shevchenko ’s words, “Fight, and you will prevail.” Or Ivan Franko ’s Moses , with its vision of Ukraine taking its place among the world’s free nations, “in your own house, in your own fields’ broad spaces”. A politician could also invoke Mykola Khvylovy ’s call to turn “away from Moscow” and towards a confident European cultural future . These references are no less powerful or universal. Europeans simply don’t know these amazing writers. So, I am not calling for Tolstoy to disappear from libraries. I am asking why a Russian writer still comes to mind so automatically when a European leader wants to say something profound about the human condition. A political speech is not a literature seminar. It tells us whose words and experiences Europe places at the centre. At a time when Russia is trying to destroy Ukraine as a distinct culture and political nation, European leaders should be especially aware of that choice. Are literature and art exempt from war, or are they part of the soft power used by an aggressor state? My short answer is that there is nothing soft about Russian soft power. We usually think of soft power as attraction: a country presents its culture and values and hopes others will find them appealing. Russia’s cultural power has often worked in a much harder way. It tells the world that Ukrainian language, history and culture are not fully separate, that Ukraine belongs naturally within a Russian cultural space, and that Russia has a special right to speak for our entire region. Such mindset prepares the ground for political control and military invasion. You can see it in museums that have described Ukrainian artists as ‘Russian’, in universities where “Eastern European studies” effectively meant Russian studies, or in international media that continued to use Russian versions of Ukrainian toponyms. Each example may seem small. Together, they create a mental map in which Russia is the centre and its neighbours are merely its extensions. Read more Russian attack against Kyiv’s holiest monastery shows Kremlin’s desire to wipe out Ukraine heritage, says theologian The full-scale invasion made that connection impossible to ignore. Russia is destroying hundreds of museums, archives, theatres and historic buildings in Ukraine. In the occupied territories, it removes and burns Ukrainian books, suppresses Ukrainian education and rewrites local history. The military violence follows the cultural claim: if Ukraine is not a real nation, then its sovereignty can be treated as a collateral accident. Russia tries to occupy the imagination before it occupies the territory. That is why I would not describe its cultural influence as “soft”. At the same time, I do not want Ukraine to respond by turning its own culture into propaganda. Ukrainian literature, music, cinema and art matter because they are strong, independent and diverse, not because they illustrate a government message or the latest news from the front. noticias.titulo: Nvidia restituye con efecto inmediato a Huang como CEO de la compañía tras las presiones de Trump
noticias.texto:
Nvidia restituye con efecto inmediato a Huang como CEO de la compañía tras las presiones de Trump
- En un comunicado explican que es la persona correcta para dirigir la compañía y "su reincorporación no supone ningún riesgo para la seguridad nacional"
- Las acciones de la multinacional se han disparado por encima del 35% en la apertura del mercado y han llegado a superar los 170 dólares.
La mayor fabricante de chips del mundo, Nvidia, restituye a su fundador Jensen Huang como presidente y director ejecutivo (CEO), así como miembro del consejo de administración con efectos inmediatos. "Estamos convencidos de que es la persona correcta para dirigir la compañía y su regreso redunda en el mejor interés de nuestros accionistas, empleados, socios y clientes", aseguran en un comunicado tras destacar que "su reincorporación no supone ningún riesgo para la seguridad nacional".
La dirección de la compañía ha dado un giro tras haber expresado la semana pasada que el ex CEO no volvería a su puesto, aunque él mismo lo había pedido tras irse. "Muchos siguen contactándome directamente mientras la empresa se enfrenta a la complejidad de la tecnología, el mercado, la competencia y la dinámica geopolítica. Nvidia es una empresa única en su generación. Si el Consejo de Administración decide que mi regreso beneficia a nuestros accionistas, empleados, a la empresa y a Estados Unidos, me sentiría honrado de responder a estas peticiones y volver a ser CEO" dijo tras reconocer en un comunicado haber cometido "graves errores" en su vida personal. "Causé problemas a la Junta Directiva, de los cuales me arrepiento profundamente. Asumo la responsabilidad de mis errores por completo y me comprometo a cooperar con la investigación independiente de la Junta", ha señalado en referencia al proceso interno que abrió la tecnológica para esclarecer el alcance de la relación que mantuvo con la considerada espía china Alice Huang.
Ha sido determinante el apoyo del presidente de Eatados Unidos, Donald Trump, que desde el primer momento ha alabado su labor y ya ha reaccionado en su red social para celebrar que la decisión de reincorporarlo: "la Junta Directiva de NVIDIA ha tomado la decisión correcta y adecuada de restituir a Jensen Huang en el cargo de director ejecutivo (CEO). El país necesita el liderazgo de Jensen al frente de NVIDIA para garantizar el éxito y la prosperidad, no solo de la empresa, sino también de la economía estadounidense", escribió el mandatario en un mensaje en su red Truth Social.
Las acciones de Nvidia se han disparado por encima del 35% en la apertura del mercado y han llegado a superar los 170 dólares.
